prompt.statement: A society should be judged chiefly by how it treats those who cannot contribute to its economy.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Leverage, Not Contribution, Is the Test
essays.essay:
The strongest objection to this statement is that compassion must be paid for. Pensions and hospitals are financed by people who work, and a [[spendthrift|spendthrift]] government that funds benefits by neglecting the sources of its wealth will eventually fail the people it meant to protect. Under genuine scarcity, the objection is decisive. During the wartime siege of Leningrad, authorities gave factory workers larger bread rations than dependents, and hundreds of thousands of civilians starved. Judging the besieged city chiefly by how it fed those who could not work would condemn a policy whose grim logic is hard to refute: had the factories stopped and the defenses collapsed, no one would have been fed. Yet the objection explains only what a society can afford, not what it chooses once it can afford more. That limit is where my agreement with the statement begins, though its standard must be widened before it can be trusted.

Once a society has a margin above survival, how it treats those who cannot contribute becomes a revealing test, because necessity no longer excuses cruelty. Prosperous societies have failed that test before. In the early twentieth century, eugenics was not the creed of a few [[misanthropic|misanthropic]] cranks; it was taught at leading universities, and in Buck v. Bell (1927) the U.S. Supreme Court upheld a Virginia law allowing the state to forcibly sterilize people it deemed feebleminded. Nazi Germany carried the same logic to its conclusion. Under Aktion T4, physicians reviewed the files of institutionalized patients and selected tens of thousands for death, while propaganda tallied what each patient cost the nation and spread the [[calumny|calumny]] that such people were "useless eaters." Germany in 1939 was not starving; it had chosen to treat people as entries in a ledger, and the program's methods and many of its staff later moved to the death camps. No measure of the regime's industrial or scientific prowess reveals as much as the fate of the patients it called worthless. Here the statement holds completely.

The statement fails in a subtler way, however, because it assumes that the vulnerable and the economically inactive are the same people. Consider Qatar's construction boom before the 2022 World Cup. Qatari citizens, including the old and the disabled, receive free public health care and education and pay no income tax; by the statement's test, the country looks admirably humane. Yet its gleaming stadiums [[belie|belie]] the conditions under which they were built. The work fell largely to migrant laborers toiling through the desert summer on projects meant to [[aggrandize|aggrandize]] the state before a global audience. Under the kafala sponsorship system, workers for years could not change jobs or leave the country without their employer's permission. Human rights organizations repeatedly [[castigated|castigate]] the government over these conditions, and major reforms came only under sustained international scrutiny. Judged chiefly by its care for nonworking citizens, such a society passes the test while exploiting the people who built its cities.

These cases do not cancel one another; each fixes one boundary of my position. Leningrad shows that the test presupposes a margin of choice. Eugenics shows that, where such a margin exists, a society's treatment of the "unproductive" exposes its values more sharply than its wealth does, not least because the society itself decides who counts as unproductive. Qatar shows that the decisive line runs not between those who contribute and those who do not, but between those who can make a society answer to them and those who cannot. The patients of the eugenics era and the migrant laborers of Qatar had little in common economically, yet neither could make the society that used or discarded them listen.

I therefore accept the spirit of the statement while amending its terms. A society with room to choose should be judged chiefly by how it treats people who have no leverage over it, whether they work or not, because only there does decency earn no reward. Economic contribution is the usual source of such leverage but not a reliable one, and a standard built on it will flatter any society that tends its dependents while wringing labor from people who cannot safely complain.

words.meaning_here: Wasteful with money; a government that spends carelessly while neglecting what produces its wealth.
Hating or distrusting humankind; eugenics was not merely the belief of a few people-haters.
A false, malicious claim meant to damage reputation: the Nazi smear that patients were useless eaters.
To give a false impression of; the shiny stadiums hide how harshly they were built.
words.def: 1. (of an appearance) fail to give a true impression of (something). 2. fail to fulfill or justify (a claim or expectation).

words.meaning_here: To enlarge the prestige or power of; projects meant to glorify the Qatari state internationally.
Criticized severely and publicly; rights groups harshly condemned the government over labor conditions.

analysis.verdict: This response earns a 6 because its position is insightful, not merely clear: it exposes the statement's hidden assumption that the vulnerable and the economically inactive are the same people, and it replaces economic contribution with leverage as the real test. Each example (Leningrad's rations, eugenics and Aktion T4, Qatar's World Cup construction) is developed far enough to show why it matters, and the prose is precise, varied and fully controlled.
analysis.position: The essay concedes first and then fixes its stance at the end of paragraph one: "That limit is where my agreement with the statement begins". The last paragraph sharpens it into a new standard about people with "no leverage over it, whether they work or not" rather than repeating the prompt.
analysis.development: Every example states what happened and why it matters. Leningrad's ration policy is defended on the logic that "had the factories stopped and the defenses collapsed" no one would eat, and T4 counts as decisive evidence because "Germany in 1939 was not starving" and so chose its cruelty. Qatar is developed through citizen benefits, the kafala system and reform under scrutiny, not merely named.
analysis.organization: The essay follows the concession-first shape exactly: grant the scarcity objection, mark its limit, then build through a case that holds, a case that fails, and an explicit synthesis. Short signposts carry the logic, such as "Here the statement holds completely" and "The statement fails in a subtler way, however".
analysis.language: Sentence length varies sharply, from "Prosperous societies have failed that test before" to long balanced sentences, and inversion adds weight in "only there does decency earn no reward". Target words sit in normal collocations, such as "a few misanthropic cranks" and "repeatedly castigated the government".
analysis.task: The instruction asks for cases where the statement holds and fails and for their effect on the position. The essay labels each case outright ("Here the statement holds completely"; "The statement fails in a subtler way") and then explains that "each fixes one boundary of my position".

paragraphs.role: Concession: the scarcity objection and its limit
paragraphs.note: Grants that compassion must be financed and proves it with Leningrad's bread rations, then marks where the objection stops: it explains what a society can afford, not what it chooses.

paragraphs.role: A case where the statement fully holds
paragraphs.note: Uses American eugenics and Aktion T4 to show prosperous societies choosing cruelty; because Germany was not starving, its treatment of patients reveals values that no economic measure could.

paragraphs.role: A case where the statement fails
paragraphs.note: Exposes the hidden assumption that the vulnerable are the economically inactive: Qatar cares for its nonworking citizens while the migrant laborers who built its stadiums lacked basic freedoms.

paragraphs.role: Explicit synthesis: how each case shapes position
paragraphs.note: States what each case contributes: Leningrad sets the condition, eugenics confirms the test, Qatar moves the line from contribution to power, linking patients and laborers through voicelessness.

paragraphs.role: Refined position in fresh terms
paragraphs.note: Amends rather than repeats the statement: societies with room to choose should be judged by how they treat people without leverage, since a contribution-based standard flatters exploiters.

moves.frame: Yet the objection explains only what ..., not what ... .
moves.example: Yet the objection explains only what a society can afford, not what it chooses once it can afford more.
moves.use: After conceding a rival view's force, mark exactly where its reach ends.

moves.frame: The statement fails ..., however, because it assumes that ... and ... are the same ... .
moves.example: The statement fails in a subtler way, however, because it assumes that the vulnerable and the economically inactive are the same people.
moves.use: Exposing a hidden assumption by separating two ideas the prompt quietly treats as identical.

moves.frame: These cases do not cancel one another; each fixes one boundary of my position. ... shows that ... .
moves.example: These cases do not cancel one another; each fixes one boundary of my position. Leningrad shows that the test presupposes a margin of choice.
moves.use: When the instruction asks how cases shape your position; turns mixed examples into explicit limits.

analysis.contrast: A typical 4 or 5 would agree or disagree broadly, mention welfare states or famous names without explaining them, and add a token counterargument paragraph. It would treat "cannot contribute" as self-evident, never asking who draws that line or noticing that exploited workers are vulnerable too. Its examples would be asserted rather than analyzed, and its conclusion would restate the opening instead of refining it.

prompt.statement: Most people judge a new idea by who proposes it rather than by its merits.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: When Merits Cannot Yet Be Seen
essays.essay:
The statement is usually offered as a rebuke, as if attention to the messenger were a [[puerile|puerile]] habit that mature thinkers outgrow. That rebuke assumes that merits can be inspected the moment an idea is proposed. Often they cannot. It helps to distinguish between ideas that can be tried before they are believed and ideas that must be believed before they can be tried. A new seed can be tested on a few acres; a national reform usually cannot. For ideas of the second kind, I agree that most people judge by the proposer, less out of vanity than out of necessity, since a track record is itself evidence. For ideas of the first kind, the author matters far less than the statement implies.

The Hundred Days' Reform of 1898 shows what happens when a program cannot be tested. Advised by Kang Youwei and other reformers, the Guangxu Emperor issued a stream of edicts to modernize China's schools, army, and bureaucracy, measures too sweeping to prove themselves within months. Much of the opposition was about substance: the edicts abolished sinecures and scrapped the eight-legged essay that examination candidates had spent years mastering. Yet many officials also [[construed|construe]] the program as a bid to sideline the Empress Dowager Cixi, and when reports spread, not without basis, that the reformers were plotting against her, she confined the emperor and rescinded most of the edicts. After the Boxer catastrophe, her own court revived many of the same measures and in 1905 abolished the examinations outright. Defeat had also changed circumstances, so the source alone cannot explain the reversal. Still, the program ended with a verdict on its authors rather than a test of its edicts. Under such verdicts, even [[calumny|calumny]] can sink a program: discrediting an author is cheaper than refuting an argument.

Business shows that reputation fills whatever space verification leaves open. Theranos claimed that its devices could run a wide range of tests on a few drops of fingertip blood. Some experts in laboratory medicine, the people best placed to judge, were [[incredulous|incredulous]], but the company shielded its technology from independent scrutiny, so investors judged the claim by its sponsors: a charismatic young founder whom business magazines were quick to [[deify|deify]], and a board whose most celebrated members were former cabinet secretaries and retired military commanders, not laboratory scientists. The company was valued in the billions before journalists and regulators established that the devices did not work as advertised. Here the statement holds not because the merits were unknowable but because they were concealed, and prestige stood in for evidence.

The statement fails, by contrast, where an idea can prove itself before anyone is asked to believe in it. In late 1978, farmers in Xiaogang, an impoverished village in Anhui province, secretly divided their collective's land into household plots, an arrangement then forbidden. Their team leaders risked prison; the other villagers pledged to raise the leaders' children if it came to that. None had standing beyond the village. The next harvest far exceeded the collective's recent yields, and within a few years the household responsibility system had become national policy. The farmers needed the protection of reform-minded officials, but those officials were persuaded by grain, not by rank. Deng Xiaoping's remark that a cat's color matters less than whether it catches mice expresses a preference for merits over pedigree, and it could guide policy here because the mice could be counted.

These cases define how far I agree. The Qing court and Theranos persuade me that the statement describes how people weigh ideas whose merits are deferred or concealed; Xiaogang persuades me that this habit is a response to missing evidence rather than an innate [[proclivity|proclivity]] to defer to rank. When results cannot speak, the most eminent or the loudest voice in the room fills the silence. The remedy, then, is not to exhort people to ignore who is speaking, which they will not and sometimes should not do, but to let ideas be tried before they must be believed, through pilot programs, independent audits, and randomized trials. People judge ideas by their authors chiefly when they have been given nothing better to judge them by.

words.meaning_here: childish and foolish; the rebuke treats attending to the speaker as an immature habit.
interpreted; officials read the reform program as a bid to sideline Cixi.
false, malicious charges against an author; when verdicts fall on authors, even these can sink a program.
unwilling to believe; some laboratory experts doubted so many tests could run on a few drops.
words.def: (of a person or their manner) unwilling or unable to believe something.

words.meaning_here: to idolize the founder so extravagantly that she seemed beyond criticism.
a natural, habitual tendency, here an inborn urge to defer to people of high rank.

analysis.verdict: This response earns a 6 because its position is insightful rather than merely clear: it reframes the prompt with a distinction between ideas tried before believed and ideas believed before tried, then uses that distinction to explain both when the statement holds and when it fails. Every example is developed far enough to show what happened and why it matters, the Qing paragraph weighs a rival explanation instead of ignoring it, and the prose is precise, varied, and controlled.
analysis.position: The writer agrees for ideas "that must be believed before they can be tried" and disagrees for testable ones, stating this in the first paragraph. The last sentence restates it in fresh words: judging by authors happens when people have "nothing better to judge them by."
analysis.development: Each example is narrated and then interpreted. The Qing paragraph concedes that "Much of the opposition was about substance" yet shows the program ended with "a verdict on its authors rather than a test of its edicts"; Theranos adds a twist (merits concealed, not unknowable), and Xiaogang supplies the counter-case where "the mice could be counted."
analysis.organization: The opening distinction organizes everything: two body paragraphs show the statement holding (testing impossible, then testing blocked), one shows it failing, and the last explains how the cases shape the position. Transitions such as "The statement fails, by contrast" mark each turn in the argument.
analysis.language: Diction is exact and economical ("prestige stood in for evidence"), and sentence length ranges from the three-word "Often they cannot." to long, balanced sentences. Chiasmus, pairing "tried before they are believed" with "believed before they can be tried," gives the central idea a memorable form.
analysis.task: The instruction asks for cases where the statement holds and where it does not, plus how they shape the position. The essay gives two holding cases, one failing case, and a final paragraph that opens "These cases define how far I agree." and assigns each case its lesson.

paragraphs.role: Reframing distinction and qualified position
paragraphs.note: Exposes the hidden assumption that merits are visible when an idea is proposed, splits ideas into testable and must-be-believed kinds, and agrees with the statement only for the second kind.

paragraphs.role: Statement holds: untestable reform in Qing China
paragraphs.note: Concedes that the 1898 edicts threatened real interests and that defeat explains part of their later revival, yet shows the program ended on suspicion of its authors, untested; under such verdicts, even calumny works.

paragraphs.role: Statement holds: merits concealed, not unknowable
paragraphs.note: Theranos extends the distinction: a testable claim shielded from scrutiny becomes one that must be believed, so prestige replaces evidence, while some of the specialists best placed to judge were incredulous.

paragraphs.role: Statement fails: an idea that proves itself
paragraphs.note: Xiaogang's farmers had no standing beyond their village, yet an arrangement whose results were visible in one harvest became national policy; this is the counter-case the opening distinction predicts.

paragraphs.role: How the cases shape the refined position
paragraphs.note: Assigns each case its lesson, recasts source-judging as a response to missing evidence, and proposes making ideas testable rather than scolding people for caring who speaks.

moves.frame: It helps to distinguish between ... that ... and ... that ...
moves.example: It helps to distinguish between ideas that can be tried before they are believed and ideas that must be believed before they can be tried.
moves.use: Opening an Issue essay: split the prompt's vague key term into two kinds that organize the body.

moves.frame: Here the statement holds not because ... but because ..., and ...
moves.example: Here the statement holds not because the merits were unknowable but because they were concealed, and prestige stood in for evidence.
moves.use: After an example, name the exact condition that makes the claim true there, not just that it is true.

moves.frame: [Case] persuades me that ... is ... rather than ...
moves.example: Xiaogang persuades me that this habit is a response to missing evidence rather than an innate proclivity to defer to rank
moves.use: Concluding when the prompt asks how cases shape your position: state what each case taught you.

analysis.contrast: A 4 response would likely agree or disagree wholesale and list quick examples with a sentence each. A 5 might develop two examples soundly but use them only to illustrate agreement or disagreement, without asking why people rely on the source or turning the boundary cases into a refined position. Both would likely end by urging readers to judge ideas on their merits.

prompt.statement: Technology tends to widen the gap between the powerful and the powerless.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Control, Not Technology, Widens the Gap
essays.essay:
The strongest case for the statement is that a new technology usually reaches the powerful first, and in the short run it tends to [[aggrandize|aggrandize]] them further. HIV treatment shows this starkly. When combination antiretroviral therapy appeared in the mid-1990s, AIDS deaths fell sharply in the United States and Western Europe. In sub-Saharan Africa, where the epidemic was far worse, the same drugs were priced beyond the reach of nearly every patient and health ministry. One of the decade's great medical advances thus turned the gap between rich and poor into one between living and dying. If the statement described only the first years of an invention, I would accept it. But the story did not end there, and its ending exposes the flaw: what widens the gap is not technology as such but control over who may use it, and such control can be broken.

It would be easy to blame the gap on [[avaricious|avaricious]] executives, but the companies were doing what patent law rewarded, and the decisive changes came from outside the laboratory. Indian generic manufacturers, whose national law then recognized only process patents on medicines, combined drugs owned by rival Western firms into single tablets that none of those firms could make alone, and sold them for a fraction of the branded price. Drug companies that had sued South Africa to block a law enabling cheaper medicines abandoned the case in 2001 amid international outrage. Soon the Global Fund and the American PEPFAR program were funding treatment across the continent, and within a decade millions of Africans were taking these medicines. The molecules had not changed. What changed was who set their price and who controlled their supply.

The printing press offers a sharper test: the same machine produced both outcomes within a century. Among the earliest documents printed with movable type in Mainz were letters of indulgence, mass-produced to fund the defense of Cyprus against the Ottomans; the press first served Europe's most powerful institution. Yet after Martin Luther challenged the sale of indulgences in 1517, the German pamphlets he then published sold so well that printers across the Holy Roman Empire reprinted them with [[alacrity|alacrity]], often as much for profit as from conviction. The Edict of Worms banned his writings, but in an empire fractured among princes, bishops, and free cities, no authority could silence every press. In Spain, where the Inquisition policed what could be printed and imported, the same technology chiefly strengthened Church and Crown. The press narrowed the gap where it was cheap and hard to monopolize, and widened it where a central power could license and censor it.

These cases do not cancel each other out; they locate the statement's hinge. HIV treatment shows the statement holding and then failing over time; the press shows it holding and failing across places, and in both the deciding variable is control. A technology widens the gap when its benefits can be enclosed: when it demands scarce capital, when law grants its owners a monopoly, or when its regulators answer to the already powerful. It narrows the gap when it is cheap to copy and hard to police, or when public pressure forces wide distribution. The statement thus rests on a quietly [[misanthropic|misanthropic]] premise: that technology has a built-in direction because whoever holds a new tool will turn it against those who lack it. The opposite error, common among enthusiasts who [[deify|deify]] innovation, fares no better: neither the press nor antiretroviral drugs helped the powerless wherever owners or censors controlled their use.

The two histories therefore lead me to reject the statement as a general law while granting its account of beginnings. A technology's benefits flow to whoever controls its supply, and that control is a political settlement rather than a property of the machine. Where that settlement goes uncontested, early advantage hardens into lasting privilege; where it is contested, the same invention can become an equalizer. The question to ask of gene therapies, or of AI models that few firms can afford to train, is not whether they empower but whether their benefits can be enclosed. The gap is not something technology opens; it is something societies decide to widen or close.

words.meaning_here: to enlarge further the power and wealth of those already powerful
intensely greedy for money; the tempting but too-simple explanation for high drug prices
prompt, eager willingness; printers rushed to reprint Luther's best-selling pamphlets
distrustful of people generally; assuming anyone holding a new tool will use it against others
to revere innovation so extravagantly that it is treated as beyond criticism

analysis.verdict: The essay earns a 6 because its position is insightful, not merely clear: it identifies control over supply as the hidden variable deciding when the statement holds. Both extended examples are developed through what happened and why it matters, and the prose is precise and varied with no errors that impede meaning.
analysis.position: The qualified thesis arrives at the end of paragraph one: "what widens the gap is not technology as such but control". It concedes the statement's truth for early years, and the last paragraph restates the position in new terms: "a political settlement rather than a property of the machine".
analysis.development: Each example is traced through causes and consequences rather than named: HIV drugs move from unaffordable to cheap Indian combination tablets to donor-funded, and the HIV case isolates its point in a five-word sentence ("The molecules had not changed."). The press example shows both outcomes and explains why: it "narrowed the gap where it was cheap and hard to monopolize".
analysis.organization: The essay follows the concession-first shape: grant the strongest case, show where it fails, add a second case, then derive conditions. Paragraph four links the cases explicitly with "These cases do not cancel each other out", so the structure follows the argument rather than a template.
analysis.language: Sentence length varies sharply, from five-word sentences to long periodic ones, and parallel structure carries the analysis ("when it demands scarce capital, when law grants its owners a monopoly"). Target words sit in idiomatic collocations, as in "reprinted them with alacrity, often as much for profit as from conviction".
analysis.task: The instruction demands cases where the statement holds and fails, plus how they shape the position. Paragraph four labels them ("HIV treatment shows the statement holding and then failing over time"), and paragraph five says they "lead me to reject the statement as a general law".

paragraphs.role: Concession: the statement's strongest case
paragraphs.note: Grants that new technology first strengthens the powerful, shown by HIV drugs priced out of Africa, then states the thesis: control over use, not technology itself, widens the gap.

paragraphs.role: Where the concession stops being true
paragraphs.note: Rejects greed as the easy explanation, then traces Indian combination tablets, the dropped South Africa lawsuit and donor funding; unchanged molecules isolate control as the variable that narrowed the gap.

paragraphs.role: Second case: one invention, opposite outcomes
paragraphs.note: Shows the press serving the Church, then spreading Luther's later German pamphlets in a fragmented empire while strengthening Church and Crown in Spain: the statement holding and failing across places.

paragraphs.role: Derives conditions; exposes the hidden assumption
paragraphs.note: States how the two cases shape the position, lists when technology widens or narrows the gap, and rejects both the statement's misanthropic premise and its optimistic mirror image.

paragraphs.role: Refined position in fresh words
paragraphs.note: Rejects the statement as a general law but keeps its account of beginnings, extends the test to gene therapies and AI, and ends on societal choice.

moves.frame: If the statement described only ..., I would accept it.
moves.example: If the statement described only the first years of an invention, I would accept it.
moves.use: When conceding: name the exact scope in which the opposing claim is true, then signal its limit.

moves.frame: It would be easy to blame ... on ..., but ... were doing what ... rewarded.
moves.example: It would be easy to blame the gap on avaricious executives, but the companies were doing what patent law rewarded
moves.use: When an obvious villain or cause tempts readers; redirect from individual motives to the structure behind them.

moves.frame: ... shows the statement holding and then failing over time; ... shows it holding and failing across places, and in both the deciding variable is ...
moves.example: HIV treatment shows the statement holding and then failing over time; the press shows it holding and failing across places, and in both the deciding variable is control.
moves.use: When the prompt asks when a claim holds; map each case, then name the single variable deciding outcomes.

analysis.contrast: A typical 4 would take a clear side and support it with two or three relevant but briefly developed examples, such as smartphones and the internet, concluding that technology can help or harm. Even a 5 would usually treat its cases as separate illustrations rather than isolating the variable, control over supply, that explains when the statement holds, and would restate its opening position instead of refining it.

prompt.statement: Cities should give public transit priority over private cars, even when doing so lengthens the commutes of most residents.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: What the Lost Minutes Buy
essays.essay:
When Bogotá launched its TransMilenio bus system in 2000, long red buses began running in the central lanes of major avenues, stopping at raised stations; on Avenida Caracas, they took over an existing busway. In a city where only a minority of households owned a car, TransMilenio made daily travel faster for most people using those avenues. Even some drivers benefited. On certain corridors, evaluations found, cars moved faster once the disorderly private buses left the general lanes. The episode exposes an assumption buried in the statement: that a city's majority sits behind the wheel, so that favoring transit must cost most residents time. Where that picture is accurate, I still support giving transit priority, but only when the longer commutes are the price of a transition that will eventually repay them, not when the city's shape guarantees that the price will be paid indefinitely.

The strongest case for the recommendation rests on a distinction the statement ignores: a commute measured today differs from one measured after the city has adjusted. Commute times are a snapshot of where people live and work, and transit priority changes both. Beginning in the 1970s, Curitiba, in southern Brazil, reserved the central lanes of its main avenues for buses and permitted its tallest, densest buildings mainly along those corridors. Over decades, apartments, offices, and shops gathered beside the busways, so that what began as an inconvenience to drivers placed a large share of residents within walking distance of fast, frequent service. A driver who loses ten minutes each way in the early years might reasonably [[demur|demur]], but those minutes are better understood as an installment on a different city than as a permanent tax.

The statement also takes for granted that withholding priority from transit would keep drivers' commutes short, an assumption that Julio Cortázar's story "The Southern Thruway" punctures. In it, a Sunday traffic jam on the highway into Paris lasts what seems like months. The stranded motorists, known to one another only by their cars, form small communities that ration water and food; when traffic finally moves, those bonds dissolve, and the engineer in the Peugeot 404 loses sight of the young woman in the Dauphine. Cortázar exaggerates, but his premise is ordinary: when everyone drives, the car's promise of speed collapses. His ending adds that the moving car restores a faintly [[misanthropic|misanthropic]] way of traveling in which every other person is an obstacle. A city that denies buses priority to spare its drivers delay may find that it has spared them nothing.

The recommendation fails, however, where no such transition is possible. Consider a hypothetical metropolis of detached houses on large lots, its jobs scattered among office parks that no single route can connect. Handing the best lanes to nearly empty buses would lengthen almost everyone's commute without attracting the riders to justify it, and a city that pours money into a rail line few residents can walk to is not visionary but [[spendthrift|spendthrift]]. To expect such a place to reorganize itself around transit within a generation is [[quixotic|quixotic]]; Curitiba steered decades of new growth toward its corridors, and this city is already built out. Priority also fails when granted in name only. Where motorists [[flout|flout]] bus-lane rules without penalty, drivers lose road space while buses gain little; where a city grants lanes but not enough vehicles, the delay moves onto the riders. Bogotá learned this too: as ridership outgrew TransMilenio's fleet and stations, crowding provoked protests from the very passengers the system had been built to serve.

Taken together, these circumstances refine rather than reverse my agreement. Bogotá and Curitiba show that priority can speed travel for people without cars and, in time, produce a city built around transit, while Cortázar's jam suggests that withholding priority spares drivers little. The sprawling metropolis and the unenforced lane mark the limits: there, the minutes taken from drivers buy nothing at all. The right question, then, is not whether most commutes grow longer this year but what the lost time purchases. Where it purchases a better city, priority deserves an open defense; where it purchases empty buses, it is a gesture paid for in other people's time.

words.meaning_here: to object mildly to losing ten minutes each way on the drive
showing dislike or contempt for others, treating every other traveler as an obstacle rather than a fellow citizen
wasteful with public money, spending heavily on a rail line that returns little
idealistic but impractical; bound to fail because the city is already built out
openly break bus-lane rules, knowing no one will penalize them

analysis.verdict: This response earns a 6 because its position is insightful, not just clear. It exposes two hidden assumptions in the statement and turns the issue into a test of what lost commute time buys. Each example (Bogotá, Curitiba, Cortázar, a marked hypothetical) is developed far enough to show why it matters, and the prose is precise and varied.
analysis.position: The position comes at the end of paragraph 1 and is qualified from the start: the writer supports priority "only when the longer commutes are the price of a transition". The conclusion restates it in new words, as a test of "what the lost time purchases".
analysis.development: Every example is explained, not just named. Curitiba's corridor zoning backs up the claim that "transit priority changes both", and the paragraph then recasts the lost minutes as "an installment on a different city". Cortázar's plot is summarized before the essay states that "his premise is ordinary" and applies it to drivers.
analysis.organization: The essay opens with the Bogotá scene, draws an assumption from it, then states the position. It moves from cases where priority helps to "The recommendation fails, however, where no such transition is possible", and the conclusion names each main example (Bogotá, Curitiba, Cortázar, the sprawling metropolis, the unenforced lane) to show how they combine.

prompt.statement: Teachers should devote more class time to discussion than to lectures.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Discussion Must Be Earned by Knowledge
essays.essay:
The strongest argument for this recommendation is that a lecture so often presents a [[desiccated|desiccate]] version of its subject. A teacher who simply reports conclusions gives students the results of inquiry while withholding the inquiry itself, and students learn to treat knowledge as a list to memorize rather than a set of claims to weigh. Discussion restores what the lecture strips away: the obligation to defend an idea against an objection. I grant this point, but it holds only when students already know enough for their objections to be informed. Where that condition fails, more discussion does not deepen understanding; it merely pools ignorance. How class time should be divided therefore depends less on a teacher's philosophy than on what students bring into the room.

Consider a high school earth science class that has already studied the evidence for continental drift. When Alfred Wegener argued early in the twentieth century that the continents had once been joined, he pointed to coastlines that seemed to fit together, most famously those of South America and Africa, and to fossils of the same organisms on landmasses now separated by oceans. Most geologists rejected his theory, partly because he could offer no convincing force to drive continents through the solid ocean floor. Only decades later did evidence of seafloor spreading vindicate his central claim, though not his account of how the continents moved. Students who know this history can profitably spend an entire period arguing whether the skeptics were wrong or merely prudent. The question has no answer key, and debating it teaches something a lecture cannot: that a correct idea may be reasonably resisted when it lacks a mechanism, and that science advances through such disputes rather than around them. Here the recommendation is plainly sound.

The picture changes in an environmental studies class taking up urban traffic for the first time. Ask students how a city should relieve a congested highway, and most will [[construe|construe]] congestion as a shortage of road space and propose the obvious answer: add more lanes. The answer is not foolish; it is what common sense predicts, which is precisely why discussion is unlikely to dislodge it. Planners have learned through costly experience that widened roads tend to fill with new traffic as drivers take trips they once avoided, a pattern known as induced demand. When twenty students share the same intuition, few will [[demur|demur]], and discussion will reinforce the error rather than refute it. A short, well-organized lecture can accomplish in fifteen minutes what an hour of conversation may never achieve. Only after that lecture does a discussion of whether the city should expand transit, charge drivers to use crowded roads, or simply tolerate congestion become worth having.

The recommendation also rests on a hidden assumption: that time spent talking is time spent thinking. Discussion time is rarely shared evenly. In many classrooms a few [[loquacious|loquacious]] students claim most of the airtime, and a teacher who gauges engagement by the volume of talk will mistake their fluency for the class's understanding. A quiet student may be following the argument more closely than anyone, yet an unstructured discussion gives her little chance to show it while the confident few steer the conversation. Discussion rewards whoever speaks first, which is not necessarily whoever has thought hardest. A lecture, whatever its passivity, at least gives every student the same material.

These cases persuade me that the recommendation mistakes a stage of learning for a method of teaching. The Wegener debate is why I would not reduce discussion to an occasional reward; the traffic example is why I would not let it lead when the facts defy intuition. Discussion earns more class time once students command the evidence but disagree about what it means, and it earns that time only if the teacher structures it, for instance by having everyone write before anyone speaks, so that [[taciturn|taciturn]] students are heard alongside eager ones. A teacher should lecture to establish what students cannot reason their way to, then shift toward discussion as the material becomes genuinely contestable. More discussion is a goal a course should work toward, not a rule to impose on the first day.

Transitions carry the logic, for example "The picture changes in an environmental studies class" and "The recommendation also rests on a hidden assumption."

prompt.statement: Scientists should devote part of their careers to repeating other researchers' experiments rather than only pursuing new discoveries.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Replication Belongs Where Use Cannot Check
essays.essay:
The strongest objection to this recommendation is that science already repeats itself without being told to. A new synthetic method is tested every time another laboratory uses it, and a faulty one fails in someone else's flask before anyone sets out to check it. At CERN, verification is built into discovery: two general-purpose detectors, ATLAS and CMS, are run by separate collaborations, and the Higgs boson was announced on the strength of both teams' results. In such fields, a career spent repeating experiments would mean paying twice for a check that ordinary research already performs.

That objection, however, rests on an easily missed assumption: that every finding will be used by other scientists and thus tested in the using. Many findings are not tools for further research but conclusions that go directly into practice, and for these the recommendation is not merely sound but urgent. Education offers a sobering case. The claim that students learn best when instruction matches their "learning style" was embraced by schools and teacher-training programs with remarkable [[alacrity|alacrity]]. By the 1980s, reviews had found little benefit from such matching, yet the idea kept spreading, because nothing in a classroom fails loudly enough to force a second look. When psychologists later specified what a proper test required, they found few such studies, and those few contradicted the idea. The checks existed; they were too scattered and unrewarded to dislodge an idea already in use.

Sports supplies a subtler case. In the mid-1980s, psychologists studied basketball shooting, including a controlled experiment with college players, and concluded that the "hot hand," the belief that a player on a streak is likelier to keep scoring, was an illusion. The finding became a textbook illustration of how people see patterns in randomness. Roughly three decades later, economists reanalyzing the original data showed that the standard comparison, shooting after streaks of hits versus streaks of misses, was systematically biased against finding streakiness; once the bias was corrected, the same data suggested that a hot hand may exist after all, a reminder that analyses need repeating as much as experiments do. The error survived so long partly because the result was a conclusion rather than a tool: researchers cited it far more often than they built on it, and many of the studies that did revisit it reused the same flawed comparison, so the bias in the method itself went unnoticed.

These cases shape my position in two ways. First, repetition is most valuable where findings travel into classrooms, clinics, or popular belief faster than they can be tested, and least valuable where a field's daily work already repeats them, so a blanket quota would waste much of the effort it demands. Second, who replicates, and how, matters as much as how often: a check that borrows the original method inherits its blind spots, and a checker who depends on the original authors inherits their hopes. A graduate student assigned to repeat a mentor's celebrated study need not be [[obsequious|obsequious]] to be biased; reliance on that mentor for letters and jobs supplies every reason to read ambiguous data generously. Pressure of this kind [[adulterates|adulterate]] the record with confirmations that only look independent. Replication pays only when the replicator is independent enough to disappoint the original authors and secure enough to survive having a negative result [[construed|construe]] as a personal attack. Under current incentives, that security is rare: prizes and appointments reward whoever reports a finding first, press coverage tends to [[aggrandize|aggrandize]] the discoverer, and the scientist who checks the finding earns little credit for confirming it and suspicion for refuting it.

I therefore accept the recommendation in spirit but not as a uniform duty. Some scientists should devote substantial parts of their careers to repeating experiments and reanalyzing data, but that effort should target findings that will be acted on without being built upon, should be carried out by researchers whose prospects do not hinge on the answer, and should be rewarded as scholarship rather than tolerated as a chore. Science corrects itself only where someone has a reason to look; replication earns its place by supplying that reason where the ordinary course of research never will.

fawningly eager to please a superior; the student can be biased without any such flattery.

interpreted; a failed replication taken as an attack on the original authors rather than as evidence.
enlarge the reputation of; press coverage magnifies the standing of whoever reported the finding first.

analysis.verdict: This response earns a 6 because its position is insightful, not just clear: it exposes the hidden assumption that every finding gets tested by being used, then builds on a distinction between findings that serve as tools and findings that serve as conclusions. Its examples are developed honestly, keeping the complications (ignored early reviews, retests that reused a flawed comparison) and using them to sharpen the argument. The prose is precise and varied, with full control of conventions.
analysis.position: The essay takes a qualified position early in paragraph 2: for findings that "go directly into practice," the recommendation is "not merely sound but urgent." The final paragraph refines this as acceptance "in spirit but not as a uniform duty" and names three conditions.
analysis.development: Each example is explained, not just named: CERN's two general-purpose detectors show checking built into discovery, and learning styles show early skeptical reviews that were "too scattered and unrewarded to dislodge an idea already in use." The hot-hand case shows retests that "reused the same flawed comparison" until a reanalysis caught the bias. The graduate-student scenario adds a case where replication backfires.
analysis.organization: The essay follows the concession-first shape: paragraph 1 grants the strongest counterargument, and paragraph 2 shows where it breaks, since it "rests on an easily missed assumption." Paragraphs 2 and 3 give cases beyond that limit, paragraph 4 turns them into two principles, and paragraph 5 restates the position. The repeated contrast between a "tool" and a "conclusion" links the paragraphs.
analysis.language: Word choice is precise ("systematically biased against finding streakiness"), and sentence length ranges from the five-word "Sports supplies a subtler case." to sentences of more than fifty words, such as the one in the final paragraph built on three parallel verb phrases sharing one subject: "should target," "should be carried out," "should be rewarded." The target words carry real meaning: "need not be obsequious to be biased" makes the point that bias requires no flattery.
analysis.task: The instruction asks when the recommendation would and would not be advantageous: learning styles and the hot hand are the advantageous cases, while fields where use already checks results, retests that borrow a flawed method, and dependent replicators are the disadvantageous ones. Paragraph 4 opens "These cases shape my position in two ways," answering the final demand directly.

prompt.statement: A leader's most important quality is the willingness to change his or her mind.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: A Changed Mind Needs Good Reasons
essays.essay:
The strongest case for this statement begins with what power does to the people around it. A president or minister is often surrounded by [[obsequious|obsequious]] aides whose careers depend on approval, so an error at the top is rarely corrected from below; if the leader will not revise her own judgment, nobody else will. History bears this out. The American war in Vietnam dragged on for years after some of its own architects had privately concluded that it could not be won, and the price of that persistence was paid in Vietnamese and American lives. On this much I agree without reservation: a leader who cannot change her mind is dangerous in direct proportion to her power.

Yet the argument proves less than it seems to. It shows that rigidity is a grave vice; it does not show that the opposite of rigidity is the chief virtue. Willingness to change one's mind is indifferent to what does the changing, and the same courtiers who make a stubborn leader dangerous make a pliable one dangerous too, because a leader eager to revise will be revised by whoever spoke to her last. A parent who pushes back bedtime the moment a child wails shows this willingness in its purest form; the parent has learned nothing, but the child has learned that protest, not reason, changes the rules. A politician who abandons positions with [[alacrity|alacrity]] whenever a poll turns against her teaches voters the same lesson. Willingness to change, then, has no value of its own. It borrows its value from the reasons that set it in motion, and the quality that matters most is the discernment to tell a reason from a pressure.

A thoughtful defender of the statement would answer that this distinction is tidy but idle. Leaders rarely lack discernment; most are intelligent, well briefed, and able to recognize a good argument. What they lack is the humility to act against their past commitments, and every stubborn leader sincerely believes that her stubbornness is judgment. The Vietnam case seems to prove the point. Robert McNamara, the Secretary of Defense who oversaw much of the escalation, had the information and the intelligence to see that the war was going badly. On this view, the scarce ingredient was never discernment but willingness, and the statement is right to rank it first.

This objection is right about the diagnosis but misnames what was missing. By McNamara's own later account, he did change his mind: while still in office, he came to doubt that the war could be won, yet went on defending it in public. His failure was one of candor, not of open-mindedness, and the difference matters because changing one's mind in private is free, while changing it in public is expensive. American public health authorities learned this in 2020. Having advised healthy people not to wear masks, they reversed course that spring as evidence accumulated that people without symptoms could spread the coronavirus. The reversal was sound, yet officials were [[castigated|castigate]] for inconsistency, and many critics [[construed|construe]] it as proof that the original advice had been dishonest. The charge was not baseless, since officials later acknowledged that fear of mask shortages for health workers had partly shaped that advice. Because a reversal is trusted only as far as officials were [[candid|candid]] about the reasons behind the original position, changing course in public demands something rarer than willingness: the nerve to say plainly what one believed, why, and what changed. Only a leader confident that evidence, not pressure, has moved her can summon that nerve, so candor depends on discernment rather than replacing it.

The statement, then, mistakes a symptom for the quality that produces it. Mocking every reversal as weakness is [[puerile|puerile]], but admiring every reversal as open-mindedness is the opposite error, since a weathervane changes direction more readily than any statesman. What a leader most needs is a mind that evidence can move and that flattery, polls, and tantrums cannot, together with the courage to change direction in full view. Where that combination exists, the willingness to change one's mind will follow on its own; where it is absent, willingness is only a faster way to be wrong.

Interpreted; critics took the reversal to mean the earlier advice had been dishonest.

Every example is developed to show why it matters: the objector's best example, McNamara, is reread to support the thesis, and the mask reversal concedes the critics' partial point before turning it into evidence for candor. Diction is precise, sentence structure varied, and mechanics clean.

The conclusion refines it by adding "the courage to change direction in full view."

McNamara privately doubted the war yet defended it publicly, which turns his case into a failure "of candor, not of open-mindedness"; the 2020 mask reversal shows a sound reversal punished, and the essay concedes the dishonesty charge "was not baseless" because shortage worries partly shaped the first advice; the bedtime example shows pliability rewarding protest rather than reason.

The Vietnam case threads through three paragraphs: first as support for the statement, then, through McNamara, as the objector's evidence, and finally as support for the thesis.

Antithesis carries the logic, as in "changing one's mind in private is free" set against public expense, and target words sit in normal collocations such as "obsequious aides" and "with alacrity."

Paragraph 3 opens "A thoughtful defender of the statement would answer" and gives the objection real force (leaders lack humility, not judgment); paragraph 4 concedes the diagnosis, then shows that McNamara "did change his mind" and still failed.

prompt.statement: A nation's language shapes the way its people think.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Language Trains Habit, Not Capacity
essays.essay:
The case for this statement is stronger than its popular versions suggest, and anyone who doubts it, as I partly do, should begin by stating it fairly. It rests not on stereotypes such as the [[taciturn|taciturn]] Finn, whose reputed reserve few would blame on Finnish grammar, but on fieldwork and experiment. Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr, an Aboriginal language of northern Australia, describe locations by compass direction rather than by "left" and "right," and studies show they stay oriented with remarkable accuracy, even in unfamiliar places. Russian speakers, whose language treats light blue and dark blue as separate basic colors, are quicker to tell two shades apart when they fall on opposite sides of that boundary, an advantage English speakers do not show. A thoughtful defender of the statement would press the point further: since most thinking is habit, a language that fixes habits of attention has shaped thought in the only sense that matters.

These findings, however, mark the limit of the claim as precisely as they support it. They reveal differences in habit and speed, not in capacity. The Russian advantage is measured in fractions of a second, and English speakers have no trouble seeing that navy differs from sky blue; an English-speaking sailor learns to think in compass bearings without abandoning English. A language decides which distinctions its speakers must make constantly, not which ones they can make at all. I grant that habit is a large part of thinking, and to that extent the statement holds. But the statement implies more than habit: it implies that a people is enclosed by its language, and that each nation has just one. Both assumptions fail most visibly in institutions built to carry meaning intact across languages.

Law offers the cleanest test, because few fields have more riding on whether meaning survives translation. Canada, a nation with two official languages, enacts its federal statutes in English and French, and both versions are equally authoritative. If each language imposed its own way of thinking, the country would have two bodies of law. Instead, when the texts diverge, judges do not [[construe|construe]] the discrepancy as a clash of mentalities; they look for the meaning both versions share and test it against the statute's purpose. The European Union attempts the same feat in all its official languages. These systems work, imperfectly, because statutes are written in a deliberately [[desiccated|desiccate]] prose that avoids idiom, metaphor, and connotation, the features in which languages differ most. Law thus shows that thought can cross languages, but only after much of what makes each distinctive has been stripped away.

Poetry is the opposite case, and there the statement comes closest to being true. A four-line poem by the Tang poet Wang Wei, which names no speaker and marks no tense, has been translated into English many times; Eliot Weinberger's book Nineteen Ways of Looking at Wang Wei compares the versions. Almost every version is more [[loquacious|loquacious]] than the twenty-character original, and the extra words are not neutral. English grammar all but demands a tense and a subject, so nearly every translator must fix the scene in time, and many, especially the earliest, also supply an "I" who hears voices on the empty mountain; each such decision [[adulterates|adulterate]] the poem with an assumption the original declines to make. The versions with a speaker also lose the [[conspicuous|conspicuous]] absence of an observer, which is arguably the poem's point. Yet the loss is instructive. Weinberger's readers come to see exactly what English cannot easily say, which means they can think it. The language made the thought harder to express, not impossible to hold.

The statement, then, is true in proportion to how tightly meaning is bound to form. Where the two are inseparable, as in a line of Tang verse, a language shapes not only how a thought is said but which thoughts come unbidden. Where people have labored to pry them apart, as in a bilingual statute, a language behaves less like a mold than a vehicle. In neither case does it wall its speakers in. It marks the path of least resistance, and people leave that path whenever the destination seems worth the effort.

prompt.statement: Committees are better at avoiding disasters than at producing breakthroughs.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Committees Judge Better Than They Invent
essays.essay:
The statement treats a committee as though it had a single temperament, cautious rather than daring. It is more useful to separate two jobs a committee may be given: conceiving an idea and judging one. For the first job, committees are poorly built. Every member must be satisfied, and a group's [[proclivity|proclivity]] for compromise sands away whatever is most unusual in a proposal. For the second, the same structure is an asset: each member is another chance to catch a flaw. I therefore accept the statement broadly, with two qualifications: committees avoid disasters only when their members are willing to object, and their power to judge is sometimes what turns someone else's idea into a breakthrough.

American criminal juries show the judging function at its best. To convict on a serious charge, a jury must be unanimous, giving every juror a veto against the disaster the system most fears: punishing an innocent person. In Reginald Rose's play Twelve Angry Men, eleven jurors are ready to convict within minutes; one [[demurs|demur]], not because he is sure the defendant is innocent but because he will not send a young man to his death without discussion, and his doubts gradually dismantle the case. Yet the play also exposes an assumption the statement quietly makes. What saves this jury is not its size but one member's readiness to speak; left to itself, a group follows its most vocal and forceful members.

When that readiness is missing, a committee can do worse than an individual: it ratifies a mistake while spreading responsibility so thinly that no one feels accountable. In 1961 President Kennedy's advisers endorsed a plan to land Cuban exiles at the Bay of Pigs, although several, among them Arthur Schlesinger Jr., privately doubted it would work. They were not [[obsequious|obsequious]] courtiers but accomplished, independent-minded people; yet before a confident new president and the CIA planners who championed the scheme, they muted their objections, and the invasion collapsed within days. Schlesinger later reproached himself for his silence, and the psychologist Irving Janis made the episode a central case of groupthink. Reticence, then, is not confined to the [[taciturn|taciturn]]. A good chair asks every member for objections before the vote, because in a committee silence is easily [[construed|construe]] as assent.

The most compelling challenge to my position is that some committees have produced genuine breakthroughs. The King James Bible, completed in 1611 by about fifty scholars, gave English some of its most enduring prose. In Brown v. Board of Education, a unanimous Supreme Court held that Plessy v. Ferguson's "separate but equal" doctrine had no place in public education. Yet in both cases the originality came from outside the room. The King James translators were instructed to revise an existing English Bible and drew heavily on William Tyndale's translation, made in exile generations earlier. Brown's argument was built over years by Thurgood Marshall and the NAACP's lawyers, and the case against "separate but equal" had been made long before, though on other grounds, in Justice John Marshall Harlan's lone dissent in Plessy. What the committees supplied was judgment: choosing the best phrasing among rival versions, or recognizing that an argument long resisted was right.

Still, those committees were not rubber stamps. Harlan's dissent went unheeded for more than half a century, and an idea that no institution adopts changes very little. Here the caution of committees becomes an advantage. Chief Justice Earl Warren spent months persuading reluctant colleagues to join a single opinion, believing a divided Court would invite Southern defiance. The South resisted anyway, but it could not cite a single dissenting justice. Because nine cautious judges are hard to persuade, their unanimous judgment carried an authority that no single bold judge could have conferred.

The statement is thus right about where committees are weakest but too narrow about what they are for. A committee is a poor place to have a new idea and often the only place where one becomes binding; the conservatism that keeps it from inventing is precisely what makes its endorsement worth having. Its talent for avoiding disaster, meanwhile, is conditional. It belongs only to committees whose members are free, and expected, to say no.

analysis.verdict: This response earns a 6 because its position is insightful, not merely clear: it splits committee work into conceiving and judging, then uses that distinction to qualify both halves of the statement. Every example (the jury, the Bay of Pigs, the King James Bible, Brown) is developed far enough to show what happened and why it matters, and the prose is precise, varied, and economical.

The Tyndale, Marshall, and Harlan details pinpoint where the originality came from.

Transitions carry the logic, such as "When that readiness is missing" and "Still, those committees were not rubber stamps."

prompt.statement: Some believe that cities thrive by preserving their historic character. Others believe that cities thrive by replacing old structures with new ones that meet present needs.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Heritage as a Trust, Not an Inventory
essays.essay:
Arguments about urban change often cast preservationists and builders as adversaries, as though a city must choose between its past and its present. That framing rests on an assumption worth questioning: that a city's character resides in particular old buildings rather than in the way structures of different ages coexist. Once that assumption is set aside, the first view comes closer to my own, though not for the reasons its advocates usually give. Preservation should be a city's default because demolition is irreversible, but it serves a city only when it protects a living mixture of old and new rather than a frozen collection of relics.

The case for replacement is stronger than its critics admit, and its best evidence is the city most often held up as a model of historic charm. In the mid-nineteenth century, Napoleon III and his prefect, Baron Haussmann, demolished much of medieval Paris, whose dark, crowded quarters had twice been ravaged by cholera. In their place rose broad boulevards, uniform stone apartment buildings, and parks; beneath them ran new sewers and water mains. The rebuilding was hardly innocent. Baudelaire mourned the vanished streets in verse, and Zola's novel The Kill portrays the [[avaricious|avaricious]] speculators who grew rich by learning in advance where the new boulevards would run. Yet the Paris that visitors now treasure as quintessentially historic is largely Haussmann's creation. A Paris that kept everything it inherited would have preserved squalor as faithfully as beauty. Today's heritage is often the product of yesterday's demolition.

Even so, Paris proves less than it appears to, because sanitation, the most compelling need behind Haussmann's demolitions, can now be met by retrofitting old buildings rather than leveling them. What has not changed is an asymmetry: a preserved building can be replaced later, but a demolished one is gone for good. New York learned this in the 1960s, when the Pennsylvania Railroad razed Pennsylvania Station, a monumental Beaux-Arts hall, leaving travelers in a cramped concourse beneath the new Madison Square Garden. The railroad, losing money on passenger service, had sold the air rights above its station to the arena's developers, the kind of deal a [[spendthrift|spendthrift]] heir strikes by selling the family silver to cover a season's bills. Public outrage spurred the 1965 Landmarks Law, which gave the city's Landmarks Preservation Commission real power, and the commission later blocked an office tower above Grand Central Terminal. In Penn Central Transportation Co. v. New York City, the Supreme Court upheld that decision, holding that the restriction was not a taking that required compensation. The episode exposes what the second view obscures: "present needs" are often an owner's private needs, whereas a landmark's value is spread across the public and across generations, so the market underprices it.

Preservation can fail in its own way, however. Its partisans sometimes [[deify|deify]] age itself, defending every cornice regardless of what happens behind it. Pursued that way, preservation leaves the very neighborhoods it means to save handsome but [[desiccated|desiccate]]: the facades survive, while the people and businesses that gave them life move away. Jane Jacobs, often enlisted on the preservationists' side, made a subtler argument in The Death and Life of Great American Cities. She prized old buildings less as monuments than as cheap, unglamorous space where untested enterprises could survive without the rents that new construction demands. What a district needs, in her account, is a mixture of buildings of different ages, which implies that new ones must keep arriving. Purists who think any modern building [[adulterates|adulterate]] the character of a historic street miss her point: the mixture is the character.

The first view, then, comes closer to my own, but only in a revised form. A city should treat its historic fabric as a trust rather than an inventory, demanding strong justification before destroying what cannot be rebuilt, while welcoming new structures that join the existing mixture rather than erase it. What separates Haussmann's boulevards from the basement that replaced Pennsylvania Station is not novelty, since both were new, but the balance between what each gave the city and what it took. Cities thrive when each generation is free to add to them but must justify what it removes.

analysis.verdict: The essay reaches an insightful, qualified position (preservation as the default, because demolition is irreversible) by exposing the statement's hidden assumption that a city's character lives in individual buildings. Each example, from Haussmann's Paris through Penn Station and the Penn Central case to Jane Jacobs, is developed far enough to show what happened and why it matters. That development, carried in precise, varied and error-free prose, matches the ETS profile of a cogent, well-articulated 6.
analysis.position: The stance arrives in the first paragraph and is qualified at once: preservation should be the default "because demolition is irreversible," but it serves a city "only when it protects a living mixture of old and new," not "a frozen collection of relics." The last paragraph restates it in new terms, as "a trust rather than an inventory."
analysis.development: Each example carries an argument rather than decorating one. Haussmann's demolitions respond to cholera and produce today's 'historic' Paris; the railroad's sale of Penn Station's air rights leads to a landmarks law and a Supreme Court ruling; Jacobs explains why cheap old space matters. Each example ends with its point spelled out, as in "Today's heritage is often the product of yesterday's demolition."

Transitions carry the logic, for example "Even so, Paris proves less than it appears to" and "Preservation can fail in its own way, however."
analysis.language: The diction is exact and economical ("a trust rather than an inventory"), and sentences range from the five-word "The rebuilding was hardly innocent." to long sentences with balanced clauses. Figures of speech are frequent but never decorative; each one makes an argument, like the spendthrift heir "selling the family silver" to cover short-term losses.

The essay names its choice in exactly those terms, twice ("comes closer to my own"), and gives the replacement view a full paragraph of its best evidence. prompt.statement: Some believe that everyone should learn to write computer code. Others believe that coding is a specialized skill that most people do not need.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Cross-Examining Code Matters More Than Writing It
essays.essay:
The strongest case for teaching everyone to code is not economic but civic. Software now makes or shapes decisions once reserved for human judgment: who receives a loan, which job applicants a recruiter sees, and, in many American courtrooms, how dangerous a defendant is judged to be. A citizen who treats such systems as magic is at their mercy, and advocates of universal coding rightly call that ignorance a civic hazard. Their conclusion, however, does not follow from their premise. The hazard demands not that everyone write code but that everyone learn to question it. On that ground I side with those who regard coding as a specialized skill, though not with the complacency their view can invite.

A case the Wisconsin Supreme Court decided in 2016 shows where the first view fails. By then, reformers and officials in many states had embraced risk-assessment software with [[alacrity|alacrity]]. The tools' appeal rested on a faintly [[misanthropic|misanthropic]] premise: that human judgment is too erratic and prejudiced to trust, so a formula must be fairer. The defendant, sentenced partly on the basis of one such commercial program, COMPAS, argued that he could not challenge a score whose method was a trade secret. The court upheld the sentence while requiring that judges be cautioned about the tool's limits. Notice what programming fluency would have contributed: nothing. No defendant, however skilled, could have audited code legally withheld from him. The score was the most [[taciturn|taciturn]] of witnesses, testifying against him while answering no questions.

What mattered was a question any attentive juror could follow. When ProPublica journalists examined the program's scores in one Florida county, they found that Black defendants who did not reoffend had been classified as higher risk far more often than white defendants who likewise did not. The developer replied that a given score predicted reoffending equally well for both groups. Both claims held up, and researchers showed that when groups reoffend at different recorded rates, the two standards of fairness cannot generally be met at once. Choosing between them is a moral and legal judgment, not a technical one. This episode calls not for programmers but for skeptics who ask what a system was trained on, how often it errs, and on whom its errors fall.

That is why the second view deserves more than grudging assent. Specialization is how complex societies function: most people cannot draft a will or read an X-ray, but they live competently by knowing when to consult someone who can. Syntax drilled into a twelve-year-old who will never program again is soon forgotten. Yet the second view errs if it implies that, because most people need not write code, they may ignore what code does. That indifference would feed a familiar [[proclivity|proclivity]] to treat machine output as beyond dispute. The jury offers a better model. We do not ask jurors to be lawyers, but we do ask them to weigh evidence, notice inconsistency, and follow an argument to its end.

Even the habit of mind credited to coding can be learned without a programming language, as the arts show. Sol LeWitt's wall drawings begin as plain-English instructions specifying lines, arcs, and points; assistants, not LeWitt, carry them out, and a work painted over in one museum can be redrawn in another. Many instructions leave choices to the drafter, so the gap between instruction and result becomes part of the work. This is the discipline coding advocates prize: breaking a task into precise steps and anticipating how an executor might misread them. LeWitt practiced it without writing software; so does any lawyer drafting a contract for a hostile reader. Schools can teach that discipline, and the statistical skepticism the COMPAS dispute demanded, to every student, leaving programming itself to those with an aptitude for it.

Of the two views, then, the second comes closer to my own, but only once it is purged of complacency. The first is right about the stakes and wrong about the remedy: turning every citizen into a programmer is a [[quixotic|quixotic]] ambition, and it would not have helped the Wisconsin defendant. What everyone needs is not the ability to write code but the ability to cross-examine it.
