prompt.statement: Some people believe that we should judge the past by the moral standards of its own time. Others believe that we should judge it by the standards we hold today.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Every Age Had Its Own Dissenters
essays.essay:
The case for judging the past by its own standards rests on a genuine insight: moral understanding is acquired, not given. Ideals we now take for granted, such as universal suffrage or the legal equality of women, required generations of argument before most people could even entertain them. To [[castigate|castigate]] a Ming dynasty magistrate for failing to champion democracy is less a moral judgment than an act of vanity, one that congratulates the present on an inheritance it did not earn. Moralizing of this kind is [[puerile|puerile]], and historicists are right to resist it. Yet their argument quietly assumes that each era held a single moral standard, shared by everyone and impossible to see beyond. That assumption is rarely true, and once it is abandoned, the view that we should judge the past by today's standards comes closer to my position, provided we separate the verdict on an act from the verdict on its author.

The opium trade between Britain and China shows how quickly the assumption breaks down. In the early nineteenth century, opium produced in India under the East India Company's monopoly was carried to China by private merchants, who [[flouted|flout]] Qing prohibitions on the drug for profit; the silver they earned, in turn, helped finance Britain's enormous appetite for Chinese tea. When the imperial commissioner Lin Zexu seized and destroyed their stocks in 1839, Britain went to war and eventually forced China to cede Hong Kong Island. Supporters of the war [[construed|construe]] it as a defense of free trade, and a strict historicist would judge it in those terms. But opinion at the time was not unanimous. Lin wrote to Queen Victoria asking how Britain would respond if foreigners sold the drug to its own people, and in the House of Commons a young William Gladstone denounced the war as a lasting disgrace. The merchants did not lack a moral argument; they chose to ignore one.

The case exposes the first view's central flaw. "The standards of its own time" usually means the standards of those who held power and wrote the record, not those of the Chinese families ruined by addiction or of the Britons who protested. The real choice, then, is not between their standards and ours but between a convenient consensus and the best moral reasoning available, and the fullest version of that reasoning is the one we hold now, shaped in part by the very dissenters the past ignored. The idea of moral progress depends on this choice. To call the abolition of slavery an advance is to measure the era before it against a standard it had not yet adopted; a consistent historicist could describe only changes in moral fashion, never improvements.

Judging by today's standards, however, does not mean distributing blame indiscriminately. Our standards readily condemn the opium trade; how much blame falls on a particular person depends on what that person knew, what alternatives existed, and whether anyone had warned of the harm. A merchant who knew the trade was illegal and ruinous bears far more responsibility than a London clerk whose tea was paid for, through a chain of commerce he never saw, by the same traffic. Present-day standards themselves insist on this distinction, because they tie blame to knowledge and choice. They also forbid distorting the evidence: an account that misrepresents what a historical figure did or believed, to score a contemporary point, is not moral clarity but [[calumny|calumny]]. The historicist's caution, in other words, is not an alternative to modern standards; it is one of them.

The past, then, should be judged by the best standards we possess, applied with the humility those standards themselves demand. We owe the dead an accurate account of what they faced and what they could have known; we do not owe them the pretense that whatever they did was right because enough of their neighbors approved. Lin and Gladstone suggest that most ages contain the materials for their own critique. Judging the past by our standards is often less an act of condescension than a belated decision to listen to those who were right at the time.

prompt.statement:
Claim: A good scientist should be more interested in disproving ideas than in proving them.
Reason: Only ideas that survive serious attempts to refute them deserve trust.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Refutation Belongs to Communities, Not Temperaments
essays.essay:
By the 1990s, many physicians were prescribing hormone therapy to women after menopause partly because large observational studies suggested it protected the heart. When the Women's Health Initiative tested the idea in a large randomized trial of healthy postmenopausal women, the combined-hormone arm was stopped early: the risks, including breast cancer and stroke, outweighed the benefits, and the promised protection against heart disease never appeared. The episode seems to vindicate the view that a good scientist should care more about disproving ideas than proving them, since a belief built on observational data collapsed once it faced a randomized test. I accept the reason behind that view nearly in full, but I [[demur|demur]] at the claim, which mistakes a standard for judging knowledge for a temperament required of every scientist.

The reason is sound because confirmation is cheap. Given the human [[proclivity|proclivity]] to notice evidence that fits what we already believe, almost any idea can accumulate supporting cases. The hormone data looked persuasive, yet the women who chose hormones tended to be wealthier and healthier than those who did not, so confounding by those advantages could account for the very association the hypothesis predicted. The physicians who relied on those studies were not foolish, but too many were [[ingenuous|ingenuous]] in treating agreement between data and hypothesis as proof, without asking what else could produce that agreement. Still, the word "serious" carries much of the weight. A [[cursory|cursory]] or underpowered study that fails to find an effect refutes nothing, and an idea that survives such a test has earned no trust. The reason holds only when the attempts at refutation are as rigorous as the evidence they challenge.

Even a true reason, however, does not deliver the claim: the reason concerns which ideas a community should trust, while the claim concerns what an individual scientist should want. The statement assumes that the skepticism science needs must reside inside each researcher. Cryptography shows otherwise. In the late 1990s, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology sought a new encryption standard through an open competition: teams submitted ciphers, and cryptographers worldwide spent years trying to break them. All five finalists withstood those attacks; the winner, designed by two Belgian researchers, prevailed largely on speed and flexibility. Survival did not set it apart, but without survival no amount of speed could have made it trustworthy. Its authors aimed to build something that would endure; the most searching attacks came from rivals and outside cryptanalysts with every incentive to find a flaw. Trust emerged chiefly from the structure of the contest, not from the temperament of the designers. To expect every scientist to attack her own hypothesis as a rival would is [[quixotic|quixotic]]; a well-designed institution makes that expectation unnecessary.

If the claim has merit, it is for a different reason: as a corrective. Because the pull toward confirmation is so strong, a scientist who deliberately leans toward doubt may end up roughly balanced. Taken literally, however, the claim would cripple discovery, since ideas need advocates before they can receive a fair test. In the early 1980s, Robin Warren and Barry Marshall argued that a bacterium, now called Helicobacter pylori, caused most peptic ulcers, a view many specialists dismissed because they blamed ulcers on stress and acid. Marshall was plainly more interested in proving his idea than in disproving it; he even drank a culture of the bacterium and developed gastritis. That stubborn advocacy kept the idea alive until the evidence vindicated the pair and earned them a Nobel Prize. Their case also exposes a false opposition in the claim: to prove their hypothesis was to refute the reigning one. Those who [[deify|deify]] refutation, as some admirers of Karl Popper do, forget that a refutation is often won by someone fighting for a rival idea.

What a good scientist should care about most, then, is neither proving nor disproving but finding out: proposing ideas boldly, exposing them to tests that could sink them, and accepting the verdict. The reason correctly names the standard that knowledge must meet; the claim errs in assigning that standard to a single temperament rather than to the communities, trials, and rivalries that do most of the refuting.

prompt.statement:
Claim: Laws should be written so that any adult citizen can understand them without legal help.
Reason: People cannot fairly be expected to obey rules they are unable to understand.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Knowable Law, Not Simple Law
essays.essay:
The statement's reason comes close to a first principle of justice: a rule that cannot be known cannot fairly be enforced. The claim built on it, however, demands far more. To require that every law be intelligible to every adult without legal help is [[quixotic|quixotic]] in a society that must regulate nuclear plants, bond markets, and clinical trials. I accept the reason, if "unable to understand" means unable by any reasonable means, but reject the claim outside a narrow core of law. Citizens are owed law that is public, stable, and knowable, not law simple enough to understand unaided. Kafka's The Trial shows why that distinction matters; South Africa's pass laws show why even knowable law is not enough.

Josef K., a bank official, is arrested one morning without having done anything wrong. He is never told the charge or shown the law he has supposedly broken, and he never gets past the court's lowest officials. The court sits in tenement attics, and when K. opens the examining magistrate's books, he finds an indecent picture and a lurid novel instead of statutes. Over the following year the case slowly [[desiccates|desiccate]] his life until little matters to him but the trial; then two men lead him to a quarry and kill him. The court's labyrinthine procedures make the novel read like a protest against legal complexity. Yet K. never learns whether the law itself is complicated. It is simply withheld.

That distinction exposes a hidden assumption in the statement: that needing legal help is what makes law unfair. K.'s misfortune is not that he needs a lawyer but that no lawyer can help him. His lawyer, Huld, receives clients from a sickbed and keeps promising a petition that never seems to be filed; Titorelli, who paints the judges' portraits, admits he has never seen a genuine acquittal. The professionals know the court's habits but not its law; the law's obscurity only [[aggrandizes|aggrandize]] them, letting each claim knowledge no one can verify. Seen this way, a [[convoluted|convoluted]] tax code that accountants explain consistently and in advance is not unfair, while a one-line rule enforced in secret would be monstrous. The reason is therefore sound, but it supports a requirement of knowability, not of unaided comprehension; understanding gained through a lawyer is still understanding. Kafka nonetheless suggests a different argument for the claim, at least for rules governing ordinary conduct: plain law constrains power, because a rule every citizen can read is harder for officials to [[construe|construe]] in their own favor.

South Africa's pass laws test this position from the opposite side. However intricate the influx-control regulations behind them, their central command under apartheid was simple: Black South Africans had to carry a passbook and produce it on demand, or face arrest. No one needed a lawyer to grasp it; its very simplicity made it an efficient instrument of control. In 1960, when the Pan Africanist Congress urged people to leave their passes at home and present themselves at police stations for arrest, protesters at Sharpeville set out to [[flout|flout]] the law precisely because they understood it; the police opened fire, killing dozens. Here the reason's condition was fully met, yet the law was no less unjust. Comprehensibility is thus necessary for fair obligation but not sufficient; the rule itself must be one a person could reasonably be asked to accept. Sharpeville also supports the alternative argument for plain law: open defiance, like obedience, requires knowing what the law says.

The statement, then, points in the right direction but overshoots. Its reason names a real condition of fair obligation; that condition, however, is that law be discoverable rather than self-explanatory, and it is only one among several. Its claim survives only in a narrower form: rules that govern everyday conduct and carry criminal penalties should be plain enough for laypeople to read, so that they can comply and officials cannot hide behind obscurity. Beyond that core, intricate law for specialists is legitimate, provided it is published in advance and explained by someone a citizen can reach. Yet even perfect clarity settles nothing about justice; a rule that everyone understands may still be one that no one should be asked to obey.

words.meaning_here: idealistic but impractical: demanding universally readable law ignores what modern regulation must cover.
drains of vitality; the case slowly leaves K.'s life dull and empty apart from the trial.
inflates the importance of Huld and Titorelli, letting them trade on knowledge no one can check.
extremely complex and hard to follow, yet still explainable by professionals.

prompt.statement: Governments should tax foods and drinks that are proven to harm health.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Tax What Producers Can Remove
essays.essay:
In 2011, Denmark began taxing foods high in saturated fat, raising the price of butter, cheese, and processed meat. Little more than a year later the tax was repealed, amid business complaints about compliance costs and customers lost to German shops. In 2018, Britain began taxing sugary soft drinks, a levy now widely judged a success. Both policies rested on the principle that foods proven to harm health should cost more; their opposite fates suggest that the principle settles very little. What matters is what a tax causes companies and consumers to do. Judged by those consequences, a health tax is wise when it targets a harmful ingredient that producers can remove, unwise when the harm is inseparable from an ordinary food, and inadequate when the danger is hidden from buyers or present at almost any dose.

The British levy worked because it was aimed less at drinkers than at manufacturers. It charged producers by sugar content, with a higher rate for the sweetest drinks and none below a threshold, and was announced two years before taking effect. That interval mattered. Many companies used it to reformulate their best-known drinks, so a substantial share of the sugar in British soft drinks disappeared. The design demanded no corporate virtue: even a purely profit-driven firm would rather cut sugar than surrender part of its margin. Nor did the levy ask drinkers to overcome their [[proclivity|proclivity]] for soda; it changed what was in the can.

Denmark's tax failed for the opposite reason. Saturated fat is not something added to butter or cheese; it is part of what butter and cheese are. Producers therefore had little to reformulate, and the burden fell on consumers. Danes did buy less butter and cream, but every household paid more, and some shopped across the border. The episode exposes an assumption buried in the statement: that harm is a property of a food, when for most foods it is a property of quantity. Butter eaten sparingly does little harm, so a tax on butter penalizes moderate eaters along with heavy ones. Many critics object on grounds of fairness, and not without reason: poorer households spend a larger share of their income on food. Yet the objection weakens when a tax changes the behavior of those it burdens: after Mexico taxed sugary drinks in 2014, purchases fell most among poorer households.

For a third kind of harm, a tax is not too blunt but too weak. Taxes work through price, and price guides only buyers who know what they are buying. Around 1900, federal law barely restrained [[avaricious|avaricious]] manufacturers, and many [[adulterated|adulterate]] their products with cheap fillers and untested preservatives. Even shoppers far from [[ingenuous|ingenuous]] could not protect themselves: no one could detect such additives at the counter, and a higher price would have warned no one. After the government chemist Harvey Wiley tested preservatives on volunteers dubbed the Poison Squad, and muckraking magazines [[castigated|castigate]] the makers of patent medicines laced with alcohol and opiates, Congress responded in 1906 not with a tax but with the Pure Food and Drug Act. Price also fails when no dose is safe. Artificial trans fats were disclosed on American nutrition labels from 2006, yet they have no established safe level of intake; in 2015 the Food and Drug Administration moved to remove them from the food supply. Taxing such a substance would merely sell people permission to be harmed.

The statement is right about the goal but wrong to treat a tax as a single instrument with a predictable effect. Whether a health tax improves health depends on whom it moves: producers who can remove a harmful ingredient, consumers who can only cut back, pay, or evade, or no one at all when the harm is invisible. Governments should therefore tax added ingredients such as sugar, in tiers that reward reformulation, and spend the proceeds on the households that pay most; they should prohibit what is hidden or dangerous at any dose; and they should hesitate to tax staple foods whose harm lies only in excess, where a modest change in diet is bought with a heavier grocery bill for the poor and a longer drive to the border.

Naive and unsuspecting; here negated: even wary shoppers could not detect the hidden additives.
Harshly criticized in public print; here, magazines attacking the makers of patent medicines.

analysis.verdict: This response earns a 6 because its position is insightful, not merely clear. Instead of answering yes or no, it sorts harmful foods into three classes and shows that the same tax has different consequences in each. Each main case is developed down to its mechanism (why Britain's levy worked, why Denmark's faltered despite lower purchases, why price cannot reach hidden harm or harm with no safe dose), and the prose is precise and varied.
analysis.position: The position arrives at the end of paragraph 1 as a three-part test: a tax is "wise when it targets a harmful ingredient that producers can remove," unwise when the harm is intrinsic to the food, and inadequate when the harm is hidden or present at almost any dose. The final paragraph restates it as concrete policy: tiered sugar taxes, outright prohibition, and caution about staples.
analysis.development: Each example is explained, not just named. Britain's levy is traced to its mechanism (tiered rates plus two years' notice led firms to reformulate), and Denmark's failure to a reason the reader can check: saturated fat "is part of what butter and cheese are." The essay even concedes that "Danes did buy less butter and cream," then shows why that gain came at a cost borne by every household.
analysis.organization: The scene-first opening contrasts two real cases, then sets up a three-part test that the body follows in order: removable ingredient (Britain), intrinsic harm (Denmark), hidden harm or harm with no safe dose (1906 law, trans fats). Signposts such as "Denmark's tax failed for the opposite reason," "For a third kind of harm," and "Price also fails when no dose is safe" make each turn visible.
analysis.language: Sentence length varies deliberately, from "That interval mattered." to long sentences built on parallel clauses in the conclusion. Diction is exact rather than ornate ("not too blunt but too weak"), and the target words sit in standard collocations: "far from ingenuous," "their proclivity for soda."
analysis.task: The instruction asks for consequences that shape the position, and the essay says so outright: "Judged by those consequences" introduces the thesis. It traces intended effects (reformulation, lower purchases), unintended ones (cross-border shopping, costs for moderate eaters and the poor), and the limits of price itself (hidden harms and harms with no safe dose), and each one changes what the essay recommends.

paragraphs.note: Restates the thesis in fresh terms (whom a tax moves), turns the three-part test into recommendations, and closes with an image that echoes the lost Danish customers from the opening.

prompt.statement: Manufacturers should be required to make spare parts and repair instructions available for every product they sell.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Repair Rights for Goods Built to Last
essays.essay:
The strongest objection to this policy comes not from appliance makers worried about margins but from makers of medical equipment, and it deserves a full hearing. A ventilator or infusion pump repaired with a counterfeit valve or recalibrated by an untrained hand can kill the patient attached to it. Few people would [[demur|demur]] at the claim that such machines should be serviced only by someone who understands them. If the policy meant mailing a schematic and a box of parts to anyone who asked, it would trade a modest gain in convenience for a real risk to life.

Yet the argument proves less than it claims. It justifies rules about who may repair a dangerous device and with what parts; it does not justify withholding manuals and components from everyone outside the manufacturer's service network. That difference became concrete in 2020, when hospitals crowded with COVID-19 patients needed every ventilator working. Many of their biomedical technicians, trained professionals who maintain such machines daily, reported that manuals, diagnostic software, or parts were restricted to manufacturer-authorized personnel. In 2018, a U.S. Food and Drug Administration review found that the available evidence did not establish independent servicing as a widespread danger to patients. Safety, in short, is an argument about competence, and manufacturers have too often stretched it into an argument for exclusivity. Repair should therefore be opened to competent outsiders; the policy's consequences must decide how far.

The case for the policy rests on a plain observation about incentives. One need not believe that manufacturers are [[avaricious|avaricious]] to see the problem; one need only notice that a firm earns little from a repair someone else performs. It usually earns more from a replacement or from its own service department. The withheld ventilator manuals served the second; the first has a longer history. In the 1920s, the world's leading lightbulb makers, among them Osram, Philips, and affiliates of General Electric, formed the Phoebus cartel, agreed to limit their bulbs to roughly a thousand hours of life, and fined members whose bulbs lasted longer. Durability that depends on goodwill alone will not last. The policy's chief intended consequence would be to change that calculation, so that a frugal household need not behave like a [[spendthrift|spendthrift]], discarding a washing machine because a door seal has failed. Since 2021, the European Union's ecodesign rules have obliged makers of washing machines, dishwashers, and refrigerators to supply spare parts for up to a decade, reserving certain parts for professional repairers, precisely the distinction the safety argument calls for. They are too new to judge, but they show that such a mandate can be specified product by product.

The same evidence, however, exposes the flaw in the word "every." A repair mandate would have done nothing against the Phoebus cartel, because a burned-out filament cannot be fixed; the fitting remedy was competition or a durability standard, not a manual. Applied literally, the policy would oblige firms to stock parts for disposable razors and five-dollar earbuds, and the cost of warehousing components that no one will ever order would fall on buyers, hardest on those who can afford only the cheapest goods. A second unintended consequence is subtler. Only an [[ingenuous|ingenuous]] regulator would assume that "available" parts are also usable. A firm could price a replacement screen at nearly the cost of a new phone, or program its devices to reject components it has not authorized, honoring the letter of the law while [[flouting|flout]] its spirit.

These consequences point toward a narrower but stronger policy than the one proposed. Manufacturers should be required to supply parts, documentation, and diagnostic tools for durable goods whose value makes repair worthwhile, for a period matched to each product's expected life, at prices that reflect cost and without software that locks out independent parts. Where a failure could injure someone, access should go to certified technicians rather than the general public; consumables and trivially cheap goods should be exempt. So framed, the rule answers the manufacturers' best objection and confronts both incentives traced above. Its proper object is not every product a company sells, but every product the company claims was built to last.

words.meaning_here: Object or raise doubts; few would object to the claim that such machines need knowledgeable servicers.
Intensely greedy for money; the essay says the problem exists even without assuming greed.
A habitually wasteful spender; repair access keeps a frugal household from having to waste like one.
Naive and too trusting; only a naive regulator would assume that available parts are automatically usable.
Openly disregarding; obeying the law's wording while plainly defying its purpose.

analysis.verdict: This essay earns a 6 because its position is insightful, not just clear. It separates competence from exclusivity, exposes the overreach in the word "every," and then lets the consequences it traces rebuild the policy. Each example (the 2020 ventilator crisis, the Phoebus cartel, the EU ecodesign rules) is explained, tied to the argument and claimed no further than the evidence allows, and the prose is precise and controlled.
analysis.position: The turn comes early, with "Yet the argument proves less than it claims," which marks where the safety objection stops. Paragraph 2 then commits to a position, "Repair should therefore be opened to competent outsiders," and leaves its reach to the consequences. Paragraph 5 states the refined version, "a narrower but stronger policy than the one proposed," and the last sentence sharpens it into "every product the company claims was built to last."
analysis.development: Every example is developed until its point is clear: the 2020 ventilator shortage shows trained technicians shut out, and the FDA review shows that independent servicing had not been established as a widespread danger. The essay then reuses the ventilators as evidence of a service monopoly and the Phoebus cartel as evidence of shortened product life. Finally it turns the cartel against the statement itself: "a burned-out filament cannot be fixed."
analysis.organization: The essay follows the concession-first shape: the concession (paragraph 1), its limit and a provisional position (2), intended consequences (3), unintended consequences (4) and the redesigned policy (5). Transitions carry the logic: "Yet," "therefore" and "The same evidence, however, exposes the flaw."
analysis.language: The diction is exact rather than ornate ("stretched it into an argument for exclusivity"), and short sentences break up long ones: "Durability that depends on goodwill alone will not last." The target words sit in ordinary collocations such as "demur at the claim," "an ingenuous regulator" and "flouting its spirit."
analysis.task: The instruction asks how consequences shape the position, and the essay makes that dependence explicit twice: "the policy's consequences must decide how far," then "These consequences point toward a narrower but stronger policy." Each feature of the final policy answers a consequence traced earlier; for example, cost-based prices close the pricing loophole from paragraph 4.

paragraphs.note: Grants the opponents' best case, that medical devices repaired badly can kill, and admits the policy read literally would be reckless, setting up the limit the next paragraph locates.

paragraphs.role: Locates exactly where the safety argument stops
paragraphs.note: Separates rules about who repairs from secrecy about how; the 2020 ventilator crisis and the 2018 FDA review show safety stretched into exclusivity. Ends with a provisional position, leaving its reach to the consequences.

paragraphs.role: Intended consequences: two incentives, history, precedent
paragraphs.note: Names two profitable alternatives to outside repair, a service monopoly (the ventilators) and replacement (the Phoebus cartel); states the household benefit; cites the EU's tiered rules as a model, not yet proven.

paragraphs.role: Unintended consequences expose the word "every"
paragraphs.note: Turns the Phoebus example against the statement's scope, then traces two side effects: storage costs falling on poorer buyers, and compliance in name only through pricing and software locks.

paragraphs.role: Refined position built from the consequences
paragraphs.note: Converts each consequence into a design feature: durable goods only, life-matched duration, cost-based prices, no software locks, certified access for risky devices; closes by redefining the policy's target.

moves.example: It justifies rules about who may repair a dangerous device and with what parts; it does not justify withholding manuals and components from everyone outside the manufacturer's service network.
moves.use: When conceding an opponent's point, to mark exactly where its logic stops applying.

moves.example: The same evidence, however, exposes the flaw in the word "every."

analysis.contrast: A typical 4 or 5 would simply agree or disagree, list benefits (less waste, lower costs) and drawbacks (safety, expense) in separate paragraphs, and end with "it depends." Its examples would be generic or merely named, such as "Europe has repair laws," without saying what they show. It would not notice that "every" sweeps in disposable goods, or that "available" parts can still be unusable.

prompt.statement: Progress in any field depends more on the questions people ask than on the answers they find.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Misdirected Fields Need Questions, Ill-Equipped Fields Answers
essays.essay:
The statement captures something real about progress, but its claim to cover any field is too broad. It assumes that every stalled field suffers from a failure of imagination, yet fields stall for two different reasons. Some are misdirected: they produce answers in abundance, but to the wrong question. Others are ill-equipped: everyone knows what to ask, but no one has the instrument, technique, or funding to settle it. The statement holds for the first kind and fails for the second, as two episodes from European history show.

As Victorian London [[burgeoned|burgeon]], cholera returned repeatedly, and the medical establishment blamed miasma, the foul air of crowded, filthy districts. The theory was not foolish, since cholera did strike hardest where the stench was worst, but it led physicians to ask what in the air was poisonous, a question that yielded speculation but no account of how the disease spread. When an outbreak struck Soho in 1854, John Snow, a physician long skeptical of miasma, asked a deceptively [[artless|artless]] question: where had the dead been getting their water? Using the register of deaths and inquiries among victims' households, he found the deaths clustered around the public pump on Broad Street; his famous map, drawn later, displayed a conclusion he had already reached. The [[anomalous|anomalous]] cases proved as telling as the typical ones. Workers at a nearby brewery with its own well were largely spared, while a widow in distant Hampstead died after drinking water fetched from the pump.

Snow's investigation is a [[paradigmatic|paradigmatic]] case of a question outrunning its answers. He never identified the organism that causes cholera. The removal of the pump handle, which textbooks have [[canonized|canonize]] as the founding moment of modern epidemiology, came after the outbreak had begun to subside, and Britain's General Board of Health dismissed his explanation. Yet his question endured because it could travel: compare the sick with the well, and ask what exposure separates them. That comparison remains the core logic of outbreak investigation. Miasma theory did later claim a success: sewers built to banish London's stench also helped keep sewage out of its drinking water. But a remedy that works for reasons its builders do not grasp cannot tell them where else to apply it. The [[profundity|profundity]] of Snow's insight lay not in a fact he established but in a frame he replaced, and here the statement is exactly right: a field trapped inside a mistaken question may stumble onto remedies, but only a better question can explain them.

The search for longitude at sea tells the opposite story. For centuries, European navigators could fix latitude from the sun but only estimate longitude, often with fatal results. Here no one lacked the right question. Scholars had known since the sixteenth century that a ship carrying an accurate clock set to home-port time could compare it with local noon to calculate longitude. In 1714 the British Parliament posed the question explicitly, offering a large prize for a practical method. Even astronomers championing a rival method, reading the moon's position against the stars, pursued the identical question; the camps competed only on answers. What was missing was a clock that could keep time through months of pitching decks and shifting temperatures. John Harrison, a self-taught clockmaker, spent decades of [[arduous|arduous]] work building one; James Cook later sailed with a copy and praised it. No reframing would have helped; progress waited on craftsmanship.

These cases shape my position: I reject the statement as a general law but accept it as a diagnosis of one kind of failure. Questions matter most when a field is misdirected, when capable people labor on a problem framed so that its solution cannot appear. Answers matter most when a field is ill-equipped, when the question is common knowledge and progress waits on technique, money, or patience. Yet a stalled field rarely announces which condition it suffers from. A government that offers a prize for a specific solution assumes the question is sound; one that funds open-ended inquiry allows that it may not be. Progress depends less on whether we prize questions or answers than on recognizing which one a field lacks.

words.meaning_here: grew rapidly; London expanded quickly in population and size during the Victorian era.
seemingly simple and unpretentious; a plain, down-to-earth question that concealed a sharp hypothesis.
deviating from the expected pattern; deaths or survivals that did not fit the pump's location.
words.def: deviating from what is standard, normal, or expected.

words.meaning_here: serving as a model, typical example of a question outrunning its answers.
elevated to revered, authoritative status in the standard story of epidemiology.
depth of intellectual insight; how far Snow's thinking reached beyond the facts he established.
requiring strenuous, prolonged effort; difficult and tiring work over many years.
words.def: involving or requiring strenuous effort; difficult and tiring.

analysis.verdict: This response earns a 6 because its position is insightful, not merely clear. It exposes the statement's hidden assumption that every stalled field suffers from a failure of imagination, replaces it with a distinction between misdirected and ill-equipped fields, and even concedes that miasma-era sewers helped before explaining why that success does not rescue the wrong question. Both examples are developed far enough to show what happened and why it matters, in precise, varied, controlled language.
analysis.position: The writer takes a qualified position in the first sentence: the statement "captures something real about progress" but "its claim to cover any field is too broad." The conclusion sharpens this into a conditional claim: the statement is "a diagnosis of one kind of failure."
analysis.development: The Snow example runs across two paragraphs: first what he asked and how he found the pump cluster, the brewery workers, and the Hampstead widow, then why it counts as "a question outrunning its answers." It concedes that miasma-driven sewers helped, then argues that a field "may stumble onto remedies, but only a better question can explain them." Longitude is explained, not just named: rival astronomers "pursued the identical question," so progress depended on Harrison's clock.
analysis.organization: The structure follows the argument rather than a template: a distinction, a two-paragraph extended example where the statement holds, a contrasting case where it fails, and a conclusion stating how the cases "shape my position." Signposts such as "The search for longitude at sea tells the opposite story." mark each turn.
analysis.language: Diction is economical and exact ("yielded speculation but no account of how the disease spread"), and sentence length varies from short verdicts ("Here no one lacked the right question.") to long sentences with embedded clauses. Target words sit in idiomatic collocations such as "a deceptively artless question" and "a paradigmatic case."
analysis.task: The instruction asks when the statement holds, when it does not, and how those cases shape the position. The essay does all three visibly: "here the statement is exactly right" for Snow, "tells the opposite story" for longitude, and "These cases shape my position" to open the conclusion.

paragraphs.role: Position and the key distinction
paragraphs.note: Exposes the statement's hidden assumption that every stall is a failure of imagination, distinguishes misdirected from ill-equipped fields, and previews two European cases that test each side.

paragraphs.role: Extended example, part one: Snow's question
paragraphs.note: Shows how miasma theory framed the wrong question, then narrates Snow's deceptively simple water question, how death records and household inquiries located the pump, and the anomalous cases that confirmed it.

paragraphs.role: Extended example, part two: why it matters
paragraphs.note: Argues that Snow answered little yet changed his field, concedes that miasma-driven sewers helped by accident, and concludes that a misdirected field may stumble onto remedies but needs a better question to explain them.

paragraphs.role: Contrasting case where the statement fails
paragraphs.note: Longitude: the question was obvious and even posed by Parliament, and rival camps shared it and competed only on answers, so progress depended on Harrison's craftsmanship, not on reframing.

paragraphs.role: Refined position and its practical stakes
paragraphs.note: States explicitly how the cases shape the position, restates the distinction in fresh words, and extends it to policy: prizes assume a sound question, while open-ended funding does not.

moves.frame: It assumes that ..., yet ...
moves.example: It assumes that every stalled field suffers from a failure of imagination, yet fields stall for two different reasons.
moves.use: Early in an issue essay, to expose a hidden assumption and introduce the distinction you will test.

moves.frame: The ... of ... lay not in ... but in ...
moves.example: The profundity of Snow's insight lay not in a fact he established but in a frame he replaced
moves.use: After narrating an example, to state precisely what it proves and turn the story into argument.

moves.frame: These cases shape my position: I reject ... as ... but accept it as ...
moves.example: These cases shape my position: I reject the statement as a general law but accept it as a diagnosis of one kind of failure.
moves.use: Opening the conclusion when the prompt asks how your cases shape your position.

analysis.contrast: A typical 4 or 5 response would agree or disagree wholesale and treat questions and answers as simple rivals. It would list several famous names, often Einstein or Newton, with a sentence each, or mention Snow without explaining why his question mattered more than his answer. It would rarely expose the statement's hidden assumption or specify when each side applies, and it would end by restating the prompt.

prompt.statement: Popular opinion is a poor guide to what is true but a reliable guide to what is workable.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Opinion Judges Acceptance, Not Efficacy
essays.essay:
In the summer of 1858, the Thames smelled so foul that the season became known as the Great Stink. Most Londoners, and many physicians, blamed cholera on "miasma," or bad air, a theory since disproved. Yet the outcry, sharpened by lawmakers who could smell the river themselves, led Parliament to empower the Metropolitan Board of Works to build Joseph Bazalgette's intercepting sewers, which carried waste downstream of the city and helped end London's cholera epidemics. The public misunderstood the disease yet demanded a remedy that worked, as the statement predicts. I accept its first half but only part of its second. "Workable" conceals two questions: whether people will accept a measure, and whether it will achieve its purpose. Popular opinion answers the first with real authority; it answers the second correctly mostly by accident, as it did in 1858.

The statement holds best when the question concerns the public itself. Google Glass, offered to early users in 2013, was a genuine engineering achievement: a small computer and camera built into an eyeglass frame. Its [[fervid|fervid]] early champions predicted such devices would soon be as ordinary as smartphones. They misjudged their neighbors. Many people disliked sitting near someone who might be recording them, several restaurants and bars banned the device, and Google stopped selling it to consumers within two years. No expert review could have overturned that verdict, because whether people will tolerate a camera at the dinner table is a social fact rather than a technical one, and the public is its most reliable witness. A device people refuse to wear, or a treatment regimen they refuse to follow, is unworkable however well it performs on paper.

The statement fails, however, when the consequences of a choice are delayed, diffuse, or invisible. In 1998 a small study, never [[corroborated|corroborate]] and later retracted, suggested a link between the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine and autism. Amid a [[cacophonous|cacophonous]] media debate that often treated the study and the contrary evidence as evenly matched, vaccination rates in Britain fell, and measles, once rare, returned in repeated outbreaks. Here popular opinion misjudged not only the truth but also what was workable, and for a structural reason: a vaccine's success is a non-event. A child who never catches measles generates no story, whereas one whose autism is first noticed soon after a routine shot generates a vivid one. Antibiotics suffer the same distortion. A patient who takes them for a viral cold recovers anyway and credits the pills, while the resistance that needless prescribing breeds emerges later, often in other people. When the public cannot see the outcome it is judging, its confidence that a practice works is no better founded than its beliefs about why.

Together these cases explain why my agreement is only partial. They do not cancel each other; they divide the territory. Popular opinion is authoritative about acceptance, which is a fact about people, and unreliable about efficacy, which is a fact about the world. Even the Great Stink reconciles the two only by coincidence: the stench and the cholera bacterium both traveled in sewage, so the false theory and the true one alike favored carrying it out of the city, though cleaner water supplies mattered too. Had the theories diverged, Londoners would have demanded the wrong cure with equal conviction. The practical lesson is to treat popular opinion as a constraint, not a compass. A health ministry that [[vacillates|vacillate]] between policies as the polls shift will drift toward whatever feels effective, while one that ignores the public will design programs no one uses. When evidence and sentiment collide, officials are tempted to [[equivocate|equivocate]] about a clear finding to calm critics, but ambiguity is precisely what fear feeds on. Issues that already [[polarize|polarize]] the public require more clarity from experts, not less.

My position, then, is that the public is the final judge of what it will tolerate and no judge at all of what will succeed once tolerated. A workable policy needs both verdicts. The Londoners of 1858 supplied the second by good fortune rather than good judgment, and a society that relies on such fortune will eventually pay, often in harms it cannot see until they arrive.

confirmed by later research; the study's claim was never supported by other studies

Every example (the Great Stink, Google Glass, the MMR scare, antibiotics) is narrated and then explained, and the opening example is reinterpreted later instead of being dropped. The prose is precise and varied, with no filler.

Diction is exact and compressed ("a constraint, not a compass"), and target words sit in natural collocations, as in "fervid early champions" and "cacophonous media debate" (paragraphs 2 and 3).

prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Admiration Follows Credit, Not Usefulness
essays.essay:
The statement captures a real pattern: every era lavishes praise on the conspicuous while overlooking much of the work that sustains it. Yet “rarely” implies that admiration and usefulness are rivals, when admiration is better understood as a response to visible, attributable evidence, which useful work often fails to produce. The statement holds, then, when the benefits of someone’s work are hidden or delayed, and it fails when those benefits are vivid and traceable or when admiration is itself the means of doing good. I therefore agree only conditionally: the claim describes how certain kinds of work are rewarded, not what admired people are like.

The statement holds most clearly when a person’s greatest achievement takes the form of an absence. In the mid-nineteenth century, London suffered repeated cholera epidemics, and the Thames, fouled by the waste of a [[burgeoning|burgeon]] city, had become little more than an open sewer. Joseph Bazalgette, chief engineer of London’s Metropolitan Board of Works, had already drafted plans for new sewers when the “Great Stink” of 1858 pushed Parliament to fund them. His intercepting sewers carried waste far downstream, and their design turned on [[recondite|recondite]] questions of gradient, flow, and pumping capacity. Together with cleaner water supplies, the system helped end epidemics that had killed thousands of Londoners. His own era honored him with a knighthood, and the Institution of Civil Engineers elected him its president, yet he never approached the renown of the era’s most celebrated figures, largely because his success consisted of deaths that did not occur. Prevention that leaves nothing to see earns respect, not reverence.

A second condition is timing: the statement holds when admirers must judge before the benefit appears. Studies of university teaching have found that the instructors whom students rate most highly are not reliably those whose students do best in later courses; a few have found the relationship reversed. Students rate a course at its end, when its pleasures are fresh and its lessons untested. A charismatic lecturer who fills each hour with entertaining digressions can send students out feeling enlightened. Fluency is easily mistaken for [[profundity|profundity]]. A colleague who insists on the effortful practice that makes knowledge last earns grumbling at the term’s end and gratitude, if ever, years later.

The pattern reverses when a benefit is vivid and traceable to a single person. In the early 1950s, polio terrified American parents: summer outbreaks closed swimming pools, and images of children in iron lungs were familiar from newsreels. When a vast field trial showed in 1955 that Jonas Salk’s vaccine worked, the public greeted the news with [[fervid|fervid]] gratitude, and Salk became a national hero within days. Both Salk and Bazalgette prevented disease, so the difference lies not in the kind of work but in whether its benefit could be traced to its author. The trial tied protection directly to Salk’s vaccine, whereas cholera’s retreat from London had several causes and no single author.

In some roles the statement fails even more completely, because admiration is the very instrument of usefulness. In April 1993, as South Africa negotiated its way out of apartheid, a white right-wing gunman assassinated Chris Hani, one of the liberation movement’s most popular leaders, and many feared retaliatory violence. Nelson Mandela, not yet president, went on national television to urge restraint, and the negotiations survived. Twenty-seven years in prison had given him unmatched moral authority, and only someone so widely revered could ask furious supporters to forgo revenge. Admiration was not a distraction from his usefulness; it was the form his usefulness took.

These cases shape my position: I accept the statement as a diagnosis of where admiration goes astray, not as a verdict on the people who receive it. The claim mistakes a bias of attention for a law of character. Much valuable work is preventive, technical, or slow to repay, and an era that [[canonizes|canonize]] only those whose contributions it can see and credit will keep underrating its Bazalgettes. Where benefits are vivid and attributable, or where trust is the medium of the work itself, admiration and usefulness converge. The fault lies less with the people we admire than with how narrowly we look.

Intensely, almost feverishly felt: the public’s gratitude when the polio vaccine was shown to work.

analysis.verdict: This response earns a 6 because its position is insightful, not merely clear. It exposes the hidden assumption that admiration and usefulness are rivals and replaces it with testable conditions: whether a benefit is visible, timely, and traceable to its author. Each of its four examples is developed far enough to show why it supports or limits the claim, and the prose is precise, varied, and nearly error-free.
analysis.position: A qualified position appears at the end of the first paragraph, “I therefore agree only conditionally,” and rests on a reason: admiration is “a response to visible, attributable evidence.” The final paragraph restates it in fresh terms, saying the claim “mistakes a bias of attention for a law of character.”
analysis.development: Every example is explained, not just named. Bazalgette’s sewers show why prevention that leaves nothing to see “earns respect, not reverence,” even from an era that knighted him, and the Hani assassination shows exactly how Mandela’s reputation did practical work. Pairing Salk with Bazalgette isolates the real variable: whether a benefit “could be traced to its author.”
analysis.organization: The paragraphs follow the conditions announced in the introduction: two under which the statement holds (hidden benefits, delayed judgment) and two under which it fails (traceable benefits, admiration as instrument). Openers such as “A second condition is timing” and “The pattern reverses” make each turn visible.
analysis.language: Diction is exact rather than ornate (“intercepting sewers,” “effortful practice,” “retaliatory violence”), and sentence length varies from long, layered sentences to short ones such as “Fluency is easily mistaken for profundity.” There are no contractions or filler transitions.

prompt.statement: Scientists should share their data publicly as soon as it is collected, before they publish their own analyses.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Share Evidence, Protect Credit and People
essays.essay:
The recommendation casts data sharing as a contest between scientists seeking credit and a public seeking knowledge. Framed that way, immediate release looks like generosity and any delay like hoarding. When data describe texts, stars, or molecules, I largely agree: the costs of delay fall on everyone, and the collector's legitimate claim is to credit for interpretation, not to control of the evidence. But the framing omits a third party, the people some data describe. Once they enter the picture, release "as soon as it is collected" can cause harm that no later analysis can repair.

No episode shows the cost of withholding evidence more clearly than the long dispute over access to the Dead Sea Scrolls. Beginning in 1947, caves near the Dead Sea yielded the oldest known manuscripts of the Hebrew Bible and hundreds of other ancient Jewish texts. The largest cache, thousands of fragments from a single cave, was entrusted to a small team of scholars with exclusive rights to publish it. The team proved [[dilatory|dilatory]]. Nearly four decades after the discoveries, much of that material remained unpublished, and scholars outside the circle could not even examine photographs of it. Defenders insisted that the editors were not lazy but [[punctilious|punctilious]], unwilling to print a reading until every letter was secure. Yet perfectionism justifies delaying one's own edition, not barring everyone else from the evidence.

The monopoly collapsed in 1991, when a California library holding a set of the photographs opened them to any researcher and an unauthorized facsimile edition appeared. Scholarship on the scrolls [[burgeoned|burgeon]], and the official editions, prepared by a team that had begun expanding before the monopoly fell, came out far faster. But the episode also revealed a legitimate interest on the editors' side. One scholar who had spent years reconstructing an important text from fragments of several copies sued when his reconstruction was printed without his permission, and Israel's courts upheld his claim. Such reconstruction is scholarship of the most demanding kind, and its results deserve protection. The case thus isolates a distinction that the recommendation blurs, between evidence and its interpretation. Releasing the photographs cost the editors only their monopoly and freed an entire field; printing the reconstruction took the one thing an editor can fairly claim. Evidence should circulate freely, but credit for interpreting it belongs to whoever did the work.

Genomics supplies the contrast, all the more striking because its flagship project is the [[paradigmatic|paradigmatic]] success of open data. In 1996, leaders of the Human Genome Project agreed to post newly assembled sequence publicly within a day, long before anyone had analyzed it, so that every laboratory could hunt for disease genes at once. That policy was safe because the reference sequence came from a few anonymous volunteers and was tied to no medical record. Studies linking genes to disease are different. In 2008, researchers showed that someone holding a person's genotype could infer whether that person had contributed DNA to a study, even from pooled summary statistics. Because inclusion among a study's patients reveals a diagnosis, the National Institutes of Health quickly moved such data behind controlled access. Withdrawal could not reach copies already downloaded, and that is the decisive point: disclosure cannot be undone, and its dangers may surface only later. If summary figures, long assumed harmless, could betray participants, then raw genetic records posted the moment they are collected would expose them far more directly. For such data, the recommendation endangers people who agreed to help science, not to be identified by it.

These cases pull my position in opposite directions, but the line between them is principled. Where data describe the natural world or the human past, an exclusive hold mainly serves delay, even when the material is so [[recondite|recondite]] that confining it to a few experts seems harmless. There, the evidence should be released promptly and credit for its interpretation protected. Where data can identify living people, speed is the wrong virtue, because those at risk never joined the bargain between scientists and the public and cannot be made whole once exposed. The question that matters, then, is not how soon scientists should share their data but whom those data can expose.

prompt.statement: Young people should work for a year before deciding what to study at university.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Work Tests Careers, Not Disciplines
essays.essay:
The recommendation rests on an appealing assumption: that a year of employment will reveal what a young person ought to study. Sometimes it does. Work is an excellent test of an occupation, because it exposes the daily texture of a job as no brochure can. It is a weak test of an academic discipline, however, and no test at all when the jobs bear no relation to the choice at hand. I therefore endorse the recommendation only for students weighing a field that leads directly to a demanding profession, and only when the year is organized around that choice. As a rule for everyone, it is more likely to postpone a decision than to improve it.

Medicine is the clearest case in which the advice pays off. In Britain, as in Vietnam and much of continental Europe, most students enter medical school straight from secondary school, committing at eighteen to an [[arduous|arduous]] course of study that lasts five or six years and leads to a single profession. A teenager who [[vacillates|vacillate]] between medicine and biochemistry has encountered both only on paper; what no classroom can tell her is whether she can endure night shifts, the physical intimacy of caring for frail patients, or the death of someone she has looked after. British medical schools recognize this gap; they generally expect applicants to have spent time in a caring role, such as working in a care home. A year in such work answers the question that matters most before the costliest years of training begin. Some students discover a vocation; others learn, far more cheaply than in the third year of medical school, that they prefer the laboratory to the bedside. Either outcome justifies the year.

The recommendation fails where work cannot imitate the field. A student torn between disciplines as [[disparate|disparate]] as mathematics and history will learn little about either in a call center or a café, and months of tedious work may [[enervate|enervate]] her, dulling the very curiosity that made the choice feel important. The danger is greater when the year has no question to answer. Europe offers a precedent. In the eighteenth century, wealthy English families often sent their sons on a Grand Tour of France and Italy straight from school, and Adam Smith, in The Wealth of Nations, judged that the young men commonly came home less capable of serious application to study or business than if they had stayed home. Smith was describing travel that passed for education but answered no question; its modern counterpart is a [[desultory|desultory]] series of jobs taken to put off a choice. Such a year serves the [[diffident|diffident]] student worst, since she is the least likely to seek out the experiences that might settle her doubts.

These examples turn my position from a general verdict into a conditional one. What matters is not work as such but the fit between the work and the decision it is meant to inform. Where a field leads to a single, demanding occupation that a young worker can sample, a year of work yields evidence worth its cost; where it does not, the year is less an experiment than a [[dilatory|dilatory]] tactic. One might object that any job builds maturity. Perhaps it does, but maturity is a different benefit from the one the recommendation promises; it argues for working before university, not for working before choosing a subject. Institutional context sharpens the point. A Vietnamese or German applicant must name a field on the application itself, so a mistake is costly and a year of testing can pay for itself. An American undergraduate can usually wait until the end of the second year to declare a major, and her introductory courses sample the disciplines more directly than any job could. For her, that exploratory year already exists inside the university.

The advice, then, deserves a narrower audience than its wording implies. Students contemplating a demanding vocation, especially where admission forces an early and expensive commitment, should spend a year doing work that resembles it. Everyone else is better served by enrolling and letting coursework do the exploring, because a job can test a career but rarely a discipline.

Every example is explained far enough to show why it matters, and the prose is precise, varied, and error-free.

prompt.statement: Schools should have older students spend part of each week teaching younger ones.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Older Students Should Tutor, Not Teach
essays.essay:
Behind this recommendation lies an old and sound intuition, preserved in the Latin proverb docendo discimus: by teaching, we learn. I largely agree, but the word "teaching" conceals a doubtful assumption: that anyone who has mastered a subject can pass it on. Older students make excellent tutors when an adult defines a narrow task and stays close at hand; they make poor substitutes for teachers when left on their own. The circumstances in which the practice has succeeded and failed suggest that schools should adopt it as supervised tutoring, not as a universal weekly duty to teach.

Consider the buddy programs common in American elementary schools, where fifth graders meet younger children weekly to read aloud or practice arithmetic. The younger child receives what a teacher with twenty-five pupils cannot provide: a patient listener who waits while he sounds out a word. The older child gains something less obvious. A [[diffident|diffident]] eleven-year-old who never raises her hand may discover, with a seven-year-old looking up at her, that she has something to offer, and that discovery can follow her back to her own desk. Explaining also tests understanding in a way that answering questions does not. A second grader's [[artless|artless]] question about why one must borrow from the tens column may reveal to his tutor that she has memorized how to subtract without ever grasping place value. Such gains, however, depend on easily missed conditions: a task narrow enough for a child to manage, and a teacher who plans the session and stays nearby to catch the tutor's mistakes.

The monitorial system of the early nineteenth century shows what happens when the same idea is pressed into service to replace teachers. In Britain, Andrew Bell and Joseph Lancaster promoted schools in which a single master instructed a corps of older pupils, who then drilled younger children in reading and arithmetic. The model spread quickly because it was cheap: one adult could oversee hundreds of children. Yet the monitors could pass on only what they had memorized, so instruction hardened into rote recitation. A monitor could tell whether an answer was right but not why a child had gotten it wrong, and the [[cacophonous|cacophonous]] schoolrooms, where many groups recited at once, could be kept in order only through rigid, almost military drill. Tellingly, the remedy kept young instructors: from the 1840s, English schools began replacing monitors with pupil-teachers, adolescent apprentices who taught under a master's supervision while being trained themselves. The system had failed, then, not because children cannot help one another learn but because they cannot stand in for the adult who knows why an answer is right.

A third circumstance, closer to the recommendation's literal wording, lies between these extremes. Imagine a high school that requires every junior to spend Friday afternoons in a second-grade classroom. Some juniors would thrive. Others, already struggling in their own courses, would lose hours they could not spare, and a few, however well meaning, would be too [[garrulous|garrulous]] to let a seven-year-old finish a sentence. Without a curriculum, the sessions would quickly become [[desultory|desultory]]: tutors would improvise games, the younger children would conclude that the period did not count, and the teacher would spend the afternoon managing two groups instead of one. The recommendation's sweeping terms, "older students" and "each week," treat as universal a practice whose value depends on who is tutoring, what is being taught, and how carefully an adult has planned the work.

These cases move my position from simple agreement to conditional agreement. The buddy programs show that the benefits are real and run in both directions; the monitorial schools show that those benefits vanish once older students must supply what only trained teachers can; the imagined high school shows that a sound practice weakens when imposed on everyone alike. Schools should therefore reserve time each week for older students to help younger ones, but should define the task narrowly, keep a teacher in charge, and match tutors to tasks rather than conscript an entire grade. Under those conditions the proverb holds for the tutors, who learn by teaching, and their pupils gain what it never promised: a patient guide only a few years older.

prompt.statement: Public libraries matter more in the digital age than they did before it.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Scarcity Relocated, Not Abolished
essays.essay:
Before the internet, a public library mattered chiefly because it held more books than most people could afford to own. That function has plainly weakened, and any honest defense of the statement must begin by admitting it. Even so, I largely agree, because the digital age has not abolished scarcity; it has relocated it. What is scarce now is not information but reliable access to it, the skill to judge it, and the time and quiet to absorb it. Libraries matter more today, but only to the extent that they relieve these new scarcities rather than cling to their old role.

The first scarcity is access, and the assumption hidden in the phrase "digital age" is that everyone lives in it equally. They do not. As schooling, job applications, and public benefits have moved online, the cost of lacking a reliable connection has risen sharply: a family without broadband was once merely inconvenienced and is now partly shut out of civic life. The COVID-19 pandemic made this vivid. When schools closed and classes moved onto screens, students without home internet struggled to attend lessons or submit assignments, and many libraries responded by lending Wi-Fi hotspots and leaving their networks on so that students could work from the parking lot after hours. That a child doing homework in a parked car counted as a solution shows how thin the alternatives were. In a print world, a household far from a library lost access to books; in a digital one, it can lose its link to school itself.

The second scarcity is judgment. The internet does not hand its users knowledge; it surrounds them with a [[cacophonous|cacophonous]] chorus of advertisers, partisans, and experts, and nothing in the medium itself separates the reliable from the merely confident. Young people raised on screens are often assumed to tell these voices apart, but a widely cited Stanford study of online reasoning found the opposite: most middle-school students tested took an advertisement labeled "sponsored content" for a genuine news story. Left to themselves, many students mistake [[desultory|desultory]] browsing for research, clicking the first plausible link and moving on. School and public librarians are among the few professionals whose job is to teach the remedy: asking who stands behind a source, checking it against others, and recognizing when a question calls for a scholarly database rather than a search engine. Before the internet, this skill was useful. Now that anyone can publish anything, it is indispensable.

The strongest challenge to my position deserves to be stated in full. Public libraries, a skeptic would say, were an answer to the scarcity of print. Andrew Carnegie financed thousands of library buildings on the conviction that working people, given free access to more books than they could buy, would educate themselves. Today even [[recondite|recondite]] scholarship once confined to university libraries can often be downloaded in seconds. If the remaining problem is connectivity, a city could subsidize broadband and laptops rather than maintain buildings full of books that, in many places, fewer people borrow. The first half of this argument is correct; a library that defines itself by its stacks is becoming [[obsolete|obsolete]]. The second half fails. A subsidized laptop without the judgment described above produces more aimless clicking, not more understanding, and offers no patient guide, no quiet room, and no place where a person may stay for hours without buying anything. It can deliver facts instantly, but rarely the [[profundity|profundity]] that comes from long, quiet hours with a demanding book. Falling loans measure only the oldest service, and treating them as proof of irrelevance tends to fulfill itself: cities that cut hours and staff because libraries seem obsolete [[enervate|enervate]] the very institutions best equipped to supply what the digital age lacks.

The statement, then, is true in a particular sense. Libraries matter more now not because books matter more, but because the distance between having information and being able to use it has widened, and the library is one of the few public institutions built to close that distance. Whether any given library matters more depends on whether it embraces that role or merely mourns the one it has lost.

aimless and unsystematic; jumping from link to link without plan or purpose
obscure and known mainly to specialists, like scholarship once kept only in university libraries
out of date; no longer useful in its old, book-storage form

Every example is developed until its relevance is explicit, and the opposing view is answered in its strongest, historically accurate form in fluent, precise prose.

Both reasons are explicitly compared with the pre-digital situation, which the prompt's word "more" requires.

Each paragraph turns on one idea, so the structure follows the argument rather than a template.

prompt.statement: In today's economy, loyalty to a single employer does workers more harm than good.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Loyalty as Bargain, Not Creed
essays.essay:
In late 2001, thousands of Enron employees learned that a single corporate failure could take both their jobs and their retirement savings. Many had put much of their 401(k) money into company stock, encouraged by executives who praised the shares even as accounting [[chicanery|chicanery]] concealed the firm's mounting debts. They were [[fervid|fervid]] believers in the company, their confidence fed by business magazines that had repeatedly celebrated Enron as one of America's most innovative companies. The episode seems to prove that loyalty to an employer is a trap. I agree that loyalty often harms workers today, but the statement misidentifies the cause: not loyalty itself but loyalty that has stopped checking whether it is returned.

The statement's pessimism rests on a real change in the bargain between firms and workers. A generation ago, an employee who stayed at a large company could often expect a pension and steady promotion. Since then, many employers have replaced guaranteed pensions with savings plans that shift risk onto employees; layoffs have come even in profitable years; and workers who switch jobs have often received larger raises than those who stay. Loyalty that asks for nothing in return thus becomes a subsidy paid by the worker. Journalism offers a starker case. After a hedge fund gained control of the Denver Post and cut its newsroom repeatedly, the paper's own editorial board publicly urged in 2018 that the Post be sold. Journalists who had remained out of devotion to the Post found themselves working for an owner whose strategy was [[inimical|inimical]] to the very work that had kept them there. Loyalty presumes a stable object, and that object can be sold out from under the worker.

The most compelling challenge to the statement is economic rather than sentimental. Commitment, its defenders argue, is an investment that compounds. A worker who stays learns an organization's unwritten rules, earns the trust that brings responsibility, and builds relationships that no resume can transfer; employers, in turn, train the people they expect to keep. If every worker treats every job as a way station, firms will rationally stop training anyone, and workers as a group will suffer. Journalism supports this view too. In 2002, when the Boston Globe's Spotlight team exposed how the Archdiocese of Boston had concealed abuse by priests, it relied on reporters who knew the city's courts and parishes intimately and on editors who had spent decades at the paper. A newsroom of short-timers could hardly have produced that story.

This objection is right about the value of tenure, yet it proves less than it seems to. The veterans' long service paid off because the Globe honored its side of the bargain: it gave the team months to report, went to court to unseal records in the abuse lawsuits, and backed its journalists against a formidable institution. That reciprocity is what separates their commitment from the Enron employees' faith. Even here, insider loyalty had limits. The investigation began in earnest only after a newly arrived editor from outside the city pressed the paper to dig deeper into a case it had already covered; the veterans had the sources, but an outsider saw what familiarity had obscured. As for the collective argument, it identifies a genuine loss but assigns the remedy to the wrong party. If firms will not train workers they cannot be sure of keeping, the solution lies in contracts and benefits that make staying worthwhile, not in asking individual workers to honor a bargain the other side has already abandoned.

Discussions of workplace loyalty tend to [[polarize|polarize]] into praise for the nimble free agent and nostalgia for the company man, yet both camps mistake the length of a commitment for its quality. A worker can stay twenty years with clear eyes, keeping skills marketable, savings diversified, and outside offers in view; such a worker loses little by staying and often gains much. What workers should [[abjure|abjure]] is not commitment but blind faith: the loyalty that keeps no ledger, asks no questions, and stakes everything on the word of people whose interests may already have diverged from their own. Loyalty harms workers only when it stops being a bargain and becomes a creed.
