intensely, even excessively, enthusiastic; their belief in Enron went beyond what was reasonable
harmful to and working against the journalism the reporters wanted to do
split into two sharply opposed camps of opinion
deliberately renounce or give up a belief or habit

analysis.verdict: This essay earns a 6 because its position is insightful, not merely clear: it moves the harm from loyalty itself to loyalty that has stopped checking whether it is returned, and every paragraph builds on that distinction. Each example (Enron, the Denver Post, the Spotlight investigation) is explained and then tied to the argument. The strongest objection is stated in its best form before it is answered.
analysis.position: The thesis comes at the end of the opening scene and qualifies the statement instead of splitting the difference: "the statement misidentifies the cause". The final sentence restates it in new words: "stops being a bargain and becomes a creed".
analysis.development: Each example goes far enough to show why it matters. Enron shows what the employees lost and how (their 401(k) money was in company stock), and the Denver Post case leads to a stated lesson: "Loyalty presumes a stable object". The Spotlight case works twice, first supporting the objection and then the rebuttal.
analysis.organization: The structure follows the reasoning: scene and position, reasons to agree, the strongest objection, the answer, then the refined position. Transitions signal logical turns rather than mere sequence, as in "This objection is right about the value of tenure" and "Even here, insider loyalty had limits."
analysis.language: The diction is precise and plain ("a subsidy paid by the worker", "sold out from under the worker"), and sentences range from short pivots ("Journalism offers a starker case.") to long, balanced sentences with semicolons and parallel lists. Target words appear in natural collocations such as "accounting chicanery" and "inimical to the very work".
analysis.task: The instruction asks for the most compelling challenge, and paragraph 3 announces it as "The most compelling challenge", stating it fairly in two parts a thoughtful economist would actually make: tenure builds firm-specific knowledge and trust, and if everyone job-hops, firms stop training. Paragraph 4 answers both parts separately instead of dismissing them.

paragraphs.note: Enron employees lose jobs and savings together; the essay states the apparent lesson, then sharpens it: the harm comes from loyalty that has stopped checking whether it is returned.

paragraphs.role: Why the statement is partly right
paragraphs.note: Describes the broken bargain (pensions, layoffs, raises for job switchers), then uses the Denver Post to show that the employer someone is loyal to can be sold.

paragraphs.role: Rebuttal: tenure pays only when reciprocated
paragraphs.note: Grants that tenure has value, shows Spotlight succeeded because the Globe reciprocated, notes that an outsider prompted the investigation, and assigns the training problem to employers.

paragraphs.role: Refined position in fresh words
paragraphs.note: Rejects both polarized camps, separates the length of a commitment from its quality, and names what workers should renounce: blind faith, not commitment.

prompt.statement: Some argue that young people learn best from the example of their elders. Others argue that young people learn best by questioning their elders.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Questioning That Mastery Has Earned
essays.essay:
Both views treat example and questioning as rival methods, as if young people had to choose between copying their elders and cross-examining them. The first view deserves more credit than it usually receives. Much of what elders know resists explanation: even the most [[garrulous|garrulous]] grandmother cannot say exactly how she can tell when the rice is done, and her granddaughter learns it by watching. Yet example transmits an elder's errors as faithfully as her skills, and only questioning lets the young tell the two apart. The second view therefore comes closer to my own position, but only once the false choice is dissolved: young people learn best by questioning elders whose example they have first studied closely enough to question well.

The career of Chinua Achebe shows how the two depend on each other. Achebe grew up in Igboland, in southeastern Nigeria, amid the stories and proverbs of Igbo elders, and from them he learned that a well-placed proverb can combine brevity with [[profundity|profundity]]: an elder who wishes to rebuke, console, or persuade reaches for a saying that does the work of a paragraph. At school and then at University College, Ibadan, he met a second set of elders, the English writers of the colonial syllabus. In both cases the teaching proceeded chiefly by example. He learned Igbo rhetoric by hearing it used and the craft of fiction by reading novels, and no amount of skeptical interrogation could have replaced that immersion. Had the story ended there, it would have vindicated the first view.

It did not end there. At Ibadan, Achebe read Joyce Cary's Mister Johnson, a celebrated novel set in Nigeria, and found its portrait of Nigerians superficial and false. Things Fall Apart was, in part, his reply, and here the second view finds its strongest support: imitation alone would have left Achebe reproducing, however skillfully, the very portrait he rejected. Yet he kept faith with the tradition he was challenging. He wrote in English, gave his hero the downfall of a classical tragic figure, and even borrowed his title from Yeats. When critics later urged African writers to [[abjure|abjure]] English altogether, he refused. An [[artless|artless]] polemic against colonial fiction would have been easy to dismiss; a novel that met the English canon on its own terms could not be. His questioning carried weight precisely because his knowledge of what he questioned was [[intimate|intimate]]. Tellingly, Achebe's own hero shows what rejection without understanding looks like: Okonkwo, who shapes his entire life in reaction against his idle father, never examines that father's example; he simply inverts it, and the rigidity that results destroys him.

China's Cultural Revolution offers a harder test, because it seems to show the second view at its most destructive. In 1966 Mao Zedong encouraged students to rebel against authority, and Red Guards, told to smash the "Four Olds" (old ideas, culture, customs, and habits), denounced, beat, and in some cases killed their own teachers. Universities first suspended admissions and then filled their places by political recommendation; the national entrance examination was not restored until after Mao's death; and millions of young people lost years of schooling. If this is what questioning elders produces, the first view looks prudent. But the Red Guards were not questioning their elders; they were obeying one. Having [[canonized|canonize]] a single elder, whose quotations they carried in a little red book, they attacked every other authority with a certainty no genuine questioner could feel. The episode refines my position rather than refuting it: questioning educates only when it spares no authority, including the one that licenses the rebellion.

Young people do learn first by example, and for a mother tongue or a craft there is no real substitute. But what they learn by example alone they hold only on loan. It becomes their own when they test it against the world they actually inhabit, as Achebe tested the English novel against the Nigeria he knew, and such testing is worth exactly as much as the mastery and independence behind it. The elders who serve the young best, then, are those who offer an example worth studying and welcome the questions that serious study provokes.

depth of insight; a short proverb can hold deep meaning in very few words
formally renounce; give up English as a language for African literature, as a matter of principle
lacking skill or craft; a crude protest that critics could easily wave aside
closely familiar; Achebe knew the English novels he challenged through deep firsthand study

analysis.verdict: This essay earns a 6 for insight and cogency, not just clarity. It shows that the prompt sets up a false choice, builds one example in depth across two paragraphs, and then tests its own position against a hard counterexample that it turns into a refinement. The diction is precise and controlled, with clear, purposeful sentence variety, and there are no errors that distract the reader.
analysis.position: The opening exposes the prompt's hidden assumption ("Both views treat example and questioning as rival methods"). The position then appears early, with its qualification built in: questioning comes closer, but only of elders whose example the young have "first studied closely enough to question well." The conclusion restates it in fresh terms ("what they learn by example alone they hold only on loan").
analysis.development: Achebe is developed in depth rather than name-dropped: what he learned from Igbo elders and colonial schooling, how Things Fall Apart answered Cary, and why keeping English and its forms made the novel impossible to dismiss. The Red Guards case is explained and then reinterpreted: "the Red Guards were not questioning their elders; they were obeying one."
analysis.organization: The essay follows the thinking. It moves from the false choice, to example, to questioning, to a counterexample, to a refined position. A counterfactual hinge links the two Achebe paragraphs: "Had the story ended there, it would have vindicated the first view." The next paragraph opens with "It did not end there."

One key claim rests on a semicolon antithesis whose halves are built in parallel: an artless polemic "would have been easy to dismiss"; a novel that "met the English canon on its own terms could not be." Each vocabulary word is the most precise choice in its sentence.

The first is credited with tacit knowledge ("The first view deserves more credit than it usually receives.") and is allowed to look right after the Red Guards ("the first view looks prudent"). The second is granted "its strongest support" in Achebe's reply to Cary, then tested against the Red Guards, who seem to show it "at its most destructive."

prompt.statement: Some believe that a nation's most important resource is its natural wealth. Others believe that its most important resource is the education of its people.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Natural Wealth Multiplies What Education Builds
essays.essay:
Framed as a contest, this question invites a misleading answer, because it treats natural wealth and education as independent assets that a nation could rank on a balance sheet. They are not independent. A mineral deposit has value only when people know how to find it, extract it, sell it and spend the proceeds wisely; crude oil seeping into nineteenth-century salt wells was a nuisance until chemists learned to refine it into lamp fuel. By education, then, I mean not merely years of schooling but the knowledge and civic competence that allow a society to govern what it owns. Understood that way, the view that education is the more important resource comes closer to my own. Natural wealth can be decisive, but only under conditions that an educated people must first supply.

The case for natural wealth nonetheless deserves a serious hearing. A nation without fertile soil, fresh water or energy faces hard limits that no curriculum can lift, and resource revenue can pay for the very schools the rival view prizes. Norway offers the [[paradigmatic|paradigmatic]] case of a windfall managed well. After oil was found off its coast in the late 1960s, much of the revenue flowed through the ordinary budget for about two decades before the government created a sovereign fund invested abroad and, later, a rule tying annual spending to the fund's expected return. Oil made an already prosperous, well-governed country far richer, yet even Norway had to learn that prudence; the fund now keeps the windfall from being consumed by a single generation. Where a resource is abundant, demand for it is strong and institutions exist to hold it in trust, natural wealth can fairly be called a nation's most important resource.

Remove that last condition, however, and the claim collapses. After the Netherlands began exporting natural gas in bulk, the inflow of foreign money strengthened its currency and squeezed its manufacturers, whose goods grew costlier abroad; economists still call the pattern "Dutch disease." Venezuela fared far worse. Holding some of the world's largest proven oil reserves, it let a single commodity dominate its exports and budget, and because the revenue flowed to whoever held the state, the struggle for control helped [[polarize|polarize]] the country. After a strike at the state oil company in the early 2000s, the government dismissed thousands of experienced engineers and managers, and the company, [[enervated|enervate]] by the purge, never regained its former output. The oil had not gone anywhere; much of the expertise to extract it had. Resource rents can even be [[inimical|inimical]] to education itself, since rulers who live on them rather than on taxes often have little need for a skilled and demanding citizenry.

Education, by contrast, compounds with use and travels with its owners. South Korea emerged from war poor and short of minerals, yet it expanded schooling with unusual determination, and over the following decades its shipbuilding and electronics industries [[burgeoned|burgeon]]. Ordinary life teaches the same lesson. Land and savings can be squandered or seized, but a nurse who emigrates with nothing except her training can rebuild her livelihood abroad, because what she knows cannot be taken from her. Even the courts, whose business is rights rather than growth, have recognized schooling as a collective asset. In Plyler v. Doe, the Supreme Court struck down a Texas law that let school districts turn away undocumented children. The majority relied chiefly on equal protection, refusing to punish children for their parents' conduct, but also warned that a permanent illiterate underclass would add to the costs of unemployment, welfare and crime. Part of the logic was prudence, not charity: an uneducated population is a liability the whole nation carries.

Natural wealth, then, is a multiplier rather than a foundation: it magnifies whatever capacity a nation already possesses, enriching Norway and destabilizing Venezuela. Education is the capacity being multiplied, though it too has a condition, since graduates who find no opportunity at home will carry their training elsewhere. A nation that must choose where to invest should still choose its people, not because minerals are worthless, but because only a society that knows how to govern a windfall can keep it from becoming a curse.

prompt.statement:
Claim: Communities should judge a new technology by its long-term effects rather than its immediate benefits.
Reason: The most serious harms of a technology usually appear only after it has become difficult to abandon.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Late Harms Call for Reversibility, Not Prophecy
essays.essay:
I accept the reason in part and the claim only in a narrower form, and the two fail in different ways. The reason captures a real pattern: some technologies do their worst damage slowly, and by the time the damage is plain, a society has rebuilt its habits and institutions around them. But "usually" overstates the pattern, and even where it holds, it does not yield the conclusion drawn from it. A community cannot judge a technology by effects that have not yet occurred, only by forecasts of them. What the reason supports is not a different yardstick but a different procedure: accept immediate benefits provisionally, and preserve the power to change course.

Consider the reason first. Antibiotic resistance fits it closely. Soon after penicillin came into general use, resistant staphylococci were spreading through hospitals, but the full cost of resistance accumulated slowly, through countless prescriptions and, later, the routine feeding of antibiotics to livestock. By the time resistance was recognized as a global threat, surgery, cancer chemotherapy and intensive care all depended on effective antibiotics; giving them up was unthinkable. Thalidomide shows why "usually" claims too much. Sold as a sedative in West Germany in the late 1950s, it caused severe limb malformations in thousands of infants, and because such malformations were rare enough to be conspicuous, physicians traced them to the drug within a few years. It was withdrawn, and abandoning it cost almost nothing. The contrast exposes a distinction the reason ignores: the reason holds for technologies whose harms are cumulative and diffuse, and fails for those whose harms are acute and traceable.

Even for that class, however, the reason does not establish the claim. Had communities in the 1940s judged antibiotics chiefly by their long-term effects, the prospect of resistance might have led them to [[abjure|abjure]] the use of these drugs, forfeiting one of the largest gains in medical history to avert a harm that can be slowed, if not eliminated. The claim rests on a hidden assumption: that long-term effects are available for inspection at the moment of decision. They are not. A community told to weigh them must weigh forecasts, and forecasts are where the rhetoric of promoters and opponents grows most [[fervid|fervid]], since neither side can be proved wrong for decades. The sound inference from the reason is narrower: because serious harms may surface late, a technology should be adopted in ways that keep its effects observable and its use adjustable.

The printing press reveals a deeper difficulty: the long term has no natural endpoint at which a verdict can be rendered. In the early sixteenth century, printed pamphlets carried Luther's arguments across the German lands faster than authorities could suppress them, and the press helped [[polarize|polarize]] Latin Christendom into hostile confessions whose rivalry fed more than a century of intermittent religious war. Yet while the worst of those wars raged, Francis Bacon counted printing, with gunpowder and the compass, among the three inventions that had transformed the world. The same decades thus supported opposite verdicts. A community bound to judge the press by its long-term effects would have had to [[vacillate|vacillate]] between condemnation and celebration, revising its verdict with each generation as new effects came into view. The long-term effects of a technology are not a fixed sum awaiting discovery; they are a running account.

The claim survives, then, but in a weaker form and for a better reason than the one offered. Long-term effects deserve deliberate weight not chiefly because harms arrive late, but because those who enjoy a technology's immediate benefits often bear only part of its distant costs: a patient who takes an antibiotic may later carry a resistant strain, but so may neighbors and future patients who never took the drug. A community should therefore accept a technology on the evidence it has, invest early in the monitoring and alternatives that keep retreat possible, and, asked whether the technology is safe in the long run, answer plainly that it does not yet know rather than [[equivocate|equivocate]]. Judging by long-term effects is not a verdict delivered once, at the threshold; it is an obligation that begins there.

to answer vaguely to dodge commitment; here, blurring whether long-term safety is actually known

prompt.statement:
Claim: Public figures should be held to a higher ethical standard than private citizens.
Reason: Their actions shape the behavior of many other people.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Trust, Not Fame, Raises the Bar
essays.essay:
For more than a decade, Lance Armstrong was less an athlete than an emblem. A cancer survivor who won seven consecutive Tour de France titles, he was all but [[canonized|canonize]] by the sports press, and millions who had never raced a bicycle wore his yellow charity wristband. Pressed about doping, he either denied it outright or [[equivocated|equivocate]], insisting that he had never failed a drug test; the truth was officially established only in 2012, when he was stripped of his titles. Commentators then asked what children who had worn those wristbands would now believe. That worry contains the statement's reasoning in miniature. I agree that public figures should be held to a higher ethical standard, but only in conduct connected to their public role, and I accept the stated reason only in part. Imitation is real, yet it is neither what made Armstrong's conduct so grave nor a reliable guide to where the higher standard belongs.

Take the reason first, because it is partly true. Read naturally, it says that others follow a public figure's example. People, especially the young, learn what is acceptable by watching those they admire, and fame multiplies the audience for every lesson. In professional cycling the effect was not hypothetical: riders of Armstrong's era later described a peloton in which doping seemed the price of competing at all, a norm that every winner who doped helped to entrench. A champion who cheats teaches rivals and admirers alike that the rules bind only the naive. To that extent the statement is right: a public figure's conduct has consequences beyond the act itself, and those consequences raise the moral stakes.

Taken as the sole ground for a higher standard, however, imitation proves too much. Admirers copy far more than a star's professional conduct; they copy her clothes, her diet, her attitudes toward marriage. If imitation alone raises the standard, every private decision of a famous person becomes a public moral question, and we arrive at trial by tabloid and social media, where a singer's divorce can draw more condemnation than a regulator's negligence. Such verdicts track visibility rather than harm. A defensible version of the claim confines the higher standard to the domain in which a person holds public trust: how a champion competes, how an official uses authority, how a scientist reports results.

The reason also proves too little, and here the history of science is instructive. In 1998 Andrew Wakefield, then a little-known researcher at a London hospital, published a paper in The Lancet suggesting a link between the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine and autism, and at a press conference he went further, recommending separate single vaccines. Investigations later showed that he had misrepresented his data; the journal retracted the paper, and British regulators struck him from the medical register. Nobody was imitating Wakefield; the parents who refused the vaccine were not copying him but believing him. He became a public figure only through the [[cacophonous|cacophonous]] press debate that followed, as British vaccination rates fell and measles cases climbed. Yet that fame was a product of trust, not its source: journalists and parents listened because a doctor had published in a leading journal. Even a [[punctilious|punctilious]] peer reviewer sees only the data an author chooses to report. The harm traveled through trust rather than imitation, which is why we expect strict honesty from anyone whose word others must accept without checking it.

That distinction recasts the Armstrong case. What made his conduct so grave was less the lesson his young admirers absorbed than the [[chicanery|chicanery]] by which he cheated riders who competed clean and deceived sponsors and fans who had invested in his story, and the intimidation he used to keep teammates silent. Those would have been serious wrongs even if no child had ever worn a wristband. The claim therefore survives, but the most [[cogent|cogent]] case for it rests on reliance, not imitation. The higher standard is a debt owed for entrusted power, not a tax levied on fame: it should rise with the trust others must place in a person's public conduct and stop where that conduct ends. Beyond that line, the famous deserve the same moral latitude as anyone else.

prompt.statement:
Claim: Inventors should not be allowed to patent discoveries made with public funding.
Reason: The public has already paid for the knowledge.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: The Public Bought Knowledge, Not Products
essays.essay:
The claim rests on an intuition that is hard to dismiss: if taxpayers finance a laboratory, it seems wrong for anyone to sell its discoveries back to them at monopoly prices. Yet the claim and its reason deserve separate verdicts. The reason is partly true, since public funding creates a legitimate public stake, but it misidentifies what the public bought. The claim, a blanket prohibition, does not follow from that reason and would often injure the very taxpayers it means to protect. What the reason supports is narrower: such patents should be permitted, but with conditions attached.

Consider the reason first. A grant pays for experiments, which yield knowledge: a mechanism, a molecule, a technique. A patent does not lock that knowledge away; the law requires inventors to disclose an invention in enough detail for others to reproduce it, in exchange for a temporary right to exclude competitors. What the grant rarely buys is the slow, expensive work that separates a promising compound from a pill on a pharmacy shelf: formulation, clinical testing, regulatory approval, and manufacturing. The reason thus assumes, without saying so, that a discovery is already a product. It is not, and patents attract the private investment that turns one into the other.

The United States once ran something close to the claim as policy. Before 1980, federal patent rules were a patchwork, and some contractors and universities were allowed to keep title to their inventions. Many agencies, however, kept title to inventions from research they funded, offered nonexclusive licenses to any firm that asked, and were frequently [[dilatory|dilatory]] in answering petitions for exceptions. Thousands of government-held patents sat unused, in part because few companies would spend years developing a drug or device that competitors could copy. The Bayh-Dole Act of 1980 let universities own their federally funded inventions and license them exclusively. University patenting soon surged, and licensing became a major source of new companies, especially in biotechnology. Economists still debate how much of that growth the law caused, but few defend the regime it replaced. A rule that seemed to honor the taxpayer had proved [[inimical|inimical]] to the taxpayer's interests.

None of this means the reason is empty. The public sometimes does pay twice, and AZT, the first approved drug for AIDS, remains the [[paradigmatic|paradigmatic]] case. The compound was first synthesized in the 1960s under a federal grant, as a cancer treatment that failed. Two decades later, a pharmaceutical company screening compounds against animal retroviruses confirmed its activity, and government scientists showed in the laboratory that it inhibited HIV and helped run its first human trial. The company patented the drug's use against AIDS and set a price that made it, at the time, one of the most expensive drugs ever sold, provoking protests from activists who pointed out that public money had helped create it. It would be easy to blame corporate [[chicanery|chicanery]], but none was needed. That is why the reason deserves a hearing: the system, working as designed, let public investment become private profit with no obligation to those who financed it.

The claim itself is defensible only in narrow cases, and there for a different reason. When the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 2013 that naturally occurring human genes cannot be patented, it did not ask who had paid for the research; it held that isolating a natural sequence is not invention. Other laboratories soon offered genetic tests that one company had controlled. Exclusivity over such discoveries buys no further development; it only obstructs others. For most publicly funded discoveries, however, the remedy is not for universities to [[abjure|abjure]] patents but to attach terms to them: commitments to reasonable pricing, royalties returned to public research, and government rights to license an invention to others when its owner fails to make it available. Bayh-Dole already reserves such rights, though agencies have proved reluctant to invoke them.

The public, then, is owed not ownership of every patent its money touches but a fair share of what those patents produce. The decisive question is not whether taxpayers paid for the knowledge but whether the products built on it reach them on terms that honor that investment.

It would rarely notice that the public paid for knowledge rather than products, or that the claim might be right for a different reason, and would end by restating its opening rather than refining it.

prompt.statement: Every citizen should be required to receive training in basic first aid.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Universal Readiness Without Universal Compulsion
essays.essay:
The case for this policy seems obvious. When someone's heart stops on a sidewalk, the minutes before an ambulance arrives largely decide whether that person lives, and during those minutes only bystanders are present. Yet the policy rests on two assumptions that deserve scrutiny: that compulsory training for every citizen is the best way to prepare bystanders, and that a trained person will act. Because a mandate's consequences depend almost entirely on its design, I support requiring a narrow core of emergency skills at points where the state already reaches people, but I oppose a literal obligation on every adult, which would cost a great deal and deliver mainly certificates.

Denmark offers the clearest evidence of what a well-built requirement can achieve. In the mid-2000s, after years of poor survival from out-of-hospital cardiac arrests, the country made resuscitation training compulsory in elementary schools and required a first-aid course of everyone applying for a driver's license. Meanwhile, defibrillators appeared in public places and voluntary courses [[burgeoned|burgeon]]. By the end of the decade, the share of victims receiving bystander CPR had roughly doubled, and the share who survived had roughly tripled. These changes likely account for much of that improvement.

How the Danish policy was built matters as much as its success, because the design reveals which consequences a mandate must produce and which it must avoid. It did not order every citizen to report for instruction; it attached training to schools and licensing offices, which most people pass through anyway, so compliance required no new machinery of enforcement. It also kept the content narrow. Schoolchildren learned resuscitation rather than a paramedic's entire textbook, and resuscitation is anything but [[recondite|recondite]]: its essentials can be taught in a few lessons, and it forgives imperfection, since even a clumsy effort by a frightened teenager keeps some blood flowing to the brain until a defibrillator arrives. Finally, the training arrived alongside other changes, including better hospital care, so I must concede that the classroom cannot claim all the credit. That concession strengthens the argument. Training is one link in a chain, and a requirement that ignores the rest of the chain will disappoint.

Germany supplies the contrasting case, and it [[corroborates|corroborate]] the Danish lesson from the opposite direction. For decades it has required anyone seeking a driver's license to complete a short first-aid course, so most German adults have been trained. If training alone produced rescuers, Germany would have ranked near the top of Europe in bystander resuscitation; instead, its rate long remained far below Scandinavia's. Nor can Germany's legal duty to help close that gap on its own: in 2016, several customers at a bank in Essen walked past or stepped over an elderly man who had collapsed in the foyer, and after he died, a court fined three of them for failing to help. The law could punish that failure afterward, but it cannot manufacture the confidence that action requires. A single course cannot reliably supply it either, especially when a teenager treats the course as one more hurdle before the driving test and makes only a [[desultory|desultory]] effort to learn. The typical failure is subtler than callousness: a [[diffident|diffident]] passerby senses that something is wrong, doubts that she is qualified to help, and [[vacillates|vacillate]] between stepping in and waiting for someone more capable, who may never come.

These consequences settle my position. The intended consequence, more bystanders willing and able to act, follows only under specific conditions; the unintended ones are easier to predict. A mandate on every citizen would have to reach adults long out of school, which would mean penalties to compel attendance; it would fall hardest on people with the least time to spare; and if it took the form of a one-time course, it would reproduce Germany's result on a larger scale: a population trained but not ready. A narrower requirement, built into schooling and licensing, confined to the few skills that save lives within minutes, refreshed periodically, and supported by defibrillators, dispatcher coaching, and laws that shield rescuers from liability, can turn hesitant onlookers into people who act. Universal readiness is worth pursuing; universal compulsion is a poor way to pursue it.

prompt.statement: Any technology that collects personal data should be required to obtain the user's explicit consent for each use of that data.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Consent Matters Only When It Is Rare
essays.essay:
The strongest argument for this policy is that the alternative has already failed. For years, a [[burgeoning|burgeon]] data industry has obtained consent once, at sign-up, through terms of service so long-winded that almost no one reads them, and has then treated that single click as permission for any purpose the data might later serve. The Cambridge Analytica affair showed where this leads. A Facebook personality quiz gathered data from the people who took it and from their friends, who had never used the app, and that data ended up with a political consulting firm that promised to target voters by psychological profile. Requiring consent for each use targets exactly this drift from one purpose to another. On this point the policy's defenders are right; where they go wrong is in assuming that more requests mean more control.

The argument breaks down at the word "each." Consent protects people only when they attend to it, and attention is the scarcest resource a policy can spend. A typical phone holds dozens of apps, each reusing data constantly: to recommend products, to detect fraud, to train software. If every such use required a fresh request, the requests would multiply until answering them became a reflex rather than a decision. As with a [[garrulous|garrulous]] colleague, the one remark that matters would go unheard. Europe has already run a smaller version of this experiment. After its rules on online tracking tightened, consent banners appeared on most websites, and users now routinely click whatever makes the banners vanish fastest. Many sites have encouraged the habit with quiet [[chicanery|chicanery]]: a bright "Accept all" button beside a faint link to a maze of toggles. Behind the banner sits a notice that [[equivocates|equivocate]] about who the "trusted partners" are and what they will do. Such consent is worse than none, because a reflexive click still shifts responsibility to the user; the company can say she agreed.

Another consequence is less visible but more serious. Much of the public value of personal data lies in uses no one foresaw when it was collected. Drug safety is a clear case: side effects too rare for clinical trials to detect often come to light only when researchers examine the health records of large populations. A rule demanding fresh consent for each such study would not merely slow this work; it would distort it, because people who answer requests differ systematically from those who ignore them, so findings from the responsive may not hold for everyone. The policy would thus burden beneficial reuses conducted openly while doing little about harmful ones that are not.

That last point exposes the policy's hidden assumption: that the danger lies in uses an honest company might propose and a user might decline. History suggests otherwise. Before World War II, Dutch officials kept population registers with [[punctilious|punctilious]] care, recording each resident's religion. Under German occupation, those records helped the authorities identify and locate Jewish residents, and historians count the registry's efficiency among the reasons a larger share of Jews in the Netherlands was deported and murdered than anywhere else in occupied Western Europe. No consent requirement would have stopped this, because the occupiers had no intention of asking. The gravest harms come from actors who never seek permission, whether a regime, a thief, or a firm willing to break the rules. Even the Cambridge Analytica data changed hands in breach of Facebook's own policies. Against such actors, the only protection is structural: collect less data, delete it sooner, and forbid certain uses outright, whatever a user has clicked.

These consequences, not any doubt about consent itself, shape my position. Explicit consent should be required, but selectively: for uses a reasonable person would not expect given why the data was collected, and for any sale or sharing of health, location, or political and religious data. Public-interest research, such as drug-safety studies, should instead face independent ethics review. Routine uses need no fresh requests, and some uses should remain forbidden however many boxes are checked. The goal is not more consent but consent rare enough that people stop to read the question. Requested constantly, permission becomes noise; reserved for the moments that matter, it becomes a real choice again.

essays.title: Filling Posts Is Not Delivering Care
essays.essay:
During the First World War, Mikhail Bulgakov, newly graduated from medical school in Kyiv, was assigned to a village hospital in Smolensk province with no senior physician to consult. The semi-autobiographical stories he later published, known in English as A Young Doctor's Notebook, show a novice amputating a mangled leg and hurrying to his textbooks midway through a difficult delivery, terrified that his inexperience will kill someone. Bulgakov's peasants did receive a doctor, which is exactly what advocates of compulsory rural service promise. Whether they received adequate care is another question, and that gap between filling a post and serving a community is where this policy should be judged. Having weighed its likely consequences, I oppose a blanket requirement that every new doctor spend two years in underserved areas, though I would support a narrower obligation built around supervision and retention.

The case for the mandate is not frivolous. Its intended consequence, a supply of physicians where few would otherwise go, is real, and the moral argument behind it is strong: in many countries taxpayers heavily subsidize medical training, including rural taxpayers who rarely see a doctor. Thailand has long required graduates of its public medical schools to work in government hospitals, an obligation that helped staff district hospitals the private market would have left empty. Some conscripts come to like rural practice and stay. If these were the only consequences, the policy would be easy to endorse.

They are not, and the first unintended consequence is the one Bulgakov dramatized: the policy places the least experienced clinicians precisely where supervision is thinnest. A new graduate in a city hospital who misreads a chest film has a senior colleague down the hall; the same graduate in a remote clinic may have no one. However [[punctilious|punctilious]] a beginner is about protocol, no protocol can reliably tell a lone clinician when a feverish child has slipped from routine illness into sepsis. A [[diffident|diffident]] newcomer, reluctant to order a costly transfer on a mere hunch, may wait until the patient is too sick to travel. The strain falls on the doctors as well. Bulgakov first took morphine to ease a severe reaction to diphtheria antitoxin, but at that isolated post the remedy became an addiction. A policy that exposes poor communities to avoidable errors in the name of equity has redistributed risk, not care.

A second set of consequences unfolds over time. Because each cohort leaves when its two years expire, an underserved town would receive a perpetual rotation of beginners, an arrangement [[inimical|inimical]] to continuity of care, which matters most for chronic diseases such as diabetes. Compulsion also invites evasion, and evasion is rarely random. In the Soviet Union, which assigned graduates to their first jobs, the well-connected often secured comfortable placements while others were dispatched to the provinces; where a buyout is permitted, as in Thailand, the burden falls hardest on those who cannot buy their way out. Finally, a mandate gives a [[dilatory|dilatory]] health ministry a cheap way to appear active. Conscripting graduates is far easier than raising rural salaries, building staff housing, or linking clinics to specialists by telemedicine, and the easy measure can become an excuse for postponing the hard ones.

These consequences, more than any abstract appeal to professional freedom, shape my position. The defensible core of the policy is reciprocity: doctors trained at public expense owe the public something. Yet an obligation experienced as punishment tends to [[enervate|enervate]] the very doctors it conscripts, souring the idealism that might have kept them in rural practice for good. The debt should therefore be repaid in a form that produces care rather than mere presence: rural rotations embedded in supervised training, a senior physician reachable by video from every placement, and incentives such as the loan repayment offered by the United States' National Health Service Corps, which turns longer service into a bargain rather than a sentence. The most durable remedy lies upstream, in admitting more students from rural backgrounds, since a rural upbringing is among the most consistent predictors of rural practice. Compulsory service can be a bridge while those measures mature; it should never be mistaken for the foundation.

prompt.statement: Most people would rather be certain than be right.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Certainty Thrives Where Mistakes Stay Hidden
essays.essay:
The statement treats certainty and correctness as rival goods, but the two are not the same kind of thing. Certainty is a state of mind that a person can produce unaided; being right is a relation between a belief and the world, and only the world can confirm it. People therefore trade the second for the first mainly when the world stays silent: when the cost of an error arrives late, falls on someone else, or cannot be traced to the decision that caused it. Where reality grades decisions quickly and on the record, most would rather be right, even when being right means admitting doubt. I accept the statement, then, as a description of how people behave when their mistakes stay hidden, but not as a verdict on human nature. The preference for certainty is less a trait than a symptom of missing feedback.

In the classroom, the statement holds even among students eager to learn. In one survey, college students named rereading more often than any other study strategy. A familiar page produces a pleasant feeling of fluency, which students take as proof of mastery. The inference is [[specious|specious]]: recognizing an explanation is not the same as being able to reconstruct it. Self-testing, by contrast, exposes gaps at once and feels like failure. In a well-known experiment, students who reread a passage several times predicted better recall than those who read it once and practiced recalling it; a week later, the second group remembered more. In effect, students choose the sensation of being certain over the work of becoming right. The cost is real but deferred: it surfaces on the examination, where it is blamed on nerves rather than on habit.

Where error surfaces promptly, unambiguously, and on the record, however, the statement fails. National Weather Service forecasters learn within a day whether it rained. Agency policy has required probability forecasts for decades, but policy can dictate the format, not the honesty of the numbers. The numbers are well calibrated: across many forecasts, a 70 percent chance of rain is followed by rain roughly 70 percent of the time. To a listener who wants a plain yes or no, such a forecast may sound noncommittal, yet the forecaster is not [[irresolute|irresolute]]: the number is a firm claim that the record will test. Nor is the probability an [[affectation|affectation]] of humility; it is the most accurate statement available, and years of daily scoring have helped keep forecasters' probabilities honest.

The most revealing case is one in which the same profession moved from one side of the statement to the other. For decades, National Football League coaches facing fourth down routinely kicked even where, as statistical analyses eventually showed, going for the remaining yards would have raised their chances of winning. The coaches were not unusually [[timorous|timorous]]; they read their incentives correctly. A failed attempt is vivid and blamed on the coach, while a punt that contributes to a loss disappears into the noise of the game. The punt thus offered certainty not about the outcome but about the coach's standing. For years, a few [[pertinacious|pertinacious]] analysts kept publishing the arithmetic, and coaches clung to their caution anyway. What eventually changed was the feedback. Analytics departments [[proliferated|proliferate]] across the league, and commentators began grading fourth-down calls against win-probability models. Once the cost of the reflexive punt became [[discernible|discernible]], fourth-down attempts rose markedly. Part of that rise came with a new generation of coaches, so temperament may explain some of it; still, the newcomers faced the same public grading, and the profession as a whole moved toward being right once being wrong became visible.

These cases turn my partial agreement into a sharper claim: people often behave as the statement predicts, but less because of their character than because of their circumstances. They settle for certainty when the world withholds the evidence that would make being right worth its discomfort, and they tend to abandon it once that evidence arrives. Anyone who wants students, coaches, or institutions to care more about being right should spend less energy urging them to be brave and more making their errors surface promptly, publicly, and in a form no one can blame on luck.

prompt.statement: Moral courage is rarer and more valuable than physical courage.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: The Danger's Source Decides Courage's Worth
essays.essay:
The statement treats moral and physical courage as two forms of one virtue, distinguished by what the brave person puts at risk: the body in one case, reputation or livelihood in the other. A more revealing distinction concerns who imposes the risk. Physical courage usually confronts a danger that the whole community also fears, such as an invading army or a spreading fire, so the community stands behind those who face it and teaches its children to [[venerate|venerate]] them. Moral courage usually confronts the community itself; those who refuse to go along risk the disapproval of the very people whose approval sustains them. Drawn this way, the distinction makes the statement right about rarity but only conditionally right about value: moral courage is worth more when the danger lies in a group's own error, and worth less when the danger comes from outside.

When the danger comes from one's own side, the statement holds. On the eve of the space shuttle Challenger's 1986 launch, engineers at Morton Thiokol, the contractor that built the solid rocket boosters, warned that the rubber O-rings sealing the booster joints might fail in unusually cold weather. Roger Boisjoly was the most [[pertinacious|pertinacious]] of them, pressing the point even after it became clear that NASA officials wanted to proceed. Thiokol's managers reversed the engineers' recommendation, and the shuttle broke apart shortly after liftoff, killing all seven crew members. When Boisjoly later testified candidly before the presidential commission, he was shunned by colleagues and eventually left the company. Nothing he did endangered his body, yet few people in his position would have paid his price, precisely because his own side exacted it. Many people who would rush into a burning building are [[timorous|timorous]] in a meeting where the boss has already decided. And no feat of physical bravery could have supplied what his testimony did: a public account of how schedule pressure had overridden engineering judgment.

When the danger comes from outside the group, however, the ranking reverses. After a reactor at the Chernobyl nuclear plant exploded in 1986, firefighters from the plant and the nearby town of Pripyat fought the resulting fires through the night, containing blazes that threatened the adjoining reactor; several of them died of radiation sickness within weeks. The explosion itself grew out of the Soviet nuclear establishment's own errors, but once the reactor was burning, the threat lay in the fire, not in anyone's judgment. Chernobyl suffered from a shortage of moral courage as well: [[irresolute|irresolute]] officials delayed evacuating Pripyat, and the Soviet government acknowledged the accident only after radiation was detected in Sweden. Yet no amount of honesty in Moscow could have extinguished a fire on a reactor roof. In those first hours, physical courage was not the lesser virtue but the indispensable one.

These cases lead me to accept the first half of the statement and to qualify the second. Moral courage is rarer for a structural reason: societies [[bolster|bolster]] physical courage with training, uniforms, and honors, but institutions seldom decorate the person whose message is that the institution itself is wrong. Its value, however, depends on two conditions that physical courage can do without. First, the dissenter must be right. Boisjoly's dissent mattered because his [[probity|probity]] was matched by technical expertise; the same stubbornness that sustains a truthful engineer also sustains the crank and the zealot. Second, dissent must eventually be heeded by someone able to act; his warning was overruled on the night he gave it and became valuable only in retrospect. A firefighter's contribution, by contrast, is complete the moment the flames go out.

The statement, then, describes the usual situation inside institutions rather than a universal ranking. Dissent is scarce wherever the group sets the price of honesty, and, provided the dissenter is right, it is worth more whenever a group's own error is the chief threat: a flawed launch decision, a cover-up, a comfortable falsehood. When the threat is a fire, a flood, or an epidemic, the person who walks toward it does the more valuable work. The useful question is therefore not which virtue deserves the crown, but which danger a situation presents and which kind of courage it is asking for.

prompt.statement: Governments should publish the raw data behind every major policy decision they make.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Publish the Evidence, Protect the Identities
essays.essay:
The recommendation treats "raw data" as a single substance, but the files behind a policy decision usually hold two different things. One is evidence: what was measured and found, such as the outcomes of a drug trial. The other is identity: who was measured, recorded in names, addresses and other details that tie each figure to a living person. Publishing evidence lets citizens test a government's reasoning; publishing identities lets anyone, now or decades from now, find the people the data describe. I therefore support the recommendation almost without reservation for evidence and oppose it for identities, and because many datasets mix the two, the real work lies in separating them.

Publishing evidence pays off most clearly when an expensive decision rests on numbers that outsiders cannot check. Preparing for pandemic influenza in the 2000s, many governments, Britain's among them, spent large sums stockpiling the antiviral oseltamivir (Tamiflu), largely on the strength of summaries of manufacturer-sponsored trials. Independent Cochrane reviewers spent years in [[dogged|dogged]] pursuit of the full clinical study reports; when they finally obtained them, their 2014 review found that the drug shortened symptoms in adults by less than a day and offered no reliable evidence that it prevented hospital admissions or serious complications. Nothing in this story requires anyone to have [[dissembled|dissemble]]. Summaries omit what their authors judge unimportant, and only the full record reveals the omissions. A duty to publish would have required governments to secure the complete reports before spending, not years afterward. This is why my support for publishing evidence is nearly unconditional. Disclosure does not presume that officials lack [[probity|probity]]; it makes their probity verifiable, and it catches the honest mistakes that integrity alone cannot prevent.

Identities are a different matter, and European history offers a grim warning. Before World War II, the Netherlands kept one of the most thorough population registers in Europe, recording for each resident such [[prosaic|prosaic]] facts as name, address, date of birth and religion. Nothing in it looked dangerous. After the German invasion of 1940, however, the occupiers used these records to identify and locate Jews, and the Netherlands lost a far larger share of its Jewish population than most occupied countries in Western Europe. Resistance fighters judged the files dangerous enough to set fire to the Amsterdam registry in 1943. The danger of personal records, in other words, depends less on who collects them than on who controls them later. Files kept behind a locked door must be stolen, seized, or handed over by a [[venal|venal]] or compliant clerk; files posted online require none of these. This is where my agreement ends: publishing identifiable data hands it to every future regime and every hostile actor, and no government can take it back.

Many real datasets contain both evidence and identities, which is why the distinction is more useful than the slogan. The Tamiflu reviewers needed to know how many patients recovered and how quickly, not who they were. In such cases a government can honor the spirit of the recommendation by publishing aggregated or de-identified data in full and giving vetted researchers supervised access to the underlying records, as many statistical agencies already do. Separation is not always possible, however. Imagine a rare disease in a village of a few hundred people: a table listing each patient's age, sex and street would identify every one of them without naming anyone. When evidence cannot be stripped of identity, the presumption should reverse: publish the methods and findings, but protect the rows.

The recommendation, then, names a real debt that governments owe their citizens but misstates what it consists of. Citizens are owed the means to check whether a policy rests on sound evidence; they are not owed one another's private lives. A citizen who demands the trial data behind a national drug stockpile is not being [[impertinent|impertinent]]; one who demands a neighbor's diagnosis is. A better rule would require every major decision to come with its evidence, released as fully as the protection of individuals allows, and would judge any release of personal records by one test: whether they would remain safe in the hands of the worst government that might someday inherit them.

prompt.statement: Individuals should keep their political opinions out of the workplace.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Leave Allegiances, Not Findings, at the Door
essays.essay:
The recommendation treats "political opinions" as a single kind of baggage that workers either carry to the office or leave at home, but the phrase covers two different things. Some political opinions are allegiances formed elsewhere: loyalty to a party, enthusiasm for a candidate, a settled view on immigration. Others are conclusions that the work itself produces, as when a chemist discovers that a common product is poisoning the public and insists that the government act. I agree that individuals should generally keep the first kind out of the workplace, especially where some colleagues hold power over others. Applied to the second kind, however, the recommendation would silence precisely the people best equipped to speak.

Consider first the ordinary office, where politics arrives from outside. An accounting firm or a software team gains nothing when the [[clangor|clangor]] of campaign arguments spills from the break room into its meetings. Colleagues who must agree on a budget or a deadline need not agree about a senator, and energy spent defending partisan identities is energy taken from the work. Hierarchy sharpens the problem. Imagine a department head who keeps a candidate's sign on her door and jokes about the other side's voters. Subordinates who vote differently will rarely object, since challenging the boss's politics would seem [[impertinent|impertinent]]; more likely, they will learn to [[dissemble|dissemble]], nodding along to protect their performance reviews. For all its political talk, the office becomes less honest: a staff that has learned to hide one conviction from the boss is unlikely to volunteer another, such as a doubt about a flawed project. By the same logic, a manager should not even ask how an employee voted.

History offers a grimmer version of the same danger. In Stalin's Soviet Union, the agronomist Trofim Lysenko rose to dominance less through evidence than through ideological fit: his claim that crops could be reshaped by their environment and pass those changes to their offspring suited a doctrine that celebrated humanity's power to remake nature. Lysenko and his allies [[stigmatized|stigmatize]] classical genetics as a bourgeois, idealist science, and geneticists who resisted lost their posts; Nikolai Vavilov, the nation's leading plant geneticist, was arrested and died in prison. Soviet biology was set back for a generation, and agriculture suffered with it. The lesson is not merely that political loyalty makes laboratories unpleasant. Once allegiance became a qualification for scientific work, it displaced the evidence that the work existed to weigh.

The recommendation fails, however, when political conviction grows out of the work rather than invading it. Around 1950 the geochemist Clair Patterson, trying to date the Earth from the lead in meteorites, found his samples contaminated by lead from his own laboratory. Getting clean measurements forced him to build one of the first ultraclean rooms and then to ask where all that lead came from. Industrial lead, he found, had become [[ubiquitous|ubiquitous]], present in seawater, polar ice, and human bodies at levels far above natural ones. He traced much of it to the tetraethyl lead added to gasoline and began arguing publicly for its removal. That was a political opinion in the fullest sense, a demand that government restrain a powerful industry, whose scientists disputed his findings for years. Had Patterson treated his conclusion as a private view unfit for professional life, the phaseout of leaded gasoline, after which Americans' blood lead levels fell steeply, might have come far later.

These cases shape my position by changing the question: what matters is not whether an opinion is political but where it comes from and what authority it claims. An imported allegiance claims the authority of the group that shares it, and at work that authority is irrelevant at best and coercive at worst. A conclusion produced by the work claims only the authority of evidence, and it can be checked by colleagues who share none of the speaker's loyalties, as Patterson's measurements eventually were. Lysenko, too, called his doctrine a finding, but he silenced those who could have tested it. An employer may therefore reasonably [[admonish|admonish]] its staff to leave campaign buttons and partisan quarrels at the door. It should never ask them to leave behind what their work has taught them.

prompt.statement: The growing use of algorithms in decision making will make institutions fairer.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Algorithms Make Bias Auditable, Not Fairness Automatic
essays.essay:
The statement assumes that fairness is a property a tool can possess, the way a thermometer can be accurate. An algorithm is something humbler: a set of rules, usually derived from past records, aimed at a goal its designers chose. It inherits any bias in those records and cannot, by itself, decide among rival ideas of fairness. I therefore doubt that algorithms will, on their own, make institutions fairer. Their real virtue is narrower. Unlike the bias behind a human hunch, an algorithm's bias can be measured cheaply and repeatedly, and measurement turns unfairness from a vague suspicion into a [[tractable|tractable]] problem. Whether that virtue is realized depends on who may examine the software.

COMPAS, a commercial tool that many American courts have used to predict whether a defendant will reoffend, illustrates both halves of this argument. Its appeal lay in replacing the [[subjective|subjective]] impressions of judges with a consistent score. In 2016, the nonprofit newsroom ProPublica obtained the scores of thousands of defendants in Broward County, Florida, and checked who was charged with a new crime within two years. Among defendants who did not reoffend, Black defendants were nearly twice as likely as white defendants to have been labeled medium or high risk. A tool adopted to check human prejudice seemed instead to [[stigmatize|stigmatize]] many Black defendants as likely reoffenders on the strength of predictions that proved false, all under the cover of arithmetic.

The vendor's reply complicated that verdict: Black and white defendants who received the same score, it noted, reoffended at roughly the same rate. Both claims were true; researchers proved the two standards cannot be met at once. When two groups reoffend at different underlying rates, any imperfect score must either mean something different for each group or misclassify the groups at different rates. Choosing between those standards is a moral decision, not a technical one. Yet the episode also showed what algorithms do well: because every score was recorded, outsiders could audit the predictions. A judge's intuition leaves a decision but no formula; it can be suspected, but it cannot be rerun.

A thoughtful skeptic would reply that this transparency was a lucky accident. Florida's public-records law handed journalists the COMPAS scores, but most algorithms that screen job seekers, tenants, and borrowers run inside private firms that reveal little to outsiders. Amazon, for instance, trained a hiring program on a decade of résumés, most of them from men. No engineer wrote a [[chauvinistic|chauvinistic]] rule, yet the system taught itself to penalize résumés containing the word "women's." Engineers neutralized that term but could not rule out subtler proxies, and the company abandoned the project; the public learned of it only through a Reuters report. Trusted uncritically, such a tool would further [[marginalize|marginalize]] women in an industry where they are already underrepresented. On this view, algorithms do not expose bias so much as launder it, lending old prejudice a [[specious|specious]] neutrality that discourages scrutiny and applying it at a scale no recruiter could match.

The skeptic is right that an algorithm no outsider may inspect offers the public little of the protection I have claimed. But the objection measures algorithms against an impartial human judgment that has never existed. When economists sent thousands of fictitious résumés to employers in Boston and Chicago, those randomly given white-sounding names received about 50 percent more callbacks than comparable ones given Black-sounding names. Exposing that bias took an elaborate field experiment; a model can be tested the same way, more cheaply and as often as needed, by anyone permitted to run it. Even the Amazon case is less damning than it appears: engineers caught the problem because the model's preferences were [[discernible|discernible]], and shelving the tool removed the evidence of bias, not the male-dominated history that produced it. The skeptic has identified a danger of secrecy, not of automation.

Algorithms will make institutions fairer, then, only when an institution declares which definition of fairness it pursues, checks its predictions against what happens, and lets outsiders examine its systems. Otherwise, automation gives familiar prejudice a faster and more confident voice. Algorithms cannot supply fairness; at their best, they make an institution's unfairness harder to deny, and therefore harder to sustain.

prompt.statement: The greatest obstacle to progress is not ignorance but the illusion of knowledge.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Ignorance Slows Progress; Illusion Stops It
essays.essay:
In 2000, as South Africa faced one of the fastest-growing HIV epidemics in the world, President Thabo Mbeki convened an advisory panel that seated scientists who denied that the virus causes AIDS beside researchers who had spent careers showing that it does. For years afterward his government delayed the public distribution of antiretroviral drugs, while his health minister promoted garlic, beetroot, and lemon as remedies. South Africa's problem was not ignorance: it had first-rate HIV scientists, the drugs were already saving lives in wealthy nations, and Brazil provided them free to all who needed them. The problem was a government that believed it knew better. I therefore largely agree that the illusion of knowledge is the graver obstacle to progress, because ignorance invites inquiry while illusion forecloses it. But the claim holds only where knowledge already exists; at the frontier of understanding, ignorance remains the binding constraint.

Art history shows how such illusions form. In 1937 Abraham Bredius, an elderly scholar [[venerated|venerate]] as a leading authority on Dutch painting, hailed a newly surfaced Supper at Emmaus as a masterpiece by Vermeer, and patrons bought it for a Rotterdam museum. Its true author was Han van Meegeren, a painter embittered by critics of his own work. Because Vermeer is so [[enigmatic|enigmatic]] a figure, with few surviving pictures, scholars had speculated that he once passed through a religious phase under Italian influence. Van Meegeren painted that missing phase, and the experts saw what their theory had taught them to expect. Only after the war, accused of treason for selling a supposed Vermeer to Hermann Göring, did he confess, and even then a few [[pertinacious|pertinacious]] connoisseurs went on defending the Emmaus. The error was not a gap in the experts' knowledge but an overextension of it.

Why are such errors so stubborn? Ignorance has no reputation to defend; an illusion of knowledge does, and so it recruits pride and identity to its side. Its holders rarely [[dissemble|dissemble]]. They believe what they say, and each public defense makes the belief harder to abandon. In South Africa, the dissidents' [[specious|specious]] arguments, which blamed AIDS on poverty and on the drugs themselves, drew strength from a well-founded distrust of the drug companies that had sued the government to block a law allowing cheaper medicines. Every concession to the evidence meant admitting error at the top of the state, so concessions came slowly; Harvard researchers later estimated that the delay cost hundreds of thousands of lives.

The strongest objection is that this argument mistakes the dramatic for the fundamental. Illusions, an opponent would say, are eventually punctured: van Meegeren was exposed, and South Africa went on to build the world's largest antiretroviral program. Genuine ignorance offers no such reprieve. More than forty years after HIV was identified, and after the failure of several large trials, some in South Africa, there is still no licensed HIV vaccine, and no amount of humility has produced one. On this view, illusion merely postpones progress that knowledge has made possible; ignorance decides whether progress is possible at all. I accept the premise but not the conclusion that ignorance is the greater obstacle. The objection treats ignorance and illusion as rivals for the same role, yet ignorance is a condition and illusion a disposition toward it. Ignorance measures how far progress still has to travel; it slows the journey, but only illusion stops anyone from setting out. Vaccine researchers know that they do not know, and even their failed trials, some with results no one expected, have shown them where not to look. An illusion blocks a route already mapped, and the self-correction the objection relies on is paid for in years and lives.

The statement, then, is right about the obstacles people build and too sweeping about the ones nature presents. Where an answer does not yet exist, as with an HIV vaccine, ignorance is the real limit, and humility is no [[affectation|affectation]] but simply the right temperament for working against it. Where the answer is already in hand, as it was in South Africa in 2000, the decisive obstacle is the confidence that one knows enough to stop looking.

prompt.statement: Small, gradual reforms achieve more than bold, sweeping ones.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Decree the Rules, Grow the Institutions
essays.essay:
The strongest case against the statement is not that bold reform is more inspiring but that half-finished reform can be worse than none. When a government frees some prices and keeps others fixed, anyone able to buy at the controlled price and sell at the market price grows rich, and these winners become [[pertinacious|pertinacious]] opponents of unifying the two prices. Reformers also have a short window before the public, worn down by hardship, grows [[restive|restive]] and turns on them. Poland's reformers grasped both dangers. In 1990 they freed most prices and made the zloty convertible for trade almost at once, and after a painful slump Poland became one of the steadiest performers in the former Soviet bloc. Russia freed most prices in 1992 but kept energy prices controlled, and traders who could buy oil cheaply at home and sell it abroad amassed some of the first great post-Soviet fortunes. On this evidence, gradualism is the habit of [[timorous|timorous]] governments, and its rewards flow to insiders.

That argument is sound, but only for one kind of reform, and so I agree with the statement for most reforms rather than for all. Prices, exchange rates and tariffs are rules: a government can rewrite them by decree, and rewriting them slowly only invites speculation. Secure property, honest courts and competent banks are institutions, and no decree can summon them into being. Even Poland was bold only about rules; it privatized its large state firms slowly, and much of its growth came from new private businesses rather than from privatized giants. Russia inverted the formula. Hesitant on energy prices, it was hasty on ownership, transferring its industry first through vouchers handed to citizens and then through rigged auctions, before courts or regulators could protect small shareholders. The result was not a nation of owners but a handful of magnates holding the country's richest assets.

Most of what a society needs to reform is institutional, and there gradual change achieves more for a reason the statement leaves unstated: it can learn. Vietnam's farm reform, which began years before the 1986 Doi Moi program, shows how. After collective agriculture left the country short of food, some provinces quietly let households farm contracted plots and keep whatever they grew beyond a fixed quota. Hanoi watched the harvests, endorsed a version of the practice nationally in 1981, and later granted families long-term rights to their land. The method was [[empirical|empirical]] rather than doctrinal: each step was a test whose failure would have stayed local and reversible, and each success converted skeptics in the leadership who would have rejected a blueprint. The process was [[plodding|plodding]], stretched across most of a decade, yet by 1989 a country that had recently imported rice was among the world's largest exporters of it. Tellingly, that same year, facing a problem of rules, the leadership moved abruptly: it freed most remaining prices and unified the exchange rate, and inflation, which had run in the hundreds of percent, fell sharply.

Vietnam's experience also answers the objection's sharpest claim, that gradualism breeds insiders who block completion. What decides the matter is not the pace of reform but the distribution of its early gains. Russia's halfway house enriched a small circle of traders exploiting a price gap; Vietnam's raised the incomes of millions of farming households, who became a broad constituency for going further. A reform that concentrates its first rewards creates a veto, while one that disperses them creates momentum. Incremental change offers a further advantage: it breaks one enormous wager into a sequence of [[tractable|tractable]] problems, each small enough to diagnose and correct when it goes wrong.

Small reforms, then, do not achieve more merely because they are small. They achieve more when the thing being changed must be grown rather than declared, and when each step creates enough winners to carry the next. Where the change is a rule that any half-measure would corrupt, hesitation is the greater danger, and a government should act at once. The sound reformer is neither bold nor cautious by temperament; she asks first whether she is resetting a rule or growing an institution, and lets the answer set the pace.
