prompt.statement: Some believe that national governments are best placed to solve environmental problems. Others believe that such problems are best solved by local communities.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Match the Authority to the Harm
essays.essay:
Arguments about who should solve environmental problems often become a contest of virtues: national governments command money, scientists, and enforcement power, while local communities possess intimate knowledge and a direct stake in the result. Both descriptions are accurate, which is why the argument rarely ends. A more useful question is where the harm falls relative to the people who cause it. When those who cause a harm also bear it and can watch one another, local communities are usually the better stewards. When the harm travels beyond them, or cannot be detected without a laboratory, only a larger authority will do. Because the most damaging problems tend to be of the second kind, the national view comes closer to my own, though for a reason its advocates seldom give.

The local view nonetheless deserves more credit than its critics allow. Elinor Ostrom shared a Nobel Prize in economics for showing that communities can govern shared resources without central control or private ownership. In one celebrated case, a Swiss Alpine village preserved its communal pastures for centuries with rules as [[prosaic|prosaic]] as this one: no household could send more cows to the summer meadow than it could feed through the winter. The arrangement worked because the pasture had clear boundaries, the villagers themselves would bear the cost of ruining it, and a cheater's extra cows grazed in full view of the neighbors. Overgrazing was therefore a [[tractable|tractable]] problem for the village and an opaque one for a distant ministry that could not know how many animals a slope could support. Ostrom and her colleagues found the same pattern in Nepal, where farmer-run irrigation systems often outperformed more modern, government-run systems. National programs that [[marginalize|marginalize]] the people who use a resource daily risk losing the cooperation they need.

Yet the local view quietly assumes those conditions, and the gravest environmental problems lack them. The geochemist Clair Patterson, while trying to date the earth from lead in meteorites, found his samples contaminated by lead from nearly everything around him. Tracing that lead to its sources, he showed that modern bodies carried far more of it than pre-industrial ones, largely because of leaded gasoline. No town could have discovered this: the poison was invisible, and measuring it demanded techniques so exacting that Patterson had to develop many of them himself. Nor could any town have solved it. A city that banned leaded fuel would still breathe the exhaust of every truck passing through, while refiners kept selling to everyone else. The remedy came only when federal regulators phased lead out of gasoline nationwide, and as they did, the lead in Americans' blood fell sharply.

The local view also assumes that a community speaks with one voice. Often the polluter belongs to the community, sometimes as its largest employer, yet its neighbors, not its shareholders, bear the harm it causes. A town whose paper mill both pays its residents and fouls its river tends to be [[irresolute|irresolute]], tightening its rules after each public outcry and relaxing them at the next threat of layoffs. The mill need not find [[venal|venal]] officials; it need only remind the council who signs the paychecks. James Madison argued in Federalist No. 10 that a single faction can dominate a small republic far more easily than a large one, and a company town is that danger in miniature. A national regulator is hardly immune to pressure, but it answers to a broader public, including the people downstream.

The same reasoning marks the limits of national governments. When chlorofluorocarbons from refrigerators and spray cans worldwide were found to be thinning the ozone layer, no single nation could halt the damage; it took an international treaty, the Montreal Protocol. The principle, then, is not that capitals are wiser than villages but that an authority must reach at least as far as the harm it addresses. Where a problem is bounded, visible, and borne by those who cause it, communities should govern it, and national governments should give them room. But air, rivers, and toxic chemicals rarely stop at town lines, so that principle assigns most of the consequential work to national governments and the treaties they sign.

prompt.statement: Some believe that a society's wealthiest members have a special duty to support public causes. Others believe that such duties belong equally to all citizens.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Equal Duty, Unequal Measure
essays.essay:
The word "duty" raises two questions that this debate tends to blur: how much a person owes, and why that person owes anything at all. The belief that the wealthy bear a special duty answers the first question well; the belief that such duties belong equally to all citizens answers the second. My position lies closer to the second view, suitably refined. Every citizen owes the same kind of obligation to public causes, one that arises from membership in a community rather than from the size of a bank account, although the amount each owes should rise with what each can afford. The wealthy owe more of this common duty, not a different one, and the only obligation peculiar to them is to ensure that their generosity never becomes a purchase.

The case for a special duty deserves a serious hearing, because on the question of amount it is largely right. If "equally" meant equal sums, the second view would be indefensible: a donation that would ruin a schoolteacher is a trivial expense for a magnate, so identical gifts would impose wildly unequal sacrifices. Large fortunes, moreover, are rarely built alone; they depend on courts that enforce contracts and public schools that train workers. Andrew Carnegie defended the first view in "The Gospel of Wealth," contending that a rich man should administer his surplus during his lifetime as a trust for the community. His giving matched his words: he financed thousands of public libraries that put books within reach of readers who could never have bought them. Americans have long [[venerated|venerate]] benefactors of this kind, and with reason.

Yet Carnegie's own program shows why amount is not the whole story. He did not simply hand towns finished buildings; in most cases he required a town to provide the site and to pledge tax money every year to run its library. The gift was a partnership, not a substitute for public support, and the libraries endured because ordinary taxpayers kept funding them for decades. A public cause stays public only when the public sustains it. The principle holds even in professional sports, where teams typically belong to the very rich. The Green Bay Packers are owned by their fans, whose shares pay no dividends and cannot be resold at a profit. That arrangement has helped keep the team in the smallest market in the National Football League, while franchises in far larger cities have been moved by owners chasing better stadium deals. A commitment spread across a community [[engenders|engender]] an attachment that no single patron, however generous, can guarantee.

There is a further reason to resist calling the duty of the wealthy "special": the word implies special standing, as if giving were a favor that earns privileges. The 2019 college admissions scandal exposed the crudest form of this bargain. Wealthy parents paid an intermediary to bribe coaches at selective universities into designating their children as recruited athletes, some for sports the students had never played competitively. The coaches were [[venal|venal]], but the parents' premise was more revealing: that wealth entitles a family to a different set of rules. Outright bribery is rare, yet its legal cousin, the extra consideration some selective colleges give to the children of major donors, rests on the same assumption. When gifts buy deference, philanthropy decays into an [[affectation|affectation]] of public spirit, and the donor's name on the building comes to matter more than the work inside it. What sets the wealthy apart, then, is not a different kind of duty but a stricter test of [[probity|probity]], because their gifts can so easily become transactions.

Duty to public causes is best understood as a single obligation that every citizen holds by belonging to a community, measured against what each can bear. The wealthy owe more of it because they can give more, not because they form a separate moral class with obligations of its own and, by implication, privileges of its own. Their one distinctive burden is to make sure that what they give remains a gift, so that the libraries, schools, and teams they help support continue to belong to the people who sustain them.

prompt.statement: Some believe that international organizations make the world safer. Others believe that they mainly limit the ability of nations to act in their own interest.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Why the Limit Is the Security
essays.essay:
It would be easy to dismiss the claim that international organizations mainly hem nations in as the grievance of [[chauvinistic|chauvinistic]] politicians, but it contains a hard truth: membership has real costs. A country that joins the World Trade Organization can have its tariffs ruled unlawful; a non-nuclear state that joins the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty forswears a weapon its neighbors might someday build and accepts inspections by the International Atomic Energy Agency. The costs also fall unevenly. Each permanent member of the Security Council can block enforcement action against itself, so the rules bind the weak more tightly than the strong. Yet the argument rests on an unstated assumption: that a nation's interest is whatever its government would choose if left entirely free. That is where the second view stops being true, and why the first comes closer to my own, with one amendment. International organizations make the world safer not in spite of limiting nations but by limiting them, and only when the limits are mutual and someone is willing to enforce them.

South America offers the clearest illustration. Under military rule, Argentina and Brazil, longtime rivals, each pursued nuclear programs that outsiders suspected could be turned toward a bomb, and neither trusted the other's assurances. After civilian rule returned, their presidents began building confidence through joint declarations and visits to each other's sensitive nuclear sites. In 1991 the two governments did something the second view would call self-defeating: they created a joint agency through which Argentine inspectors examine Brazilian facilities and Brazilian inspectors examine Argentine ones. Each nation surrendered the freedom to enrich uranium in secret and gained what no unilateral policy could deliver, the assurance that its rival had done the same. Years of routine inspections [[engendered|engender]] a durable trust that summit declarations alone could not have sustained, and the feared arms race never came. Here the limit did not compete with the national interest; it was the national interest.

Still, the first view is not true merely because an organization exists, as Rwanda in 1994 shows. United Nations peacekeepers were already in the country when the genocide began, and their commander had warned headquarters months earlier of a plan to exterminate Tutsi. Within days, peacekeepers guarding refugees at a Kigali school were ordered out, and the refugees were massacred soon afterward. Then an [[irresolute|irresolute]] Security Council, shaken by the murder of ten Belgian peacekeepers, cut the force to a few hundred troops rather than reinforce it. An organization able only to [[admonish|admonish]] the killers may be worse than none, because its presence invites people to rely on protection it will not provide. Yet Rwanda hardly vindicates the second view. Nothing restrained the powerful states from pursuing their interest; they simply judged it to lie in staying away. The failure was too little constraint, not too much.

Why, then, does the second view sound so plausible? The answer lies partly in journalism. News coverage rewards conflict, so a deadlocked Security Council debate reaches every front page, while an inspection that finds nothing amiss reaches none. The press resembles a fire bell: its [[clangor|clangor]] announces the blaze, never the fire that failed to start. But the safety cooperation produces consists largely of fires that fail to start: the weapon not built, the border war not fought. The Argentine-Brazilian agency has worked quietly for more than three decades, yet few outsiders have heard of it. Readers who know these bodies only through headlines see their costs vividly and their benefits hardly at all, and may mistake an imbalance in coverage for an imbalance in fact.

The two views are less opposed than they first appear. International organizations do restrict nations; the real question is whether the restriction is reciprocal, verifiable, and backed by members willing to pay to uphold it. Where those conditions hold, as between Argentina and Brazil, surrendering a freedom is how a nation serves its interest. Where they fail, as in Rwanda, the danger is not that the organization binds its members too tightly but that it binds no one while appearing to protect everyone. Nations buy security with their freedom of action; the best international bodies make that bargain credible.

prompt.statement:
Claim: Cities should make public transportation free.
Reason: When transit is free, more people use it, which reduces traffic and pollution for everyone.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Free Fares Serve Riders, Not Roads
essays.essay:
Free public transportation is never truly free; the only questions are who pays for it and why. A city can abolish fares for two quite different reasons. It can treat transit as an environmental lever, a way of pulling drivers out of their cars, or as a civic entitlement, like a paved street or a library, that residents should not have to buy one trip at a time. The argument before us rests entirely on the first rationale. I largely reject that reason, but I accept a qualified version of the claim, on grounds the argument never offers.

The environmental reason is [[specious|specious]]: it sounds like simple arithmetic, since more riders should mean fewer cars, but it assumes that every new passenger is a former driver. When Tallinn, the Estonian capital, abolished fares for its residents, ridership did rise, yet researchers found that much of the new demand came from people who had previously walked, while car traffic changed little. That result is unsurprising once one asks why people drive. Their reasons are [[prosaic|prosaic]]. The car is faster, it goes door to door, and it spares its owner a [[tortuous|tortuous]] route with two transfers. For most drivers the fare is the smaller cost of a trip and time the larger; removing the first while ignoring the second will not empty the roads.

The cities celebrated for making transit compete with the car have usually attacked time rather than price. Curitiba, in southern Brazil, became a global model not by giving rides away but by giving buses their own lanes and having passengers pay before boarding, so that buses ran almost like a surface subway; Bogotá later adapted the design for TransMilenio, which also charges fares. No one abandons a car to sit on a [[plodding|plodding]] bus stuck in the same traffic jam, however cheap the ticket. And where the goal is less traffic, the most direct tool runs counter to the claim: Stockholm cut traffic in its center by charging drivers, and London's own congestion charge helped pay for more buses.

Yet the claim can survive the failure of its reason, because the second rationale is far stronger. For a low-wage worker on a city's outskirts, the fare is not a trivial price but a daily toll on the ability to earn a living. Latin America shows how sharply that burden is felt. In São Paulo in 2013, a group called the Free Fare Movement led protests against a small increase in bus and subway fares; the protests grew into Brazil's largest demonstrations in two decades, and the increase was revoked. In Santiago in 2019, a metro fare increase prompted students to jump the turnstiles en masse. The increase landed on a city whose residents were already [[restive|restive]] over pensions and the cost of living, and the protest soon widened into a national reckoning with inequality, announced each night by the [[clangor|clangor]] of pots and pans banged on balconies. Neither movement was about congestion or air quality. Both began as fights over access: who can afford to reach the jobs, schools, and clinics a city concentrates.

Even this stronger case holds only under a condition the claim omits. Fares fund service, and a city that abolishes them without replacing the revenue will soon run fewer and shabbier buses, betraying the riders free transit was meant to help; a free bus that comes every forty minutes is a hollow benefit. Luxembourg could make public transport free nationwide partly because fares had covered only a small fraction of the system's costs. A city that depends on the fare box may do better with deep discounts for low-income riders, which can deliver most of the gain in access at much lower cost.

Free transit, then, is best defended as what it is: a transfer to the people who ride, not a cure for the people who drive. A city that wants cleaner air must make transit fast and driving costly. A city that wants fairer access may reasonably make transit free, so long as it replaces every dollar the fare box once collected; otherwise it has simply traded the burden of the fare for the burden of the wait.

prompt.statement:
Claim: Employers should not ask job applicants about their previous salaries.
Reason: Basing pay on past pay carries past unfairness into the future.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Price the Job, Not the Person
essays.essay:
A mathematics consultant at a California county education office discovered that male colleagues, some hired after her for the same work, were earning more. The county did not cite their qualifications; its pay schedule simply set each newcomer's pay at a modest premium over his or her last salary, and her previous employer had paid her less. A disparity created elsewhere had been imported intact, and a federal appeals court held that prior pay could not justify it. The case seems to vindicate both the claim and its reason, but it vindicates them unequally. I agree that employers should not ask applicants what they used to earn. The reason, however, is true but insufficient: it proves too much, and the stronger case rests on what a past salary measures.

The reason deserves more respect than skeptics give it. Because raises are usually calculated as percentages of current pay, a gap at hiring never closes; in dollars, it widens with every raise. Nor is the reported figure a neutral fact. It may have been set by a [[chauvinistic|chauvinistic]] manager, by an employer in a field long dismissed as women's work, or in a negotiation the applicant was too inexperienced to win. History offers a starker precedent. After Reconstruction, several Southern states imposed literacy tests on voters but exempted men whose ancestors had been eligible to vote before Black men were enfranchised. These grandfather clauses never mentioned race, yet the scheme disenfranchised Black citizens as surely as an explicit ban, because it made yesterday's exclusion the test of today's eligibility. The Supreme Court struck down Oklahoma's version in 1915, recognizing that a neutral-sounding appeal to the past can disguise discrimination.

Yet the reason, taken alone, cannot sustain the claim, because nearly every hiring criterion carries past unfairness forward. A degree from a selective university reflects, in part, family wealth; a senior title reflects who was chosen for promotion. If transmitting old inequities disqualified a question, an employer could ask nothing at all. What sets salary history apart is its weakness as evidence: a diploma, however unequally distributed, certifies what an applicant can do, whereas a salary records only what another employer agreed to pay. Its apparent precision is [[spurious|spurious]]; the number reflects that employer's budget, region, and leverage as much as the applicant's ability. A public school teacher who joins a software company brings needed expertise and a salary that says almost nothing about her value there. The deeper problem is not that the question is [[impertinent|impertinent]], although many applicants find it so, but that its answer misleads.

The question also corrupts the negotiation it is meant to inform. The employer learns the applicant's number while revealing nothing about its own range, and because past pay often goes unverified, the exchange rewards applicants willing to [[dissemble|dissemble]] and penalizes those too scrupulous to round up. A company that would never knowingly reward dishonesty has built a hiring step that does exactly that.

Still, a ban is a weaker remedy than it looks. Economists who studied "ban the box" laws, which bar employers from asking about criminal records early in hiring so that applicants are not [[stigmatized|stigmatize]] by an old conviction, found that the callback gap between otherwise similar white and Black applicants widened: some employers apparently guessed who had a record. A rule meant to keep former offenders from being [[marginalized|marginalize]] cast suspicion on Black applicants with no record. An employer barred from asking about salary may likewise infer it from an applicant's sex or previous employer. Removing a question does not remove the inference.

The defensible position is therefore narrower and more demanding than the one stated. Employers should not ask about past pay, not merely because the number carries old unfairness, since much of a résumé does, but because it measures the wrong thing and favors the stronger party in bargaining. The prohibition should cover volunteered figures too, since a misleading number does not improve by being offered. And because silence invites guessing, the ban works best alongside a posted salary range for every opening. An employer that prices the job rather than the person no longer needs to ask what someone else decided an applicant was worth.

prompt.statement:
Claim: People should read widely outside their own field.
Reason: The most useful ideas often come from connecting distant areas of knowledge.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Breadth That Serves Depth
essays.essay:
The reason behind this claim has impressive evidence on its side. In 1838 Charles Darwin read Thomas Malthus's essay on population, a bleak argument that human numbers, unchecked, grow faster than the food supply, and found in it the mechanism he needed: if far more creatures are born than can survive, any variation that improves the odds will tend to be preserved. Two decades later Alfred Russel Wallace, recalling the same essay during a fever in the Malay Archipelago, reached the same conclusion independently. Natural selection, perhaps biology's most consequential idea, arose from just such a distant connection. Yet the same example shows where the reason stops being true. I agree that people should read widely, but the reason misdescribes where the most useful ideas come from and overlooks the surest benefit of such reading.

Notice who made the connection. Countless politicians and clergymen read Malthus, but those who found a law of biology in his pages were naturalists with years of specimens behind them. The spark came from outside their field; the tinder had been gathered within it. The reason thus hides an assumption: that a connection's value lies in the distance between fields rather than in the depth of the mind that joins them. It also overrates how often valuable ideas arise this way. Leaps across disciplines are memorable but [[sporadic|sporadic]]. Many ideas of equal consequence come from sustained, often [[plodding|plodding]] work on one problem. James Watt conceived the separate condenser, which made steam power far more economical, by studying a model Newcomen engine he was repairing until he saw that it wasted much of its steam reheating a freshly cooled cylinder. A mentor who [[admonishes|admonish]] a doctoral student to master her own literature before sampling others is not being narrow; she is describing how most useful work gets done.

Even if the reason were wholly true, it would not by itself establish the claim. If distant connections are valuable but rare, a society might entrust them to a few polymaths or to interdisciplinary teams of specialists. Why, then, should each person read widely? The answer partly rescues the reason: a connection cannot be delegated, because no one thinks to consult an expert in a field whose relevance he cannot yet see. As an undergraduate, Claude Shannon took a philosophy course that introduced him to George Boole's algebra of logic. Later, working with relay circuits at MIT, he recognized that switches, which are either open or closed, obey the same rules as propositions, which are either true or false. That insight helped found digital circuit design, yet few engineers would have thought to ask a logician. Breadth matters because it lets one mind hold both halves of a connection that no committee would know to assemble.

Still, if invention were the only payoff, wide reading would be a lottery ticket; most readers never make a Darwinian leap. The claim rests more securely on a different reason: reading outside one's field improves judgment within it. A discipline left to itself tends to [[venerate|venerate]] its traditions, and its members forget that some assumptions were inherited rather than argued for. An outsider would notice, but outsiders' questions usually sound [[impertinent|impertinent]] to insiders. Wide reading lets a specialist ask them herself. A hypothetical epidemiologist who has read some anthropology may never turn that reading into a discovery, yet when her model predicts that a vaccination campaign will succeed, she is more likely to ask whether the community trusts the vaccinators, a question her equations do not contain. That benefit requires real engagement; reading done merely to quote the Stoics at dinner is an [[affectation|affectation]], yielding neither connections nor perspective.

I therefore accept the claim and only half of its reason. Distant connections do produce some of our most valuable ideas, but they come rarely, and usually to minds already deep in one field; the reason mistakes an occasional byproduct of breadth for its purpose. The dependable return on reading outside one's field is the ability to see that field as a stranger would: to tell which of its assumptions reflect the world and which merely reflect custom. Breadth is worth recommending when it serves depth, neither replacing it nor decorating it.

prompt.statement: Every adult citizen should be required to complete one year of national or community service.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Mandatory Service Must Be Universal, Useful, Civic
essays.essay:
Champions of compulsory national service often [[admonish|admonish]] young adults for their self-absorption and hold up as models those who already serve: the graduate who teaches in a rural school, the retiree who runs a food pantry. A requirement, however, does not simply multiply such people. It enlists the reluctant alongside the eager, so its consequences differ in kind, not merely in scale, from those of volunteering. The policy's strongest justification is a benefit that only compulsion can supply: universality. A duty that binds everyone places side by side citizens whose paths would otherwise never cross. I support the requirement only where it can secure this benefit without the harms that compulsion tends to bring, and I oppose it elsewhere, because there its unintended consequences would overwhelm its intended ones.

When the duty truly falls on everyone, the effects can be profound. The French Third Republic made military service a near-universal experience for young men, and the historian Eugen Weber argued that the barracks, along with the schoolroom and the railroad, helped forge a single nation from a [[heterogeneous|heterogeneous]] rural population whose members often spoke Breton, Occitan, or another regional language at home. The same mechanism runs in reverse once exemptions can be bought. The Union's draft law of 1863 allowed a drafted man to escape service by paying a three-hundred-dollar commutation fee, and fury at that provision helped ignite the New York draft riots. A compulsory year riddled with exemptions for the wealthy or well connected would [[engender|engender]] not solidarity but the bitter conviction that sacrifice is for other people. That danger makes my first condition universality in fact, not merely in law.

Even a truly universal program faces a dilemma in the work it assigns. If conscripts perform necessary labor, institutions come to depend on them. For decades, Germany's civilian alternative for conscientious objectors supplied hospitals, nursing homes, and ambulance crews with young men; when conscription was suspended in 2011, welfare organizations warned of serious shortfalls, and the government created a voluntary federal service partly to fill them. Required service can thus become a hidden subsidy that lets employers postpone hiring trained, paid staff. Yet if the state avoids that trap by inventing busywork, it produces a [[restive|restive]] cohort of young adults who conclude, reasonably, that their year is being wasted, and who carry that cynicism into later life. My second condition is the narrow ground between these failures: work that is needed but chronically left undone, such as tutoring struggling students or clearing brush in fire-prone areas, and that supplements professional services instead of replacing them.

Finally, service must cultivate loyalty to fellow citizens rather than hostility toward outsiders or dissenters. Here the French example cuts the other way. The same schoolrooms and barracks that, in Weber's account, made peasants into Frenchmen also nursed a longing for revenge against Germany after the loss of Alsace-Lorraine, and a program designed to instill love of country can easily become a school for [[chauvinistic|chauvinistic]] nationalism. Dissenters face a parallel danger. During the First World War, some British women handed white feathers to men out of uniform to brand them cowards; a service mandate that offered objectors only a grudging alternative would [[stigmatize|stigmatize]] them in much the same way. Germany again offers a partial answer: its civilian service, long regarded with suspicion, eventually came to be seen by many as an ordinary and honorable choice. A civic rather than martial purpose, with equal standing for civilian and military paths, is therefore my third condition.

My support for the policy, then, is conditional, but the conditions are concrete: a duty that spares no one, work that adds to professional services rather than replacing them, and a civic purpose that gives civilian and military paths equal honor. A government prepared to guarantee all three could justify claiming a year from every citizen. Where any one is missing, the policy turns against its own aims: it breeds resentment instead of solidarity, displaces the workers it should complement, and teaches suspicion of foreigners and dissenters alike. There, a generously funded voluntary program would forgo some of the mixing that only compulsion achieves, but it would avoid harms that a poorly designed mandate makes nearly certain.

prompt.statement: Cities should charge drivers a fee for entering their busiest districts during peak hours.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Charge Drivers Only Where They Can Choose
essays.essay:
Debates over congestion charges usually turn on whether drivers deserve to pay. The more useful question is what the charge will make people do. The proposal rests on an unstated assumption: that many rush-hour drivers could travel another way, or at another time, if given a reason. Where that assumption holds, a peak-hour fee works well. Where it fails, the fee taxes people for circumstances they cannot change. I therefore support such charges conditionally, and the conditions emerge from tracing what the policy would set in motion.

Where alternatives exist, the consequences favor the fee. The notion that a toll-free road costs nothing is [[specious|specious]], as anyone who has sat through three light cycles downtown knows: at rush hour it is priced in time, and everyone pays whether the trip is an emergency or an errand. Much of that price falls on people who never chose to drive: passengers on a [[plodding|plodding]] bus stuck behind single-occupant cars. In Manhattan, most people entering the business district during peak hours already arrive by train or bus, and those who drive tend to be wealthier than those who ride. A fee that thins car traffic thus charges a comparatively affluent minority and returns time to the bus riders stuck behind them. That consequence, more than the revenue, is what inclines me toward the policy. Stockholm bears this out: its 2006 trial charge began amid widespread opposition, yet after months of lighter traffic, a majority of city voters backed making it permanent. When enough trips can shift in timing or mode, congestion becomes a [[tractable|tractable]] problem: a modest price moves the marginal driver onto a train or into an earlier hour.

The logic collapses when drivers have no real alternative. Consider a hypothetical hospital orderly whose shift begins during the morning rush and whose only other option is a bus that would add hours to her day. Since she cannot reasonably change when or how she travels, the fee will only shrink her paycheck. Multiply her by every home health aide and line cook in the same bind, and an efficient price becomes a regressive tax on inflexibility. A second consequence lands outside the zone. New Jersey sued to block New York's charge, arguing that the federal environmental review had not adequately weighed the traffic and exhaust that detouring drivers would push into its towns. The program survived the challenge, but the objection was not frivolous: a cordon removes some cars but merely relocates others, often toward neighborhoods with little say in the decision. These two consequences are why my support stops short of a universal rule.

Yet these consequences dictate the policy's design rather than defeat it, and they expose a trap. The instinctive response to a [[restive|restive]] electorate is to keep the fee low and grant exemptions, but exemptions tend to [[proliferate|proliferate]] once the first is conceded, and each weakens the incentive the fee exists to create. A [[timorous|timorous]] council can thus produce a charge too cheap to deter discretionary trips and too porous to fund better transit: the resentment of a new tax without the faster streets that might justify it. New York's plan, halted weeks before its scheduled 2024 launch, revived months later at a lower price, and defended in court when federal officials moved to revoke approval, shows the pressure such a policy must withstand. Surviving that pressure requires a visible return: buses that move, trains that come more often, and discounts aimed narrowly at low-income workers with no other way in.

Cities should price their busiest streets at peak hours, but the justification is empirical rather than moral: it depends less on what drivers deserve than on whether driving at that hour is truly a choice. A charge is warranted where most travelers have, or can soon be given, a reasonable alternative; where the revenue is legally earmarked for improving that alternative; and where the city sets a price high enough to change behavior and watches the zone's edges for displaced traffic. Without those conditions, the policy burdens those least able to adapt while barely easing traffic. With them, it rations scarce road space more fairly than the rush-hour queue it replaces.

prompt.statement: Governments should tax individuals' wealth, not just their income.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Tax Wealth Where It Can Be Seen
essays.essay:
In 2021 ProPublica, drawing on leaked IRS data on the richest Americans, reported that Jeff Bezos, the founder of Amazon, had paid no federal income tax in two separate years and, in others, taxes that were tiny beside the growth of his fortune. Nothing in the reporting suggested he had broken the law. Most of his fortune consisted of Amazon shares, and in the United States the rise in a share's value is not taxed until the share is sold. The episode exposes an assumption built into the income tax: that economic gains arrive as transactions the government can see. For the very rich, they often do not. I therefore accept that governments should tax wealth, not merely income. Yet when I trace the consequences of the usual proposal, an annual levy on each person's net worth, I conclude that wealth should be taxed when a transaction reveals its value, not on an official's yearly guess.

The intended consequences are worth wanting. A nurse pays tax on every paycheck, while a founder whose shares double in value owes nothing on the gain and can borrow against them to live comfortably, because loans are not income. If the shares pass to heirs, a lifetime of gains is never taxed as income at all. Taxing wealth would close this gap and draw revenue from those most able to pay. It would also check a form of power that income statistics miss. Bezos bought The Washington Post; other fortunes bankroll political campaigns or shape the priorities of global health programs. Fortunes that compound untaxed can [[marginalize|marginalize]] the elected institutions through which ordinary citizens govern themselves.

The trouble begins with an objection so [[prosaic|prosaic]] that it rarely appears in the moral case for the policy: someone must decide what a fortune is worth. Wages are reported by employers, but wealth is a [[heterogeneous|heterogeneous]] collection of assets, many of which have no price until they are sold. Shares of a public company are easy to value; a private startup, a family farm, or a painting is not. Even a market price can be fleeting. A biotechnology firm's shares can lose most of their value in a day when a late-stage clinical trial fails, so a founder assessed on January's valuation might, by March, owe tax on a fortune that has largely vanished. Germany learned how estimates corrode such a tax: in the mid-1990s its constitutional court ruled that the wealth tax treated taxpayers unequally, because real estate was assessed at outdated values far below those applied to financial assets, and the tax, never repealed, has been suspended since 1997. An annual levy built on appraisals would also [[engender|engender]] systematic undervaluation, and with it an industry devoted to making fortunes look smaller.

Europe's record points the same way. Most European countries that once levied an annual wealth tax have abandoned it; Sweden abolished its tax in 2007, and in 2018 France replaced its levy with one on real estate alone. Capital is mobile, and so are its owners: after Norway raised its wealth tax in 2022, several of its richest citizens moved to Switzerland. Even where the wealthy stay, the tax depends on the [[probity|probity]] of the officials who value their holdings, a quality no statute can guarantee. Where assessors are poorly paid, discretion over the value of a private company becomes something to sell, and a [[venal|venal]] official can supply a low appraisal as readily as a building permit.

These consequences do not defeat the case for taxing wealth; they redirect it. The statement distinguishes income from wealth, but the line that matters runs elsewhere: between values a market has observed and values an official must estimate. Governments could treat a large loan secured by appreciated shares as a sale, tax lifetime gains when assets pass to heirs, and raise taxes on large inheritances. Estates still require appraisal, but a dispute that arises once a generation is more manageable than an annual one. Such measures reach the gains ProPublica exposed without asking the state to price every startup each January. Governments should tax wealth, then, but they should tax it where it can be seen: when it is sold, borrowed against, or handed down.

prompt.statement: The most important lessons a person learns are learned outside formal education.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Life Teaches Judgment; School Spares the Cost
essays.essay:
The claim that life's most important lessons are learned outside the classroom has the comfortable ring of a commencement-speech [[platitude|platitude]], and like most platitudes it is half true. Its hidden assumption is that school and experience are rival teachers. In fact, much of any curriculum was first learned outside a classroom, often at great cost, and then written down so that others need not learn it the same way. I agree with the statement only for lessons that resist being written down; for lessons too costly to learn twice, formal education is not the lesser teacher but the only responsible one.

Consider Ignaz Semmelweis, whose career at first seems to vindicate the statement. In the 1840s, Vienna General Hospital ran two maternity clinics, and women in the one that trained medical students died of childbed fever far more often than women in the one that trained midwives. The medicine he had been taught blamed such fevers on bad air or the women's constitutions. The decisive clue came instead from the morgue: a colleague cut by a student's scalpel during an autopsy died of an illness much like the mothers'. Semmelweis reasoned that students were carrying something from the corpses they dissected to the women they examined, and he required handwashing in a chlorinated lime solution. Deaths fell sharply. The most important lesson of his career came from the wards and contradicted his lectures. Yet he could read that evidence only with a trained clinician's habits, comparing two groups of women admitted on alternating days and discarding rival explanations one by one. Experience supplied the clue; education supplied the eyes to see it.

The lesson Semmelweis never learned, however, decided his fate. He was slow to publish, and when he finally wrote at length he was [[pugnacious|pugnacious]] rather than persuasive. In open letters he accused prominent obstetricians of murder, as though no honest physician could [[gainsay|gainsay]] a claim that, before germs were understood, seemed to lack a mechanism. A more [[sagacious|sagacious]] reformer would have foreseen that insults turn doubters into enemies. Rebuffed and increasingly erratic, Semmelweis died in an asylum; his idea prevailed only after germ theory, developed by Pasteur and others, explained it. No lecture could have taught him how to hold a conviction without contempt for those who did not yet share it. Here the statement holds in full, and his failure helped delay a reform that could have saved many mothers.

Other lessons are too dangerous to leave to experience, an [[indiscriminate|indiscriminate]] teacher that instills false confidence as readily as insight. In the mid-1980s the Therac-25, a computer-controlled radiation therapy machine, gave massive overdoses to several patients, some of whom died. Experience had taught its makers to trust software carried over from earlier models; they did not grasp that in those models hardware interlocks had silently caught its errors. Without such interlocks, quick edits by an operator could trigger a subtle timing flaw, and operators used to frequent, cryptic error messages sometimes simply resumed treatment. The case is now a staple of software engineering courses, where students learn, without harming anyone, that past reliability does not prove safety. Medicine follows the same logic: a surgeon should not discover the course of an artery through a patient's [[profuse|profuse]] bleeding. For such lessons, learning outside formal education means learning at someone else's expense.

These cases do not cancel each other; they divide the territory, and that division is my position. The statement confuses where a lesson originates with where a person should learn it. Semmelweis's lesson, like most worth knowing, originated outside a classroom; formal education lets later generations learn it without repeating the harm. What no school can transmit is the judgment that governs how knowledge is used. Semmelweis shows that knowledge without judgment can be powerless; the Therac-25 shows that experience without codified knowledge can be lethal. About the lessons of judgment, learned in life or not at all, the statement is right. About everything that can be written down, it is wrong; heeding it would mean paying again for knowledge already bought at a terrible price.

prompt.statement: Science has done more to change how people think than to change how they live.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Tools Travel Farther Than Reasoning
essays.essay:
The statement treats thought and life as separate arenas and asks which one science has changed more. That framing hides a more useful distinction. Science produces knowledge, which changes people only when they grasp it, and tools, which work whether or not anyone understands them. Where science offers only knowledge, the statement is largely true; where it offers tools, the statement is false, because people can live by science's products without ever reasoning in its terms. Since tools reach far more people than ideas do, I largely disagree with the statement. One case, however, fits neither category neatly, and it suggests that the decisive question is not whether science changes thought or life but whose thought it changes.

Discoveries that answer questions of meaning rather than solve practical problems show the statement at its strongest. Darwin's theory of natural selection improved no harvest and shortened no journey, yet it unsettled the educated public's sense of humanity's place in nature. The ground had been prepared. Geologists had already shown that whole species had vanished, and Tennyson's In Memoriam, published nearly a decade before Darwin's book, grieved over a nature that seemed careless of what it made. Darwin deepened that unease by explaining how species could arise without a designer, and the disquiet was anything but [[evanescent|evanescent]]: a generation later, Thomas Hardy, an early admirer of Darwin, built novels around a universe indifferent to the people struggling within it. What farmers and factory hands made of these ideas is largely [[conjectural|conjectural]], because so few of them recorded their beliefs, but the change in what writers and their readers believed is unmistakable. Here science transformed thinking and, for decades, left daily life almost untouched.

The statement fails, however, wherever science hands people a tool. Smallpox, which for centuries killed and disfigured people across much of the world, was declared eradicated in 1980. That victory required years of [[sedulous|sedulous]] effort by health workers who tracked down each remaining case and vaccinated anyone who might have been exposed. Eradication changed how everyone lives: no parent now fears the disease, and no child needs the vaccine. It did far less to change how people think. Most people now accept that germs cause disease, but they accept it on authority, much as their ancestors accepted that sickness rose from foul air; the content of the belief has changed, while the way of arriving at it has not. Public memory of epidemic disease has also proved short-lived, and vaccine skepticism draws strength from the very success that has spared parents the sight of the illnesses vaccines prevent. Science can remake how a person lives without touching how that person reasons.

The most revealing case lies between these extremes, in the courts. When DNA testing entered American courtrooms in the late 1980s, it supplied evidence far harder to [[gainsay|gainsay]] than a witness's memory, and it soon began freeing people who had spent years in prison for crimes they did not commit. Studied together, those exonerations showed a pattern: most had involved confident but mistaken eyewitness identifications. Those mistakes proved readily [[explicable|explicable]], because psychological research had shown that memory is reconstructed rather than replayed and that a witness's confidence can grow after the event. Some courts now instruct jurors about the fallibility of memory, and many police departments have changed how they conduct lineups. Science thus changed how a profession thinks, and that change altered the lives of defendants and victims who may never read a word of the underlying research.

These three cases shape my position in different ways. The Victorian literary record confines the statement's truth to science that offers understanding without tools; the history of smallpox shows that tools travel much farther than the reasoning behind them; the courtroom shows where the two categories meet. On balance, science has changed how people live more widely than how they think, yet its most consequential work occurs when it changes the thinking of the few people whose decisions govern the lives of many. The statement's error is to treat thought and life as competing outcomes, when in the cases that matter most the first is the route to the second.

prompt.statement: Art that challenges its audience is more valuable than art that comforts it.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Honesty, Not Discomfort, Measures Art's Worth
essays.essay:
The statement treats challenge and comfort as rival ingredients sealed inside a work of art, as though paintings and songs could be ranked by how much of each they contain. Both words, however, describe a relationship between a work and a particular audience at a particular moment, so the real question is what a given audience needs. I agree with the statement only when an audience's ease depends on something it has declined to examine. When an audience already knows the hard truth and lacks the strength to bear it, comfort is the more valuable thing art can offer.

The history of science supplies a case in which challenge is clearly worth more. In 1768 Joseph Wright of Derby painted An Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump, a candlelit rendering of the demonstrations traveling lecturers performed as entertainment. The lecturer has pumped the air from a glass vessel in which a white cockatoo is struggling; one girl hides her eyes while another stares up in dread. The lecturer himself, his hand at the valve that could let the air back in, looks straight out of the canvas, as if asking the viewer whether to continue. Wright was fascinated by the new science, yet he would not let his audience enjoy its marvels without registering their cost. A picture of pure wonder would have flattered spectators whose pleasure depended on not thinking about the bird; Wright's version makes every viewer a party to the decision.

Sports supply the opposite case. In 1989 a crush at an FA Cup semifinal at Hillsborough Stadium killed nearly a hundred Liverpool supporters, and police and newspapers falsely blamed the fans themselves. The bereaved did not need art to teach them that life is fragile or that institutions can lie; they had learned both at terrible cost. What they needed was the song Liverpool crowds had long sung at Anfield, a Rodgers and Hammerstein show tune that promises no one will walk alone and that became a hymn of shared mourning. A deliberately unsettling work at the memorials would have been not brave but cruel. Nor was this comfort passive. Solidarity that soothes a grieving community can also [[galvanize|galvanize]] it, and the families pressed their case for more than a quarter century, until new inquests ruled that their relatives had been unlawfully killed. The real rival of challenging art is not comfort but its counterfeit: the [[soporific|soporific]] music piped into waiting rooms, which soothes by asking nothing and saying nothing.

Challenge has its counterfeit as well. Much art marketed as provocative is merely [[tendentious|tendentious]]: it delivers the artist's conclusions ready-made and treats the discomfort it causes as proof of courage. A [[pugnacious|pugnacious]] artist who mistakes picking a fight for making a point leaves viewers nothing to think through, only a side to choose. Worse, when the audience already shares the artist's politics, the supposed challenge is only a [[platitude|platitude]] in a darker key. Even genuine challenge is a means, not the source of value. When José Feliciano sang a slow, guitar-accompanied rendition of the national anthem before a 1968 World Series game in Detroit, he provoked a storm of complaints from listeners who heard disrespect in an unfamiliar sound. Today such personal interpretations are routine, and his version shocks no one. Had its value lain in the shock, it would have expired with the shock; it endures because it was always a heartfelt reading of the anthem in a voice the crowd had not expected.

These cases do not leave me halfway between agreement and disagreement; they show that the statement measures the wrong thing. The contest that matters is between honesty and evasion, and both challenge and comfort can serve either. Challenge earns its value by disturbing an ease built on not looking; comfort earns its value by steadying people who have already seen the worst. Art that merely lulls or merely scolds is worth little in either guise. I would rank works, then, not by how uneasy they leave us but by whether they give an audience the truth it most needs, which is sometimes a reproach and sometimes a promise that no one will walk alone.

prompt.statement: Companies should let employees decide for themselves where and when they work.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Freedom in Proportion to the Work
essays.essay:
In the spring of 2020, American newspapers emptied their newsrooms almost overnight, yet the presses kept running. Reporters interviewed sources from their kitchens, editors trimmed copy on laptops, and the morning edition still landed on doorsteps. That summer, the owner of the New York Daily News announced that the paper's newsroom would close for good. If even a daily paper, an enterprise organized around a nightly deadline, can function without a shared room, why should any company dictate where and when its people work? I accept the recommendation as a default but not as a rule. The phrase "for themselves" assumes that employees both bear and understand the consequences; where they do, autonomy should be generous, and where they do not, the company needs a say.

The assumptions hold best where work is individual and its results are easy to see. A reporter covering a trial works better in the courthouse hallway than at a desk across town, and a story filed by six o'clock [[obviates|obviate]] any need to know where its author spent the afternoon. The same holds for tax returns and software: the product is the evidence of effort. The familiar objection, that unsupervised employees become [[indolent|indolent]], misdiagnoses the problem. A worker inclined to idle can do so at a desk as easily as at home, and a manager who can judge only attendance cannot judge much of anything. The gains are concrete. An employee spared a two-hour commute recovers time for sleep, a family can trade a cramped apartment near the office for a more [[salubrious|salubrious]] neighborhood, and a parent who can start at seven and stop at three may keep a job she would otherwise leave.

The first assumption, that the employee alone bears the consequences, fails when work is tightly coupled in time. Even the pandemic newsroom granted freedom of place, not of hours: a late story still cost an editor, a copy desk, and a page designer their evening. The real problem with flexible hours is therefore coordination, not idleness. When one teammate works at midnight and another at dawn, a question that would take thirty seconds across a table becomes a day-long exchange of messages. The trouble is [[nettlesome|nettlesome]] rather than dramatic: small delays, recurring daily, that fall mostly on colleagues, not on the person who chose the odd hours. IBM, long a champion of telecommuting, applied the same coordination logic to place in 2017, when it called thousands of remote employees back to regional offices so that teams could work side by side. The reversal may have been too sweeping, but the point stands: autonomy that costs a lone analyst little can cost a team a great deal.

The second assumption, that employees understand those consequences, fails less visibly with people who are still learning. The reporters who filed from their kitchens in 2020 had built their sources and judgment in crowded newsrooms, by overhearing a veteran coax a reluctant official or watching an editor rescue a muddled opening paragraph. A reporter hired that spring inherited none of this and could not miss what she had never seen. Letting her decide for herself presumes that she knows what she needs, which is exactly what a beginner cannot yet know. A company that sends its newest employees home has not granted them freedom so much as quietly canceled their apprenticeship, and the bill arrives years later, when there are too few seasoned editors to promote.

These cases do not refute the recommendation; they mark its boundary. The courthouse reporter shows that freedom of place pays off whenever the work is self-contained and its quality visible. The late story shows that freedom of hours must yield where colleagues absorb the cost, and the stranded newcomer, that autonomy is a poor substitute for training. The sensible policy, then, is a generous default with a few firm anchors: shared core hours, fixed deadlines, and side-by-side apprenticeships for newcomers. Such a policy will satisfy neither the [[intransigent|intransigent]] manager who equates presence with productivity nor the employee who regards any office day as an imposition. It will, however, give each employee as much freedom as the work itself can bear.

lazy; habitually avoiding effort once no supervisor is watching
of a place: pleasant, clean, and healthful to live in, unlike a cramped apartment near the office
irritating and recurring; the trouble is a steady run of small delays, not one crisis
unwilling to compromise; a manager who will not budge from requiring office presence

prompt.statement: Cities should invest in public spaces before they invest in new roads.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Capacity Roads Can Wait; Access Roads Cannot
essays.essay:
The recommendation treats public spaces and roads as rivals for the same budget, but the rivalry is partly illusory: in most cities streets already make up the largest share of public space, and the real question is what they should be asked to do. The decisive variable is whether a city suffers from too much traffic or too little access. Where an established network is merely congested, I agree that public space should come first. Congestion is [[nettlesome|nettlesome]], but a new road tends to fill with the traffic it invites, whereas a park or square improves daily life without adding cars. Where neighborhoods lack basic access, the order should be reversed, because there the missing road is not an irritation but a barrier.

Seoul's restoration of the Cheonggyecheon shows the recommendation at its most persuasive. For decades this downtown stream lay buried beneath a surface road, with an elevated expressway running overhead. By the early 2000s the expressway was deteriorating, and the city chose to tear it down rather than repair it; by 2005 a stream-side park, set below street level, had taken its place. The opposition was [[clamorous|clamorous]]: merchants feared for their trade, and critics predicted that closing a major artery would paralyze downtown. The paralysis never came. The city overhauled its bus network at about the same time, many drivers changed routes or left their cars at home, and traffic adapted far faster than forecasts assumed.

Why it worked matters more than the fact that it did. Removing the expressway [[obviated|obviate]] costly repairs, so part of the park's price was money Seoul would have had to spend on the old structure anyway; and because broad avenues and subway lines ran parallel on either side, the lost lanes could be absorbed. A noisy corridor of trucks and buses became a channel of running water, its banks measurably cooler in summer than nearby streets. Yet admirers abroad, [[profuse|profuse]] in their praise, tend to pass over the costs. The stream is fed largely by water pumped from the Han River at considerable expense, and the relocation of the corridor's merchants and vendors set off a bitter dispute that dragged on for years. Public space is neither free nor automatically benign; it paid off in Seoul because the city already had the roads it needed.

The opposite circumstance appears at the edges of many fast-growing cities. On the newer fringes of Hanoi, Dhaka, or Lagos, houses often rise faster than streets, along lanes too narrow for a fire truck and dirt tracks that turn to mud each rainy season. There the shortage is not of places to linger but of the ability to arrive, and a plaza built first would beautify a district that an ambulance cannot enter. The [[mundane|mundane]] work of grading, paving, and draining a street is the prior public good. It also does more than any plaza to make a district [[salubrious|salubrious]], since a drained lane holds no standing water for mosquitoes to breed in. Once that work is done, residents usually make the street itself a public space, with vendors' stalls by day and children's games at dusk. Postponing such roads would honor the recommendation's letter while defeating its purpose.

These cases do not leave me halfway between agreement and disagreement; they show where the line falls. Seoul demonstrates what public space can achieve once a network is complete; the unpaved fringe exposes what the same priority costs before it is. The recommendation is right about roads that add capacity and wrong about roads that create access. American law offers a template. A 1966 federal statute forbade approving highways through public parks when a feasible and prudent alternative existed, and after federal officials approved routing an interstate through Memphis's Overton Park, the Supreme Court ruled in 1971 that the approval was subject to searching judicial review and could not stand if it was [[arbitrary|arbitrary]]. Parkland, the Court added, could be taken only in truly unusual cases. The interstate never crossed the park. That is the form the recommendation should take: not a fixed sequence, but a strong presumption in favor of public space that only a demonstrated need for access can overcome.

prompt.statement: Governments should consult citizens directly, through referendums, on major decisions.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Knowable Stakes and Free Dissent, Not Magnitude
essays.essay:
When public demands grow [[clamorous|clamorous]], a referendum can look like a government's most honest response: rather than presume to know what citizens want, it simply asks them. That appeal is real, but the recommendation conceals an assumption. A referendum does not discover what citizens want; it records their answer to a question someone else has written, at a moment someone else has chosen. Whether direct consultation helps therefore depends less on how major a decision is than on two conditions: whether voters can judge the concrete consequences of their choice, and whether those posing the question leave them free to answer it. I endorse referendums when both conditions hold. When either fails, I would leave the decision to elected representatives, who at least answer for the details.

Stockholm's congestion charge shows how advantageous a referendum can be when the first condition is met. A fee on cars entering the city center was unpopular, and a vote on the idea alone would have been a contest of predictions. Instead, the charge ran as a full-scale trial for several months in 2006 before residents were asked whether to keep it, a sequence born of a parliamentary bargain, not a plan to inform voters. By voting day, Stockholmers had lived with the policy, and the difference on the roads was plain to see. City voters approved the charge in an advisory referendum, and it became permanent the following year. The margin was thin. Several neighboring municipalities voted no, and the vote did not end the dispute. It did change what the dispute was about: people were judging an experience rather than a forecast. This case alone keeps me from rejecting the recommendation outright.

Britain's 2016 referendum on leaving the European Union shows the same condition failing, and the failure had nothing to do with the decision's importance. The ballot offered two options, but leaving was not a single policy. It was a family of possibilities, from close alignment with Europe to a clean break, each with different consequences for trade, migration, and the Irish border. No voter, however [[sagacious|sagacious]], could know which version a "leave" vote endorsed, because none had yet been negotiated. Every claim about leaving's effects was therefore speculative; Britain held the contest of predictions that Stockholm had avoided. The narrow result settled a direction without a destination. Parliament then split into [[intransigent|intransigent]] factions. Each claimed to speak for the people and denounced compromise as [[perfidy|perfidy]]. Far from resolving a hard question, the referendum returned it to legislators in a more poisonous form.

The second condition, freedom to answer, matters most where governments are least trustworthy, yet the recommendation leaves governments in charge of consulting. In 2016, Thailand's military government put its own draft constitution to a vote. The referendum law restricted criticism of the draft, and activists were arrested for distributing leaflets urging a "no" vote. A loaded supplementary question asked whether, for the sake of continuing reform, an appointed Senate should help choose the prime minister during a transition. Both passed, and in 2019 the appointed senators helped keep Prayut Chan-o-cha, leader of the 2014 coup, in power. The junta needed no [[skullduggery|skullduggery]] at the ballot box; it had tilted the contest openly, by law, before anyone voted. The vote let the junta claim popular [[sanction|sanction]] for arrangements designed to entrench it. Switzerland, where citizens can force a national vote on a new law by gathering signatures and both sides campaign freely, shows the corrective: neither the agenda nor the argument belongs to the government alone.

These cases move me from the recommendation's blanket rule to a narrower one. "Major" is the wrong trigger: Britain voted on one of its most consequential postwar choices and Stockholm on a traffic fee, yet only the second asked voters something they could evaluate. Governments should put a question directly to citizens when its consequences can be stated concretely, or, better yet, experienced in advance, and when opponents are as free to campaign as the government is. Under those conditions, a referendum yields something no legislature can manufacture: consent given with eyes open. Without them, it yields only the appearance of consent, which can be more dangerous than no consultation at all.

prompt.statement: People should be judged by their intentions rather than by the outcomes of their actions.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Judging Foresight, Not Bare Intentions
essays.essay:
The strongest case for judging people by their intentions rests on what philosophers call moral luck. Imagine two drivers who leave the same party equally drunk. One reaches home without incident; the other strikes a child who darts into the road. Only the timing of a child's step, which neither driver controlled, separates them, and a verdict that condemns the second far more harshly than the first seems to punish misfortune rather than wrongdoing. Few would [[gainsay|gainsay]] the lesson: actual outcomes are an unreliable gauge of character. Yet the example, examined closely, does not support the statement. It supports a different standard, one that judges people by the consequences they could reasonably foresee and by the care they took to avoid them.

Neither driver, after all, intended to hurt anyone; each meant only to get home. A defender of the statement might reply that choosing to drive drunk itself reflects a culpable state of mind, and that is true. But recklessness cannot be defined without reference to outcomes: it is the willingness to run a foreseeable risk of harm. Once "intention" is stretched to cover what a person foresaw or should have foreseen, it is no longer the alternative to outcomes that the statement proposes. The argument from moral luck therefore shows not that outcomes are beside the point, but that we should weigh the outcomes a person risked rather than only those that happened to occur. By that measure both drivers stand condemned, though only one was unlucky.

The standard is most demanding where a role carries an explicit duty to anticipate consequences, as a journalist's does. In 2014 Rolling Stone published a harrowing account of a gang rape at a University of Virginia fraternity, intended to expose how lightly universities treated sexual assault. By all appearances the reporter and editors acted from conviction, but the story rested almost entirely on one student's account, and the magazine never independently contacted the friends she said she had met that night. Within weeks the account began to unravel. A review by Columbia's journalism school concluded that routine reporting would probably have led editors to reconsider; the magazine retracted the article, and an associate dean it had depicted as indifferent won a defamation suit. The editors' credulity is [[explicable|explicable]], since the story confirmed a pattern they had reason to believe was real. Yet verification exists precisely because conviction is not evidence, and skipping it harmed the very cause the magazine meant to serve, handing anyone inclined to doubt the next victim a ready-made excuse.

Postcolonial Africa shows both the weight of intentions and their limits. Mobutu Sese Seko helped [[oust|oust]] Patrice Lumumba, the prime minister who had made him army chief of staff, and later spent three decades plundering the country he renamed Zaire. Julius Nyerere of Tanzania, by contrast, lived modestly and pursued a sincere vision of rural self-reliance. Both presided over economic decline, yet to equate Nyerere's errors with Mobutu's [[perfidy|perfidy]] would be absurd. Still, Nyerere's sincerity did not protect the farmers his policies uprooted. His ujamaa program sought to gather scattered households into cooperative villages with schools and clinics; when many refused to move, resettlement became compulsory and sometimes forcible, and the disruption contributed to severe food shortages. Because intentions are always [[conjectural|conjectural]], inferred from conduct rather than observed, the clearest evidence of a government's aims is how it responds when the people it means to help resist or suffer. Nyerere's government answered resistance with compulsion, putting loyalty to a design ahead of the farmers it was supposed to benefit.

"It is the thought that counts" is a harmless [[platitude|platitude]] when a birthday gift disappoints; as a rule for judging editors and heads of state, it becomes a license for carelessness. Intentions rightly separate the treacherous from the merely mistaken, and that distinction deserves to survive. But an intention worth calling good includes a serious effort to learn what one's actions will do. People should therefore be judged by what they meant together with what they took the trouble to foresee, and the more power they hold over other lives, the more foresight we are entitled to demand.
