prompt.statement: Free speech must include the right to say things that most people find offensive.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Offense Is Not Injury
essays.essay:
The most serious challenge to this statement is not a plea for good manners. It is the argument that some offensive speech attacks free expression itself: by humiliating and frightening its targets, it drives them from public life, so that protecting the speaker silences the people spoken about. The case usually cited is Skokie, Illinois, a Chicago suburb where many Holocaust survivors had settled. In 1977 a small and [[pugnacious|pugnacious]] neo-Nazi group announced plans to demonstrate there in uniforms bearing swastikas, and the choice of town was widely understood as deliberate. No one can [[gainsay|gainsay]] the anguish of residents who had survived the camps and now faced that spectacle at their own village hall. If the right to offend shelters such a performance, the objection asks, why should a decent society honor it?

I nonetheless agree with the statement, with one qualification: free speech must protect what offends, but not necessarily what injures. The objection runs these together. Offense is a reaction in the listener, and the statement measures it by headcount, by what "most people" find objectionable. Injury is something words do to a particular person. A cross burned on a Black family's lawn to intimidate them may be punished, as the Supreme Court has held, not because most people find it repugnant but because it is a threat delivered to one household. Threats, targeted harassment, and incitement to imminent lawless action can all be restricted without asking how many people they offend. The Skokie demonstration fell on the other side of that line: its message was vile, but it addressed the public in a public place, and residents could stay away. Federal courts struck down the village's ordinances against it, and the group never marched there. That answer will console no survivor. Its claim is narrower: tolerating the demonstration cost less than giving a village council the power to silence whatever it finds too offensive.

That power, not the demonstration, is the real issue, and history gives little reason to trust majorities with it. In 1925 Tennessee made it a crime for public school teachers to teach that humans descended from lower animals. The law reflected a conviction common across the state: that human evolution was not merely mistaken but blasphemous. When a high school teacher, John Scopes, agreed to test the law, he was convicted and fined; the verdict was overturned on a technicality, but the statute stayed on the books for more than four decades. The offense many Tennesseans took was sincere, and its target was what is now the organizing principle of modern biology. A free speech principle that excluded whatever most people find offensive would not merely have tolerated that law; it would have supplied its rationale. Scientific claims that unsettle cherished beliefs routinely provoke [[clamorous|clamorous]] protest, and the volume of protest has never been evidence that the claims were false.

The objection also assumes that the power to suppress offensive speech would serve the vulnerable. In practice it falls to whoever is already in charge. Southern congressmen and their allies found petitions against slavery not merely [[nettlesome|nettlesome]] but offensive and inflammatory, so from 1836 to 1844 the House of Representatives shut them out without debate, first by tabling them on receipt and later by refusing to receive them at all. The speech those rules muffled came from citizens pleading for people who had no right to petition. Anyone [[sanguine|sanguine]] that today's majorities would draw the line more wisely should remember that every majority considers its own sense of offense the decent one.

Free speech, then, must include the right to offend, though not because offense is valuable in itself. Much offensive speech is crude, false, or [[tendentious|tendentious]], and those who invoke the right are seldom heroes. The right must cover them anyway, because a protection extended only to what most people already accept would protect nothing that needed protecting. What it need not cover is speech that works as a weapon against a particular person. Where intimidation ends and mere offense begins will remain a hard question, and courts will sometimes misjudge it. Still, the line belongs at what words do to someone, not at how many people they upset.

prompt.statement: An education that never changes a student's beliefs has failed.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Changing How We Believe, Not What
essays.essay:
Read literally, the statement is false. A student who arrives with sound convictions and leaves holding all of them has not necessarily been failed by her teachers. Read for its spirit, however, the claim is nearly right, provided we distinguish what a person believes from how she believes it. An education that leaves both untouched, so that the graduate holds the same convictions for the same unexamined reasons, has failed, even if every one is true. The change that matters is less often a reversal of opinion than a shift in its grounds.

No life illustrates this distinction more vividly than John Stuart Mill's. His father, James Mill, directed the boy's education with [[sedulous|sedulous]] care and a clear purpose: to raise a champion of Jeremy Bentham's [[utilitarian|utilitarian]] philosophy. Mill began Greek at three, had studied logic and political economy by thirteen, and was publishing in defense of Benthamite reform as a teenager. By every conventional measure the experiment succeeded. Then, at twenty, Mill asked himself whether he would be happy if every reform he had been trained to pursue were accomplished at once, and had to answer no. Months of depression followed.

The collapse is [[explicable|explicable]] in the terms Mill himself later supplied. His education had made him superb at reaching conclusions but had left his attachment to them too weak to withstand scrutiny; relentless analysis, he decided, had worn away the feelings that give convictions their force. He recovered not through a new doctrine but through experiences his training had neglected: a memoir that moved him to tears, and Wordsworth's poetry. He remained a utilitarian and a reformer, but a different one, attentive to the cultivation of feeling and critical of Bentham's narrow view of human nature. Decades later, in On Liberty, he generalized the lesson: even a true opinion, if it is never contested, comes to be held as a "dead dogma." Mill's central conclusions survived his crisis; his way of holding them did not, and that change completed an education his father had left unfinished.

The most compelling objection deserves a full hearing. Education, a thoughtful critic might say, should aim at knowledge and skill, leaving convictions to the student; a teacher who tallies the beliefs she has altered has become a missionary. History shows where that ambition leads. After 1933 the Nazi regime purged teachers, rewrote textbooks, and eventually made membership in the Hitler Youth compulsory, transforming what a generation of young Germans believed about race, nation, and duty. By the statement's test, the Hitler Youth passes easily, while a rigorous course confirming students' accurate beliefs might fail; that test measures the wrong thing.

Much of this I accept: changed conclusions prove nothing by themselves, and a teacher bent on making converts has mistaken her job. Yet the Nazi case confirms the distinction rather than refuting it. The regime changed what young Germans believed but ensured that they held the new beliefs in exactly the wrong way: on authority, as a test of loyalty, with doubt treated as betrayal. Its pupils emerged not more open to revision but more [[intransigent|intransigent]], and many fought for the regime long after its defeat was certain. Mill's crisis made old conclusions answerable to experience; Nazi schooling made new conclusions answerable only to power. The critic's alternative is also unstable: teaching students to weigh evidence while exempting their convictions from the weighing teaches hypocrisy. Nor does my position favor the [[pugnacious|pugnacious]] instructor who treats every inherited conviction as an enemy. The student who arrives convinced that cruelty is wrong should leave convinced still, but able to say why.

The statement, then, mistakes a common symptom for the disease. A curriculum that only confirms what students already think is usually [[soporific|soporific]], and the claim is right to distrust it. The failure, however, lies not in unchanged conclusions but in convictions that were never exposed to the risk of being wrong. An education succeeds when it alters the terms on which a student holds her beliefs, so that each becomes something she can defend and could, given good reason, surrender. Sometimes the surest evidence of such an education is an old belief held in a new way.

prompt.statement: Some people believe that the main purpose of education is to prepare students for work. Others believe that its main purpose is to teach students how to think, whatever work they eventually do.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Judgment Is Built on Particular Material
essays.essay:
It is tempting to dismiss the first view as philistine, but it rests on a point few would [[gainsay|gainsay]]: students enroll, and families pay tuition, in the expectation of a livelihood, and a graduate who reasons elegantly but can do nothing an employer needs has been poorly served. Defenders of the second view reply that jobs change or vanish while the habit of careful reasoning lasts. Both camps, however, assume that a school must choose between preparing students for work and teaching them to think. My own position is closer to the second view, but narrower. Stated abstractly, "teaching students how to think" is a [[platitude|platitude]], praised at every commencement and rarely defined, because no one learns to think in general. Anyone who has sat through a workshop on "critical thinking skills" knows how little such instruction changes the way people reason, and research on the transfer of learning suggests why: reasoning practiced in one domain rarely carries over to an unrelated one. We learn to think about something, and that something is often the material of our eventual work.

American legal education offers a clear illustration. Through much of the nineteenth century, an aspiring lawyer typically apprenticed in a practitioner's office, copying documents and absorbing routines, or memorized rules summarized in lectures. In the 1870s, Christopher Columbus Langdell, dean of Harvard Law School, replaced the lecture with what came to be called the case method. Students read the actual opinions in which appellate judges had resolved disputes and, under persistent questioning, had to extract the governing principles themselves, test them against altered facts, and defend their conclusions. Despite early resistance, the method dominated American law schools by the early twentieth century and still anchors the first-year curriculum.

This history defeats the dichotomy from both directions. Law school is frankly vocational, yet the case method prepares students for a way of reasoning, not a list of tasks. Hours of close reading teach a student to notice which facts a court treated as decisive, to distinguish an unfavorable precedent rather than ignore it, and to anticipate the other side's argument. These habits are not a preliminary to the lawyer's work; they are the work. The judgment that makes a litigator effective, the sense of which argument a skeptical judge will accept and which concession costs nothing, grows from that early discipline, not from a general course in reasoning. The method's blind spot is just as instructive. For generations, practitioners complained that new lawyers could dissect an appellate opinion but had never drafted a contract or counseled a client. That complaint helped [[galvanize|galvanize]] law schools into building clinics where students represent real clients under supervision. Reasoning that never touches practice proved as incomplete as practice that never invites reasoning.

A contrasting case shows where the first view is simply right. An apprentice electrician spends years learning to wire buildings to the National Electrical Code, and no homeowner wants one inclined to reason about grounding from first principles. The code condenses long experience of fires and shocks into rules that [[obviate|obviate]] dangerous trial and error; in such a trade, preparation for specific work is rightly the chief purpose of training. Even so, the first view is incomplete. No code anticipates every century-old house with brittle wiring in its walls; the electrician who opens such a wall must decide how rules written for other circumstances apply here, much as a lawyer fits precedent to new facts. Apprentices learn that judgment not in a seminar but beside a seasoned electrician, on particular jobs.

The first view, then, holds to the degree that a student's future work can be specified in advance and reduced to rules. For some occupations it largely can, and there training for the task properly comes first. For most students, whose eventual work is unknown even to themselves, and for every profession whose problems outrun its rules, the deeper purpose of education is to cultivate judgment. But judgment is never taught in the abstract; it is built through [[sedulous|sedulous]] engagement with particular material, often material that resembles real work. The best schools therefore refuse the choice the statement offers: they teach students to think by giving them something worth thinking about.

prompt.statement: Some believe that people should save for the future even at the expense of present enjoyment. Others believe that people should live fully in the present.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Save What Keeps, Spend What Perishes
essays.essay:
In the Stanford studies known as the marshmallow test, a researcher left a preschooler alone with a choice: ring a bell and eat one small treat at once, or wait for the researcher's return and receive two. Children who held out were later reported to be more academically successful, and the finding hardened into a parable about the rewards of deferral. Decades later, researchers at the University of Rochester added a twist. Children whose experimenter had just broken a promise of better art supplies gave in far sooner than those whose experimenter had kept it; for them, eating the treat was not weakness but sound inference. The test, in other words, may measure trust in the future as well as self-control, and that is the right lens for this debate. The view that we should save even at some cost to present enjoyment comes closer to my own, but only in a refined form: we should defer pleasure when the future reward is reasonably secure and the present good will keep, and seize the present when the opportunity is perishable.

The case for living in the present deserves more respect than its critics grant. At its best, it is not a license for an [[indolent|indolent]], pleasure-seeking life but an observation that some goods cannot be banked. Money deposited at thirty can be withdrawn at sixty; an afternoon with a four-year-old cannot. The years when a child begs for a parent's company, when one's knees can handle a mountain trail, when an aging mother still recognizes her son: such seasons are [[evanescent|evanescent]], and no account balance will buy them back. Moreover, the saver's arithmetic rests on assumptions about the future that are [[conjectural|conjectural]] at best. Illness, layoffs, and early death do not consult anyone's retirement plan, and a person who postpones every pleasure for a distant payoff may, like the Rochester children whose promised art supplies never arrived, be waiting on a promise that will never be kept.

Even so, I side with the savers, because the uncertainty that the present-minded invoke is the best argument for a reserve. The illnesses and layoffs that may cancel a distant reward can also strike next month, and a family with [[scant|scant]] savings lives fully in the present only until the first missed paycheck or broken transmission; after that, the present is consumed by high-interest debt and dread. Savings, in this sense, are less a gift to one's older self than a shield for the current one. The sacrifice is also smaller than it looks. The thrill of a new phone or a bigger car fades quickly, a pattern psychologists call hedonic adaptation, so much of what saving costs is pleasure that would have evaporated anyway. What prudence usually asks us to give up is not joy but its short-lived imitation.

The law shows how institutions can make the future more trustworthy. In American bankruptcy, debtors can generally shield much of their retirement savings from creditors, so a nest egg built through years of restraint survives a single financial collapse. Yet bankruptcy judges also grant a discharge that erases many remaining debts, giving the honest debtor what courts have long called a fresh start rather than years of garnished wages. The law thus secures a floor beneath the future while refusing to sentence the present to endless repayment. It acts like the reliable adult in the Rochester study: it keeps its promise to the saver without demanding that a whole life be spent on yesterday's obligations.

The deeper flaw in the debate is its assumption that saving and enjoyment are rivals. Often they are not. A daily walk and a home-cooked dinner cost little and give pleasure at once, yet their [[salubrious|salubrious]] effects accumulate over decades. Where the two aims genuinely collide, the rule a [[sagacious|sagacious]] person follows is simple: save what keeps, and spend what does not. Put money away, because money will wait; do not postpone the trip with an aging parent or a child's bedtime story, because those will not. Understood this way, living fully in the present is not the opposite of prudence but one of the things prudence is for.

prompt.statement: Some argue that the news media should present only facts and leave interpretation to readers. Others argue that the media have a duty to explain what the facts mean.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Interpretation Is Unavoidable, So Make It Visible
essays.essay:
The argument that the news media should present only facts rests on an assumption that rarely survives scrutiny: that facts can be conveyed without interpretation at all. Every news report reflects choices about which facts to include, which to lead with, and what to call them, and such choices are interpretive. For that reason, the second view comes closer to my own position, with one qualification. The media's real duty is not simply to explain what facts mean but to keep those explanations visible, so that readers can see where reporting ends and inference begins.

The case for leaving interpretation to readers deserves a serious hearing, because it springs from a legitimate fear. A newsroom that sees itself as an explainer can slide into [[tendentious|tendentious]] coverage, deciding what a story means before the evidence is in and arranging the facts to fit. Coverage of the bombing at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics is a sobering case. Within days, news outlets reported that the security guard who had spotted the unattended backpack was under FBI scrutiny, and the reporting soon hardened into a tale of [[perfidy|perfidy]]: a guard who had supposedly planted the bomb so that he could be hailed for finding it. The theory was entirely [[conjectural|conjectural]]. The guard was never charged, and another man eventually pleaded guilty to the attack. Yet the episode does not vindicate the facts-only view as neatly as it seems. The report that set off the frenzy did not hand readers a bare fact: beside the true news that investigators suspected him, it asserted that he fit the profile of a lone bomber, an inference delivered in the flat voice of fact. What wronged him was not explanation but interpretation disguised as reporting, and the bare fact alone would likely have invited the same conclusion. He needed honest explanation, beginning with the reminder that suspicion is not evidence.

Bare facts mislead partly because they are never as bare as they look, a point sports fans grasp better than most. Even the box score, perhaps the most fact-bound form in journalism, embeds judgments: an official scorer decides whether a misplayed ball counts as a hit or an error, and that ruling can change a pitcher's earned run average. Accurate statistics can also mislead when no one explains them. For decades, hitters were judged chiefly by batting average and runs batted in, although the first ignores walks and the second depends on teammates reaching base. The Oakland Athletics of the early 2000s won consistently on one of baseball's smallest payrolls. Part of that success is readily [[explicable|explicable]]: the club had three superb young starting pitchers. But Michael Lewis's Moneyball showed a broad readership another cause: Oakland bought on-base percentage cheaply because the market undervalued it, as analysts such as Bill James had argued for years. The numbers had been public all along; what most fans lacked was someone to explain them.

Withholding explanation is not neutrality, and in education the cost is easy to see. When a newspaper ranks a city's schools by average test scores, no one can [[gainsay|gainsay]] the numbers themselves. Yet many readers skim the list and conclude that the highest-ranked schools teach best. Research since the Coleman Report of 1966 has found that such averages closely track students' family backgrounds, so a ranking printed without that context endorses a misleading inference by omission. Explaining what the scores measure, and what they cannot, is not an editorial indulgence but part of reporting them accurately. Here, however, the first view earns its due, because explanation carries obligations of its own. It should be labeled as explanation, show its reasoning, and admit what evidence would overturn it, so that readers keep the very independence that the facts-only camp rightly prizes.

The decisive line, then, runs not between facts and interpretation but between interpretation that announces itself and interpretation that hides inside an apparently neutral account. A press that declines to explain does not leave readers free; it leaves them alone with inferences that headlines, rankings, and omissions have already shaped. The better course is to explain openly, mark the limits of what is known, and trust readers to argue back.

prompt.statement:
Claim: Laws should expire automatically unless they are renewed.
Reason: Laws that no one reviews outlive the problems they were written to solve.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Legislative Inertia Needs Review, Not Expiration
essays.essay:
The reason offered here is largely true, but it supports a far more modest conclusion than the claim. Statutes do outlive the circumstances that produced them, because repealing a law takes effort and leaving it alone takes none. Automatic expiration, however, is a costly remedy for that inertia. It assumes that a deadline will make legislators rethink a law, when it may only make them reenact it, and that we can tell when a problem has been solved. Sunset clauses suit laws written for an emergency; as a universal rule, they would exchange the dead weight of obsolete law for the constant threat of obstruction.

The reason deserves more credit than defenders of legal stability usually give it. In 1879 Connecticut made it a crime to use contraception. By the mid-twentieth century the law was rarely enforced, yet reformers failed for decades to persuade the legislature to repeal it, and it took the Supreme Court, in Griswold v. Connecticut (1965), to bar its enforcement against married couples. In a legislature the status quo wins ties: a law needs no majority to survive, only the absence of a majority to kill it. An expiration date would have reversed that burden, and might have [[obviated|obviate]] the long repeal campaign: the law's defenders, not its critics, would have needed the votes.

Even if the reason is granted, it does not establish the claim, because a deadline forces lawmakers to renew or abandon a law, not to rethink it. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 required certain jurisdictions to obtain federal approval before changing election rules, a temporary requirement that Congress renewed several times, most recently in 2006. Lawmakers were hardly [[indolent|indolent]] during that renewal; they held extensive hearings and compiled a voluminous record of continuing discrimination. Yet they reenacted, unchanged, the formula that decided which jurisdictions were covered, though it rested on data from the 1960s and early 1970s. In Shelby County v. Holder (2013), the Supreme Court struck the formula down on essentially the ground this reason offers: it reflected conditions that no longer prevailed. The case also exposes the reason's hidden assumption. The dissent countered that discrimination had receded precisely because preclearance was working, and events soon lent that argument force: within months North Carolina enacted a sweeping election law that a federal appeals court later found was designed to disadvantage Black voters. When a law prevents a harm, the harm's absence can look like proof that the law is obsolete, and the gains such a law secures may prove [[evanescent|evanescent]] once its protection is removed, whether by a court or by expiration.

Judged on its own merits, the claim faces a further objection: automatic expiration hands leverage to whoever is willing to let a law die. Where forty-one senators can block a bill by filibuster, every expiring statute becomes a hostage, and an [[intransigent|intransigent]] faction could repeal by obstruction what it could never repeal by vote. The debt ceiling, though a borrowing limit rather than a sunset clause, shows such leverage at work: the 2011 standoff prompted the first downgrade of the federal government's credit rating by a major agency. Deadlines also invite [[skullduggery|skullduggery]]: provisions that could never survive open debate can be slipped into a hurried renewal bill that few members have read and none can afford to defeat.

The defensible position, then, is narrower: automatic expiration fits laws born of a crisis, such as the statute Congress passed weeks after September 11 to expand surveillance. Several of its powers were written to lapse, and a 2015 deadline, arriving after leaks had exposed the bulk collection of Americans' telephone records, gave reformers the leverage to end the practice. In such cases the claim holds, but for a reason other than the one offered: not because unreviewed laws linger, but because emergency powers rest on a forecast that may prove wrong. For such powers, the leverage that makes expiration dangerous elsewhere becomes a safeguard. For other laws, the reason justifies only mandatory review that requires lawmakers to explain why a statute still serves its purpose. A law should be made to justify its continued existence, not forced to survive a deadline that rewards whoever most wants it gone.

prompt.statement:
Claim: People should stop following the news for several weeks each year.
Reason: Constant exposure to news distorts people's sense of how dangerous the world is.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Proportion, Not Silence, Corrects the News
essays.essay:
Many American parents who roamed freely as children now hesitate to let their own children walk alone to a friend's house. Asked why, they rarely cite local crime figures; more often they recall a televised abduction from some distant town, replayed until it felt like a threat next door. Yet abductions by strangers remain rare, while far more common dangers to children, such as car crashes and drowning, seldom reach the national news. This familiar pattern makes the reason behind the claim hard to dismiss: constant exposure to news does warp people's sense of danger. I accept that reason, with one amendment, but I reject the remedy built on it. A yearly blackout addresses how often people follow the news, when the trouble lies in what the news selects and how audiences read it.

The reason holds because news is, almost by definition, a record of the unusual. A plane crash is reported; the thousands of uneventful flights that day are not. A newscast is [[profuse|profuse]] in its warnings and stingy with its denominators: it tells viewers that one child was taken, not how many millions came home safely. Through much of a long decline in American crime, most people told pollsters that crime was rising nationwide while judging their own neighborhoods far more calmly; they knew their streets through experience and the nation through the news. But the reason, as stated, is incomplete. News does not simply make the world seem more dangerous; it relocates danger. It magnifies the vivid and rare, such as terrorism and shark attacks, while the [[mundane|mundane]] hazards that kill far more people, such as heart disease and traffic accidents, almost never lead a broadcast. The distortion is one of misallocation as much as magnitude.

That amendment explains why a periodic blackout is the wrong cure. If the problem were sheer volume, silence might restore judgment. But a reader who spends a few weeks without news does not emerge with better denominators; she returns to the same stream with the same habits, and whatever calm the break produced proves [[evanescent|evanescent]]. The courts, which have long accepted that publicity can corrupt judgment, offer an instructive contrast. In Sheppard v. Maxwell, the Supreme Court ruled that an Ohio physician convicted of murder had been denied a fair trial: a [[clamorous|clamorous]] local press had campaigned for his arrest and presumed his guilt, and the trial judge had done too little to keep that publicity from the jurors. The law's remedy, however, is narrow. Judges instruct jurors to avoid coverage of their case and, in extreme cases, sequester them, because a verdict must rest only on evidence admitted in court. No judge orders the public to stop reading newspapers. Abstention works when it protects a specific judgment from a specific contamination; imposed on everyone once a year, it protects nothing in particular.

None of this means a break from the news is worthless. A few weeks away may well prove [[salubrious|salubrious]], though for reasons that have little to do with risk: rest, attention reclaimed from an [[omnipresent|omnipresent]] phone, and time for the people and problems within one's reach. That is a different argument, and it supports a personal choice rather than a general prescription. As a rule for everyone, moreover, the claim ignores those who cannot afford to look away. A family in a hurricane's path or a nurse during an outbreak cannot responsibly go dark; sometimes the danger on the screen is real and near. Someone worried about distortion would do better to change the diet than to fast: drop [[tendentious|tendentious]] outlets that inflate threats to serve a cause, read rather than scroll, and ask of every alarming story how often such things happen.

What emerges is a split verdict. The reason identifies a genuine flaw but understates it: the news distorts not only how dangerous the world seems but where its dangers appear to lie. The claim answers that flaw with the bluntest instrument available. Silence cannot teach proportion, and proportion is what the overexposed reader lacks. What corrects the picture is not a few weeks of ignorance each year but a daily habit of setting every vivid story beside the ordinary numbers it leaves out.

prompt.statement: Governments should pay students a small monthly allowance for staying in school until they complete secondary education.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Stipends Work Only When Precisely Aimed
essays.essay:
In rural Bangladesh, many girls once left school around puberty, often to be married. A modest stipend for secondary schoolgirls, piloted in the early 1980s and extended across the countryside in the 1990s, was paid only if they attended regularly, earned satisfactory marks, and remained unmarried. Female enrollment climbed until girls outnumbered boys in secondary classrooms, a gain researchers credit only partly to the stipend; new schools and garment jobs also mattered. Such a record makes the proposed policy look obvious, but the stipend helped because it was aimed at a specific obstacle; an allowance for every student might not. I support paying students to stay in school, but only as a targeted, conditional measure coupled with investment in the schools themselves, and it is the policy's likely consequences, intended and unintended, that impose these limits.

The strongest case for the allowance begins by correcting an assumption. Skeptics tend to picture the dropout as [[indolent|indolent]], someone the state must now bribe into a classroom, but in poor households the reality is usually the reverse. A teenage girl leaves school because her family needs her wages or her labor, or because an early marriage relieves the household of a dependent. Bangladesh's marriage condition was designed to [[forestall|forestall]] precisely that outcome. Mexico's Progresa program tested this logic in the late 1990s. It paid poor rural mothers whose children stayed in school, offered larger grants at the secondary level, where the pull of work grows strongest, and introduced benefits first in randomly selected villages. Comparisons with villages still awaiting the program showed enrollment rising most sharply at the transition to secondary school, exactly where the allowance offset the greatest sacrifice. The results [[galvanized|galvanize]] governments as far away as the Philippines and Indonesia into launching similar programs. For such families the allowance is not a bribe but compensation, and its power to keep their children in school is why I favor the policy at all.

The policy as stated, however, would pay students without distinction, and here the consequences grow less benign. An [[indiscriminate|indiscriminate]] allowance would flow mostly to families whose children would have finished school anyway, so much of its cost would buy no change in behavior. Even means-tested programs face this charge. England's Education Maintenance Allowance, which paid poorer teenagers to stay in education after sixteen, was scrapped in the early 2010s partly on the grounds that most recipients would have stayed without it. Fair or not, the argument carried the day, revealing a second danger: a program that cannot show it changes behavior soon loses political support. Waste is thus not merely an accounting problem; it endangers help for the students who truly need it. I would therefore confine the allowance to regions and groups where dropout rates show that staying in school carries a real cost.

A subtler consequence concerns what the money buys. A payment tied to attendance rewards the merely present student exactly as it rewards the [[sedulous|sedulous]] one, and reviews of cash-transfer programs worldwide have found that they raise enrollment far more reliably than test scores. A stipend can fill a classroom; it cannot make the lesson worth attending, and no allowance [[obviates|obviate]] the need for trained teachers and adequate materials. Finally, any benefit keyed to a register invites [[skullduggery|skullduggery]], from headmasters padding their rolls with phantom pupils to families enrolling children who seldom appear. Such abuses do not justify abandoning the policy, but they demand independent audits and payments tied to progress as well as presence, as Bangladesh's requirement of satisfactory marks recognized.

The consequences, then, do not argue against paying students; they argue for paying the right students for the right things. Directed at households for whom a teenager's schooling is a genuine sacrifice, conditioned on attendance and achievement, and financed alongside better teaching, a small monthly allowance can change lives at modest cost, as it helped to do for a generation of Bangladeshi girls. Paid to everyone and verified by no one, the same allowance would mostly reward what families were already doing and fill classrooms that teach too little. The value of the idea lies less in the payment than in the precision of its aim.

prompt.statement: Every country should guarantee its citizens free access to the internet.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: A Right Held Against the State
essays.essay:
Few would [[gainsay|gainsay]] the claim that a person without internet access is now at a disadvantage. Such a person cannot easily apply for many jobs or reach public services and, where the press is captive, cannot read news that has not first passed through official hands. Politicians of every stripe are accordingly [[profuse|profuse]] in their praise of "digital inclusion." Yet the statement rests on two assumptions worth examining: that free access is the same thing as open access, and that whoever guarantees access will be content to leave it alone. I support guaranteeing free access to the open internet, but only if the guarantee restrains the state as well as obliging it to pay. It is the policy's likely consequences, intended and otherwise, that lead me to attach that condition.

The strongest argument for the policy is civic rather than economic. In December 2010, a young street vendor in Sidi Bouzid, a poor town in Tunisia's neglected interior, set himself on fire after local officials confiscated his produce. Tunisia's tightly controlled press said little, but residents used their phones to film the protests that followed and posted the footage to Facebook, where Al Jazeera found it and broadcast it back into the country. The images [[galvanized|galvanize]] Tunisians in cities far from Sidi Bouzid, and within a month President Ben Ali had fled. What mattered was not that Tunisians could shop or stream online but that ordinary people, once connected, could report what official media would not. A guarantee of free access would extend that capacity to the rural and the poor, precisely the citizens a market left to itself serves last.

The word "free," however, raises a [[nettlesome|nettlesome]] question that would return with every budget: who pays? If the state does not, someone else will, and that payer will expect something in return. Facebook's Free Basics program, rolled out in dozens of developing countries, gave mobile users free access to a menu of services admitted under Facebook's rules, with Facebook prominent among them. In India, critics argued that free access to a curated corner of the web is not access to the internet at all, and that the arrangement let one foreign company decide which sites the poor would see; in 2016 the national telecom regulator banned such differential pricing, ending the program there. A country that guarantees free access on the cheap invites exactly this substitution. The guarantee is worth having only if it covers the open internet, which means the public must bear the cost, whether by subsidizing users or providers, rather than leaving the bill to a sponsor who will want to set the menu.

A second consequence is less obvious and more dangerous: the more a government pays for a network, the more firmly it is likely to hold the off switch. In January 2011, as protesters filled Cairo, the Mubarak government ordered Egypt's providers to cut nearly all internet traffic for about five days. Ugandan authorities shut down access on the eve of the 2021 presidential election. Shutdowns timed to elections are a modern instrument of electoral fraud: they need not touch a single ballot, yet they make it far harder for reports of intimidation or [[skullduggery|skullduggery]] at the polls to spread widely. Both governments acted through their power over licensed providers; a state that also financed, and perhaps owned, the country's free connections would find the switch even closer at hand. Any guarantee must therefore be written as a limit on government as well as a promise from it, forbidding shutdowns without the [[sanction|sanction]] of an independent court and keeping the network's daily operation at arm's length from whoever holds power.

My answer, then, is a conditional yes. Free access deserves a guarantee, but the guarantee means something only if it is a right citizens hold against their governments rather than a service governments dispense and withdraw at will. Defined that way, as open access that is publicly financed and legally shielded from shutdown, it would put within every citizen's reach the capacity that let Tunisians with phones help topple an autocrat. Defined loosely, it would hand a corporation or a state the power to decide what a nation may read, and when.

lavish in expressing something; politicians praise digital inclusion freely, even excessively.
jolted people into sudden, vigorous action; the footage stirred Tunisians elsewhere to protest.
troublesome and recurring; the question of who pays keeps causing difficulty every budget.
underhanded, deceitful dealing at the polls, used to gain an electoral advantage.
official permission or approval; a shutdown is allowed only if an independent court approves it.
words.def: 1. a threatened penalty for disobeying a law or rule. 2. official permission or approval for an action.

analysis.verdict: This response earns a 6 because its position is insightful as well as clear. It exposes two assumptions hidden in the statement and makes its support depend on them. Its two main examples, Tunisia and Free Basics in India, are developed far enough to show what happened and why it matters for the policy, and the language is precise, varied, and error-free.
analysis.position: The first paragraph commits to a qualified yes: it backs "free access to the open internet," but only if "the guarantee restrains the state as well as obliging it to pay." The condition grows out of two named assumptions, so the position takes on the issue's complexity from the start.
analysis.development: Each body paragraph pairs one consequence with concrete evidence: Tunisia shows the civic benefit, Free Basics shows what cheap "free" access becomes, and two brief shutdown cases, Egypt and Uganda, show the state's off switch. Each paragraph ends with its lesson for the policy, such as the point that a guarantee would extend the capacity to report "to the rural and the poor."
analysis.organization: Paragraph 2 grants the policy its strongest case. The two assumptions named in paragraph 1 then become the subjects of paragraphs 3 and 4. Transitions carry the logic: "however" turns from benefit to cost, and "A second consequence is less obvious and more dangerous" raises the stakes.
analysis.language: The diction is exact ("a curated corner of the web", "a modern instrument of electoral fraud"), and sentences range from the blunt seven-word "My answer, then, is a conditional yes." to long, balanced constructions. Target words sit in standard collocations: "profuse in their praise", "a nettlesome question", "skullduggery at the polls", "the sanction of an independent court".
analysis.task: The instruction asks how the policy's consequences shape the position, and the essay shows this openly. Each body paragraph ends by stating what its consequence means for the policy ("The guarantee is worth having only if it covers the open internet"; "Any guarantee must therefore be written as a limit on government"). The conclusion then combines those conditions into the final answer.

paragraphs.note: Two brief cases, Egypt and Uganda, show governments cutting access when it matters most; a state that paid for access could hold the switch more firmly. The paragraph turns this into legal limits on shutdowns.

paragraphs.role: Refined position: a right against the state
paragraphs.note: Restates the answer as a conditional yes in new words. Ends by recalling both risks at once: a corporation or a state deciding what a nation may read, and when.

Its examples would be named rather than developed, and the consequences would sit beside the position instead of reshaping it. It would rarely question what "free" means or notice that the guarantor could also become the censor.

prompt.statement: The more information people have, the harder it becomes for them to make good decisions.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: The Problem Is Sorting, Not Abundance
essays.essay:
The statement treats "information" as a single quantity, as if it could be weighed by the pound. In practice the word covers two things. Raw information is the unsorted stream of claims, rumors, and data that reaches a person; organized information is the same material, checked for reliability and arranged around a specific question. The distinction matters because the statement is largely true of the first and largely false of the second. More information does make good decisions harder when its volume [[outstrips|outstrip]] anyone's capacity to sort it; when information arrives already structured around a decision, however, more of it usually produces better choices. The enemy of judgment is not abundance but the absence of a filter.

Brazil's 2018 presidential election shows raw information at its most corrosive. Television still mattered, but WhatsApp groups became a major channel of persuasion, and in them Brazilians received a daily [[hodgepodge|hodgepodge]] of genuine news clips, partisan memes, doctored images, and voice messages of unknown origin. Researchers who studied widely shared images in public groups found many false or misleading. Voters did not lack information; they were saturated with it. A forwarded message carries no reliable mark of where it began, so a fabricated video and a newspaper report arrive looking equally authoritative. Each additional message added not knowledge but work. When claims cannot be checked, people fall back on cruder cues, such as who forwarded a message or whether it flatters their own side. Here the statement holds, and for a precise reason: the medium had [[severed|sever]] information from the editors and sources that once vouched for it.

Nigeria's response to Ebola in 2014 shows the opposite. When an infected traveler collapsed in Lagos, the case seemed to [[portend|portend]] an urban epidemic. Officials demanded more information, not less: teams traced hundreds of exposed people and set out to check each one daily for three weeks. For the epidemiologists running the response, every daily check answered a question posed in advance: has this contact developed a fever, and if so, who must be isolated next? The data flowed into an emergency operations center built on the staff and systems of Nigeria's polio program, so reports reached people trained to verify them and charged with acting on them. The system was not airtight: one contact slipped out of monitoring and carried the virus to Port Harcourt. Tellingly, that lapse came from too little information, not too much, and the same system then traced the new cluster. The outbreak was held to about twenty cases, and the World Health Organization declared Nigeria free of Ebola that October. Far from paralyzing anyone, each new observation sharpened the next decision.

Set side by side, the two cases explain why my agreement is so narrow. Brazilian voters and Nigerian epidemiologists were both flooded with information; what separated them was whether anyone had sorted it first. I therefore reject the remedy the statement implies. If abundance itself were the danger, the cure would be to restrict what people may know. Rationing information might leave them less [[befuddled|befuddled]], but it would not make them better informed: it removes precisely the checks that expose error and hands the sorting to whoever controls the supply. The better answer is to rebuild filters. During the campaign, a coalition of newsrooms called Comprova pooled reporters to check viral claims, restoring part of the editorial function the messaging apps had stripped away. Individuals can build filters too: a [[circumspect|circumspect]] reader, one who treats every unsourced claim as doubtful until a credible outlet confirms it, can ignore most of what crosses her screen at little cost.

The statement, then, mistakes a failure of organization for a surplus of information. More information [[hampers|hamper]] judgment only when it arrives faster than any person or institution can sort it. Where that condition holds, as it did on Brazilian phones in 2018, the statement describes the experience accurately but misnames its cause. Where it does not, as in the Lagos operations center, more information is simply more evidence, and evidence is what good decisions are made from. The useful question is not how much information people have but whether anyone has sorted it before they must act.

words.def: 1. divide by cutting or slicing, especially suddenly and forcibly. 2. put an end to (a connection or relationship); break off.

words.meaning_here: signal coming danger; the single case looked like a warning of a citywide epidemic

It reframes the prompt by separating raw information from organized information and argues that the deciding variable is filtering, not volume. Both examples are developed down to their mechanisms (even the Lagos response's one lapse becomes evidence for the thesis), and the prose is precise and varied, with no errors that obscure meaning.

Nigeria shows why more data helped ("every daily check answered a question posed in advance"), and even its lapse "came from too little information, not too much."

Paragraph 2 tests raw information, paragraph 3 tests organized information, and paragraph 4 compares them ("the two cases explain why my agreement is so narrow"). Paragraphs 2 and 3 each end by saying what their case proves ("Here the statement holds, and for a precise reason"; "each new observation sharpened the next decision").

Contrasts such as "added not knowledge but work" sharpen the argument without ornament.

prompt.statement: A city is defined more by its ordinary neighborhoods than by its famous landmarks.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Landmarks Record, Neighborhoods Decide
essays.essay:
The strongest case against the statement is Hiroshima. Few people outside Japan could describe a single Hiroshima street, yet the skeletal dome left standing near the hypocenter of the 1945 atomic bombing is internationally famous. The city has embraced that identity: it built a memorial park at its heart, and every August its mayor reads a peace declaration addressed to the world. To call Hiroshima a city defined chiefly by its residential districts would be perverse. Where a landmark embodies an event or a faith larger than the city itself, as the dome does, or as the Kaaba does for Mecca, the landmark is the definition, and the statement fails.

Yet notice what kind of definition the dome supplies. It tells the world what Hiroshima means; it says almost nothing about how the city lives, works, or renews itself. Even that meaning is borrowed from ordinary life. The dome was an exhibition hall for the prefecture's products, and the memorial park was laid over Nakajima, a busy downtown neighborhood destroyed in a single morning. The ruin moves visitors because it stands in for ordinary streets and the people who filled them. This exposes the assumption hidden in the statement's [[dichotomy|dichotomy]]: that landmarks and neighborhoods compete for the same role. They do not. A landmark can fix what a city means to outsiders, but only its neighborhoods determine whether it remains a living city, and when the two pull apart, the neighborhoods decide the city's fate. I therefore agree with the statement for the city as a place people inhabit, and reject it only for the rare city whose landmark stands for something larger than the city.

Venice shows what happens when a city keeps its landmarks and loses its neighborhoods. St. Mark's Basilica and the Rialto Bridge are restored, and millions of visitors photograph them every year. Headlines dwell on [[boorish|boorish]] tourists who picnic on church steps or swim in the canals, but the deeper loss is quieter. Since the 1950s the historic center has lost most of its residents, first to modern housing and jobs on the mainland and more recently to tourism: apartments have become short-term rentals, and grocers and hardware stores have given way to souvenir shops. Once the crowds leave each evening, whole quarters go dark, their shutters closed because no one lives behind them. The city has even begun charging day-trippers an entry fee on its busiest days, as a museum would. Nothing that appears on a postcard has vanished, yet Venice as a city is plainly [[waning|wane]]. If landmarks defined a city, Venice would be thriving.

Shenzhen offers the reverse case. It has no landmark most of the world could name, yet few modern cities have a sharper identity. When China designated it a special economic zone in 1980, it was a [[somnolent|somnolent]], largely rural border area. Within four decades its economic output had surpassed that of neighboring Hong Kong, and it had become one of the world's chief centers of electronics design and manufacturing. What defines it is not a tower but a district like Huaqiangbei, where multistory markets house a [[hodgepodge|hodgepodge]] of stalls selling capacitors, circuit boards, and phone screens. That density has made the district remarkably [[fecund|fecund]] ground for invention: an engineer can sketch a device in the morning, buy its parts a few blocks away by afternoon, and hold a working prototype within days, a pace that draws hardware start-ups from abroad. Shenzhen is defined by ordinary, unglamorous blocks, and the definition is accurate.

These cases mark the boundary of the statement rather than refuting it. Hiroshima persuades me to limit the claim; Venice and Shenzhen persuade me to keep it. A landmark defines a city only when the city has become, above all, the keeper of something the wider world needs to remember or revere, and even in Hiroshima the landmark draws its force from the ordinary life it commemorates. Everywhere else, a city is what its neighborhoods sustain: the trades they shelter, the inventions they make possible, the [[comity|comity]] that lets residents and visitors share the same streets. Landmarks record what a city has been; its ordinary streets decide what it will become.

prompt.statement: A government's legitimacy depends more on what it achieves than on how it was chosen.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Selection Confers Legitimacy; Results Test It
essays.essay:
After the 2000 election, Americans spent five weeks arguing about hanging chads while comedians made [[mordant|mordant]] jokes about a democracy that could not count its ballots. When the Supreme Court halted the Florida recount, Al Gore, despite winning more votes nationwide, conceded. He disagreed with the Court but accepted its decision; he did not [[repudiate|repudiate]] the result. George W. Bush took office having accomplished nothing as president, yet most Americans who resented the outcome accepted his right to govern. The episode exposes what the statement overlooks: a government must be obeyed before it has achieved anything, so its initial legitimacy can rest only on how it was chosen. I therefore largely disagree: selection grants a government its authority, and achievement decides, within limits, whether that authority survives.

The statement does hold when a government fails at tasks nearly every citizen considers basic. Fernando de la Rúa won Argentina's presidency fairly in 1999, inheriting a recession that deepened into a financial crisis by late 2001. To halt a bank run, his government sharply limited withdrawals, cutting people off from their savings. Crowds filled the streets chanting that every politician should go, dozens died, and de la Rúa resigned, leaving the presidential palace by helicopter. His mandate was impeccable, and the recession's origins under his predecessor partly [[exculpated|exculpate]] him; neither fact saved him. When a government cannot safeguard savings, secure food supplies, or keep people safe, few citizens care how it was chosen, because such failures are judged by a standard everyone shares.

The opposite case is more revealing. Augusto Pinochet seized power in Chile in a 1973 coup, and by the late 1980s his regime could boast a strong economic recovery. In a 1988 plebiscite on extending his rule, the regime campaigned on that record, yet a majority voted no. Economics mattered, since many poor Chileans had seen little of the recovery; to them, the regime's proudest achievement was hardly an achievement. But for many voters, growth did not excuse a regime that had killed or disappeared thousands of its opponents. More telling still, the regime had written this vote into its own 1980 constitution, itself approved in a plebiscite few observers considered fair. A government confident that results alone confer legitimacy would not have bothered with ballots; Pinochet's did, which suggests that its architects believed their rule needed the appearance of consent.

The law builds the same priority into its rules. American courts ordinarily enforce foreign judgments as a matter of [[comity|comity]], without retrying the case, but not judgments from systems lacking impartial tribunals or due process. A federal appeals court refused to enforce a judgment from Liberia's courts during its civil war; it asked not whether the judgment was correct but whether those courts could then be trusted to decide fairly.

Process carries this weight because the statement rests on a false hidden assumption: that citizens agree on what counts as achievement. In a divided society they rarely do. A tax cut is a triumph to one voter and a betrayal to another; performance cannot win the loser's consent, but a fair procedure can, by giving him reason to accept a result he dislikes. Authority resting on results alone is also brittle. Most of us have seen a self-appointed leader run a project: others follow her while things go well, but at her first misstep, people who have been exchanging [[furtive|furtive]] glances object openly, and everyone remembers that no one chose her. Singapore and the Gulf monarchies, which lean heavily on performance, seem to contradict this, yet neither rests on results alone: Singapore's ruling party keeps winning elections, and the monarchies invoke dynastic tradition. Performance sustains their authority; it did not create it.

Argentina and Chile thus fix the limits of my position. When a government fails to provide what everyone needs, performance can [[supersede|supersede]] pedigree; when a regime that seized power asks to be judged by its record, even a respectable record may not redeem it. Between those extremes, where most politics takes place, legitimacy rests chiefly on selection, because a fair choice is the only ground winners and losers can share. Results can strip a government of its standing, but they can rarely confer it.

prompt.statement: Young researchers should choose the most important problem in their field rather than the problem they are most likely to solve.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Choose the Important Problem When It Ripens
essays.essay:
The recommendation flatters ambition, and ambition deserves some flattery: fields advance when someone attacks their central questions rather than their margins. Yet the advice rests on a hidden assumption, namely that importance and solvability are fixed properties of a problem and pull in opposite directions. In fact, solvability depends on when a problem is attempted and with what tools. I therefore accept the recommendation only conditionally. A young researcher should commit to the most important problem when a new method or new evidence has made it tractable, and should otherwise choose a solvable problem on the road to the important one.

The mathematician Andrew Wiles illustrates both branches of this position. As a boy, Wiles read about Fermat's Last Theorem, a deceptively simple claim that had defeated mathematicians for more than three centuries, and resolved to prove it. As a doctoral student, however, he chose not to pursue it and, on his supervisor's advice, studied elliptic curves. Had he followed the recommendation then, he would probably have spent his formative years on a problem no one knew how to approach and emerged with nothing. This is the circumstance in which the advice does real harm: the problem is famous largely because every available method has failed against it. Wiles's choice was [[circumspect|circumspect]] rather than timid, and elliptic curves, a [[fecund|fecund]] area of number theory, made his reputation.

Then the problem changed around him. In 1986 Ken Ribet proved that Fermat's Last Theorem would follow from an unproved conjecture about elliptic curves. The most celebrated open problem in mathematics became a problem in Wiles's specialty, and a more important one, since solving it now meant tackling a central conjecture of the field. At last the recommendation and prudence pointed the same way. Wiles worked largely in secret for about seven years, announced a proof in 1993, and repaired a serious gap the following year with Richard Taylor. The timing was [[felicitous|felicitous]], but he could exploit it only because he had spent a decade in the field through which the problem now ran; though he had to learn new techniques, the idea that closed the gap drew on his early training. The wise early choice, then, was neither option the recommendation offers: it was a tractable problem adjacent to the important one, followed by full commitment once the two converged.

A contrasting case tests whether this position is merely a counsel of caution. In 1951 James Watson, then in his early twenties, and Francis Crick, still a doctoral student, set out to solve the structure of DNA, which Watson believed held the secret of heredity. Here, following the recommendation was plainly advantageous. Their first attempt, a hasty model built partly on a figure Watson misremembered from a seminar, failed embarrassingly, and their laboratory director told them to leave DNA to others. The humiliation proved [[salutary|salutary]]: returning to DNA early in 1953, they took the evidence more seriously, above all Rosalind Franklin's X-ray images and Erwin Chargaff's base ratios. They [[eschewed|eschew]] experiments of their own and built models from evidence others had gathered; within weeks they had the double helix. Why did audacity succeed here when it would have failed Wiles as a student? Because, by the time they returned, the problem was ripe: the decisive evidence existed, and Crick had already helped work out how a helix scatters X-rays. Unlike Fermat's theorem, DNA's structure was elusive because data were still arriving, not because generations had failed, and the premature first attempt cost the pair embarrassment, not a career.

Far from refuting my position, the contrast sharpens it: the recommendation offers sound advice about direction but poor advice about timing. Following it pays off when an important problem has recently become tractable, when the young researcher already commands the relevant field, and when failure is cheap enough to survive. It is costly when ambition outruns method, as when a problem's fame rests on a long record of failure and the researcher would stake the years in which a career is built. Ambition disciplined by these conditions keeps the great problem in view without pretending it is ready; it works on what it can solve until what matters most comes within reach.

prompt.statement: Managers should spend at least one day a month doing the work of the people they supervise.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: When a Day on the Job Teaches
essays.essay:
The recommendation rests on an assumption it never states: that doing someone's job for a day reveals what it is like to do that job every day. Sometimes it does. When a novice can perform the work competently, or when the manager once did it and has fallen behind, a monthly shift exposes problems that reports conceal. When the work demands expertise the manager lacks, or when the manager's presence alters the very work being observed, the same shift yields either danger or theater. I therefore agree with the recommendation in the first two circumstances and reject it as a universal rule, since its value depends less on the calendar than on what the day can teach.

The clearest case for the recommendation is work that is easy to learn but hard to summarize. Amazon became known for sending its managers, senior executives included, to spend days answering customer-service calls. The work suits the practice: a newcomer with [[rudimentary|rudimentary]] training can handle routine calls under supervision, mistakes are easily corrected, and callers cannot be coached. A return-rate chart reports how often a product comes back; an afternoon of angry callers reveals why, and a manager who has heard the same complaint again and again reads that chart differently. The shared ordeal also builds goodwill between the call center and the corner office as no town-hall speech could.

Less obviously, the practice matters most for managers who think they already know the job. Many newspaper editors began as reporters, but the reporting they remember may predate the pressure to file for the web within the hour and to verify viral footage. Their knowledge is not absent but confidently obsolete, which is worse, because it passes for expertise. Newsroom lore celebrates the [[irascible|irascible]] editor who berates a reporter for a thin story; an editor who spent last Tuesday chasing a source who never called back is likelier to ask what went wrong before assigning blame. Here a monthly day of reporting is less a gesture of solidarity than a [[salutary|salutary]] correction of stale judgment.

The recommendation fails, however, where the work requires training the manager does not have. A hospital executive with a finance degree cannot spend a day titrating medication drips, and no airline would let an unlicensed chief executive fly a passenger jet. Enforcing the rule in such settings produces either a sanitized tour or a [[boorish|boorish]] intrusion, in which an executive barges onto a ward and second-guesses seasoned nurses in front of their patients. The underlying goal, direct contact with the work, is better served by disciplined observation, which endangers no one. Toyota calls this principle genchi genbutsu, roughly "go and see for yourself," and expects its managers to study problems on the shop floor rather than through reports.

A subtler failure occurs when the manager's presence changes the work being sampled. Employees who know the boss is coming will [[feign|feign]] contentment, tidy the stockroom, and hide the improvised workarounds that keep the operation running, and a predictable monthly visit is the easiest kind to stage. The CBS series Undercover Boss turned this problem into a premise: executives work entry-level jobs in their own companies in disguise, since an announced visit would yield only performance. Yet episodes typically climax with the executive rewarding a few memorable employees, which recasts systemic problems as personal stories. A [[mordant|mordant]] critic might ask why a company needed a wig and a film crew to learn what any cashier could have told it. The real defect is a culture in which bad news never travels upward, and no monthly ritual cures that.

These cases shape a position that is conditional but not vague. Managers do drift from the work they oversee, most dangerously when they fail to notice. Where the work can be learned in a day or was once the manager's own, and where the visit cannot easily be staged, a monthly shift is cheap insurance. Elsewhere, managers should watch closely, ask without defensiveness, and make it safe for subordinates to report what is broken. The test is not how many days a manager spends in a subordinate's job but whether the manager returns knowing something the reports omitted.

prompt.statement: People should be wary of advice from anyone who profits from their following it.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Aim Wariness Where Profit Enters
essays.essay:
Taken as a reflex, this recommendation is sensible; taken as a rule, it proves too much. Nearly everyone who gives expert advice profits when it is followed: the surgeon is paid to operate, the lawyer to litigate, the tutor to keep tutoring. A person who discounted all such counsel would be left with the opinions of friends, who may be disinterested but are seldom expert. The statement also rests on a hidden assumption, namely that an adviser's gain must come at the listener's expense. Sometimes it does; often the two rise and fall together. I therefore accept the recommendation only in a narrower form. The useful question is not whether an adviser profits, but where in the advice the profit enters, and wariness should be aimed precisely there.

Following the recommendation strictly would be a mistake for an injured person weighing a lawsuit in the United States, where personal-injury lawyers commonly work on contingency. Such a lawyer collects a share of any recovery, often a third, and nothing if the case fails. When the lawyer urges a client to sue, the lawyer stands to profit if the advice is followed, yet the condition attached to that profit is strong evidence that the advice is sound: few attorneys invest months of potentially unpaid work in a claim they expect to lose. A client who dismissed this counsel as self-interested would be discarding the very signal that makes it credible. The same arrangement, however, contains a point of divergence. The lawyer bears most of the cost of preparing for trial but receives only a fraction of any larger verdict, so an early settlement can suit the lawyer better than the client, and the lawyer's enthusiasm for trial may [[wane|wane]] while a trial would still serve the client. At that moment a [[circumspect|circumspect]] client should demand reasons, and the profession's own rules agree: the decision to settle belongs to the client.

For the congregations of Chaucer's Pardoner, by contrast, following the recommendation would have been plainly advantageous. The Pardoner carries a bag of pardons and a glass case of pig bones that he passes off as holy relics, and before country parishes he [[feigns|feign]] piety to sell them. His sermon, remarkably, condemns greed, and the tale he tells to illustrate it, in which three revelers find a heap of gold and murder one another for it, is morally impeccable. The [[mordant|mordant]] irony of the portrait is that the advice is true: avarice really does destroy those it possesses. What is false is the remedy he sells. When he tries the same pitch on his fellow pilgrims after openly confessing his methods, the Host answers with a [[boorish|boorish]] insult that is nonetheless sound in its instinct. The lesson is not that a profiteer's every word is false; a listener could accept the Pardoner's sermon and still refuse his relics. Suspicion belongs at the point where the speaker's gain begins.

Together, these cases shape my position into two tests. The first is alignment: does the adviser gain only when the listener gains, or can the adviser profit while the listener loses? The second is visibility: is the gain disclosed, as a contingency fee is in a signed agreement, or concealed, as the Pardoner's is from parishioners who cannot tell pig bones from a saint's? The second test also exposes something odd about the recommendation: it is least needed where it is easiest to follow. No one has to be told to distrust a [[furtive|furtive]] peddler who cannot hold a customer's gaze; the real danger is the adviser whose manner is open and whose interest is not.

I would therefore revise the recommendation rather than discard it. People should ask not merely whether an adviser profits, since nearly every competent adviser does, but whether the adviser would profit even if the listener lost, and whether the listener can see the arrangement. Where gain is shared and visible, as in a lawyer's decision to take a case, reflexive suspicion squanders good counsel. Where gain diverges or is concealed, as in a push for a quick settlement or the offer of a relic, wariness is the listener's best protection.
