prompt.statement: Neighborhoods that grow without a master plan are usually more livable than those designed in detail.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Plan the Skeleton, Free the Flesh
essays.essay:
The statement trades on an appealing picture: the crooked lane, the corner bakery, neighbors who have known one another for decades. Such places often feel more humane than districts drawn whole on a drafting table, but I disagree that the absence of a master plan explains their appeal. The most livable neighborhoods usually have a firmly planned skeleton: the streets, drains, open spaces, and street walls that no household can coordinate alone. What they leave unplanned is the flesh: the shops and dwellings behind those walls, which residents remake over generations. Detailed design fails when it reaches into the flesh; unplanned growth fails when it neglects the skeleton.

Paris illustrates both halves of this claim. Before the 1850s, its center had grown by unplanned accretion into a [[hodgepodge|hodgepodge]] of crooked lanes, overbuilt courtyards, and open gutters. That city looks charming in old photographs; it was miserable to live in. Cholera tore through Paris in 1832 and again in 1849, and the cramped, poorly drained central quarters suffered badly. Under Napoleon III, the prefect Georges-Eugène Haussmann imposed something close to the [[antithesis|antithesis]] of organic growth. He cut broad boulevards through the old quarters, laid sewers and water mains, carved out parks, and prescribed the height and alignment of the buildings lining the new streets.

What makes Haussmann's Paris instructive, however, is the line it drew. The plan governed the skeleton in exacting detail, yet it stopped at the uniform facades it prescribed. Ground floors went to whatever businesses tenants chose, and the apartments above were divided and recombined as the city changed. Those sidewalks and storefronts have proved remarkably [[fecund|fecund]], sprouting cafés, bakeries, and bookshops that no prefect ever drew on a map. It was a [[felicitous|felicitous]] division of labor: the state settled what individuals could not coordinate, and individuals settled everything else. The project had real costs, notably the displacement of poor families to the city's edge. Still, Paris owes its livability far more to Haussmann's skeleton than to the medieval tangle it replaced.

The strongest challenge to this view comes from the planned capitals of the twentieth century, above all Brasília, inaugurated in 1960 and among the most prescriptive master-planned cities ever built. Its layout came from the planner Lúcio Costa and its principal buildings from the architect Oscar Niemeyer, men of real talent and egalitarian ambition. Every function received its own sector, from the ministries to the residential superblocks, all linked by expressways. Critics have long called it a city built for cars rather than people, whose ceremonial core turns [[somnolent|somnolent]] once the ministries close. The workers who built it had no place in the plan and settled in satellite towns, where most of the Federal District's population now lives. A thoughtful opponent would generalize: no planner, however brilliant, knows enough about how people will live to design a neighborhood in advance, so it is wiser to let one grow.

That lesson is right about Brasília but wrong about the remedy. Its superblocks still have devoted residents; what failed was not careful design but zoning so rigid that few unforeseen uses could take root. The flesh pushed back anyway: shopkeepers reversed the planned orientation of their storefronts. The limits of a planner's knowledge argue for modest plans, not for none. No household can lay a sewer, reserve land for a park, or widen a lane once a thousand homes have closed in around it, which is why the [[precarious|precarious]] informal settlements of fast-growing cities so often lack clean water, drainage, and lanes wide enough for a fire truck. Even the organic quarters we celebrate are survivors, most of them later fitted with planned sewers, while many districts that bred epidemics were cleared and forgotten. Setting Brasília beside the best of unplanned growth rather than its worst stacks the deck.

Livability, then, depends less on whether a neighborhood was planned than on what its planners chose to decide. Residents are a far richer source of ideas than any planning office, but they need a frame to build on. The neighborhoods that age best are those whose authorities were exacting about the few things only they could provide and [[forbore|forbear]] from deciding the rest.

prompt.statement: Modern medicine has made people too reliant on experts to manage their own health.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Reliance Misplaced, Not Excessive
essays.essay:
The most compelling case for this statement is not that experts give bad advice but that deference becomes a habit. A patient who demands antibiotics for a cold, a runner who needs a sleep score to know she is rested, and a dieter who reaches for a weight-loss injection rather than changing her meals share one trait: each has handed to an expert, or to an algorithm, a judgment people once made for themselves. Such deference, a thoughtful critic would say, erodes a capacity, much as a student with a tutor at her elbow never learns to check her own work. I grant the pattern but not the diagnosis, which assumes that reliance on experts and self-management compete for a fixed supply of responsibility. They do not. Modern medicine has not made people too reliant on experts; it has made reliance easy to misplace, so that people defer where their own observation suffices and trust themselves where it fails.

Type 1 diabetes shows precisely where that assumption breaks down. People with the disease manage it more continuously than almost any other patients: they count carbohydrates, calculate insulin doses, and adjust for exercise and illness. They do this because of experts, not in spite of them. Newly diagnosed patients are often overwhelmed by carbohydrate ratios and correction doses; diabetes educators make mastering those calculations a central aim of care. The best of them [[eschew|eschew]] the role of oracle, since no one could live normally while phoning a clinic before every meal. They are tutors of a kind the critic overlooks, measuring success by how little their students eventually need them. In time, a patient's knowledge of her own body can [[outstrip|outstrip]] anything a specialist infers from a quarterly visit. Here reliance on expertise is the route to self-management, not its rival.

The opposite error, trusting oneself where one's judgment is compromised, appears most starkly in American football. For generations, a player who "got his bell rung" returned to the game on his own word that he was fine. Yet a concussed player is often disoriented; the faculty he needs to judge his fitness is the very one that was injured. When pathologists began finding brain damage from repeated head trauma in former players, the National Football League spent years disputing the evidence; only under pressure from Congress and retired players' lawsuits did it grow more [[circumspect|circumspect]]. Today a player suspected of a concussion cannot return until medical staff, including a neurotrauma consultant unaffiliated with his team, clear him. That independence matters: a team with a game to win has its own reasons to misjudge his fitness. Removing the decision from the athlete does not violate his autonomy; it recognizes that self-assessment fails when the self is impaired. Patients who stop their blood pressure pills because they feel well make the same mistake more quietly: hypertension usually causes no symptoms.

The critic's most persuasive example, the weight-loss injection, looks different in this light. Unlike antibiotics for a cold, drugs such as semaglutide genuinely work, which is why some worry that their popularity [[portends|portend]] a generation of passive patients. That outcome is possible but not inevitable: regulators approved these drugs as an adjunct to diet and exercise, not a replacement, so the risk turns on how they are prescribed. None of this [[exculpates|exculpate]] the profession. A brief appointment leaves time to write a prescription but rarely to explain what else must change; a system that rewards the first over the second will produce exactly the dependence the critic fears. The fault lies in how expertise is delivered, not in reliance itself.

The statement, then, mistakes a problem of direction for a problem of quantity. Patients need to become more discerning, not more independent, asking whether their own perception is reliable enough to act on. Whether one is rested, whether a cold is improving, and what belongs on a dinner plate are questions most people can answer for themselves; whether blood pressure is silently climbing and whether a dazed mind is fit to play are not. The goal is not less reliance on experts but reliance placed where the self cannot see.

words.meaning_here: Deliberately avoid, on principle, taking on the role of an all-knowing authority.
Exceed or surpass; the patient's self-knowledge comes to exceed what a specialist can infer.
Cautious and weighing consequences; the league finally became wary of returning head-injured players.
Signals that something bad is coming: a generation of passive, drug-dependent patients.
Clears of blame; the argument does not free the medical profession from responsibility.

Sentence length varies sharply, from the three-word "They do not." to long sentences that build in stages. Target words sit in normal collocations, such as "eschew the role of oracle" and "grow more circumspect."

prompt.statement: Some argue that governments should focus on preventing problems before they arise. Others argue that, because resources are limited, governments should focus on solving the problems that already exist.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Scarcity Argues for Disciplined Prevention
essays.essay:
The strongest case for concentrating on existing problems comes not from shortsightedness but from humility about the future. A problem that already exists is certain: its victims can be named, its causes examined, and the effect of a remedy measured. A problem that has not yet arisen is a forecast, and forecasts are often wrong. The Maginot Line is a [[salutary|salutary]] reminder of what a wrong forecast costs. In the 1930s France fortified its German border for a slow, static war like the last one; in 1940 the German thrust came instead through the Ardennes, a forest French commanders had judged nearly impassable to tanks, and France fell within weeks. With resources limited, every franc sunk into concrete for the wrong war is a franc withheld from present needs. This skepticism deserves respect, but it calls for disciplined prevention rather than none, and the preventive view, held to that discipline, comes closer to my own.

The case for remedy rests on an assumption it never states: that present and future problems are unrelated, so money spent preventing one does nothing to relieve the other. Yet many existing problems are earlier ones left unprevented, and their costs grow while governments wait. Where a harm is foreseeable, its mechanism understood, and its costs compounding, the damage from waiting will eventually [[outstrip|outstrip]] the cost of acting, and deferral becomes not thrift but borrowing at ruinous interest. Under those conditions, scarcity is an argument for prevention, not against it. Even the Maginot Line indicts only misdirected prevention: it guarded against a symptom of a danger rooted partly in how the previous war ended.

Europe's two postwar settlements show that the real choice is often not between preventing and solving but between two ways of solving. In 1919, at Versailles, the victorious Allies answered an existing problem, the devastation of France and Belgium, by holding Germany liable for sweeping reparations. To John Maynard Keynes, who resigned from the British delegation in protest, the terms [[portended|portend]] economic chaos and a thirst for revenge. Historians debate how much the payments harmed Germany, but the grievance they fed became a weapon against its [[precarious|precarious]] new democracy. After 1945, facing a continent in rubble, the United States and Western Europe solved a similar problem differently. The Marshall Plan helped finance the region's recovery, former enemies included, and the European Coal and Steel Community, a French proposal, placed French and West German coal and steel under a common High Authority. Both met present needs while attacking causes of future conflict: the misery on which communist parties fed, and national control of the industries of war. Together they helped turn France and Germany, enemies in three wars within a century, into partners bound by shared interest rather than mere [[comity|comity]].

If prevention can pay so handsomely, why do governments neglect it? One reason is that successful prevention erases its own evidence. In the late 1990s, governments and businesses spent heavily repairing software that stored years as two digits and might read 2000 as 1900, an error that could cascade through interconnected systems. When the new year brought only scattered glitches, many concluded the threat had been exaggerated. Whether every dollar was needed is still debated, but the effort met all three conditions: the harm was foreseeable to the day, its mechanism was well understood, and every delay made repairs costlier as the deadline neared. The remedial view's preference for certainty thus conceals a bias. A budget process that rewards only visible rescues is [[myopic|myopic]] by design: it cannot tell a prevented disaster from one that was never coming, so it counts both as waste.

My position, then, is that prevention deserves first claim on scarce public money, but only where it has earned that claim. When a harm is foreseeable and its costs compound, waiting does not conserve resources; it postpones a larger bill. When a threat is merely imaginable, governments should [[forbear|forbear]] from building fortifications against it and attend to the hardship in front of them. And when they turn to existing problems, they should ask the question that separated Versailles from the Marshall Plan: will this remedy remove the cause, or merely pay for the damage?

words.meaning_here: Beneficial by teaching a useful though painful lesson, here about what a wrong forecast costs.

prompt.statement: Some people think that success at work depends mainly on talent. Others think that it depends mainly on persistence.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Talent at the Gate, Persistence Inside
essays.essay:
Debates about whether talent or persistence drives success at work usually treat the two as rival endowments, measured on one scale, so that one must outweigh the other. In practice they operate at different stages of a career. Talent largely decides who is admitted to a demanding field; persistence largely decides who succeeds once inside it. For that reason, the view that success depends mainly on persistence comes closer to my own, provided that persistence means not mere stubbornness but sustained, adaptable effort that turns ability into results.

The case for talent deserves more respect than its critics grant it. In some kinds of work, natural gifts set a ceiling that no amount of effort can raise. Pelé was seventeen when he scored twice for Brazil in the 1958 World Cup final; countless Brazilian boys played just as obsessively and never approached that level. To tell them they simply did not want it enough would be both false and cruel. Employers act as if they share this view: a soccer club will indulge an [[irascible|irascible]] forward who wins matches long after it would have released an even-tempered, hardworking one who does not. The persistence view also suffers from a quieter flaw. Its favorite stories, of the writer rejected by publisher after publisher before finally landing a best seller, are told by survivors; nobody interviews the many who persisted just as long and failed.

Yet the talent view describes the gate to a profession better than the competition inside it. Elite sports may be an exception, but in most work, once a field has screened its entrants, differences in raw ability narrow, and a trait that barely varies within a group cannot explain much of what separates its members. At a major newspaper, nearly every reporter was hired partly for the ability to write clean, often [[felicitous|felicitous]] prose on deadline, which is precisely why that skill distinguishes so few of them. The Watergate investigation shows what does. When the White House dismissed the 1972 break-in at Democratic National Committee headquarters as a "third-rate burglary," much of the national press lost interest. Two young reporters on The Washington Post's metro desk, Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein, did not. Their method was largely drudgery: working through lists of campaign employees, knocking on doors at night, and calling back people who had already hung up on them. Many of those they approached [[feigned|feign]] ignorance or shut the door. A highly placed FBI source helped, but by Woodward's own account he mainly confirmed what their legwork had uncovered. Tolerance for rejection, more than superior brilliance, let them [[outstrip|outstrip]] more senior political reporters and helped keep the scandal alive until the Senate opened its own inquiry.

Even where talent is beyond question, persistence decides what it becomes. Wangari Maathai was formidably able: she was the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate and later taught at the University of Nairobi. It is tempting to [[ascribe|ascribe]] her achievements to that brilliance, yet brilliance alone would probably have produced only a distinguished academic career. What made her consequential was her decision in the 1970s to organize rural Kenyan women to plant trees, one nursery at a time, and to keep at it for decades despite [[boorish|boorish]] taunts from officials, repeated arrests, and a police beating that left her unconscious. Nor did she merely repeat herself: concluding that forests could not be protected under an unaccountable government, she widened the movement into a campaign for democratic reform. The Green Belt Movement she founded planted tens of millions of trees, and in 2004 she became the first African woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. Her talent made her credible; her persistence made her matter.

The persistence that counts is not the blind insistence of someone who mistakes obstinacy for resolve, nor the endless repetition of a failed approach; it is effort that survives discouragement while learning from it. Survivors' stories cannot show that such effort guarantees success, and I do not claim it does. My claim is narrower: talent decides who gets through the gate, but among those already inside, success goes mostly to whoever keeps knocking after the first doors close.

prompt.statement:
Claim: Students should study the history of science alongside science itself.
Reason: Knowing how ideas were discovered teaches students how to think, not merely what to think.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Honest History Serves Citizens, Not Just Thinkers
essays.essay:
I agree that students should learn the history of science alongside science itself, but the reason offered is weaker than it looks. It rests on a tidy [[dichotomy|dichotomy]] between how to think and what to think, and it assumes that history belongs automatically on the first side. History does not. A history taught as a procession of geniuses, or as a [[somnolent|somnolent]] recital of names and dates, is merely more material to memorize. History teaches thinking only when it preserves the dead ends, the reasonable doubts, and the winners' errors. Its most valuable lesson, moreover, is one the reason overlooks: how scientific claims gain or lose acceptance, true or not.

The work of Ignaz Semmelweis shows what the reason gets right. In the 1840s, the Vienna General Hospital ran two maternity clinics, and women in the one staffed by physicians and medical students died of childbed fever far more often than those in the midwives' clinic. Because admissions alternated daily between the clinics, differences among the patients could not account for the gap. Semmelweis discarded one explanation after another. Atmospheric 'epidemic influences' could not explain why two clinics under one roof differed, and neither changing the mothers' delivery position nor rerouting a priest's bell-ringing procession, thought to terrify patients, made any difference. The decisive clue came when a colleague, cut by a student's scalpel during an autopsy, died of an illness resembling childbed fever. Semmelweis inferred that physicians and students were carrying something from corpses to mothers; when he required them to wash their hands in a solution of chlorinated lime, deaths fell sharply. The philosopher Carl Hempel later used this episode to teach the logic of hypothesis testing, a [[felicitous|felicitous]] choice: a student who retraces these steps learns why a comparison group matters and how rival hypotheses are eliminated, lessons no bare rule about hygiene can teach.

Yet the second half of the story is more [[edifying|edify]]. Many leading physicians [[repudiated|repudiate]] his conclusions, and it is tempting to dismiss them as fools. The record is more complicated. Semmelweis offered no convincing mechanism in an age before germ theory; his explanation indicted the very doctors asked to accept it; and he waited more than a decade to publish a full account. He was also [[irascible|irascible]], and in open letters he branded prominent critics as murderers. The lesson here concerns less the logic of discovery than the reception of evidence: a correct finding does not become shared knowledge until it is published, explained, and argued for, and experts are slow to accept conclusions that implicate them. This, rather than the reason's appeal to thinking, is the stronger case for the claim. Few students will become scientists; nearly all will become citizens who must judge which scientific claims should guide public policy.

Stalin's Soviet Union offers a contrasting case, one in which the reason's hidden assumption fails. The agronomist Trofim Lysenko won official favor by promising rapid gains in crop yields and by denouncing Mendelian genetics as bourgeois. His allies supplied a history to match, casting the dispute as a contest between practical Soviet science and reactionary Western theory. Geneticists lost their posts, the eminent plant scientist Nikolai Vavilov died in prison, and genetics was effectively banned for years. Soviet students thus learned biology with a history attached, yet that history taught them exactly what to think. The Semmelweis story invites the same abuse: told as the martyrdom of a lone genius at the hands of fools, it flatters every crank who treats expert rejection as proof of brilliance. The remedy is not less history but more candid history, willing to show authorities in error, including those who write the curriculum; the Lysenko affair itself belongs in every biology course.

The history of science, then, deserves its place beside science, but the reason given makes only half the case. Honest history can teach students how to think; legend merely teaches them what to admire. The fuller justification is civic. A citizen who understands why Semmelweis was rebuffed and Lysenko embraced knows that a sound finding may need years to win acceptance, and that official endorsement alone never makes a claim true.

prompt.statement:
Claim: Schools should assign less homework.
Reason: Time for play and rest is as important to children's development as time for study.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Protect Rest Where It Is Actually Lost
essays.essay:
The reason behind this claim is stronger than defenders of homework usually admit. Play and rest are not rewards for learning but part of it: sleep consolidates the day's lessons, and unstructured play teaches children to negotiate rules and tolerate frustration. I accept the reason almost without reservation. Its force runs out, however, at the step from reason to claim, which silently assumes that homework is what consumes children's play and rest and that the assignments eliminated would have taught little. Neither assumption holds generally. The claim is right for young children, though mainly for a different reason, and wrong as a blanket rule for adolescents, whose lost sleep has causes besides homework and whose learning depends more on practice outside class.

Adolescent sleep shows both the truth of the reason and its insufficiency. Every first-period teacher has faced rows of [[somnolent|somnolent]] teenagers. This is not laziness: at puberty the body's clock shifts later, making early sleep difficult. Linking chronic sleep loss to inattention, depressed mood, and car crashes, the American Academy of Pediatrics has urged middle and high schools to start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. The evidence vindicates the reason. It is tempting to [[ascribe|ascribe]] teenage exhaustion to homework, but the academy counts homework as one cause among several, alongside extracurriculars, after-school jobs, and late-night screens, and its central remedy is a later first bell. At high-pressure schools that assign hours of work nightly, homework may well be the main cause. Elsewhere, lighter assignments alone would not rescue a student whose body resists sleep until late and whose class begins before eight. A true reason can call for a remedy other than the one proposed.

For young children, by contrast, I agree that schools should assign less homework, perhaps none in the earliest grades, though the better argument is that such homework accomplishes very little. Large research reviews find almost no link between homework and achievement in elementary school, and a clearer one in high school. Early homework also measures the household more than the child, rewarding a quiet table and a parent free to help. Two European educators who differed over play nonetheless agreed that young children learn by doing, not by sitting at desks. Friedrich Froebel, who opened the first kindergarten in nineteenth-century Germany, filled it with blocks, songs, and gardening, convinced that play is how a young child's mind grows. Maria Montessori [[eschewed|eschew]] make-believe and called children's activity work rather than play, yet she organized her first school in Rome around materials children chose and worked with at their own pace. A worksheet sent home to a six-year-old trades that kind of learning for a poorer one, whatever one thinks of play.

With adolescents the case reverses. Much of what high school demands, from solving equations to sustaining an argument, is mastered through solitary practice that class time cannot accommodate. A difficult problem set can be [[salutary|salutary]] in the way a hard workout is: unpleasant while it lasts and precisely what produces the gain. What deserves cutting is busywork, the copied definitions and rote exercises dispatched with minimal thought. Such assignments invite [[furtive|furtive]] copying in the hallway. Worse, they teach students to [[feign|feign]] an understanding they have never built. The total burden is often a [[haphazard|haphazard]] accumulation: each teacher assigns what seems a reasonable amount, and no one adds them up. A school that coordinated assignments and discarded the empty ones might well assign less, but as a byproduct of better design, not as its goal.

The reason, then, is sound, but it argues for protecting children's time rather than for any particular cut. A school should ask not how much homework it assigns but what each assignment displaces and produces. For a seven-year-old, homework displaces play and yields little measurable learning, so it should shrink or disappear. For a sixteen-year-old, the right assignment builds skills no lecture can, and lost sleep must be traced to its real sources, whether an early bell, a bright screen, or, at a high-pressure school, the homework itself. Taking rest seriously means defending it against whatever actually consumes it, a more demanding standard than simply assigning less.

Claim: Historical figures should be judged by their whole lives rather than by their best-known deeds.
Reason: Reputations built on single achievements distort our understanding of history.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Whole Lives for People, Consequences for Deeds
essays.essay:
The word "judged" does double duty in this claim. We judge historical figures to assess their character, and we judge them to understand what their deeds did to the world. For the first purpose the claim is right, though for a reason the prompt never offers: character is a pattern, and no single act, however famous, reveals a pattern. For the second purpose the claim holds only when the rest of a life shaped the fate of the famous deed; otherwise, folding in the whole biography blurs history. The reason names a genuine distortion, but the claim draws the wrong lesson from it.

Consider first a case where the whole life is indispensable. Ignaz Semmelweis is remembered for a single insight: in the 1840s, at a Vienna maternity clinic, he showed that having doctors wash their hands in chlorinated lime sharply reduced deaths from childbed fever. The popular version casts him as a lone genius defeated by hidebound colleagues. The fuller record is less flattering and more illuminating. Semmelweis waited more than a decade to publish his evidence in full and then answered critics with [[mordant|mordant]] open letters that held them responsible for the deaths of mothers. His [[irascible|irascible]] manner made it easy for skeptics to dismiss the message along with the messenger. His temperament does not excuse their indifference, but it helps explain why a lifesaving idea spread so slowly, a question the legend cannot even pose.

Fritz Haber shows where the claim breaks down, and where it does not. Before World War I, he devised a method for synthesizing ammonia from atmospheric nitrogen; scaled up by Carl Bosch, it made synthetic fertilizer cheap and now sustains much of the world's food supply. During the war, Haber also championed and personally supervised Germany's first large-scale chlorine attack, at Ypres in 1915. Judging the man requires the whole life: the harvests his chemistry made possible cannot [[exculpate|exculpate]] him from his part in the gas war. Judging the deeds calls for a finer line. When the British blockade cut Germany off from Chilean saltpeter, Haber's ammonia was turned into nitrates for explosives, and his zeal for the war belongs in that chapter of its history. Beyond that chapter, blending the two deeds would be a category error: synthetic nitrogen fertilizer feeds no fewer people because the inventor of its key process helped poison soldiers, and chlorine was no less lethal because its chief advocate had also made bread from air.

The reason deserves separate scrutiny, because it is true but insufficient. Reputations built on single achievements do distort history, yet the usual distortion lies less in what they omit from the hero's life than in whom they omit from the story. Jackie Robinson's 1947 debut with the Brooklyn Dodgers is remembered as one man's triumph of courage. Such stories are told to [[edify|edify]], and this one does, but it sidelines the Black press, where writers such as Wendell Smith of the Pittsburgh Courier had long campaigned for integration, and the Negro Leagues, where Robinson had played and where generations of Black athletes had displayed talent the major leagues refused to see. Stretching the account across Robinson's whole life, from the seasons in which, as promised, he [[forbore|forbear]] from answering racist taunts to his later civil rights activism, would deepen the portrait of one man while leaving him just as alone in the frame. The fault lies in the frame's width, not its length. What the reason supports is a different claim: that achievements should be judged alongside everyone who made them possible.

My position, then, is conditional but firm. People should be judged by their whole lives, not because single achievements distort history but because character reveals itself only over time. Deeds should be judged by their consequences, and the rest of a life belongs in that judgment only when it shaped those consequences: Semmelweis's temper shaped the fate of his discovery, whereas Haber's gas did nothing to diminish the harvests his ammonia sustains. The reason diagnoses a real ailment; the claim it is meant to support prescribes the wrong treatment. The remedy for heroic distortion is not a longer biography but a more crowded history.

words.meaning_here: Bitingly harsh and stinging in tone, describing Semmelweis's letters attacking his critics.
Quick to anger by nature; describes Semmelweis's habitual hot temper.
Free from blame; the good harvests do not clear Haber of guilt for the gas.
Morally instruct or uplift readers, as heroic stories about Robinson are meant to do.
Deliberately and patiently refrained; Robinson, as promised, did not answer racist taunts.

analysis.verdict: The essay earns a 6 for insight and cogency, not just clarity: it exposes the ambiguity in "judged," sets a causal condition for when a whole life matters, and evaluates claim and reason separately. Each of its three examples is developed far enough to show why it bears on a specific condition, and the language is precise, varied, and nearly error-free.
analysis.position: The writer accepts the claim for judging character, accepts it for judging deeds only when the rest of a life "shaped the fate of the famous deed," and finds the reason true but too weak to support the claim. The conclusion labels this stance "conditional but firm."
analysis.development: Each example does a distinct job: Semmelweis shows a life that shaped a deed's fate, Haber a life where the test splits (the war redirected his ammonia into explosives, but the gas never touched the harvests), Robinson the people a legend sidelines. Each is explained, not just named: Semmelweis's letters "held them responsible for the deaths of mothers."
analysis.organization: The essay is organized by conditions rather than pro and con: paragraph 2 shows where whole-life judgment is indispensable, paragraph 3 applies the test within one life, and paragraph 4 treats the reason alone. The conclusion cites both scientists to state the test in one sentence.
analysis.language: Diction is exact and compact ("less flattering and more illuminating"), and sentence length ranges from short verdicts ("Judging the deeds calls for a finer line.") to long balanced sentences. The closing medical metaphor stays controlled and keeps diagnosis and prescription apart.
analysis.task: The instruction demands separate verdicts, and the essay delivers them visibly: the claim is right "for a reason the prompt never offers," while the reason is "true but insufficient," because the distortion it names comes from omitted people, not omitted years.

paragraphs.note: Restates the position in fresh terms (people by whole lives, deeds by consequences), names the claim's better reason, contrasts Semmelweis with Haber, and separates the reason's diagnosis from the claim's prescription.

Its conclusion would repeat the introduction instead of sharpening it into a test.

prompt.statement: Governments should make every adult an organ donor unless that person chooses to opt out.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Earn Trust Before Presuming Consent
essays.essay:
In nearly every country, the demand for kidneys, livers, and hearts far [[outstrips|outstrip]] the supply, and patients die on waiting lists while organs that might have saved them are buried or cremated. Presumed consent is attractive because it harnesses a well-documented habit: most people accept whatever option is preselected for them. Yet the statement rests on a hidden assumption, namely that the shortage is chiefly a problem of paperwork, of willing donors who never registered. When I trace the policy's likely consequences, I conclude that it deserves support only where three conditions hold: hospitals can identify donors and recover their organs, the public trusts those hospitals, and the opt-out is so easy and widely known that silence genuinely signals assent. Where these conditions fail, the policy can shrink the very supply it is meant to expand.

Spain shows what the policy can accomplish when the first condition is met, and how little the law achieves alone. Spain adopted presumed consent in 1979, yet its donation rate barely moved for roughly a decade. The change came only after 1989, when a new national transplant organization attacked the obstacles that had [[impeded|impede]] donation, placing trained coordinators in hospitals to find potential donors and talk with grieving families. Spain went on to reach, and has long held, the world's highest rate of deceased donation, although its physicians still consult families and [[forbear|forbear]] from invoking the presumption whenever relatives refuse. The statute served mainly as a backdrop that marked donation as the social norm; the additional organs came from investment in people and procedures. A government that passes the law without that investment should expect a symbolic gain and little else.

Where the second condition is missing, the outcome can be the reverse. In 1997 Brazil made every citizen a presumed donor unless he or she recorded an objection on an identity document. The early public reaction [[portended|portend]] the law's collapse. Many Brazilians, particularly poor citizens who doubted that public hospitals would fight to save them, feared that a presumed donor might be declared dead too readily, and large numbers registered as non-donors. Within two years the government had retreated, returning the decision to families. The lesson is not that Brazilians were selfish. It is that people who might have donated freely [[repudiated|repudiate]] a system that seemed to claim their bodies in advance. Where the state has not earned trust, presumed consent turns a gift into a seizure, and citizens guard their bodies accordingly.

The third condition addresses a subtler problem that persists even where trust is high: presumed consent succeeds because people do not act, and inaction is not agreement. Kazuo Ishiguro's novel Never Let Me Go is no forecast of real policy; its donors are clones raised to give up organ after organ until they die. Yet many readers are troubled by the characters' passivity. They never try to escape, and the most they hope for is a few years' deferral. The effect is deliberate: the novel shows how a system can extract enormous sacrifices by making them the expected course of life. An opt-out law is incomparably gentler, but it draws on the same inertia. Those who never opt out will include not only the willing but also people who never see the notices, cannot read them, or are [[befuddled|befuddled]] by the forms required to refuse. Unless refusal is simple and actively publicized, and families keep a voice, the policy will count among its donors many people who never knowingly agreed.

These consequences, more than any abstract principle about who owns the body, determine my position. Presumed consent is sound policy, but it belongs at the end of a reform, not the beginning. A government that has built a trusted transplant system and made refusal as easy as checking a box can adopt an opt-out law and expect more organs. A government that lacks these foundations should refrain from presuming anyone's consent and invest first in the institutions that make consent meaningful; otherwise it risks the Brazilian outcome, in which a measure meant to save lives teaches citizens to withhold the gift altogether. The state may presume consent only after it has earned the presumption.

prompt.statement: Countries should replace standardized national examinations with assessments designed by teachers.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Shrink National Exams, Do Not Abolish Them
essays.essay:
Every examination serves two audiences with different questions. A teacher asks what a student has learned and what she needs next; a university that has never met her asks how she compares with thousands of students taught by others. Assessments designed by teachers answer the first question far better than any national test, and a country that wants its schools to educate students rather than merely rank them should give teachers more authority over grading. Yet the proposal to replace national examinations entirely assumes that the second question will vanish with the test. Its likely consequences convince me that it will not, and that countries should shrink national examinations rather than abolish them.

The policy's intended consequence, assessment that serves learning rather than ranking, is real, as Finland shows. Finland [[eschews|eschew]] high-stakes standardized testing for nearly all of a child's schooling; academic-track students sit a national examination only at the end of upper secondary school. Until then, assessment belongs to teachers, who must hold a master's degree and are free to write questions that [[elicit|elicit]] their students' misconceptions instead of drilling for an annual test. Finnish students ranked at or near the top of the early PISA comparisons, though no single policy explains that result. But the Finnish model rests on teachers selected and trained with unusual care, a condition most countries cannot quickly replicate, and even Finland keeps a national examination precisely where students compete for university places. The strongest case for the policy does not actually implement it.

The first unintended consequence is a loss of comparability, and the history of medical education shows its cost. In his 1910 report on North American medical schools, Abraham Flexner described a [[hodgepodge|hodgepodge]]: a few rigorous university faculties alongside many for-profit schools that admitted nearly anyone who could pay and offered little laboratory or bedside training. State licensing boards existed, but their standards varied so widely that a diploma, even with a license attached, said little about what a physician knew. His report helped close many of the weakest schools; accreditation and common examinations later gave the degree a shared meaning. Leaving all final assessment to teachers would recreate the old problem in miniature: an admissions officer reading a transcript from an unfamiliar school would know little more than a patient reading a diploma in Flexner's day. The reform carried a warning, too: all but two of the schools that trained Black physicians closed in its wake. A common standard is only as fair as its designers; that lesson argues for reforming national examinations, not discarding them.

The second consequence is subtler: abolishing the exam does not abolish competition for scarce places; it merely drives that competition underground. When the pandemic canceled England's A-level examinations in 2020, the exam regulator, fearing grade inflation, adjusted teachers' estimated grades with a model that leaned heavily on each school's past results, so strong students at historically weak schools were marked down. Amid public outrage, the regulator [[repudiated|repudiate]] its own model within a week, and students received whichever grade was higher, the teacher's or the model's; the share of top grades reached a record. The whole affair was hardly [[edifying|edify]], but it exposed what the policy assumes away: without a common examination, the only practical way to compare students from different schools is to judge them partly by their schools, the very inequity reformers hope to remove. Making teachers' marks the sole gate to university also invites [[furtive|furtive]] maneuvering, from a parent's quiet appeal to a tutor's unacknowledged hand in a portfolio. A national examination, whatever its flaws, is often the one moment when a gifted student at an unremarkable school is judged on her work alone.

Weighed together, these consequences point not to a contest between trusting teachers and trusting tests but to a division of labor. Teachers should design most of the assessment students encounter, because that is where testing can teach, while a lean national examination remains at the few junctures where strangers must compare students and a common yardstick is [[indispensable|indispensable]]. Replacing the exam outright would leave classrooms freer but the path to opportunity murkier, and the students least able to work its quiet channels would pay.

analysis.verdict: This earns a 6 because the position is insightful, not merely clear: the essay splits assessment into two audiences and shows that the sorting function survives the exam's abolition. Every example (Finland, Flexner, England in 2020) is described and then explicitly tied to a consequence that shapes the position, and the prose is precise, varied, and essentially error-free.

The essay also admits costs on its own side, noting that schools training Black physicians closed after the reform.
analysis.organization: The body moves from the intended consequence (Finland) to two unintended ones (lost comparability, hidden competition), signposted by "The first unintended consequence" and "The second consequence is subtler." Each paragraph closes by stating how its evidence bears on the position.
analysis.language: Diction is exact rather than ornate: "what the policy assumes away," "drives that competition underground," "a common yardstick." Short verdicts such as "The strongest case for the policy does not actually implement it" alternate with long sentences built on colons and semicolons.

The conclusion opens with "Weighed together, these consequences point," showing that the consequences decide the position.

prompt.statement: Plastic packaging should be banned for products that can be sold without it.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Judge a Ban by Its Substitutes
essays.essay:
In many supermarkets, a cucumber arrives sealed in a skin of plastic film while the apples beside it sit loose in a bin. The cucumber could plainly be sold bare, as it was for generations. Yet the film slows moisture loss and keeps the vegetable firm for days longer, so stripping it away would likely send more cucumbers to the trash, along with the water, fertilizer, and fuel spent to grow and ship them. The statement quietly assumes that whatever can be sold without plastic should be. I support banning a great deal of plastic packaging, but the test should be what happens after the plastic disappears, not whether a product can survive the trip to the checkout without it.

The intended consequences of a ban are real, and they justify one wherever packaging does nothing but decorate: the plastic window in a cardboard pasta box, or the shrink-wrap over a box that already protects its contents. Removing such plastic costs almost nothing. Where waste collection is [[rudimentary|rudimentary]], the case for a ban extends even to packaging that does some work. When Kenya outlawed plastic carrier bags in 2017, it was responding to bags that clogged drains, worsened flooding, and turned up in the stomachs of slaughtered cattle. Backed by some of the world's harshest penalties, the ban visibly reduced that litter. It also brought complaints from traders, uneven enforcement, and bags smuggled in from neighboring countries. Still, the episode taught a [[salutary|salutary]] lesson: a habit that had seemed permanent proved changeable once the law forced the issue.

The trouble begins when a ban reaches packaging that does real work, because plastic is rarely replaced by nothing; it is replaced by something heavier. A life-cycle assessment by the Environment Agency of England and Wales found that a paper bag must be used about three times, and a cotton tote more than a hundred times, before its carbon footprint falls below that of a conventional plastic bag used once. A shopper who [[eschews|eschew]] plastic but takes a fresh paper bag on every trip is thus trading a visible harm, litter, for an invisible one, emissions. Where bags choke drains, as in Kenya, that trade may be worth making; where waste is reliably collected and buried, it often is not. Add the cucumber's lesson about food waste, and a blanket ban could enlarge the very footprint it was meant to shrink. None of this [[exculpates|exculpate]] the packers and retailers who wrap produce in plastic purely for display; it means only that the law must separate packaging that protects a product from packaging that merely advertises it.

History suggests what separates a wise ban from a merely satisfying one. The 1987 Montreal Protocol, which phased out the chlorofluorocarbons that were thinning the ozone layer, is often called the most successful environmental treaty ever. It worked because it was gradual, targeted comparatively few chemical producers rather than billions of consumers, and could rely on workable substitutes. Yet even this triumph carried an unintended cost. The hydrofluorocarbons that came to replace ozone-depleting chemicals in refrigerators and air conditioners spare the ozone layer but trap heat far more powerfully than carbon dioxide. Their use soared with demand for cooling in fast-growing economies, a trend that [[portended|portend]] substantial future warming; in 2016, nations amended the treaty to phase the gases down. The lesson is not that bans fail; it is that whatever replaces a banned product deserves the same scrutiny as the product itself.

Taken together, these consequences point toward a narrower, sturdier policy than the statement proposes. Plastic that merely decorates a product should go, and governments need not wait for perfect data to remove it. Plastic that preserves food, keeps medical supplies sterile, or replaces something heavier should stay until a substitute proves better over its whole life, not merely at the moment of disposal. Where the evidence is mixed, a [[circumspect|circumspect]] government will prefer a price to a prohibition: Ireland's 2002 levy on plastic bags cut their use sharply yet left shoppers free to buy one. The right question is not whether a product can be sold without plastic, but whether the world is better off when it is.

analysis.verdict: This response earns a 6 because its position is insightful, not merely clear. It exposes the statement's hidden assumption that what can be sold without plastic should be, replaces it with a test based on consequences, and names the conditions, such as weak waste collection, under which a broader ban makes sense. Each example is developed until its relevance is explicit, and the prose is precise and varied, with no errors.

analysis.development: Each main example carries a distinct consequence: the cucumber shows food waste, Kenya shows that weak waste collection can justify banning even working packaging, the Environment Agency study shows heavier substitutes, and Ireland's levy shows a price as the alternative to a ban. The Montreal Protocol turns these into a general principle: "whatever replaces a banned product deserves the same scrutiny."
analysis.organization: The essay moves from scene to hidden assumption to position, then from intended consequences to unintended ones to a historical principle, and ends with the policy those consequences imply. Callbacks such as "the cucumber's lesson about food waste" and "as in Kenya" link the paragraphs.
analysis.language: The diction is economical and exact, as in "trading a visible harm, litter, for an invisible one, emissions." Short pivots such as "Yet even this triumph carried an unintended cost" break up longer sentences. Target words sit in natural collocations: "a salutary lesson," "a circumspect government will prefer a price."
analysis.task: The instruction asks the writer to let consequences shape the position, and the essay does this visibly. prompt.statement: A tradition deserves to survive only if its followers can explain the reasons for it.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Scrutiny Should Scale with Harm
essays.essay:
The statement makes a tradition's worth depend on whether its followers can recite its rationale on demand. Behind that standard lies an unstated assumption: that the reasons for a practice reside in the minds of the people who perform it. Often they do not. Many traditions carry knowledge in the practice itself rather than in anyone's account of it, and demanding that followers explain such a tradition confuses their eloquence with its value. Yet the demand is exactly right in one class of cases: a tradition that imposes [[onerous|onerous]] costs on people who never chose to bear them has no claim to continue unless those costs can be justified. I therefore accept the statement's demand for justification when a tradition inflicts serious harm and reject it as a general rule.

Foot-binding in China shows the statement at its strongest. For centuries, families bound young girls' feet, folding the four smaller toes beneath the sole until the foot was permanently deformed and leaving many women in lifelong pain. When reformers in the late nineteenth century demanded reasons, defenders could invoke beauty, female modesty, family refinement, and Han Chinese identity, but for many households the decisive reason was blunter: an unbound daughter would not marry well. That reason was self-perpetuating, since bound feet mattered for marriage only because other families still demanded them. Reform societies attacked this weakness, asking families to pledge together neither to bind their daughters nor to let their sons marry women with bound feet. Those pledges, along with official bans, public campaigns, and economic change, helped the practice fade over several decades, though it lingered longest in rural areas. The demand for reasons was legitimate because the cost fell on children who could not consent. Against such a burden, a [[perfunctory|perfunctory]] "this is what we do" is no answer, and neither is a reason resting only on the custom's momentum.

The statement fails, however, when a tradition's value lies in practice rather than in explanation. In the 1970s, development planners urged Balinese farmers to abandon the planting calendar of the island's water temples and grow high-yielding rice as often as possible. Pest outbreaks and water shortages followed. The anthropologist J. Stephen Lansing later showed that the temple calendar, a ritual cycle through which farmers paid [[obeisance|obeisance]] to the goddess of a crater lake, synchronized fallow periods across large blocks of neighboring fields, depriving pests of food while dividing scarce water among villages upstream and down. The planners had seen only religion where there was also ecology. By the statement's test, as the planners applied it, the tradition deserved to die; in fact, it encoded a solution the experts had missed. The case exposes a second unstated assumption: that explaining a tradition means explaining it in the vocabulary of whoever is asking.

A further flaw lies in the test itself: it measures fluency rather than soundness. Defenders of a dubious custom can manufacture a rationale with enough [[verisimilitude|verisimilitude]] to satisfy a skeptic, while followers of a sound practice may defend it clumsily or not at all. Cities offer a familiar version of this problem. When an old quarter of narrow, shaded lanes and courtyard houses is slated for redevelopment, the planners' case arrives in [[limpid|limpid]] prose, complete with cost estimates. Residents often fall back on [[mawkish|mawkish]] reminiscences about childhood. Judged by fluency, the residents lose. Yet in hot climates such quarters frequently evolved to keep homes cool without machines, a virtue missing from both the residents' memories and the planners' estimates. Clumsy advocacy does not [[preclude|preclude]] soundness, and polished advocacy does not guarantee it.

These cases shape my position in two ways. Foot-binding shows that some traditions must answer for themselves; the Balinese temples and the old quarters show that the answer need not come from followers, or in their words. What a tradition owes, then, is not a fluent explanation from its followers but the capacity to withstand scrutiny from anyone, and that scrutiny should grow stricter as the harm a practice inflicts increases and as the freedom of those who bear it shrinks. A tradition should not survive merely because it is old, but neither should it die merely because those who keep it cannot say why.

prompt.statement: Small towns preserve community better than cities do, but cities preserve individual freedom better than small towns do.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Chosen Community Makes Freedom Possible
essays.essay:
The statement rests on a familiar contrast: a [[mawkish|mawkish]] picture of the small town, all front porches and casseroles, set against the liberating anonymity of the city. I agree that the contrast captures something real, but only under a narrow condition. The claim holds when community means mutual surveillance, because then community and freedom are not two goods that happen to be unevenly distributed; the watchfulness that creates the one is the very force that curtails the other. It fails when community means the capacity of people to act together, since that kind of community often makes urban freedom possible.

The Great Migration of African Americans out of the rural South shows the statement at its strongest. In the small towns of the Jim Crow South, community was not the opposite of oppression but its instrument. The intimacy that brought food to a grieving family also let the sheriff, the landlord, and the storekeeper know which Black resident had spoken out of turn. A [[laconic|laconic]] warning from one of them often sufficed. When it did not, the distance between public [[opprobrium|opprobrium]] and violence was short. The Black-owned Chicago Defender urged Southern readers to come north, and Pullman porters carried copies into towns where authorities tried to suppress it. Northern cities had their own segregation and their own riots, but they offered something the small town could not: indifference. This was not the indifference of neighbors, since many migrants settled near relatives, but of a city too large to track anyone's past. To a stockyard foreman, a migrant from Mississippi was [[fungible|fungible]] labor. Being interchangeable was an indignity but also a liberation, because no Chicago employer or police officer knew or cared whether a man had once refused to yield the sidewalk to a white neighbor.

Sophiatown, the Johannesburg neighborhood the apartheid government razed, is where the statement collapses. Sophiatown was poor and overcrowded, yet it held a community as tight as any village. Black, Coloured, Indian, and Chinese residents lived side by side, and Black South Africans could own land there, a right denied them in most other cities. Its churches, jazz clubs, and [[clandestine|clandestine]] shebeens sustained a defiant culture. The [[urbane|urbane]], irreverent writers of Drum magazine, several of whom lived there, chronicled that culture and went undercover to expose abuses on farms and in prisons. In Sophiatown, community did not restrict freedom; it produced it. The government grasped this more clearly than the statement does. Beginning in 1955, it forcibly removed residents to distant, segregated townships, rebuilt the area for whites, and renamed it Triomf, Afrikaans for "triumph." Johannesburg remained as large as ever; what the bulldozers destroyed was the community, and the freedom it had sheltered went with it.

These two cases shape my position by exposing the variable that the statement mistakes for size. The Jim Crow town enforced an ascribed community, one whose rules a person inherited at birth and could escape only by leaving. Such a community necessarily trades off against freedom, and small towns, where everyone is visible, supply this kind of community in abundance. Sophiatown's community, by contrast, was chosen: it grew from churches and clubs that people joined freely and from a press they read and wrote for. Chicago's migrants built the same kind in Bronzeville's storefront churches and clubs. That second kind of community is a precondition of freedom rather than its rival. Cities generate it more readily, not because they are large, but because density lets people with uncommon beliefs find one another. Neither pattern is guaranteed: a small town can sustain voluntary associations, and a city neighborhood can be stripped of them by a state that fears what they make possible.

I therefore accept the statement only for community of the first kind, and even then only as a description of what small towns and cities tend to make easy, not of what they must do. Community that binds people by birth and watches them closely will cost some freedom wherever it appears; community that people choose is the means by which they defend their freedom. The better question to ask of any place, large or small, is which of the two it allows to flourish.

prompt.statement: Cities should allow homes, shops, and workplaces to be built side by side rather than separating them into distinct zones.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Separate by Harm, Not by Label
essays.essay:
Separating land uses began as a [[beneficent|beneficent]] reform. In nineteenth-century Europe's industrial cities, [[rapacious|rapacious]] landlords crowded workers into damp tenements beside the factories, and keeping smoke away from bedrooms was a matter of public health. The recommendation implies that this remedy has outlived its disease, and for most buildings it has. But the statement rests on a hidden assumption: it treats "workplace" as a single kind of place, when a dentist's office and a chemical plant are both workplaces. Cities should mix uses by default, I will argue, but keep separating activities by the harm they impose on neighbors rather than by the kind of building they occupy.

Paris shows how much a city gains when ordinary uses mingle. When Baron Haussmann rebuilt the capital for Napoleon III, the apartment houses lining his new boulevards were mixed-use neighborhoods stacked vertically. Shops occupied the ground floor, prosperous families took the principal floor with its long balcony, and servants slept under the mansard roof. A resident could buy bread, consult a notary, and walk to work. The boulevards mixed uses more than they mixed classes, since the rebuilding drove many working families toward the eastern districts and suburbs. Streets like these are seldom deserted, and steady foot traffic keeps small shops solvent. Visitors often credit this vitality to [[urbane|urbane]] Parisians lingering over coffee; much of it is really an artifact of the buildings.

Yet Paris did not thrive by abolishing separation; it thrived by drawing the line in the right place. Under Napoleon I, a decree sorted workshops into three classes by the nuisance they caused and kept the most noxious apart from dwellings. Butchering moved from the crowded center to slaughterhouses on the city's edge, which Haussmann later consolidated at La Villette. The baker and the tailor stayed; the slaughterhouse left. Paris mixed what was compatible and expelled what was harmful, and that principle, not a general faith in proximity, is the lesson I draw. Even compatible neighbors need rules: a [[boisterous|boisterous]] bar beneath a bedroom window calls for limits on its hours, not a ban on bars near homes.

Bhopal marks the limit of my agreement. There, a pesticide plant run by Union Carbide's Indian subsidiary stood among crowded neighborhoods, many of them informal settlements that had grown up beside its fence. When methyl isocyanate escaped one night in December 1984, the heavy gas drifted low over sleeping families, and thousands died. Whatever caused the leak, proximity largely decided who suffered worst. To file such a facility under "workplaces" and let homes press against it would be [[cavalier|cavalier]] about human life. Where an activity can kill its neighbors, separation is not a planner's prejudice but the safeguard that remains when every other one fails. Those who need it most are the poor, who settle on land that is cheap precisely because of what sits next to it.

Much of the United States commits the opposite error. American suburban zoning still largely follows the Euclidean model, named for the Ohio village whose ordinance the Supreme Court upheld in 1926, and it routinely forbids even a corner grocery on a residential street. Whoever proposes one must seek a rezoning and often endure a [[fractious|fractious]] public hearing. Some neighbors raise fair concerns about parking and noise; the most [[truculent|truculent]] among them treat any change as an invasion. Meanwhile, every errand requires a car, so children and elderly people who cannot drive depend on others. Here the recommendation would be plainly advantageous, because a corner grocery does its neighbors little harm, and rules on hours and parking, not a ban, can manage what harm it does.

These cases refine rather than reverse my agreement. The question a city should ask of any building is not whether it is a home, a shop, or a workplace but what it sends across the property line: noise, traffic, fumes, or the risk of catastrophe. Judged that way, nearly every shop and office belongs beside homes, and a few industries belong nowhere near them. A city that sorts buildings by label rather than by harm can err in both directions at once, outlawing the corner bakery while letting houses creep up to a chemical plant's fence.

prompt.statement: Engineers should be held personally responsible for foreseeable harms caused by the products they design.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Punish Buried Warnings, Not Foreseeable Risk
essays.essay:
Judged with the [[magisterial|magisterial]] confidence of hindsight, almost every harm a product causes looks foreseeable. Cars crash, drugs have side effects, and every machine eventually fails in ways its designers could have predicted. Read literally, the recommendation would leave few people willing to design anything, so in that form it is not [[tenable|tenable]]. Read narrowly, however, it captures something essential: when an engineer has foreseen a specific danger, has the authority to prevent or disclose it, and sets it aside anyway, personal responsibility is not only fair but necessary. I agree with the recommendation only in this narrower form, and two cases, one Brazilian and one American, show why.

In January 2019, a tailings dam at an iron-ore mine owned by the Brazilian company Vale collapsed near Brumadinho. A torrent of mining waste buried the mine's own cafeteria and offices and swept downstream, killing about 270 people. The disaster was not unforeseen; it was foreseen and filed away. The dam used the inexpensive "upstream" design that had also failed at the Fundão dam near Mariana three years earlier, sending mud down the Rio Doce to the Atlantic. Months before the collapse, engineers from the auditing firm TÜV SÜD declared the structure stable, even though, as later investigations reported, their own analysis showed a safety margin below what accepted practice demanded.

In circumstances like these, following the recommendation is plainly advantageous. The harm was foreseeable in the most concrete sense: someone had calculated it, written it down, and signed off anyway. What failed was not knowledge but will. The auditors did not design the dam, but a stability declaration is the engineering judgment that keeps a design in service; signing one makes the signer part of that design's chain of responsibility. An auditor paid by the company it audits naturally hopes for further [[lucrative|lucrative]] work. At Brumadinho, that dependence appears to have [[vitiated|vitiate]] the very independence the audit existed to supply. Corporate penalties rarely change such incentives, because a firm can absorb fines and public [[opprobrium|opprobrium]] as costs of doing business; the outrage over Mariana did not prevent Brumadinho. A signature that could send its author to prison is different. Personal liability gives the engineer a reason to refuse that no client, however [[rapacious|rapacious]], can bargain away. Prosecutors later charged TÜV SÜD engineers, along with Vale executives, with homicide. For the engineers who signed, the charge was just: the signature, not the embankment, was where the system broke.

Following the same rule in a different circumstance would do real harm. In the 1990s, American safety standards required frontal airbags to protect an unbelted adult man, so the bags inflated with tremendous force. Engineers knew such force could kill a small child or short adult seated close to the airbag, and in that decade it did. Yet airbags saved far more lives than they took. Had each engineer been personally liable for every foreseeable death, the rational course would have been to refuse the work, and that refusal would have [[precluded|preclude]] the widespread use of a technology that, on balance, protected the public. The harm was not concealed; it was the acknowledged price of a tradeoff regulators set in the open, and collective learning reduced it through warning labels, rear seating for children, and bags that adjust their force to the occupant. Worse, personal liability would have rewarded silence, since any engineer who documented the danger would have been drafting the case for the prosecution.

Taken together, the two cases sharpen my position rather than reverse it. They differ less in the scale of the harm than in what engineers did with what they knew. At Brumadinho, a specific danger was measured and then certified away; with airbags, a statistical danger was published, debated, and steadily reduced. Personal responsibility should therefore attach not to foreseeability as such, which applies to nearly every design, but to the suppression of foresight: to the engineer who identified a particular hazard, could have halted or disclosed it, and chose to sign instead. So confined, the rule would not deter engineers from building risky but beneficial things; it would arm them against the people who pay them to look away.

prompt.statement: Citizens have a duty to vote even when no candidate represents their views.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: The Ballot as Question, Not Mirror
essays.essay:
The statement invites an objection that seems decisive: if no candidate speaks for me, my vote can only misrepresent me. That objection treats a ballot as a vehicle for self-expression. But a ballot asks a narrower, more practical question: which of these people will hold this office? In any large and [[fractious|fractious]] electorate, a candidate who mirrors one's views is a lucky accident, not a precondition for having an answer. I therefore largely agree that citizens have a duty to vote even when no candidate represents them, with one limit: the duty binds only when the ballot poses a real question.

The 1991 governor's race in Louisiana shows the distinction at work. In the open primary, the reform-minded incumbent, Buddy Roemer, finished third, leaving a runoff between Edwin Edwards, a former three-term governor long dogged by corruption allegations, and David Duke, a state legislator and former Ku Klux Klan leader. Roemer's supporters and many others now had to choose between a man they considered dishonest and one they considered dangerous. Neither represented their views. The race is remembered for a bumper sticker that told voters, with grim candor, to vote for the crook because it was important. Turnout was unusually high, and Edwards won easily.

The lesson lies in the voters' reasoning, not the outcome. Those who chose Edwards were not endorsing his record; the bumper sticker admitted as much. They were answering the question the ballot actually posed, and on that question they held a firm view. A citizen who stayed home because neither man represented her would not have escaped the choice; she would merely have let others make it, and the cost of her scruples could have fallen on the Black and Jewish Louisianans whom Duke had long vilified. The duty to vote does not wait for a candidate worth admiring.

The most compelling challenge concedes that Duke was worse and attacks the habit instead. If citizens reliably settle for the lesser evil, parties learn that bad candidates carry no penalty, and the choices never improve; Louisiana did get the crook it was promised, since Edwards was later convicted of racketeering. Staying home, on this view, is the only refusal left. It would be [[churlish|churlish]] to wave this argument away; the dynamic it describes is real. Yet it rests on an assumption that [[vitiates|vitiate]] it: that abstention is heard as protest. A nonvoter looks exactly like a citizen who did not care; dissent has force only where it is counted. In the Baseball Hall of Fame's election, a player must appear on three quarters of the ballots sportswriters cast, and a blank ballot counts as cast. A writer who finds every candidate unworthy can decline to vote, which changes nothing, or return a blank, which raises the bar for everyone; in 2013, when Barry Bonds and Roger Clemens first became eligible, a handful of writers did just that. A write-in or third-party vote lets a citizen say "none of these" without vanishing from the count.

A contrasting case shows where the duty ends. For most of Soviet history, each district offered a single, party-approved candidate. A voter could cross out the name, but doing so meant stepping into a booth, a conspicuous act when nearly everyone else dropped the unmarked ballot into the box, which counted as approval. Official turnout approached one hundred percent. Voting there was a [[perfunctory|perfunctory]] ritual meant not to decide anything but to display unanimity. No [[tenable|tenable]] account of civic duty could oblige a Soviet citizen to take part, because the ballot posed no question; participation was itself the endorsement the regime was manufacturing.

The duty to vote, then, does not rest on finding a candidate who speaks for us; it rests on the fact that someone will hold power whether or not we take part. Where the alternatives differ sharply, as they did in Louisiana, abstaining does not keep one's hands clean; it hands the decision to others. Where the candidates are nearly [[interchangeable|interchangeable]], a blank or protest ballot still discharges the duty. Only where the result is fixed in advance does the obligation dissolve, because there is no decision left to hand over.
