prompt.statement: Children today are given too little freedom to take risks.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Which Risks, Not How Much Risk
essays.essay:
The case against overprotecting children usually rests on [[mawkish|mawkish]] nostalgia: barefoot summers, scars from tumbles out of trees, errands run alone at seven. Such memories lend the statement a certain plausibility, but they prove little, since only the survivors of risky childhoods are left to reminisce. I nonetheless agree with the statement, provided we discard its hidden assumption: that risk is a single quantity, to be rationed in larger or smaller doses. Children today are shielded too thoroughly from one kind of risk, the graded and recoverable kind that builds judgment, while left exposed, often unsupervised, to another kind that teaches little and forgives less.

A more rigorous case comes from medicine, and it rests on evidence rather than the [[hackneyed|hackneyed]] appeal to childhood memory. Around the turn of this century, health authorities in Britain and the United States advised keeping peanuts away from allergy-prone infants, in some cases until age three. The logic seemed unimpeachable: if a food might provoke a dangerous reaction, postpone the encounter. Peanut allergy nonetheless kept growing more common. London researchers then found that Jewish children in Britain had peanut allergy at roughly ten times the rate of Jewish children in Israel, where babies routinely eat peanut-based snacks. That contrast prompted a trial that randomly assigned several hundred high-risk infants to eat peanut foods regularly or to avoid them entirely. By age five, the children who had eaten them were far less likely to be allergic, and American guidelines now recommend early introduction for such infants.

The instructive point is that no one in this episode was careless. Parents followed expert advice, and the advice followed a near-universal intuition: that the safest dose of a danger is zero. Yet the immune system learns tolerance through early, modest contact, so avoidance did not preserve safety; it foreclosed the learning that would have produced it. Judgment develops along similar lines. A child learns how high is too high, or how to weather a [[tempestuous|tempestuous]] friendship without adult rescue, through small, survivable mistakes. A childhood that withholds those mistakes does not abolish the danger; it postpones the lesson until the stakes are higher. Tellingly, a mainstay of treatment for anxiety disorders is graded exposure: [[deliberate|deliberate]], incremental encounters with the very situations a frightened patient has learned to avoid. Judgment is not an immune response, but the logic carries over: some capacities are built only through contact with the thing they guard against.

The most compelling objection is that this argument romanticizes a past that was often lethal. Earlier generations rode unrestrained in cars and grew up in homes where any toddler could open the aspirin bottle; many children did not survive those freedoms. Car seats and child-resistant caps curtail children's freedom exactly as the statement deplores, yet both are credited with sharply reducing the deaths they target; if paternalism is ever [[beneficent|beneficent]], it is here. Every call for more risk, the opponent concludes, gambles with lives that modern caution has saved. I concede the facts, but they mark the statement's boundary rather than refute it. The hazards those measures guard against share three features: a child cannot perceive them, cannot learn from them in small doses, and often cannot survive a single mistake. A toddler who swallows a handful of pills learns nothing. The tall tree, the solo trip to the park, and the playground quarrel differ on every count: their dangers are visible and incremental, and their usual price is a bruise or a bad day.

By this test, our caution is less excessive than misplaced. Many children forbidden to visit a park alone carry a smartphone that admits strangers and audiences no parent can see, and online risks have exactly the profile we should fear. A stranger in a chat window offers none of the cues a stranger on a sidewalk does and can impersonate a classmate with unsettling [[verisimilitude|verisimilitude]]; a photograph shared at thirteen may circulate indefinitely. Children do need more room for risk, but only for the visible, graduated, recoverable kind that forms judgment. The remedy is not fewer restraints but redistributed ones: give back the park and the climbing tree, and guard the screen far more closely.

prompt.statement: Some people believe that the best way to reduce crime is to punish it severely. Others believe that crime is reduced most effectively by addressing the conditions that produce it.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Certainty and Conditions, Not Severity
essays.essay:
In 2022, social media videos showed how to start certain Kia and Hyundai models with little more than a screwdriver and a USB cable; unlike most cars sold in the United States, those models lacked an electronic immobilizer. Thefts soon multiplied in city after city. Penalties for auto theft had not softened, and young people had not suddenly lost their moral bearings; the most [[parsimonious|parsimonious]] explanation is that a crime had become easy and its method widely known. The episode shows why I side, with one qualification, with those who would reduce crime by addressing the conditions that produce it. The qualification is that "conditions" must include not only crime's deep social roots, such as poverty and neglect, but also the opportunities a society leaves open and the likelihood that an offender will be caught.

The case for severe punishment, though often couched in [[truculent|truculent]] rhetoric, deserves a fair hearing because it rests on something true: people respond to consequences. Prison also incapacitates, since a burglar behind bars cannot break into homes. A stern sentence, moreover, declares certain acts intolerable. For crimes of [[deliberate|deliberate]] calculation, such as accounting fraud, prison surely gives some would-be offenders pause. Yet this view conflates two properties of punishment that work differently: how harsh it is and how likely it is. The eighteenth-century jurist Cesare Beccaria argued that a moderate but certain penalty impresses the mind more than a terrible one that might be escaped. Modern research largely bears him out, with one refinement: what deters most is the chance of being caught. A U.S. National Research Council review concluded that making already long sentences longer adds little deterrence. Severity still counts, but it is discounted by the perceived odds of capture; a low chance of detection [[vitiates|vitiate]] even the most fearsome threat. An impulsive sixteen-year-old who has just watched a how-to video is not weighing the sentencing code.

Critics often caricature the conditions view as merely [[beneficent|beneficent]], a kindness to offenders at their victims' expense. The evidence suggests otherwise. In a randomized trial begun in Elmira, New York, in the late 1970s, nurses visited disadvantaged first-time mothers from pregnancy until their children turned two. By adolescence, the children of unmarried, low-income mothers who were visited had been arrested less often than comparable children whose mothers were not visited. That is not leniency; it is prevention. Yet the trial also exposes a weakness in the conditions view as usually stated. Its payoff became measurable only years later, and only as arrests that never happened, which makes such programs easy to cut and of no comfort to a neighborhood frightened tonight. Worse, if "conditions" means only poverty and family disadvantage, the view becomes an alibi for inaction rather than a defensible position, since no city council can abolish poverty before the next election.

Medicine offers a better model than either camp's slogan. A cardiologist who opens a blocked artery during a heart attack does not conclude that prevention is pointless; acute care and prevention answer different questions. Punishment is the acute response: it is owed to victims, it expresses the community's [[opprobrium|opprobrium]], and it removes a few dangerous people from circulation. A health system that funded only emergency rooms would be cruel and ruinously expensive; a justice system that relies chiefly on ever-longer sentences makes the same mistake. The deeper point is that the effective part of the first view is a version of the second. Certainty of capture is itself a condition, created by investigators who actually solve cases, much as a car's vulnerability to theft is created by its makers.

I therefore stand closer to those who would address the conditions of crime, provided the phrase is read broadly enough to include opportunity and detection as well as disadvantage. Punishment should be sure and proportionate rather than spectacular. Money spent lengthening sentences that already deter little would do more good if spent on solving crimes, designing them out of everyday products, and reaching vulnerable families years before a child's first arrest. A society that wants less crime should ask not how much it can make offenders suffer but how many offenses it can make difficult, unprofitable, or unnecessary.

harsh and aggressively combative in expression, as in tough-on-crime speeches
conscious and intentional; describes calculation in which an offender weighs costs against gains

analysis.verdict: This response earns a 6 because its position is insightful, not just clear. It splits the punishment view into severity and certainty, then folds certainty of capture into a broader definition of conditions. Every example, from the Kia thefts to the Elmira trial, is described and then tied explicitly to the argument, and the prose is precise and varied.

The Kia thefts show crime tracking opportunity; Beccaria and the National Research Council separate severity from certainty, refined to "what deters most is the chance of being caught"; and the Elmira trial shows root-cause prevention working, but slowly. prompt.statement: Some believe that organized sports teach young people cooperation and discipline. Others believe that they teach young people to value winning above everything else.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: The Game Teaches, Adults Distort
essays.essay:
That sports build character is one of the most [[hackneyed|hackneyed]] claims in public life, recited at every awards banquet and rarely examined. Its cynical counterpart, that sports teach children to worship victory, is hardly fresher. Both rest on a shared assumption: that "organized sports" is a single teacher delivering a single lesson. In fact the phrase joins two things. One is the game, with its rules, positions, and practice; the other is the apparatus of coaches, parents, leagues, and rankings that decides what counts as success. The game reliably teaches cooperation and discipline; the conviction that winning outweighs everything else comes from the apparatus, and only when adults choose to teach it. The first view therefore comes closer to my own, provided it concedes how easily adults [[vitiate|vitiate]] the game's lessons.

Consider what the game demands on its own terms. A basketball team whose best player refuses to pass can lose to a weaker team that moves the ball, and children often grasp this before any coach explains it. A relay sprinter's months of solitary training count for nothing if she and her teammate have not rehearsed the baton exchange. Discipline is equally built in: free throws improve only through repetition whose payoff arrives weeks later, the kind of delayed reward adolescents most resist. Temperament, too, is reshaped. A [[tempestuous|tempestuous]] fifteen-year-old who would gladly argue with a teacher learns to hold his tongue with a referee, because a technical foul gives the opponent free throws and the cost lands on his teammates. None of this requires an inspiring coach; the lessons are embedded in the rules, which is why they surface even in mediocre programs.

Still, it would be [[churlish|churlish]] to deny the second view its due, and a Saturday beside a youth soccer field shows why. Sidelines fill with angry parents who berate teenage referees over offside calls, and because officials cite abuse from adults as a leading reason they quit, many leagues face a [[dwindling|dwindling]] supply of referees. At the extreme, adult ambition turns into fraud: a Bronx team was stripped of its victories at the 2001 Little League World Series after it emerged that adults had falsified its star pitcher's birth certificate; he was two years over the age limit. Discipline is the habit of holding oneself to a standard; what win-obsessed programs instill is closer to [[obeisance|obeisance]] to whoever controls playing time. And the twelve-year-old who stalks past the handshake line after a loss is often reproducing manners he learned on the sideline. Notice, though, who is doing the teaching. None of these lessons comes from the rules of soccer or baseball; each comes from adults who treat a children's game as a referendum on themselves.

The clearest evidence that this second lesson is a choice rather than a necessity comes from public policy. Norway's national sports confederation, a publicly subsidized body, bars national championships for children under thirteen and limits published results and rankings for the youngest players. Skeptics predict that children spared early rankings will never learn to strive, yet Norway finished first in the overall medal count at both the 2018 and 2022 Winter Olympics. Those medals have many causes, from national wealth to the winter itself, so the case cannot prove that postponing rankings produces champions. It shows something narrower: rankings can wait. A society can keep the games, the practice, and the teammates, delay the championships and standings, and still produce athletes who win when winning matters. The fixation on winning, in short, is a policy, and policies can be revised.

Organized sports, then, are less a single teacher than a channel that adults control. The game sends a steady signal of cooperation and discipline, and those adults decide whether to let it through or drown it out with standings, trophies, and sideline fury. That is why I side with the first view, and why the second deserves to be heard as a warning rather than dismissed as cynicism. The question worth asking of any youth league is not whether its children play to win, since every game invites that, but whether the adults running it have mistaken the score for the point.

prompt.statement:
Claim: Students learn more from failure than from success.
Reason: Failure forces people to examine their methods, whereas success lets them repeat methods without understanding why those methods worked.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Failure Is a Prompt, Not a Teacher
essays.essay:
That failure is the best teacher has become a [[hackneyed|hackneyed]] theme of commencement speeches, and like most clichés it survives because it is partly true. Still, the claim and its reason deserve separate verdicts. The reason identifies a genuine asymmetry: a failure demands an explanation, whereas a success seldom invites one. But a demand for explanation is not an explanation, and the reason never asks whether the scrutiny that failure provokes arrives at the truth. I therefore find the claim [[tenable|tenable]] only under three conditions: the failure must be informative, the learner must know enough to interpret it, and the lesson drawn from it must remain open to revision.

When a failure is informative and the learner is equipped to read it, it can teach what no success could. After Venezuela's First Republic collapsed in 1812, Simón Bolívar, in exile in Cartagena, wrote a manifesto dissecting the defeat. Among the causes he named was a federal constitution that divided authority among the provinces while royalist forces advanced; the remedy, he concluded, was centralized command. Had the republic survived, its leaders might well have credited federalism with saving it; only the collapse revealed when federalism breaks down. This is the strongest case for the claim, and it rests on a different foundation from the one the reason offers. Failure teaches more not simply because it forces people to examine their methods, but because it locates the limits of a method, something success by its nature cannot do.

Remove either condition, and the claim weakens quickly. Much failure is [[laconic|laconic]]: a form rejection or a red mark on an exam announces that something went wrong without saying what. To a learner who cannot diagnose the problem, such a verdict breeds discouragement more often than insight. Research on mathematics instruction offers an indirect parallel: beginners often learn more from studying worked examples than from unaided problem solving, yet struggling with a problem before instruction can deepen understanding when a teacher then explains why the attempts failed. What helps novices is not failure but explained failure. Even a gifted writer can be stalled by failure's silence. For years, by his own account, Gabriel García Márquez failed to write the novel about his grandparents' house that became One Hundred Years of Solitude. The abandoned drafts told him only that something was wrong. The answer came from a success he remembered: the impassive tone in which his grandmother had recounted ghosts and omens as though they were household news, a tone that lends [[verisimilitude|verisimilitude]] to the impossible. Failure supplied the motive to keep searching; success supplied the method.

The reason has a deeper weakness. It is attractively [[parsimonious|parsimonious]], resting the whole contrast on a single mechanism, but examining one's methods is not the same as understanding them. Failure can teach the wrong lesson, or a right lesson held as though it could never expire. Bolívar is again instructive. His conviction that only strong central authority could hold a young republic together outlasted the emergency that produced it: once independence was essentially won, his draft constitution for Bolivia provided for a president for life, and liberal comrades-in-arms saw in it a monarchy under another name. A failure had taught him something true about 1812; it could not tell him whether that truth still held in peace. The reason [[skirts|skirt]] this problem entirely, as though any lesson a failure prompts must be correct and permanent. It also overstates the opposite case: success permits complacency but does not require it, and students can be taught to interrogate their correct answers as rigorously as their mistakes.

I accept, then, the reason's premise that failure provokes scrutiny more reliably than success does, but not its implication that scrutiny yields understanding. Failure is a better prompt than it is a teacher. Students learn more from it than from success when the failure is specific enough to diagnose, when they or their teachers know enough to diagnose it, and when they hold the resulting lesson provisionally. Absent those conditions, a well-examined success teaches more than a mute defeat. The question that matters is not whether an outcome was good or bad, but whether anyone has worked out why it happened.

prompt.statement:
Claim: Leaders should be chosen for their character rather than their expertise.
Reason: Expertise can be borrowed from advisers, but judgment cannot.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Character Cannot Judge Without Expertise
essays.essay:
No leader can master every field her decisions touch. A university president who waited to acquire [[encyclopedic|encyclopedic]] knowledge of every department would never decide anything. On settled questions, technical knowledge is largely [[fungible|fungible]]: one competent tax attorney will give much the same advice as another. The stated reason thus begins with a genuine insight. A leader can hire expertise by the hour, but she cannot hire someone to decide which hired expert to believe; at the end of every chain of delegation, that judgment remains hers. So far, the argument holds. It breaks down at the next step, because it assumes that the judgment it rightly prizes springs from character alone, when much of it is built from expertise. My verdict is therefore divided: the reason is only half true, and the claim is only half right, since character matters, though not for the reason given and not in place of expertise.

The trouble is that advisers seldom agree on the questions that matter most, and even a briefing written in [[limpid|limpid]] prose cannot tell a leader whether to trust it over the one on the next desk. Consider Billy Beane's Oakland Athletics, as Michael Lewis portrayed them in Moneyball. Saddled with one of baseball's smallest payrolls, Beane heard from two camps of experts: veteran scouts, who judged players largely by how they looked and moved, and analysts, who argued that neglected statistics such as on-base percentage better predicted winning. Beane sided with the analysts, and the approach helped his vastly outspent team reach the postseason repeatedly. His choice took nerve, but it was not an act of character alone. Beane had once been a first-round draft pick whom scouts adored and who never became the star they predicted; he knew from experience how their eye could deceive. Pressed this far, the reason undercuts its own claim: if judgment cannot be borrowed, and judgment rests partly on expertise, then that portion of expertise cannot be borrowed either.

Public education shows the mirror image: character working alone. For years, many American school districts taught beginning readers through "three-cueing," a method that encouraged children to guess unfamiliar words from pictures and context rather than sound them out. Prestigious education professors promoted the approach with [[magisterial|magisterial]] confidence. Grant that the administrators who adopted it were devoted to their students. What they lacked was enough grounding in reading research to question their advisers, so their conscientiousness took the form of [[obeisance|obeisance]] to credentialed authority. Only after cognitive scientists and journalists publicized decades of evidence favoring systematic phonics did states begin to restrict the method. Character did not protect those children, because without expertise it could not recognize the danger.

Still, the claim's case for character survives on different grounds. Character matters not because judgment cannot be borrowed but because expertise is morally neutral: it amplifies whatever purposes a leader brings to it. Enron's executives, celebrated as the cleverest in American business, used their command of accounting rules to hide the company's debts until it collapsed in 2001; their expertise served their dishonesty instead of restraining it. Yet the statement conflates character with judgment. Honesty and courage are traits of character; judgment is the capacity to weigh competing claims, and it can fail in the most virtuous person. Even if the reason were wholly true, it would support choosing leaders for judgment, not for character. Indeed, an honest leader who cannot follow her advisers' arguments is apt to side with whichever one is most [[urbane|urbane]] and self-assured, mistaking polish for proof.

Leaders, then, should be chosen neither for character alone nor for expertise alone but for judgment: character disciplined by enough expertise to interrogate the experts. How much expertise that demands depends on the field. Where knowledge is settled and advisers largely agree, counsel is interchangeable, and integrity can carry most of the load. Where evidence is contested and trusting the wrong adviser is costly, as it was in Oakland and in countless classrooms, a leader needs knowledge of her own, not to replace her advisers but to know which of them has earned her trust. Character makes a leader willing to listen; expertise tells her whom to believe.

prompt.statement: Large companies should be required to publish the ratio between the pay of their highest- and lowest-paid workers.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Who Counts Decides Whether Disclosure Works
essays.essay:
The strongest objection to mandatory pay-ratio disclosure is that the number describes the shape of a business more than the conduct of its managers. A supermarket chain that pays its cashiers well above the going rate will still report a far larger ratio than a consulting firm whose lowest-paid employees are junior analysts, even if that firm is [[parsimonious|parsimonious]] with their raises. Ranked across industries, the ratio rewards companies for having no low-wage jobs rather than for paying their lowest-paid workers well, and a public that reads it as a verdict on corporate virtue will be misled.

That objection is correct, but its force ends at the boundary of an industry. Within a single sector, where rival firms hire the same kinds of workers, and within a single firm over time, the ratio becomes informative: if one retailer's ratio doubles in a decade while its competitors' hold steady, something has changed in how that company divides its revenue. I therefore support the requirement, though not in the form the statement proposes, because the policy's merit lies entirely in its consequences, and those consequences turn on a detail the statement treats as trivial: which worker counts as the lowest paid.

The intended consequence is restraint through publicity, and publicity alone can change corporate behavior. When Congress created the Toxics Release Inventory in 1986, it required American factories to report releases of listed toxic chemicals but imposed no new emission limits; it simply made the figures public. Newspapers and environmental groups turned the data into lists of each region's worst polluters, and reported releases fell steeply in the following years, in part because companies sought to stay off those lists. A pay ratio could operate the same way. Amid proxy statements that are notoriously opaque, it would be the one figure a reporter or a cashier could grasp at a glance. A board tempted to indulge a [[rapacious|rapacious]] chief executive would know that its generosity would appear as a single, quotable multiple. Few directors are indifferent to the [[opprobrium|opprobrium]] that such a number can attract.

The same history, however, exposes the policy's danger. Researchers later found that part of the decline existed only on paper, reflecting changes in how plants estimated emissions rather than in what they emitted. A pay ratio invites cruder manipulation still. The cheapest way to shrink it is not to raise the lowest wage but to move the lowest-paid workers off the payroll, handing cleaning, security, and food service to contractors whose employees do the same work, often for lower wages and fewer benefits, yet no longer appear in the denominator. For a company that already treats such workers as [[fungible|fungible]], the change is a matter of paperwork. The economist David Weil has documented how [[pervasive|pervasive]] this "fissuring" of employment has become. The statement's version, keyed to the single lowest-paid worker, is especially exposed: one part-time employee can swing the figure, and outsourcing that job improves it overnight. A policy meant to curb inequality by shaming firms would then deepen it while reporting that it had narrowed.

These consequences, more than any abstract principle of fairness, determine my position. A disclosure requirement deserves support only if it is built to withstand the incentives it creates. It should compare the top executive's total compensation with the median worker's pay, as the Securities and Exchange Commission's rule under the Dodd-Frank Act already does, so that one employee's pay cannot [[vitiate|vitiate]] the comparison. It should count workers supplied by long-term contractors, so that outsourcing cannot flatter the number. And it should be published beside the firm's own past ratios and its industry's average, so that the supermarket is judged against other supermarkets rather than against consulting firms.

The real question, then, is not whether the public deserves to know how a large company divides its rewards; it plainly does. The question is whether the number it receives will measure that division or merely teach firms to redraw their boundaries. A ratio that counts only the workers a company chooses to keep on its books describes its accounting; one that counts everyone whose labor it depends on describes its choices. Only the second deserves the force of law.

prompt.statement: Schools should ban mobile phones during the school day.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Phone Bans Work Only When Enforced Equally
essays.essay:
Debates about banning phones in schools usually pit distraction against convenience, but that framing hides the variable that decides whether a ban succeeds. A ban is not one policy but two: a rule and a method of enforcing it. The rule can be as [[laconic|laconic]] as a sign on the classroom door, but the consequences of enforcing it matter as much as its intent. Weighing those consequences, I support banning phones for the whole school day for children and young adolescents, but only if the school itself bears the cost of enforcement, collects the devices rather than merely forbidding their use, and writes narrow exceptions into the rule. A ban that lives mainly on paper, or that is enforced against some students and not others, is worse than no ban at all.

Brazil offers an instructive test. In early 2025, after Rio de Janeiro had tested a restriction in its city schools, the country enacted a national law limiting students' use of phones in public and private schools, not only during lessons but also during recess. That the measure cleared a famously [[fractious|fractious]] Congress suggests the problem was visible across political lines. The inclusion of recess is the revealing detail. Legislators were not simply shielding lessons from the buzz of notifications; they were trying to reclaim the hours in which children learn to talk to one another face to face. A phone carries the [[tempestuous|tempestuous]] friendships of early adolescence into every corridor, so that a curt reply in a group chat can unsettle a thirteen-year-old for an entire afternoon. Just as important, no single student can put her phone away without missing what everyone else is seeing. A universal rule relieves each child of a choice that none can make alone, a benefit no teacher's discretion can supply.

The drafters also anticipated unintended consequences, and their choices show what a defensible ban looks like. It would be [[churlish|churlish]] to deny that a phone can aid learning, whether as a calculator, a camera, or a dictionary, and the law sensibly permits use under a teacher's direction. It also exempts students who need a device for a disability or a health condition, and it allows use in emergencies, a provision that matters in Rio, where armed clashes between police and gangs regularly close schools in some neighborhoods. These exceptions make the ban a firm default rather than an absolute. Yet no statute confiscates a single phone. Whether the law yields calmer classrooms or a daily contest of wills will depend on whether schools have lockers or pouches, and on whether teachers are spared the [[onerous|onerous]] work of policing pockets.

New York City shows what happens when those conditions are ignored. For years its public schools officially banned phones, but the rule was enforced mainly where students passed through metal detectors, and those schools served disproportionately poor Black and Latino students. Many paid nearby vendors, often a dollar a day, to hold their phones until dismissal. In schools without scanners, enforcement was [[perfunctory|perfunctory]], and phones stayed in pockets. When the city lifted the ban in 2015, officials pointed to this inequity, along with parents' wish to reach their children. The system had shifted the cost of enforcement onto the students least able to pay it. The episode does not show that bans fail; it shows that their gravest risk is not lingering distraction but injustice. A rule applied only to poorer students teaches every student that rules are selective.

Followed to their consequences, the competing arguments resolve into a conditional answer. The benefits of a ban are real and largely social, and they materialize only when the rule is universal, so that no child stands alone as the exception. The costs fall on whoever must enforce the rule and whoever cannot afford to obey it. A school should therefore ban phones only if it is prepared to absorb those costs itself, and it should loosen the rule as students near adulthood, when learning to set a phone aside becomes more valuable than being made to. What matters, in the end, is less whether phones belong in school than whether a school will pay for a ban that binds everyone equally.

prompt.statement: A leader's greatest achievements are usually the problems he or she prevented rather than the ones he or she solved.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Averted, Deferred, and Unforeseen Problems
essays.essay:
Anyone who has worked in a hospital knows this paradox: when the infection-control team does its job well, nothing happens, and someone on the budget committee soon asks why the team exists. The statement rightly extends this insight to leadership. Prevented problems leave no evidence, and the leaders who avert them are often [[reticent|reticent]] about their success, since warning of a crisis can trigger it. Such leaders receive less credit than they deserve. Yet the word "usually" rests on two hidden assumptions: that a problem averted stays averted, and that leaders choose the problems they face. Neither holds reliably. Prevention is a leader's greatest achievement only when it removes a danger rather than postponing it, and only when the leader had a chance to act before the crisis arrived.

Earl Warren's career shows the statement at its strongest. When Warren became Chief Justice in 1953, Brown v. Board of Education had already been argued once, and the justices were divided over whether to overturn "separate but equal." A split decision would have been a gift to segregationists, since any dissent would give them a respectable authority to cite. Warren, an [[adroit|adroit]] politician and former governor of California, set out to prevent that outcome. For months he courted the hesitant justices one at a time. He then drafted an opinion plain enough for any newspaper reader to follow, declining to write a [[trenchant|trenchant]] indictment of the South and focusing instead on what segregation did to Black children. The Court ruled unanimously. That unanimity was arguably Warren's most consequential achievement, yet what it prevented is invisible by nature: no one quotes the dissent that was never written.

The sequel reveals the limits of prevention. A year later, the Court, again speaking through Warren, tried to head off Southern defiance by returning the cases to the lower courts with instructions to desegregate "with all deliberate speed." The [[conciliatory|conciliatory]] phrase was meant to purchase compliance with patience; it purchased delay instead. Prince Edward County, Virginia, one of the districts in the original litigation, closed its public schools for years rather than integrate them. Elsewhere, resistance hid behind a show of bureaucratic [[torpor|torpor]]. School boards adopted [[byzantine|byzantine]] pupil-placement rules, admitted a token handful of Black students, and waited. A decade after Brown, only a tiny fraction of Black children in the Deep South attended school with white classmates; not until the late 1960s did the Court demand desegregation at once. The problem had not been prevented but postponed, and the cost fell on children who had no voice in the bargain. Warren's two decisions therefore sharpen my position: averting a problem is an achievement, but deferring one merely disguises failure as foresight.

A contrasting case exposes the statement's second assumption. In 1982, several Chicago-area residents died after taking Extra-Strength Tylenol capsules laced with cyanide. The poison had been added after the bottles reached stores, a crime no one at Johnson & Johnson could reasonably have foreseen. The company's chairman, James Burke, could only respond: he pulled Tylenol capsules from shelves nationwide at great cost, warned consumers not to take them, and within two months brought the drug back in triple-sealed packaging. His response is still taught as a model of crisis management. For leaders who face problems they neither chose nor could foresee, solving is not a lesser achievement than preventing but the only one available. This case narrows my agreement further, confining the statement to leaders who had the luxury of acting first.

The statement is best read, then, not as a ranking but as a correction, one that rightly asks us to credit the unwritten dissent and the outbreak that never began. Foresight deserves the highest praise when it detects a danger early and ends it for good; when it merely postpones a reckoning, or when a crisis arrives without warning, repair is the greater work. Nor are the two rivals, for the best solutions harden into prevention. Since the Tylenol murders, federal rules have required tamper-evident packaging on most over-the-counter medicines, and the seal on a new bottle of aspirin now guards, unnoticed, against a repeat of the crisis Burke had to solve.

prompt.statement: Laws change behavior more slowly than culture does.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Law Outruns Culture When Witnesses Enforce It
essays.essay:
On a single morning in September 1967, every driver in Sweden moved from the left side of the road to the right. Twelve years earlier, voters had overwhelmingly rejected the change in a referendum, yet when the switchover day arrived, a whole nation's driving behavior changed within hours. If law always lagged behind culture, that morning could not have happened. I agree with the statement only for a particular kind of behavior: conduct that peers admire and witnesses would rather shield than punish. Where conduct is visible and ordinary people have reasons to police it, law can outrun culture and even pull culture along behind it.

Sweden's switch succeeded for reasons that generalize. After four years of preparation and publicity, the instruction was unmistakable: on the appointed morning, keep right. Compliance was visible to everyone on the road, and once other drivers had switched, no sane motorist would stay on the left; the law did not have to change anyone's preference, only to tell everyone when to move together. Ireland's 2004 ban on smoking in workplaces worked similarly. Smoke was a fixture of the Irish pub, and many publicans fought the measure. Yet smokers grumbled and then [[acquiesced|acquiesce]], stepping outside, because a cigarette cannot be hidden in a crowded room and because publicans, who faced fines, had every reason to enforce the rule themselves. Soon a smoky pub seemed odd. The law did not wait for culture to change; it created the culture that now sustains it.

Dueling tells the opposite story. In the 1620s, the Count of Bouteville, a notorious duelist, defied Louis XIII's renewed ban by fighting in a Paris square. His powerful relatives begged for mercy, but Richelieu warned that a pardon would destroy the edict's authority, and the king, refusing any [[conciliatory|conciliatory]] gesture, had him beheaded. Yet the practice survived. Before the Revolution, duelists arranged [[surreptitious|surreptitious]] meetings or passed off planned fights as chance encounters; in the nineteenth century, duels were fought openly, reported in the press, and seldom punished. The law failed because those who knew of a duel, from seconds to magistrates, often shared the code of honor behind it, and because the penalty that mattered most was social: declining a challenge was [[tantamount|tantamount]] to confessing cowardice, a verdict peers enforced far more reliably than any court. In England, a fatal duel had long counted as murder, though juries were reluctant to convict; the practice faded only in the mid-nineteenth century, when respectable opinion came to [[deride|deride]] it as absurd rather than honorable. Here the statement holds: the law had long been on the books, yet behavior changed only after the culture did.

These contrasting cases keep my agreement partial, and they expose an assumption buried in the statement: that culture is the nimble force and law the sluggish one. Culture can be remarkably [[lethargic|lethargic]]. The English code of honor took generations to soften, and Swedish voters showed no wish to switch sides until the law compelled them. Speed depends less on which force acts than on what kind of behavior it targets. A law works quickly when its command is clear, when compliance is visible, and when those who see violations have their own reasons to enforce it. It works slowly, if at all, when violators can hide or when witnesses share the code the law attacks. Change goes deepest and lasts longest when the two pull together: American drunk-driving deaths fell substantially in the 1980s and 1990s, as Mothers Against Drunk Driving made the act shameful while legislatures stiffened penalties, each reinforcing the other.

The statement, then, mistakes a condition for a rule. Where law polices conduct that peers admire and witnesses shield, such as dueling, it merely drives the practice underground or into open defiance, and the decisive work falls to culture. Where it governs public conduct that anyone can watch, it can change behavior overnight, as in Sweden, and then reshape the attitudes that were supposed to resist it, as in Ireland. The real question is not whether law or culture moves faster, but whether a particular law enlists the eyes and interests of ordinary people or must work against them.

prompt.statement: Wealthy donors should fund causes that governments neglect rather than causes that are already popular.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Fund Beginnings the Public Will Finish
essays.essay:
The recommendation rests on sound arithmetic. A million dollars added to a cause that already attracts hundreds of millions changes little, while the same sum given to a cause that no one funds can change a great deal. I accept that arithmetic, and I agree that wealthy donors should look first to what governments neglect. The statement, however, goes astray in treating government neglect as an empty space that private money can simply fill. A gift to a neglected cause can draw a government into a responsibility it has failed to take up, or it can excuse the government from that responsibility indefinitely. The recommendation is wise under the first condition and self-defeating under the second.

The case for the recommendation is clearest when a cause becomes popular overnight. When fire tore through Notre-Dame de Paris in April 2019, several of France's richest families pledged hundreds of millions of euros within a day, though an earlier appeal for repairs had struggled to raise money. Need had not drawn the donors; spectacle had. No one doubts that so [[numinous|numinous]] a place deserves restoration, but the cathedral belongs to the French state, whose president vowed that night to rebuild it. The gifts thus covered a cost the state had already accepted, and generous tax breaks meant that taxpayers would still bear part of it. Meanwhile, churches owned by cash-strapped villages went on crumbling. The pledges also put the donors in an [[invidious|invidious]] position: protesters who had spent months demanding economic relief asked why fortunes could appear overnight for stone but not for people. One donor family made the conciliatory gesture of renouncing its tax break, but the question remained: it was the arithmetic restated in moral terms.

Yet avoiding crowded causes is only half of a giving strategy, and the recommendation says little about the other half: how to fund what is neglected. Andrew Carnegie's library program shows that such giving works best when it draws the government in. Around 1900, cities such as Boston already ran tax-supported libraries, but many smaller American towns had none, and Carnegie paid to build well over a thousand libraries, many in just such towns. His most [[adroit|adroit]] move was the standard condition attached to his grants: the town had to supply the site and commit public money, year after year, to stock, staff, and maintain the building. Carnegie bore the large initial cost that had stalled local governments, while the ongoing service became a public duty. Many of those buildings still house public libraries, a sign that his gifts did not replace public responsibility but spread it.

The same generosity goes wrong when outside money replaces the state instead of enlisting it. Haiti, often called a "republic of NGOs," shows how. For decades, international charities, financed by private donors and foreign governments alike, have run clinics, schools, and water projects that the state did not provide, and after the 2010 earthquake most relief money again flowed around Haitian institutions rather than through them. Each project met a real need. The charities bore no [[animus|animus]] toward the state, and its weakness, rooted in dictatorship and poverty, was not their doing. Unlike Carnegie's grants, however, most of these gifts asked nothing of the state, and together they produced a patchwork of services answerable to distant funders. As critics in Haiti and abroad have argued, they left the government with little pressure and little money to build services of its own. Outside generosity did not rouse the state from its [[torpor|torpor]]; it made that torpor affordable.

Taken together, these examples shape a position narrower than the recommendation but no less firm. The rush to rebuild Notre-Dame confirms its central insight: money that chases a cause into the headlines buys little the state would not have bought anyway. Carnegie's libraries and Haiti's clinics refine it, showing that neglect is a reason to give but not yet a plan for giving. Wealthy donors should seek out what governments neglect, but they should pay for beginnings rather than for permanence and insist, as Carnegie did, that the public take up what the gift has started.

prompt.statement: Countries should teach every child at least two languages from primary school onward.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Lived Versus Decreed Bilingualism in Schools
essays.essay:
Debates about language in schools usually treat bilingualism as a single good, but it comes in two kinds. Lived bilingualism is the kind a society already practices, where a child needs a second language to talk with neighbors or continue her education. Decreed bilingualism is the kind a ministry designs: officials choose a language in the capital and assign it to every classroom, whether or not anyone nearby speaks it. The recommendation is wise when it formalizes the first kind and doubtful, sometimes harmful, when it imposes the second. Its weakness is its silence on the question that matters most: which second language, and chosen by whom.

Paraguay shows the recommendation at its most persuasive. Unusually for the Americas, an indigenous language, Guaraní, is spoken by most Paraguayans, the great majority of whom do not identify as indigenous, and it shares official status with Spanish. A child raised in Guaraní in the countryside needs Spanish to read a contract or enter a university; a child raised in Spanish in Asunción needs Guaraní to talk easily with much of the country. Children who grow up with both become [[adroit|adroit]] at sensing which language a conversation calls for, Guaraní among friends and Spanish in a government office. For these children, schooling in both languages adds no exotic subject; it formalizes a competence they are already building. Starting early makes sense here, because a child's [[inborn|inborn]] capacity for language thrives on constant use, and in Paraguay the second language is waiting outside the school door.

The same early start yields far less where the second language has no life beyond the classroom. Many school systems schedule a foreign language for a few short lessons a week, sometimes taught by teachers who barely speak it, in towns where nobody else does. The prospect of a fluent seven-year-old is [[tantalizing|tantalizing]], but under those conditions youth confers little advantage; studies of classroom learners find that later starters often catch up with early ones. Nor are the hours free. A primary curriculum must ration its time. Where many children finish the early grades unable to read fluently in their first language, an hour of mandated English or French is an hour taken from the literacy on which every later subject depends. There, following the recommendation trades literacy for a gesture.

Decreed bilingualism does real harm when the second language becomes the medium of instruction rather than a subject. A child who chatters in her home language can turn [[reticent|reticent]] in a classroom conducted in one she barely understands, and her silence is easily mistaken for slowness. Apartheid South Africa supplied the starkest case. The government ordered that several subjects in Black schools be taught in Afrikaans, a language that many pupils, and many of their teachers, spoke poorly. Students saw Afrikaans as the language of their oppressors, and they refused to [[acquiesce|acquiesce]]: in June 1976 thousands of schoolchildren in Soweto marched against the policy. Police opened fire, and the ensuing uprising became a turning point in the struggle against apartheid. Soweto shows that choosing a language is never neutral; a mandate that serves the state rather than the child becomes an instrument of exclusion.

These cases do not lead me to reject the recommendation, but they change what I think it should say. Paraguay persuades me that a second language belongs in primary school wherever it is already part of a child's world. The thin weekly lesson reveals that a uniform mandate ignores cost, and Soweto warns that the choice of language cannot be left to whoever holds power. I would [[amend|amend]] the recommendation: every child should be taught first in her own language and then, once she can follow them, in the other languages her community lives in, with that choice made locally rather than in the capital; a further language belongs only where it can be taught well enough to matter. That standard would demand two or three languages across much of Africa while sparing an underfunded school in a monolingual town a bilingualism it cannot deliver. A second language is a real gift, but only when it opens a door the child has reason to walk through.

prompt.statement: An original work of art is always more valuable than a perfect copy of it.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Better Witnesses, Not Always Better Art
essays.essay:
Whether an original is worth more than a perfect copy depends on what we ask a work of art to do. As evidence of what one person did at one moment, the original is always worth more, and for a better reason than snobbery: a copy is perfect only by the standards of the moment that made it, while the original can answer questions no one has yet thought to ask. But a painting is also an experience, and when the original can no longer provide it, a copy may be worth more. The statement is right about originals as documents and wrong to say "always" about them as works of art.

Vermeer's Girl Reading a Letter at an Open Window shows why. Decades ago, X-rays revealed a picture of Cupid hidden on the back wall, and scholars long assumed Vermeer himself had painted it out. Laboratory analysis later showed that someone else had covered it long after the canvas was finished, and Dresden conservators removed the overpaint. Any reproduction made earlier, however faithful to the [[pellucid|pellucid]] light falling through the open window, would have preserved a stranger's alteration as if it were Vermeer's decision. A copy records only what its makers knew how to measure. Its limit is knowledge, not skill: even a [[polymath|polymath]] versed in chemistry, optics and art history cannot reproduce evidence no one yet knows to look for. The original is a witness we can cross-examine each time our instruments improve.

The strongest challenge to this defense is an [[astringent|astringent]] one: critics of the cult of the original call it superstition. If a copy is truly perfect, they argue, viewers have the same experience before either object, so the premium on the original reflects scarcity and quasi-religious reverence for the artist's touch, not anything in the work. The forger Han van Meegeren seems to prove their point. Leading experts hailed his Supper at Emmaus, a pastiche rather than a copy of any known Vermeer, as a masterpiece, and it was bought for a Rotterdam museum. After the war, accused of selling Hermann Göring a supposed Vermeer, Christ and the Adulteress, van Meegeren confessed that he had forged it, the Emmaus and several other "Vermeers." Disbelieved at first, he painted a new "Vermeer" under supervision; once a technical commission confirmed his story, the canvases came to be [[derided|deride]] as crude fakes, though not a brushstroke had changed. Yet what changed was not the paint but the information. The experts had prized the paintings as testimony about Vermeer, and as testimony they were false; lowering their value was [[rational|rational]], not snobbish. Many viewers now find the forgeries unmistakably of their own era; their perfection existed only for eyes of that time.

That answer also marks the statement's limit. If an original's special value lies in its testimony, then where a work matters chiefly as an experience, a copy can be worth more. Veronese painted The Wedding at Cana for the refectory of San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice, so that monks would dine beneath a banquet at which Christ performs his first miracle. Napoleon's troops carried it off to Paris; today it hangs in the Louvre opposite the Mona Lisa, where crowds photographing the smaller picture stand with their backs to it. Whatever [[numinous|numinous]] quality the miracle held for monks at table is hard to feel in that crush. A facsimile made from high-resolution scans now hangs on the wall for which the original was painted. The canvas in Paris remains the better witness, but [[divorced|divorced]] from its setting it no longer works as Veronese intended; in Venice, the copy does. One might object that the copy's value is wholly borrowed. True, but borrowed value is still value, and the question is which object now delivers it.

An original, then, is always the more valuable document and only sometimes the more valuable work of art; the statement goes wrong by treating these as a single value. We should guard originals as we guard primary sources, since they may still tell us something new, while admitting that the experience a painting was made to give sometimes travels better in a faithful copy than in the object itself.

prompt.statement: Profit is a better motivator of useful innovation than prestige.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Profit Wins Only When Payment Tracks Benefit
essays.essay:
The statement assumes that whatever motivates innovators will also steer them toward usefulness. Neither motive does so directly. Profit rewards what buyers will pay for; prestige rewards what peers admire. I largely agree: of these two proxies, profit usually tracks usefulness more faithfully, because it comes from an innovation's users rather than from its judges. That advantage holds only when those who need an innovation can pay in proportion to its value. Where they cannot, profit misleads as badly as prestige, and the remedy is not to abandon financial reward but to redesign it.

The eighteenth-century search for longitude shows why it matters who hands out a reward. Parliament's 1714 prize for a practical way to fix a ship's east-west position drew in John Harrison, no gentleman [[polymath|polymath]] but a provincial carpenter turned self-taught clockmaker. The Board of Longitude funded him with grants for decades, and the Royal Society gave him its Copley Medal. Yet when his fourth timekeeper proved remarkably accurate on a voyage to Jamaica, the astronomers on the Board, partial to a rival lunar method, met his clock with [[astringent|astringent]] criticism and fresh demands for trials. The full prize remained a [[tantalizing|tantalizing]] prospect; Parliament made him a final award only in his old age. A reward open to anyone with a working result had summoned an outsider with a better idea; but in part because it was administered by judges invested in a rival approach, it stalled much as prestige can. The reward that spread the invention came from users: once commercial makers simplified the chronometer, navies and merchant fleets bought it in growing numbers over the following century.

The most compelling challenge to my position comes from medicine, where those who most need an innovation are often least able to pay. Oral rehydration solution, a mixture of salt, sugar, and water, was developed in Dhaka and Kolkata in the 1960s. During the 1971 war that created Bangladesh, physicians in refugee camps short of intravenous fluids gave cholera patients the oral solution, and deaths fell sharply. It has since saved millions of children from fatal dehydration. Firms did sell packaged versions, but a mixture anyone could make promised little profit among poor families whose children were dying. Even in wealthy markets profit can fail: many large drug companies have abandoned antibiotic research, because a genuinely new antibiotic must be held in reserve to slow resistance and therefore sells little. An opponent could fairly conclude that in medicine profit is not merely an imperfect guide to usefulness but a perverse one, and that scientists seeking their colleagues' esteem have filled the gaps markets left.

I accept the diagnosis but not the cure. These cases show that profit fails where payment and need diverge; they do not show that prestige succeeds there. Esteem may have sustained the researchers who devised oral rehydration, but it did not carry the solution into millions of homes. Public health agencies and charities did, distributing packets or, like BRAC in Bangladesh, teaching mothers to mix it themselves. Nor can admiration pay for the large clinical trials a new antibiotic requires. A more promising response is to reward usefulness itself: Britain has begun paying drug makers a fixed annual fee for certain antibiotics, regardless of how much is prescribed, so that firms profit from keeping effective drugs available. The scheme is young and unproven, but it aims at the right target. I am no [[apologist|apologist]] for the pharmaceutical industry; my claim is narrower. When profit misfires, the better bet is to change what is paid for, not to hope that the regard of colleagues will carry a molecule from laboratory to patient.

Profit, then, is usually the better motivator of useful innovation, not because money counts for more than honor, but because, and only where, payment tracks benefit. The hunger for esteem is as [[inborn|inborn]] as the appetite for gain, and it will keep scientists chasing principles whose uses no one can foresee. Turning a principle into something that reaches patients or sailors, however, demands years of unglamorous work that admiration seldom rewards. Where no buyer will pay for that work, the answer is to create one.

prompt.statement: Some argue that technology companies should be responsible for the content on their platforms. Others argue that only the people who create the content should be responsible for it.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Responsibility Should Follow Control
essays.essay:
A false health claim that reaches millions of people has two causes: the person who invented it and the machinery that put it in front of them. Epidemiologists draw a similar line between the source of an infection and the conditions that turn a single case into an outbreak. The debate over platform responsibility usually ignores this distinction, treating "content" as a single object for which one party alone bears the blame. Restore that distinction, and the view that technology companies should be responsible comes closer to my own, but only in a qualified form: a company answers for content to the extent that it controls how far that content travels.

The creator-only view deserves more credit than its critics allow; it is not merely a talking point for industry [[apologists|apologist]]. When a platform is a passive conduit, holding it liable for what passes through would be [[tantamount|tantamount]] to blaming the telephone company for a threat made over its lines. American law learned this lesson the hard way. In the mid-1990s, a New York court ruled that the online service Prodigy could be held liable for an allegedly defamatory message on one of its bulletin boards, reasoning that because Prodigy screened posts, it had acted as a publisher; a rival that exercised no editorial control had earlier escaped liability. The incentive was perverse: the company that tried to remove harmful material was exposed to liability for trying. Congress responded with Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which shields platforms from liability for users' posts while protecting their freedom to moderate. Where a company neither selects nor promotes what users say, the creator-only view is right, because the creator alone decided both what to say and to whom.

Those conditions, however, no longer describe the largest platforms. YouTube, Facebook, and their rivals do not simply carry messages; they rank them, recommend them, and decide which ones billions of people see first. In early 2019, YouTube announced that it would recommend fewer videos that misinform viewers in harmful ways, such as those promoting bogus cures for serious illnesses. Uploaders authored those falsehoods, but the announcement made plain that their audience had depended partly on YouTube's recommendation engine, a dial the company itself controlled. Nor is such reach accidental. Internal Facebook research, made public by a whistleblower in 2021, found that a News Feed change meant to encourage meaningful interaction among friends had instead rewarded divisive, outrage-provoking posts. An algorithm harbors no [[animus|animus]] toward public health; it measures only reaction, and few things provoke reaction as reliably as fear and anger. Such a platform is no longer a telephone line. It is the crowded, unventilated room in which one infected guest sets off an outbreak.

Control is not the only test; responsibility also follows knowledge. Ordinary users are often [[flummoxed|flummoxed]] when one post spreads while another vanishes, and because platforms disclose little about how their ranking systems work, even regulators struggle to see inside them. The companies that build those systems, by contrast, can measure what they amplify and how widely. A pharmacist is not to blame for a physician's misdiagnosis, but one who notices a dangerous drug interaction and dispenses the pills anyway shares the blame. Likewise, a company that learns its design is spreading medical falsehoods and simply [[acquiesces|acquiesce]] in the result, because engagement is profitable, cannot claim to be a bystander. Yet the Prodigy episode marks the limit of this reasoning. Platforms should be judged on the design and foreseeable effects of their systems, not held liable for every post; otherwise they will either abandon moderation or delete anything contentious.

The view that platforms bear responsibility therefore comes closer to the truth, provided responsibility is measured by control rather than by the mere presence of content on a server. My position is not a [[conciliatory|conciliatory]] gesture toward both camps; it is a principle that cuts against each of them. Creators answer for what they say. Platforms answer for what they choose to amplify and for harms they can foresee and prevent. Responsibility [[divorced|divorced]] from control breeds censorship; control divorced from responsibility breeds impunity. A public still struggling to tell medical fact from fiction can afford neither.

prompt.statement: Some argue that progress in medicine depends mostly on new technology. Others argue that it depends mostly on better access to the treatments that already exist.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: The Best Cures Are Built to Travel
essays.essay:
Champions of new technology make a point that is hard to dismiss: every drug an aid program distributes was once an invention, and no amount of distribution can deliver a cure that does not exist. Public health workers offer an [[astringent|astringent]] reply: the world is short not of cures but of the will to deliver them. Diarrhea, pneumonia, and malaria still rank among the leading killers of young children in poor countries, although medicine has known how to prevent or treat all three for decades; for much of humanity, the gap between what medicine can do and what it actually does dwarfs the gap between today's medicine and tomorrow's. The access view comes closer to my own, with one amendment: the debate assumes that technology and access are rivals, when many of medicine's most consequential inventions have been inventions of access.

Oral rehydration therapy shows why. Cholera kills by draining the body of water and salt, and a severe case can turn a healthy child into a [[lethargic|lethargic]], sunken-eyed one within hours. By the mid-twentieth century, physicians could reliably reverse this with intravenous fluids, but the cure required sterile supplies, needles, and trained staff. For a family in rural Bengal it was [[tantalizing|tantalizing]]: proven, yet often hours away by foot or boat. In the late 1960s, researchers in Dhaka and Calcutta showed that most patients could instead drink a solution of glucose and salt, because glucose helps the gut absorb sodium and water even during cholera. During the 1971 war that created Bangladesh, when intravenous fluid ran short in refugee camps in India, the physician Dilip Mahalanabis had patients drink the solution, and far fewer died than was usual in the camps. Notice what kind of invention this was. It worked no better than an intravenous drip; it worked almost anywhere.

Still, a remedy known only to physicians could not help children who never saw one. The decisive work in Bangladesh was educational. In the 1980s, the nongovernmental organization BRAC sent health workers door to door to teach mothers to make the solution at home from a pinch of salt and a fistful of gur, an unrefined cane sugar, stirred into water, eventually reaching millions of households. The design was shrewd: the workers' pay depended on how well the mothers, quizzed later by monitors, could recall the recipe, so BRAC paid for learning rather than mere visits. The case cuts against the technology view twice over. The invention mattered because it removed a barrier to access, and even then it reached the sick child only after someone had taught her mother.

HIV gives the technology view its strongest case and my own position its hardest test. For more than a decade after AIDS appeared in the early 1980s, condoms, sterile needles, and screened blood could slow its spread, but no campaign of access could have saved those already infected, because no drug yet existed that could durably control the virus. Only combination antiretroviral therapy, which arrived in the mid-1990s, made the infection a manageable chronic illness; here new technology was plainly the binding constraint. Yet at first the drugs cost far more than most African patients or governments could pay, and price drew an [[invidious|invidious]] distinction between an infected person in London, who could expect to live, and one in Lusaka, who could expect to die. The drugs reached millions of Africans only after generic manufacturers slashed prices and international programs paid for treatment.

The contrast refines my position rather than reversing it. Held strictly, each view leaves its partisans [[flummoxed|flummoxed]] by half of the HIV story: before the mid-1990s, a person with AIDS needed a discovery; afterward, one in Zambia needed a lower price and a clinic. The rivalry the statement sets up is therefore partly [[illusory|illusory]]: invention sets the limit of what medicine can do, access decides who benefits, and each becomes the binding constraint at a different moment. Because remedies already exist for many conditions that still kill the poor, most progress available today lies in delivery, and the inventions most worth celebrating are often humble ones, like a solution of salt and sugar, that let an established cure travel where doctors and drips cannot.

A 5 might develop oral rehydration well, but it would still treat technology and access as rivals and stop at choosing access, without the counterexample that shows when each view holds. This essay reframes the rivalry and tests it against HIV.

prompt.statement:
Claim: Societies should honor teachers as highly as they honor doctors.
Reason: Teachers shape every other profession, including medicine.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Honor Teachers for Judgment, Not Influence
essays.essay:
Few people object to praising teachers; the harder question is whether they deserve the standing societies reserve for physicians, and why. I agree with the claim, provided that "honor" means substantive regard—selective entry, fair pay, and trust in professional judgment—rather than an annual round of flowers and speeches. The stated reason, however, is true but insufficient, and it even works against the claim. It locates a teacher's worth in what her pupils later become, a standard that draws an [[invidious|invidious]] distinction between the teacher of a future cardiologist and the teacher of a future welder. That standard is also unworkable, as American courts discovered when they confronted its mirror image.

In Peter W. v. San Francisco Unified School District, decided in 1976, a young man who had graduated from high school reading far below the level his diploma implied sued the district for negligent instruction. A California appellate court rejected the suit, and most American courts have since followed its reasoning. The court found no workable standard of care, since educators disagree about how children should be taught. More telling still, it found causation too uncertain to establish: a child's learning depends on family, health, peers, and motivation as well as on any classroom, so no one could say which teacher, if any, had caused the failure. Medicine is different: a sponge left inside a patient is an unmistakable error, traceable to one operation and to the named surgeon and team who performed it.

The court's logic about blame applies equally to credit: if no single teacher can be blamed for a graduate who never learned to read well, none can take credit for one who became a surgeon. A physician may remember the biology teacher whose [[pellucid|pellucid]] explanations first made living cells seem knowable, but that contribution is mingled with dozens of other teachers' work, a parent's encouragement, and the student's own effort. Much of medicine's prestige is built from debts that patients can trace to a named doctor; influence so [[diffuse|diffuse]] leaves few such debts behind. The stated reason thus names the very feature that keeps teachers from being honored as doctors are: because they shape everyone collectively, society seldom sees what any one of them has done. The claim survives, but on a different foundation. Teachers, like physicians, exercise expert judgment on behalf of people who cannot yet, or cannot now, protect their own interests, in situations no rulebook anticipates. That responsibility, not their pupils' later careers, merits equal honor.

Finland offers a contrasting case that tests both reasons. If influence alone earned honor, the societies that esteem teachers most would be those that most loudly credit them with producing doctors. In Finland, teaching is neither [[derided|deride]] nor merely sentimentalized; it is often said to compete with medicine and law for the most able students. Accounts of that status seldom invoke the doctors teachers trained, or any belief that good teaching is an [[inborn|inborn]] knack; they point to policy. The country set [[stringent|stringent]] entry requirements for teacher education, required master's degrees of its schoolteachers, and then trusted them, declining to rank teachers by their students' test scores. Yet teachers there were esteemed as nation-builders long before those measures, so the policy may be as much a result of their prestige as its cause. Either way, Finland met the California court's problem, the absence of an agreed professional standard, by certifying judgment at the door rather than measuring outcomes, which remain as tangled there as anywhere. Medicine enjoys both routes to esteem, visible results and certified judgment; teaching can never fully have the first, but the second can sustain it.

The comparison with medicine is therefore worth keeping, but as a standard to meet rather than a debt to collect. Teachers rightly take [[umbrage|umbrage]] at the old gibe that those who cannot do, teach. Yet the usual rejoinder, that they taught those who do, shares the gibe's flaw: both sayings measure teaching by something other than itself. A profession earns a physician's standing when a society selects the profession's members with care and then defers to what they decide. Teaching deserves that standing on its own terms, whether or not any of its pupils ever practices medicine.
