prompt.statement:
Claim: Online anonymity does more harm than good.
Reason: People behave worse when they cannot be held accountable for what they say.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Anonymity Is Always Anonymity From Someone
essays.essay:
After German reunification, the files of the Stasi, East Germany's secret police, were opened to the citizens it had watched, and many discovered that those who had spent years filing [[surreptitious|surreptitious]] reports on them were colleagues, neighbors, and sometimes their own spouses. Few episodes show more painfully what people will do when their victims cannot see them. Yet the informers were hardly free of accountability; they answered to handlers who expected results. What their concealment removed was accountability to the people they harmed. Anonymity, in other words, is always anonymity from someone, and that fact governs how far I accept the argument. The reason it offers is largely true, but it describes only one effect of concealment. The claim built on it, that online anonymity does more harm than good, fails as a general verdict, and where it does hold, it holds for a different reason.

Judged on its own terms, the reason is sound. Accountability to an audience restrains people, and removing it lowers the price of cruelty. A man who would never voice his [[animus|animus]] toward women in front of his colleagues can voice it nightly from a throwaway account and never answer for it. But the reason treats accountability as though it punished only bad speech. Being identifiable makes a speaker answerable to everyone who can hurt him, the powerful as well as the fair-minded. In the late 1760s, a writer calling himself Junius used a London newspaper to attack the king's ministers, and eventually the king himself, when such attacks could be prosecuted as seditious libel. His criticism could be so [[trenchant|trenchant]] because no one could find him; scholars still dispute who he was. Online, the same cover protects people who are [[reticent|reticent]] for good reason: the civil servant who has witnessed fraud, or the patient who wants to ask about HIV testing without his neighbors finding out. Anonymity makes some people behave worse and others speak more honestly; the reason counts only the first.

Even if the reason were wholly true, the claim would need more: evidence that anonymity is a major source of online abuse, so that removing it would leave the internet better rather than merely quieter. South Korea ran a partial version of that experiment. In the late 2000s, it made users of high-traffic websites verify their identities before commenting, though they could still post under nicknames; several years later, its Constitutional Court struck the rule down, finding that it had chilled legitimate expression while barely reducing malicious comments. Anonymity from the law, it seems, was not a major cause of abuse there. Readers still saw only nicknames, however, so the rule never tested accountability to an audience; a law printing every name would, but only by exposing the civil servant and the patient to the people they fear. A fair tally must also separate injury from offense: a threat is a harm, but an anonymous post ridiculing a cabinet minister is not, however much [[umbrage|umbrage]] the minister takes.

Where the claim does have force, it is for a reason the argument never mentions. The gravest harm of online anonymity is not that individuals grow nastier but that one actor can pose as a crowd. According to American investigators, Russia's Internet Research Agency ran networks of social media accounts posing as American activists on both sides of divisive issues. The damage lay not in rudeness but in counterfeit consensus, and it calls for targeted remedies: platform rules against coordinated deception, and court-ordered unmasking of those who threaten or defraud. A rule requiring every speaker to be identifiable, by contrast, would be [[tantamount|tantamount]] to a rule that only the safe may speak freely.

The argument, then, gets the psychology right and the arithmetic wrong. Removing accountability does loosen restraint, but restraint is not always a virtue, and who does the restraining matters as much as what is restrained. The Stasi's informers hid from their victims to serve power; Junius hid from power to defy it. Online anonymity shelters both kinds of people, and on an internet that reaches countries where dissent is punished, the sensible course is to keep the shelter and police its abuses rather than tear it down.

prompt.statement: Cities should ban billboards and other commercial advertising from their streets and public spaces.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Signs That Belong, Ads That Rent
essays.essay:
Few people object to the sign above a bakery door, yet few would tolerate a soft-drink advertisement projected onto the facade of a cathedral. Both are commercial messages in public space, so commerce alone cannot explain the difference. The bakery sign belongs to its place: it is posted by someone who works there and tells passersby what lies inside. The projected advertisement merely rents its place, borrowing the attention that a [[numinous|numinous]] building commands to sell an unrelated product. Billboards are humbler versions of the second transaction, and the most [[trenchant|trenchant]] objection to them is not that they are ugly but that they sell something neither the advertiser nor the landlord owns: the attention of people who cannot close a street the way they close a magazine. Cities should therefore ban rented advertising, except where it visibly pays for public goods, and protect the signs that belong to the street. The consequences of each choice explain where these lines fall.

In most large cities, streets without billboards remain a [[tantalizing|tantalizing]] prospect; São Paulo is the rare one that turned the idea into law. Its Clean City Law, which took effect in 2007, stripped billboards from Brazil's largest city while merely capping the size of storefront signs, roughly the line drawn above. The intended consequence followed: facades long hidden behind vinyl became visible again. The unintended consequence was more instructive. With the billboards gone, residents could see favelas and decaying buildings that the advertising had screened from view, and the city's inequality became harder to ignore. A ban on rented advertising does more than tidy a city; it makes the city look at itself. The costs proved bearable: despite industry warnings of lost jobs, advertisers moved much of their spending to other media, and polls showed broad public support. Those consequences persuade me that the core of the policy is sound.

A ban as broad as the statement proposes, however, would also sweep away signs that belong to the street, and there its consequences turn harmful. In many African and Latin American cities, street advertisers include tailors, barbers, and market traders, for whom a hand-painted sign is often the only affordable medium. In Ghana in the 1980s and 1990s, traveling video clubs hired local artists to paint posters, frequently on reused flour sacks, which they hung at the entrance to each night's screening. The posters were frankly commercial, yet each belonged to its venue as surely as a bakery sign does; they supported many painters and now hang in galleries abroad. A blanket ban would have erased them. Its burden would fall unevenly: a beverage company can move its budget to television, but a neighborhood barber cannot. A policy meant to shield the public from corporate saturation would punish the smallest sellers most, reason enough to exempt signs that belong to their place.

The hardest case is advertising that pays for public goods. Journalism once thrived on it: the penny papers of the 1830s were cheap because advertisers paid what readers could not, putting daily news within reach of working people. Cities strike a similar bargain when contractors build bus shelters in exchange for ad panels. [[Apologists|apologist]] for street advertising cite such deals, and they are partly right: ban the panels without replacing the revenue, and riders who cannot afford cars will wait in the rain. Journalism offers a warning as well. When newspaper advertising collapsed, many publications turned to sponsored content designed to [[mimic|mimic]] their own reporting. Such [[surreptitious|surreptitious]] advertising is harder to discount than any billboard, and a city that drives every advertisement off its streets may likewise find brands paying for murals that pass for public art. The bargain should survive, then, but only in the open: clearly labeled and limited to the infrastructure it funds.

Traced to its consequences, the policy earns not one verdict but three. Billboards that rent the street should go; signs that belong to it should stay; advertising that pays for public goods may remain on visible terms. A city need not purge commerce from its streets. It need only refuse to let anyone sell the attention of passersby, except on terms the public has openly accepted.

prompt.statement: Secondary schools should start the school day no earlier than 8:30 in the morning.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: A Later Bell Needs a Budget
essays.essay:
Debates about school start times tend to treat 8:30 as a number on a bell schedule, but a start time is really two clocks at once. One is biological: the hour when an adolescent brain is ready to learn. The other is social: the hour around which bus routes, parents' jobs and afternoon sports are arranged. The policy targets the first clock, where it is persuasive, yet most of its unintended consequences arrive through the second. I therefore support barring secondary schools from starting before 8:30, but only as a funded reorganization of the community's day, not as a bare decree.

Measured against the biological clock, the intended consequences are substantial. Many parents are [[flummoxed|flummoxed]] when an early-rising child becomes a teenager who cannot be roused at seven. The reason lies in biology: during puberty the body begins releasing the sleep hormone melatonin later in the evening, which is why the American Academy of Pediatrics has recommended that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30. A sixteen-year-old who cannot fall asleep before eleven but must board a bus at 6:45 will arrive at school [[lethargic|lethargic]], however motivated she may be. Adults who [[deride|deride]] such students as lazy mistake physiology for character. Skeptics predict that teenagers will simply stay up later, but the evidence suggests otherwise. When Seattle moved its high school start times nearly an hour later, researchers found that students did not merely shift their bedtimes; they slept about half an hour longer on school nights and reported less daytime sleepiness. The first-period [[torpor|torpor]] that teachers have long accepted as a fact of adolescence turns out to be partly an artifact of the timetable.

The social clock is where the unintended consequences accumulate, and advocates who wave them away do the policy no favors. Many American districts run their buses in tiers: the same bus carries high school students at dawn, then middle schoolers, then young children. Move the high schools to 8:30, and a district must either buy more buses or shift young children into the earliest slot, a swap that does less harm to their sleep, since they tend to wake early anyway, but leaves seven-year-olds waiting at bus stops in the dark. Administrators handed such a mandate without new money are stymied by this arithmetic. Families face a parallel problem. When South Korea's Gyeonggi Province pushed its schools to begin at 9:00 in 2014, the aim was to let students sleep and eat breakfast, yet some of the sharpest objections came from dual-income parents who left for work long before the new bell. Such burdens fall hardest on families with the least control over their own hours.

These consequences shape my position not by settling whether to adopt the policy but by dictating how. The harms of early starts fall on adolescents every school day and compound over years: lower achievement, poorer mental health and, among new drivers, more car crashes. The costs to the social clock are largely financial and logistical, so money and planning can shrink them; a RAND Corporation analysis concluded that the gains from later starts, through better academic performance and fewer crashes, would outweigh the added transportation costs within a few years. The harder problem is political. Because the benefits of extra sleep are [[diffuse|diffuse]] and gradual, while the costs land on identifiable people the week the schedule changes, an unfunded mandate invites its own repeal. A district that merely [[acquiesces|acquiesce]] to a rule it cannot afford will cut whatever corner is cheapest, and the backlash can discredit the reform itself.

The real question, then, is not whether teenagers need more sleep but whether a community will reset the social clock along with the bell. An 8:30 start backed by money for buses, a phased timetable and before-school supervision for children whose parents leave at dawn is likely to deliver what its advocates promise. The same start imposed by fiat risks trading drowsy teenagers for stranded children and resentful parents before it is quietly reversed. I would adopt the policy, but I would judge every version of it by whether it pays for the second clock as seriously as it honors the first.

prompt.statement: A nation's investment in basic research matters more to its long-term prosperity than its investment in applied technology.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Discovery for Leaders, Application for Followers
essays.essay:
Few claims about national policy sound more high-minded than this one, and questioning it can seem [[iconoclastic|iconoclastic]]. Yet the statement quietly assumes that knowledge stays where it is produced, so that a country's laboratories enrich the country that pays for them. In fact, published discoveries cross borders almost freely, while the people and industries able to exploit them do not. For a nation at the technological frontier, basic research is the more important long-term investment; for a nation still catching up, applied technology usually matters more.

The statement holds at the frontier because basic research is the richest source of new possibilities, with payoffs too distant and unpredictable for markets to finance. Admittedly, tinkering can also open new paths: the steam engine [[antedated|antedate]] the science of thermodynamics and helped inspire it. But tinkering has limits. Early radio builders used semiconductor crystals as detectors but could improve them only by trial and error until quantum theory explained how electrons move through solids. The founders of quantum mechanics were not trying to build a product; they wanted to [[elucidate|elucidate]] the structure of the atom. Two decades later, though, their work made the transistor possible. That theory, largely European, was open to all; what the United States had built, in its universities, was a generation of physicists fluent in it. In 1947 a team of them at Bell Labs, charged with developing a solid-state amplifier, built the first transistor, the seed of an industry America led for decades. A frontier nation can borrow discoveries from its peers, but only if it employs scientists able to absorb them; a leader that stops paying for discovery soon finds it cannot even copy well.

The statement fails, however, for nations well behind the frontier, whose scarce resource is not knowledge but the ability to use it. Postwar Japan is the clearest case. Rather than pour limited capital into fundamental science, Japanese firms licensed foreign inventions and concentrated on improving and manufacturing them. A small Tokyo company, later renamed Sony, licensed transistor patents developed at Bell Labs and built compact radios sold worldwide. Multiplied across industries, this strategy helped make Japan, within a generation, the world's second-largest capitalist economy. The knowledge 1950s Japan needed was already written into licensable patents; basic physics would have yielded findings rivals could use as freely as Japan, while engineering and production built advantages that stayed home. Tellingly, once Japan had caught up, its government expanded support for basic science, a tacit admission that imitation has a ceiling.

These cases shape my position in two ways. First, they show that the statement's truth depends on a nation's distance from the frontier: the same physics enriched the United States, which trained scientists to use it first, and Japan, which invested in applying it. Second, they expose a false choice: the statement treats basic and applied research as rivals, yet even at the frontier the returns to the first depend on the second. The transistor itself came from a laboratory with a commercial goal; the mRNA vaccines show this more plainly. For years, Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman studied why synthetic mRNA provoked harmful inflammation, work that funders were [[skittish|skittish]] about supporting. Their discovery that chemically modified RNA could evade immune sensors came more than a decade before COVID-19; once the vaccines succeeded, the press [[lionized|lionize]] the pair. Yet their insight became a vaccine within a year of the outbreak only because applied work was ready: academic labs and small firms had developed lipid nanoparticles to carry RNA into cells, and Moderna and BioNTech had spent a decade learning to formulate and manufacture mRNA medicines. Basic research created the possibility; applied capacity decided who could seize it, and how fast.

The statement, then, is right about leaders, wrong about followers, and incomplete about both. A leader must keep funding discovery, which replenishes both the ideas every economy uses and the scientists who exploit them first; a follower gains more by mastering what others have found. Long-run prosperity goes not to the nation that favors one investment over the other, but to the one that knows which of the two its stage of development has left scarce.

prompt.statement: A civilization's art does more than its politics to shape how later generations judge it.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Admired for Art, Judged by Politics
essays.essay:
The strongest case for the statement comes from civilizations whose political life has vanished from the record. Bronze Age Crete left a script, Linear A, that remains [[inscrutable|inscrutable]], so how the Minoans were governed is largely unknown. Palaces and seals survive, and deciphered Linear B tablets [[elucidate|elucidate]] how Knossos was run, but only in its final phase, under Mycenaean Greek control. The Minoans' most eloquent remains are their frescoes: dolphins, lilies, and young athletes vaulting over a charging bull. Arthur Evans, who excavated Knossos in the early twentieth century, read these images as the portrait of a graceful, peaceful people, and that portrait still shapes how textbooks and museums present Minoan life. Yet the case exposes the statement's hidden condition: the silence of the political record. Where that record survives and still matters to the living, later generations base their verdict on politics, and art becomes a secondary witness.

Even in Crete, the artistic verdict proved fragile. Evans's restorers rebuilt the fragmentary frescoes so freely that the peaceful portrait was partly his own making, and a later, more [[iconoclastic|iconoclastic]] generation of archaeologists questioned it, pointing to weapons and to apparent evidence of human sacrifice at a hillside shrine. Where the political record is full, art loses its power to decide the case. The 1936 Berlin Olympics are remembered for two achievements: Leni Riefenstahl's Olympia, a film still admired for its inventive camera work, and the four gold medals Jesse Owens, a Black American, won at the very Games the Nazi regime had staged as a propaganda showcase. The regime financed the one and hosted the other; later generations admire both, yet they judge the regime by neither. They judge it by the [[premeditated|premeditate]] murder of millions, and in that light the film's beauty becomes evidence of how carefully the regime managed its image, while Owens's victories read as a rebuke to its racial doctrine. Nor did Germany's artistic inheritance soften the verdict; postwar writers made it part of the indictment by asking how the nation of Goethe and Beethoven could build death camps.

The deciding variable, then, is not how much art or politics a civilization left behind but whether its politics still answers questions later generations are asking. Education shows how that selection happens. The American founders, schooled in Livy, knew the story of Cincinnatus, the farmer who accepted absolute power during a military crisis and then returned to his plow. They [[lionized|lionize]] him, hailing Washington as an American Cincinnatus, because the story spoke to their fear that a victorious general might make himself king. Rome had magnificent art, from its portrait busts to the Pantheon, yet the Rome these men judged was a political Rome: a republic to imitate and an empire to avoid. A student today still tends to meet Rome through its Senate and its fall, and Egypt through its pyramids and tomb paintings. Egypt's divine kingship offers modern democracies few lessons, so its art is left to speak for it.

These cases shape my position into a conditional one. The statement holds when a civilization's political record is lost, as in Minoan Crete, or when that record no longer bears on anyone's choices, as with the pharaohs. It fails when the record is both legible and consequential, as with Rome, whose republic became a model, and Nazi Germany, whose crimes became a warning. The statement quietly assumes that later generations weigh art and politics as neutral jurors weigh two exhibits. They are not neutral. They consult whichever record speaks to their hopes and fears, and politics, which decides how people are governed, imprisoned, freed, or killed, usually speaks to those concerns more directly than any fresco can.

Art is the default witness: it testifies when no one else can, and its testimony endures because objects outlive institutions. But a witness is not a judge. A civilization may be admired for what it made, yet it is judged by how it treated the people within its reach, and that judgment waits only for the evidence to survive and for a later generation to need it. The more such evidence survives and still matters, the less its art can do to change the verdict.

prompt.statement: Governments should try out major new policies in a few regions before adopting them nationwide.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Fit the Test to How Effects Travel
essays.essay:
The case for piloting a major policy before adopting it nationwide seems self-evident: it is cheaper to discover a flaw in three provinces than in thirty. Yet the recommendation quietly assumes that a region is a miniature of the nation. For many social programs that assumption holds, and for them a regional trial is not merely [[judicious|judicious]] but close to obligatory. For policies whose effects cross borders, or whose value lies in being uniform, it fails, and a staggered rollout ranges from useless to dangerous. Whether a government should pilot a policy, then, depends less on how ambitious the policy is than on how its effects travel.

Mexico's Progresa program of the late 1990s was not strictly a regional pilot, but it shows the recommendation's logic at its best. It gave poor rural mothers modest cash grants on condition that their children attended school and the family visited health clinics. Such a scheme invited obvious doubts: that handouts would breed dependency, and that the conditions were unenforceable. Rather than settle the argument by decree or let it [[fester|fester]], the government built a test into the program's rollout: in an evaluation sample of about five hundred villages, roughly two-thirds were randomly chosen to receive benefits first, while the rest waited more than a year as a control group. Because the two groups differed mainly in timing, researchers could attribute any gap to the program itself, something national statistics, however comprehensive, could never have done. Enrollment rose, especially among girls entering secondary school, and young children in participating families were sick less often.

The deeper payoff, however, was political rather than statistical. In 2000 the party that had governed Mexico for seven decades lost the presidency, a change that put the program at risk, because incoming administrations had a long habit of scrapping their predecessors' signature initiatives. Without hard evidence, opponents could have dismissed Progresa as [[profligate|profligate]] welfare spending and let it die. Instead, the new government renamed it Oportunidades and extended it to the cities, and its design was copied across Latin America and beyond. The trial had turned an ideological quarrel into a measurable question, and the answer outlasted the government that asked it. Examining why this trial succeeded helps [[elucidate|elucidate]] when such a test is worth running. A family's decision to keep a daughter in school barely affects the next village, so little of the program's effect leaked into the control villages; the results arrived while the decision was still open; and the data were opened to outside researchers, so no government could quietly bury the findings.

A regional trial, in other words, pays off only when a few places can stand in for the whole. Sweden's switch from left-hand to right-hand traffic in 1967 shows a case in which they cannot. Testing that change in a few provinces would have turned every provincial border into a point where drivers had to swap sides, manufacturing the very collisions the reform aimed to prevent. The whole country therefore switched on a single day. Contagious disease poses a subtler problem. If a few provinces vaccinate while their neighbors wait, infection and immunity both cross the border, so a simple regional comparison understates the benefit. Yet spillover does not rule out testing: in Guinea in 2015, researchers vaccinated rings of contacts around new Ebola cases, some rings at once and others after a delay, and still detected strong protection. That design, however, followed chains of transmission rather than administrative borders.

These cases leave me in qualified agreement. Progresa persuades me that staged testing should be the default for programs whose effects stay local and appear quickly, since evidence can shield a good program from its critics and the next government. The Swedish switch convinces me that some policies cannot be tested piecemeal at all; the Ebola trial, that for policies whose effects spread, the question is how to draw a test's boundaries rather than whether to test. Above all, a pilot helps only a government willing to be proved wrong by it. Officials left [[crestfallen|crestfallen]] by a bad result can still learn from it; officials who explain it away have merely postponed their mistake.

words.meaning_here: showing good judgment; a sensible, well-measured choice for programs whose effects stay local
to worsen by being left unresolved; the dispute over Progresa growing more bitter without a test
recklessly wasteful; how opponents might have labeled the program's spending without evidence

visibly deflated and disappointed; officials who take a bad trial result to heart

analysis.verdict: This earns a 6 for insight and cogency, not just clarity: it exposes the hidden assumption that a region is a miniature of the nation and turns it into a usable test, which is how a policy's effects travel. Its examples are developed rather than name-dropped: Progresa gets two full paragraphs, each counter-case explains how a regional pilot would fail, and the Ebola trial shows that spillover calls for a different design rather than no test. The prose is precise and controlled, with varied sentences.
analysis.position: The thesis closes paragraph 1: whether to pilot depends on "how its effects travel," not on how ambitious the policy is. It is qualified from the start, since pilots are "close to obligatory" for some policies while a staggered rollout "ranges from useless to dangerous" for others. The conclusion refines rather than repeats it: a default for local programs, plus a question about "how to draw a test's boundaries."
analysis.development: Progresa is developed in depth: the design, the doubts it faced, the randomized delay that created a control group, the findings, and why the evidence let the program survive a change of government. The essay admits Progresa "was not strictly a regional pilot" and uses it to show what a trial is for: attribution, which national statistics cannot give. The counter-cases explain mechanisms ("a point where drivers had to swap sides," "infection and immunity both cross the border"), and the Ebola trial shows that spillover demands a different design, not abandoning tests.
analysis.organization: The structure follows the argument, not a template: the thesis, an extended example in two stages (statistical result, then political payoff), and the conditions behind its success. The hinge "A regional trial, in other words," turns the first condition, that effects stay local, into a principle and tests it against two counter-cases, ending with a concession ("Yet spillover does not rule out testing") that sets up the refined conclusion.
analysis.language: Diction is exact rather than ornate ("stand in for the whole"). Short, flat sentences such as "The whole country therefore switched on a single day." land a point after a long build-up, while the longer sentences in paragraphs 2 and 3 use colons and semicolons to hold multi-part claims together ("Such a scheme invited obvious doubts: that handouts would breed dependency"). The closing contrast is clean: "officials who explain it away have merely postponed their mistake."
analysis.task: The instruction asks for cases where piloting helps, cases where it does not, and how those cases shape the position. Paragraphs 2 and 3 give the favorable case; paragraph 4 gives two unfavorable ones and a trial that worked by abandoning regional lines. The conclusion says outright which example taught what: "Progresa persuades me that" and "The Swedish switch convinces me that."

prompt.statement: Organizations should reward employees for reporting their own mistakes.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Reward the Report, Not the Error
essays.essay:
Early in 2020, the Nobel laureate Frances Arnold retracted a paper her laboratory had published in Science the previous year because its central results could not be reproduced. She accepted responsibility publicly and was widely praised for her candor. The applause, however, obscured an uncomfortable asymmetry. A laureate can afford such honesty; a postdoctoral researcher, understandably [[skittish|skittish]] about any blemish on a thin record, may well stay silent. Rewarding employees for reporting their own mistakes is, at its best, a way to extend Arnold's security to everyone, and I largely endorse it. My agreement rests on three conditions: the reward should attach to the report rather than to the error, it should usually take the form of protection rather than payment, and it should never extend to misconduct that was planned.

A reward for admitting an obvious error is [[superfluous|superfluous]]; the recommendation earns its keep where a mistake is invisible to all but the person who made it. Imagine a nurse who realizes, an hour later, that she has given a patient the wrong dose. If she once watched a colleague confess a similar slip and leave the supervisor's office [[crestfallen|crestfallen]], holding a written warning, she will probably say nothing. She will [[ruminate|ruminate]] over the error alone, while the look-alike vials that caused it stay side by side on the shelf. Aviation offers a working alternative. Under the Aviation Safety Reporting System, which NASA administers on behalf of the Federal Aviation Administration, a pilot who promptly reports an inadvertent violation is generally spared fines and license suspension, and the report is stripped of identifying details. The reward is immunity, not money, and its value emerges in aggregate, when many reports expose a confusing taxiway or an ambiguous radio instruction that no single pilot could have recognized as a pattern. Errors that would otherwise [[fester|fester]] unseen become data from which an entire industry learns. This case persuades me that the recommendation's strongest justification is information for the institution, not fairness to the individual.

The same program marks the recommendation's limits. Its immunity does not cover deliberate violations or criminal acts, and that exclusion is essential. A reward that applied to [[premeditated|premeditate]] misconduct would let an employee plan a fraud, enjoy the proceeds, and confess on the eve of discovery, turning candor into an escape hatch. A cash bonus for each self-reported mistake would fail differently. When the French colonial administration in Hanoi, fearing plague, paid a bounty for rat tails in 1902, officials soon noticed tailless rats in the streets, apparently released to keep breeding. Paying for evidence of an act, rather than for the desired outcome, invites people to manufacture the evidence. Employees paid per confession would flood the system with trivial reports or discover that small errors had become profitable. In either circumstance, following the recommendation literally would corrupt the honesty it is meant to encourage.

A subtler limit appears when a mistake harms someone outside the organization. Golf expects players to call penalties on themselves, and at the 2010 Verizon Heritage, Brian Davis did so on the first playoff hole, reporting that his club had brushed a loose reed in a hazard on his backswing. The two-stroke penalty ended his chance at a first PGA Tour victory and handed the title to Jim Furyk. Admirers praised his sportsmanship, but few would argue that his honesty should have erased the penalty, which existed to protect the other competitors. Organizations must draw the same distinction. When a self-reported error has injured a customer or a patient, the reward should honor the disclosure while leaving the remedy intact; gratitude for a confession is no substitute for making the injured party whole.

These cases leave me with a narrower version of the recommendation than its wording suggests. Organizations should reward disclosure itself, chiefly by guaranteeing that an honest mistake, promptly reported, will bring protection and visible correction rather than punishment. They should not pay for mistakes, pardon schemes, or let candor cancel what is owed to others. Arnold's retraction cost her some public embarrassment and little else; the real task is to make confession that survivable for people with far less standing than a Nobel laureate.

Unnecessary, because an error everyone can already see needs no incentive to be disclosed.

Target words sit in natural collocations, such as "skittish about any blemish on a thin record."

Hidden, honest errors (the nurse, aviation) favor the recommendation; premeditated misconduct, cash bonuses and harm to outsiders do not, and sentences like "This case persuades me that" make the shaping explicit.

prompt.statement: Societies should value stability more than innovation.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Stable Rules, Not Frozen Arrangements
essays.essay:
The statement assumes that stability and innovation compete for a society's loyalty, so that more of one must mean less of the other. That assumption hides an ambiguity. "Stability" can mean preserving existing arrangements, or it can mean a durable framework of rules within which arrangements can change without bloodshed. I agree that societies should value the second kind of stability more than any particular innovation. I disagree that they should value the first, because a society that guards its arrangements against change tends to become not stable but brittle.

Tokugawa Japan offers the strongest case for the statement. After more than a century of civil war, the Tokugawa shoguns built an order designed to prevent change. They froze a hereditary divide between samurai and commoners, banned Christianity, and [[immured|immure]] their subjects within the archipelago, forbidding them to travel abroad on pain of death. Trade with Europe shrank to a single Dutch post on an artificial island in Nagasaki harbor. The result was more than two centuries without a major war. Nor was this peace sterile: Edo grew into one of the world's largest cities, literacy spread well beyond the elite, and a [[sophisticated|sophisticated]] urban culture of woodblock prints, kabuki, and haikai poetry took shape. If preserving arrangements ever paid for itself, it did so here.

Yet the peace was bought by freezing outcomes rather than building a capacity to absorb change, and its costs accumulated unseen. Contradictions [[festered|fester]] beneath the calm: samurai lived on fixed stipends while the commercial economy grew, and many fell into debt to the merchants whom Confucian doctrine disdained as unproductive. When physicians in Edo compared a Dutch anatomy text with the dissection of an executed criminal, they found that the Chinese-derived charts their profession revered were wrong, an [[iconoclastic|iconoclastic]] conclusion that energized the study of Western science. The regime, however, remained hostile to any knowledge that might unsettle the political order; in the 1830s, scholars of Western learning who questioned its policy of firing on foreign ships were punished. When American warships arrived in 1853, the shogunate could neither resist nor adapt quickly enough, and within fifteen years it had collapsed. Tokugawa Japan did not escape change; it merely postponed change until change arrived all at once, on someone else's terms.

The most compelling challenge to my position comes from the opposite catastrophe. If Tokugawa Japan shows the price of stillness, China's Great Leap Forward shows the price of daring. Determined to vault into industrial modernity, Mao Zedong herded peasants into vast communes and diverted labor to backyard steel furnaces; the famine that followed killed tens of millions. A thoughtful opponent would point to an asymmetry here. The losses of excessive caution are usually forgone gains, whereas the losses of a failed innovation can be irreversible, and they fall on people who never chose the gamble. A culture that [[lionizes|lionize]] bold visionaries, on this view, invites its leaders to wager lives that are not their own.

I grant the asymmetry, but the Great Leap supports my distinction rather than refuting it. China did not suffer because it valued change too highly; it suffered because it had dismantled the stable rules that let a society learn it is wrong. The Anti-Rightist Campaign of 1957 had already taught intellectuals that criticism was dangerous. When Defense Minister Peng Dehuai criticized the Great Leap in a 1959 letter to Mao, he was purged, and local officials, understanding the lesson, kept reporting fantastical harvests. The state requisitioned grain according to those figures, stripping villages that were already starving. A framework that protected dissent and honest statistics would have exposed the error quickly; its absence let the error compound for years.

Tokugawa Japan and Mao's China failed as mirror images of each other: one prized stillness, the other upheaval, and neither could hear bad news. What a society should value most, then, is neither stability nor innovation as such but the stable machinery of self-correction: independent courts, a free press, peaceful transfers of power, honest data. With that machinery secure, a society need not be [[skittish|skittish]] about experiment, because its mistakes will surface and be reversed; without it, neither caution nor daring will protect it for long.

prompt.statement: Globalization has made the world's cultures more alike than different.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Shared Goods, Separate Meanings
essays.essay:
Walk through any major airport and the statement seems self-evident: the same denim, the same coffee chains, the same pop songs leaking from the same earbuds. Globalization has plainly standardized the inventory of daily life. Yet the statement rests on a hidden assumption: that people who share objects therefore share a culture. A culture is less a collection of goods than a system for assigning them meaning, and at that level the world remains stubbornly various. I therefore agree with the statement only under one condition: when a community loses the institutions that transmit its meanings, above all its language. Wherever those institutions survive, globalization tends to supply new material for difference rather than erase it.

In Japan, many families have long marked Christmas Eve with a strawberry sponge cake and, since a KFC marketing campaign in the 1970s, with a bucket of fried chicken. The chicken is American and the holiday nominally Christian, yet the ritual is neither: in a largely non-Christian country, Christmas is an occasion for families and couples, not for worship. A family in Kentucky would find the custom nearly [[inscrutable|inscrutable]]. Here is the real mechanism of so-called homogenization: a global brand [[gratifies|gratify]] appetites that exist everywhere, for convenience and novelty, but the meaning attached to the purchase is supplied locally. Products converge; the cultures that absorb them do not.

European history shows that convergence can provoke the very differences it seems to threaten. In the eighteenth century, French plays, manners, and philosophy [[enchanted|enchant]] the courts of Europe: Frederick the Great wrote in French and hosted Voltaire, and Russian aristocrats spoke French among themselves. Elite European culture was, if anything, more uniform then than now. Among German writers, resentment of that prestige [[festered|fester]], and Johann Gottfried Herder turned it into a doctrine: that each people expresses a distinct spirit through its language and songs. His argument [[antedated|antedate]] Napoleon's conquests; French occupation later made it urgent, and the Brothers Grimm gathered German folk tales under a Napoleonic regime. Conquest sharpened the reaction, but cultural prestige had provoked it first.

The same dynamic now operates through public policy. France requires radio stations to play a minimum share of French-language songs. South Korea has long required cinemas to screen domestic films on a minimum number of days each year. Korean cinema, sheltered in part by that quota, went on to produce Parasite, the first non-English-language film to win the Academy Award for Best Picture. In both countries, distinctiveness was not a residue that globalization had yet to erase; it was a deliberate project, and in Korea's case a lucrative export.

The most compelling challenge to my position is that the distinction between objects and meanings is too convenient. Language is not a surface, and languages are vanishing: linguists warn that many of the world's roughly seven thousand languages are no longer learned by children. When a language dies, its songs, jokes, and names for plants and places die with it, and no local twist on fried chicken can replace them. Some of this loss was imposed outright: the same French state that now shields French songs from English once punished Breton children for speaking their language at school. Much of the rest is economic: parents stop passing on languages the global economy does not reward. This objection is correct, and it marks precisely the condition under which the statement holds. But notice who suffers such losses: small communities without a state, a school system, or a broadcast market of their own. The threat to difference is therefore not exchange as such but unequal access to the institutions that carry meaning into the next generation.

Globalization has thus made cultures more alike in what they buy than in what they mean. Where a community has lost the means to reproduce itself, the statement holds, and the loss is often irreversible. Elsewhere, shared goods become raw material for [[divergent|divergent]] rituals, and pressure from a dominant culture tends to provoke, rather than suppress, the cultivation of difference. Whether the world grows more uniform, then, depends less on how much it trades than on whether small peoples, not only large ones, retain the power to raise their children in their own language.

prompt.statement: Some people believe that a good leader must above all be decisive. Others believe that a good leader must above all be a good listener.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Listen for Unwelcome Evidence, Then Commit
essays.essay:
The statement treats decisiveness and listening as rivals, asking which quality a leader must possess "above all." That framing rests on an ambiguity in the word "listener." Listening can be a form of deference, or it can be a form of inquiry. The deferential listener gathers opinions and lets their combined weight steer the outcome. The inquiring listener seeks out, and takes seriously when it arrives, unwelcome information that might overturn the plan already in mind. Against the first, the case for decisiveness is overwhelming. Against the second, it largely dissolves, because a decision can be no better than the information its maker was willing to hear. My own position lies closer to the view that a leader must above all listen, but only in this second, more demanding sense.

Those who prize decisiveness are right about what listening as deference produces. A leader who canvasses every constituency will hear most from those with the most time and influence, and will be tempted to prefer a [[scintillating|scintillating]] presentation to a dull but accurate report. Such a leader can also defer a decision indefinitely. There is always another stakeholder to consult, and a mind inclined to [[ruminate|ruminate]] over every new objection will never run out of reasons to wait. Organizations run this way are rarely tyrannical; they are [[feckless|feckless]], commissioning studies instead of producing results. When delay carries its own cost, as in a fire, a bank run, or an epidemic, refusing to choose is itself a choice, usually a poor one.

Yet decisiveness without the second kind of listening imposes costs that are easy to overlook, because they fall on people who were never in the room. Robert Moses, who shaped New York's parks, bridges, and highways for decades, was decisiveness incarnate. He built at a pace no deliberative body could have matched, and many of his projects, from Jones Beach to the region's parkways, still serve millions. His strength was a [[synoptic|synoptic]] view of the region as one network of roads, but no such view can show what a particular route will do to a particular street. When he drove the Cross Bronx Expressway through East Tremont, he treated the [[vociferous|vociferous]] protests of its residents as obstacles to be overcome rather than as information to be weighed, and dismissed an alternative route that critics said would have spared many of their homes. The expressway was finished; the neighborhood along its path deteriorated. Moses did not fail through indecision. He failed through a confidence so complete that it made listening seem unnecessary.

The second kind of listening, by contrast, is often what makes decisive action possible. When cholera struck London's Soho district in 1854, most medical authorities believed it spread through foul air. The physician John Snow suspected contaminated water, and by tracing the households of the dead he found that deaths clustered around a public pump on Broad Street. The parish board that heard his evidence was skeptical of his theory, yet it ordered the pump's handle removed. It did not need to believe Snow; it needed only to take him seriously. The sequence is the point: the board acted decisively because it had first listened to an argument that cut against [[entrenched|entrenched]] medical opinion. Its decisiveness was the last step of its listening, not a rival to it.

The two cases suggest when each view holds. Removing a pump handle could be undone in minutes; an expressway cannot be unbuilt. When a decision is cheap and reversible, as the board's was, decisiveness has the stronger claim. When it is costly and permanent, as Moses's was, listening must come first. Acting on partial evidence is sensible when an error can be corrected tomorrow; it is reckless when the error will outlast the people who made it. The two failures are also asymmetric. A leader who listens but hesitates can be pushed toward a choice by events; a leader who decides but does not listen cannot be told that the choice was wrong. That asymmetry is why I side, finally, with the listener, provided that listening means seeking out and heeding the evidence one would rather not hear and then committing to whatever plan survives it.

prompt.statement: Some believe that tourism enriches the places people visit. Others believe that tourism gradually destroys what made those places worth visiting.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Tourism Destroys by Default, Enriches by Design
essays.essay:
Whether tourism enriches a place or hollows it out depends on a question both views pass over: enriches whom? Each speaks of a place as though it were a single beneficiary, when those who profit from visitors and those who live among them are often different groups. Of the two positions, the second comes closer to my own, though not for the reason its advocates usually give. Tourism does not ruin a destination simply by crowding it. It ruins one when the gains flow to some people and the costs settle on others, and that split is the default rather than the exception. Where a community closes the gap, tourism can enrich.

Venice offers the strongest case for the first view, one that deserves a serious hearing. The city's reliance on strangers [[antedates|antedate]] modern tourism by centuries. Medieval pilgrims bound for the Holy Land embarked from its harbor, and eighteenth-century travelers on the Grand Tour came for its Carnival and opera. The beauty that has [[enchanted|enchant]] visitors ever since is costly to maintain, and the city's economy now depends on what visitors spend. Anyone who insists that tourism simply ruins Venice must explain what would sustain the city without it. On this point the enrichment view is correct. A place no one visits is not thereby preserved; it is often simply abandoned.

Yet the same city shows how enrichment turns into erosion. Apartments have become short-term rentals, rents have climbed beyond local families' reach, and bakeries and hardware stores have given way to shops that [[gratify|gratify]] the day-tripper's appetite for masks and trinkets. The historic center's population has fallen by more than half since the 1950s. For years cruise ships towered over the palaces along the Giudecca Canal, and residents' committees grew [[vociferous|vociferous]] in demanding a ban. Officials were slow to [[heed|heed]] those demands, partly because the ships brought revenue. Resentment [[festered|fester]] as the remedy stalled: a national limit was suspended by a regional court, and a ban on large ships in those waters took effect only in 2021, two years after one slammed into a dock and as UNESCO weighed listing Venice as endangered. The pattern is the point. Cruise lines and absentee landlords collected much of the gain, while residents paid in rents, crowds, and vanished shops. What visitors came for was never a set of facades but a living city, and the costs of their visits were driving that city out.

A contrasting case tests whether this account explains success as well as failure. When the Guggenheim Museum opened in Bilbao in 1997, the city was a declining industrial port few travelers considered worth a detour. Financed largely by Basque public authorities within a wider program of urban renewal, the museum drew visitors worldwide and gave the city a new identity; planners still speak of the "Bilbao effect." Tourism was only one force in Bilbao's revival, but it enriched rather than eroded the city, and two features explain why. First, the public bore the risk, owned the asset, and reaped much of the return in jobs, taxes, and civic pride. Second, the attraction was built to receive visitors, a fact that exposes an assumption hidden in the destruction view: that whatever makes a place worth visiting exists before visitors arrive and can only be used up by them. A museum is designed to be consumed; the daily life of a neighborhood is not. Tourism destroys most readily where the attraction is ordinary life itself, because visitors displace the very thing they came to watch.

The second view, then, is the truer account of what tourism does when left alone; the first describes what a place can achieve only when it sets the terms. The cure for Venice is not to wall the city off behind turnstiles and reservations, which would complete its conversion into a museum, but to make those who profit from visitors answer to those who live among them, through housing reserved for residents, caps on short-term rentals, and fees that fund local services. Tourism enriches a place only when the people who live there, and not merely those who sell it, collect the rewards.

paragraphs.note: Traces rentals, depopulation, and the long-stalled cruise-ship ban, then names the mechanism: outsiders collected the gains while residents paid the costs, driving out the living city visitors came for.

paragraphs.note: Shows tourism, as one force within wider renewal, enriching where the public owned the asset and the attraction was built for visitors, exposing the destruction view's assumption that a place's worth predates tourism.

paragraphs.role: Refined position and concrete remedy
paragraphs.note: Restates the thesis as default versus achievement, rejects walling Venice off as self-defeating, and closes on who collects the rewards, echoing the opening question.

moves.frame: ... does not ... simply by .... It ... when ...
moves.example: Tourism does not ruin a destination simply by crowding it. It ruins one when the gains flow to some people and the costs settle on others
moves.use: State a thesis by replacing the obvious cause with the real mechanism.

moves.example: Anyone who insists that tourism simply ruins Venice must explain what would sustain the city without it. On this point the enrichment view is correct.
moves.use: Give the opposing view a genuine concession before turning against it.

moves.example: a fact that exposes an assumption hidden in the destruction view: that whatever makes a place worth visiting exists before visitors arrive
