analysis.contrast: A typical 4 or 5 would list pros (jobs, cultural exchange) and cons (pollution, crowds), mention Venice or Barcelona in a sentence each without explaining what happened, and conclude that both views have merit and tourism needs balance. It would not ask who gains and who pays, would not test its claim against a counterexample, and would close by restating the introduction.

prompt.statement:
Claim: Historical novels teach history better than textbooks do.
Reason: People remember stories far longer than they remember facts.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Novels Spark Curiosity; Evidence Earns Belief
essays.essay:
Whether historical novels teach history better than textbooks depends on what "teaching history" means. If it means transmitting a reliable record of the past—what happened, in what order, and on what evidence—then the textbook, for all its dullness, is the better instrument. If it means conveying what the past felt like to those who lived it, novels often succeed where textbooks fail. I accept the claim only in this second, narrower sense, and even there for a reason other than the one offered. The reason itself, that people remember stories longer than facts, is largely true, but it supports less than it seems to, and in one important respect it works against the claim.

Hilary Mantel's novels about Thomas Cromwell have [[enchanted|enchant]] readers who would never open a study of Tudor government, and what those readers retain is more than a plot. They come away understanding how precarious power was at the court of Henry VIII and how uncertain the break with Rome looked to men who could not know whether it would last. A textbook's [[synoptic|synoptic]] account of the English Reformation can state the facts, but because it is written with hindsight, events seem foreordained. Mantel's dialogue instead places the reader inside moments whose outcome no one yet knew. This, not memorability, is why the claim sometimes holds: novels restore the contingency of the past, and grasping that contingency is much of what historical understanding means.

The stated reason fares worse in the first sense, the transmission of an accurate record. Stories do outlast facts, but their durability comes from their form, not their [[veracity|veracity]]. Mantel's portrait of Thomas More as a cold persecutor of heretics is one many historians consider unfair, yet readers absorb it as confidently as the rest. Gone with the Wind offers a starker case. Its nostalgic picture of the plantation South, complete with loyal slaves and predatory carpetbaggers, shaped how generations of Americans imagined slavery and Reconstruction. W. E. B. Du Bois's Black Reconstruction, which slightly [[antedated|antedate]] the novel, had already challenged that picture, documenting, for instance, the public schools that Reconstruction governments established. The scholarship existed; the story won. A forgotten fact leaves a gap that later instruction can fill, but a vivid error becomes [[entrenched|entrenched]] and must be dislodged before anything true can replace it. The reason is therefore true but insufficient: to support the claim, it needs a further premise, that the stories novels tell are accurate, and no novelist is obliged to make them so.

The same distinction exposes a second limitation, one concerning evidence. Even an ambitious novel tends to deliver a thesis rather than a method. In War and Peace, Tolstoy repeatedly halts his account of Napoleon's invasion of Russia to [[ruminate|ruminate]] on what moves history, insisting that the combined wills of countless ordinary people matter more than the orders of emperors. The reader receives this serious argument as the author's conviction, not as a conclusion to be tested. A good textbook, by contrast, can set rival interpretations and primary sources side by side, teaching the skill on which every other historical lesson depends: distinguishing a well-supported account from a merely compelling one. A student who has learned that skill can judge the next historical novel she reads; a student who has absorbed only stories cannot.

A defender of the claim might reply that an accurate textbook nobody remembers teaches nothing at all. The objection has force, but it argues for better textbooks and for reading novels alongside them, not for ranking novels above them. Nor are memorable stories the novelist's monopoly: Barbara Tuchman's The Guns of August recounts the opening weeks of the First World War in prose as [[scintillating|scintillating]] as any novelist's, yet it cites its sources. If stories teach because they stick, the reason favors narrative history as much as fiction. The strongest case for historical fiction is not that its stories stick but that it makes the past feel inhabited and undecided, turning indifferent students into curious ones. A novel can create the desire to know what happened; only a work that shows its evidence can tell a reader which of the stories she remembers deserve to be believed.

words.meaning_here: delighted and captivated readers, drawing in people with no prior interest in Tudor history
giving a broad, comprehensive overview of the whole Reformation at once
accuracy; whether a story actually matches what historically happened
words.def: conformity to facts; accuracy./habitual truthfulness.

words.meaning_here: came earlier in time than; Du Bois's book appeared shortly before the novel
firmly lodged in popular memory and hard to remove or correct
words.def: (of an attitude, habit, or belief) firmly established and difficult or unlikely to change; ingrained.

words.meaning_here: reflect deeply and at length, in long digressions, on what drives historical events
brilliantly lively and clever; describes how vividly Tuchman's history is written

analysis.verdict: The position is insightful, not just clear. The essay splits "teaching history" into two tasks and then judges the claim and the reason separately: the claim is right for a different reason, and the reason is true but insufficient. Each example (Mantel, Gone with the Wind versus Du Bois, Tolstoy, Tuchman) is developed to show what happened and why it matters, and the prose is precise, varied and error-free.
analysis.position: The first paragraph states a qualified thesis: the writer accepts the claim "only in this second, narrower sense" and warns that the reason "works against the claim." The last sentence restates it in new words: novels create the desire to know, but evidence decides what to believe.
analysis.development: Every example ends with an explanation of why it matters. Mantel shows contingency, then returns as a warning (her More is a portrait "many historians consider unfair"). Gone with the Wind versus Du Bois shows a vivid error beating scholarship that already existed, and Tolstoy shows a novel delivering "a thesis rather than a method."
analysis.organization: The opening distinction between an accurate record and lived experience organizes the body. Paragraph 2 takes the second sense; paragraphs 3 and 4 take the first, including its "on what evidence" clause. Transitions name the logical link, as in "The same distinction exposes a second limitation."
analysis.language: The diction is exact rather than ornate ("durability comes from their form, not their veracity"), and sentence length varies sharply, from the six-word "The scholarship existed; the story won." to long, balanced sentences. Target words sit in normal collocations such as "synoptic account," "ruminate on" and "prose as scintillating."
analysis.task: The instruction asks for separate verdicts on the claim and the reason, and the essay gives both openly. The claim "sometimes holds" for a reason unrelated to memory (contingency), while the reason is "true but insufficient" because it depends on an unstated premise that novels are accurate. The last paragraph adds that the reason favors "narrative history as much as fiction."

paragraphs.role: Distinction, then a two-part position
paragraphs.note: Splits "teaching history" into transmitting an accurate record and conveying lived experience. Accepts the claim only for the second and previews that the reason is true yet partly self-defeating.

paragraphs.role: Where the claim holds, and why
paragraphs.note: Mantel's Cromwell novels show readers events before anyone knew the outcome. The writer credits contingency, not memorability, so the claim is right for a different reason.

paragraphs.role: Reason tested: memory is not accuracy
paragraphs.note: Readers absorb Mantel's contested More as confidently as the rest; Gone with the Wind's vivid error beats scholarship that already existed. Concludes that the reason needs an unstated premise: that novels are accurate.

paragraphs.role: Second limitation: novels lack a method
paragraphs.note: Tolstoy's digressions deliver a thesis readers cannot test. Textbooks can set sources side by side and teach how to judge accounts, including the next novel a student reads.

paragraphs.role: Counterargument answered; refined position
paragraphs.note: Grants that a forgotten textbook teaches little; Tuchman's history shows memorable narrative need not be fiction. Ends by assigning novels the job of creating curiosity and giving evidence the final word on what to believe.

moves.frame: Whether ... depends on what "..." means.
moves.example: Whether historical novels teach history better than textbooks depends on what "teaching history" means.
moves.use: Opening a prompt whose key term hides two meanings; then judge the claim under each.

moves.frame: This, not ..., is why the claim sometimes holds: ..., and ... is much of what ... means.
moves.example: This, not memorability, is why the claim sometimes holds: novels restore the contingency of the past, and grasping that contingency is much of what historical understanding means.
moves.use: Agreeing with a claim while rejecting the reason the prompt gives for it.

moves.frame: The reason is therefore true but insufficient: to support the claim, it needs a further premise, that ...
moves.example: The reason is therefore true but insufficient: to support the claim, it needs a further premise, that the stories novels tell are accurate
moves.use: Claim-and-reason prompts: grant the reason, then expose the hidden assumption it relies on.

analysis.contrast: A typical 4 or 5 would evaluate the claim and the reason separately but less sharply: it would argue that stories are memorable, concede that novels can be inaccurate, and develop relevant examples, but it would not explain why vivid inaccuracy turns memorability into a liability, notice that the claim might hold for a different reason (contingency), or see that memorability favors narrative history as much as fiction.

prompt.statement:
Claim: Companies should pay employees to learn new skills.
Reason: Workers who keep learning become more valuable to the companies that train them.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Pay for Learning, Not for Loyalty
essays.essay:
The strongest objection to this claim is an old one: a skill a company pays for need not stay with the company. Economists since Gary Becker have predicted that firms will be [[skittish|skittish]] about funding general training, the kind any employer rewards, because a trained worker can take such skills to a better-paying rival. I grant the objection its full force, but notice where it lands: it damages the reason far more than the claim. Workers who keep learning do become more valuable, but not reliably "to the companies that train them." Against the claim, however, the objection fails at its unstated premise, that a company's only return on training is a skill it can keep. Drop that premise, and the claim survives: companies should pay employees to learn, but the stated reason is half true and, even where true, insufficient.

Consider the federal courts. Each year their judges hire young lawyers as clerks on government salaries and teach them, draft by draft, how a judicial opinion is built. Most clerks leave within a year or two, often for law firms that pay generous signing bonuses. By the prompt's reasoning, the courts would look [[profligate|profligate]], spending public money on talent that private firms will harvest. Yet the arrangement persists, because a judge's return never depended on keeping the clerk. A judge gets present work that improves as the clerk learns, and mentoring that launches careers repays the judge in reputation: feeder judges, who regularly send clerks on to the Supreme Court, attract the strongest applicants precisely because their clerks move on. Training here pays off while the clerk learns and again after the clerk leaves, two returns the prompt never considers.

Taken as the sole justification, the reason also invites abuse, since a company that trains workers only because they become valuable to it will want them to stay. Hollywood studios of the 1930s and 1940s spent heavily on publicity and coaching to build stars, then bound their contract players for up to seven years, the longest term California would enforce. Standard contracts also let a studio suspend an actor who refused a role and add the suspension to the end of the term. This deliberate evasion of the legal limit could keep performers bound past seven years, until Olivia de Havilland sued Warner Bros. and won a ruling that seven years meant seven calendar years. The studios cared more about controlling stars than recouping coaching costs, so the parallel is inexact, but their logic is the prompt's reason standing alone: money spent making a worker valuable becomes a claim on the worker. That logic is [[exploitative|exploitative]], however generous the spending. Employers who now make departing workers repay their training costs have simply taken the prompt's reason literally.

Even where the reason holds, it is too thin to support a "should." That learning makes workers more valuable shows that companies have an incentive to pay, not an obligation; a good night's sleep also makes workers more valuable, yet no one argues that employers must pay for it. What distinguishes job skills is that the company often decides which skills are needed and how quickly they change. A hospital that adopts a new electronic records system has, by its own choice, made familiar skills obsolete; it should pay for the remedy whether or not the retrained staff stay. The duty is therefore strongest where the employer, not the market, sets the pace of change, and weakest where an employee chooses to learn what the job does not require.

A [[judicious|judicious]] employer, then, pays for learning as a cost of doing business, not as a down payment on a worker it expects to keep. The manager who is [[crestfallen|crestfallen]] when a newly certified employee resigns has misread the transaction. Even an employee who [[premeditated|premeditate]] her departure before finishing the course has betrayed no one; the training never purchased loyalty, and pretending otherwise leads back to the studio contract. Companies should pay employees to learn, but because of what learning yields whether or not the worker stays and what employers owe for the changes they impose, not because a better worker will be theirs to hold.

words.meaning_here: wary and reluctant to commit money, fearing the trained worker will leave
recklessly wasteful with public money, spending it on training that benefits private firms
unfairly using money spent on workers as a claim to control them
words.def: making use of a situation or treating others unfairly in order to gain an advantage or benefit.

words.meaning_here: showing good sense and careful judgment about why and how to spend
visibly disappointed when the hoped-for loyalty fails to appear
planned in advance, with a hint of wrongdoing that the sentence then denies

analysis.verdict: This response earns a 6 because it does exactly what the instruction asks: it judges the claim and the reason separately, accepting the first and showing the second is half true and insufficient. Its examples are developed until their relevance is explicit, it concedes where its studio parallel is inexact, and it defines when the duty to pay is strongest; the language is precise, varied, and controlled.
analysis.position: The position is clear and qualified by the end of paragraph 1: the claim survives, but "the stated reason is half true and, even where true, insufficient." Its insight is exposing the hidden premise that a company's only return on training is a skill it keeps, and paragraph 4 sharpens it by saying where the duty is "strongest" and "weakest."
analysis.development: Each example is explained, not just named: the clerkship paragraph says who pays, who gains, and why judges still train, concluding that training "pays off while the clerk learns and again after the clerk leaves." The studio example is handled honestly: the essay admits "the parallel is inexact" and then names the shared logic, that money spent on a worker "becomes a claim on the worker."
analysis.organization: The essay follows the concession shape: objection granted, limit found, position built from that limit. Topic sentences such as "Taken as the sole justification, the reason also invites abuse" announce each step, and the final paragraph links back to "the studio contract."
analysis.language: Sentence length ranges from the four-word "Consider the federal courts." to long sentences controlled with colons and semicolons. Diction is exact ("a down payment on a worker it expects to keep"), and target words sit in natural collocations, such as "skittish about funding general training."
analysis.task: The essay keeps claim and reason apart: paragraph 2 shows the claim is right for a different reason, and paragraph 4 shows the true part of the reason proves only that "companies have an incentive to pay, not an obligation."

paragraphs.role: Concession, its limit, and the split verdict
paragraphs.note: Grants that trained workers can leave, then shows this undercuts the reason, not the claim. Exposes the hidden premise that training's only return is a kept skill, and states the position.

paragraphs.role: Claim holds for a different reason
paragraphs.note: Federal clerkships: judges train clerks who soon leave, yet gain present work and, through reputation, stronger applicants. Builds from paragraph 1's limit by showing training pays off without retention.

paragraphs.role: The reason, taken alone, invites abuse
paragraphs.note: Studio contracts, the suspension clause that stretched them past California's seven-year limit, and de Havilland's suit show investment turned into a claim on workers; the inexact parallel is conceded, and repayment clauses update it.

paragraphs.role: A true reason is still insufficient
paragraphs.note: Separates incentive from obligation with the sleep analogy, supplies a stronger reason (a company whose choices make skills obsolete owes retraining), then defines where that duty is strongest and weakest.

paragraphs.role: Refined position in fresh words
paragraphs.note: Recasts paid learning as a cost of doing business, uses the crestfallen manager to deny that even a planned departure is betrayal, recalls the studio contract, and restates the claim on new grounds.

moves.frame: I grant the objection its full force, but notice where it lands: it damages the ... far more than the ....
moves.example: I grant the objection its full force, but notice where it lands: it damages the reason far more than the claim.
moves.use: Claim-and-reason prompts: concede an objection, then say exactly which of the two it defeats.

moves.frame: That ... shows that ... have an incentive to ..., not an obligation; ...
moves.example: That learning makes workers more valuable shows that companies have an incentive to pay, not an obligation
moves.use: When a reason proves only self-interest but the claim says "should": separate motive from duty.

moves.frame: The ... is therefore strongest where ..., not ..., ..., and weakest where ....
moves.example: The duty is therefore strongest where the employer, not the market, sets the pace of change, and weakest where an employee chooses to learn what the job does not require
moves.use: After testing a claim, define the conditions: where its duty holds most firmly and where it fades.

analysis.contrast: A typical 4 or 5 would agree with claim and reason, listing training's benefits such as productivity, morale, and retention, supported by a hypothetical company or a famous name left undeveloped. It might note that trained workers can leave, but as a minor drawback, not as the fact that splits the claim from the reason. It would rarely offer a better reason or trace where the stated one leads.

prompt.statement: Governments should fund free childcare for all families.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Build Capacity Before Abolishing Childcare Fees
essays.essay:
Proponents and opponents of universal childcare tend to be equally [[vociferous|vociferous]]. They dispute its effects on children and on parental choice, but their loudest quarrel is often over cost: whether the state can afford the bill. That framing conceals the assumption on which the proposal rests, namely that price is the only barrier between families and good care. Abolishing fees does not build a classroom or train a teacher; it multiplies demand. The consequences of the policy therefore hinge on two conditions its slogan ignores: whether the supply of good care can grow as fast as demand, and whether the care children receive is better than the care it replaces. Where both conditions hold, governments should fund free childcare for all families. Where either fails, the same promise wastes public money and can harm the children it is meant to help.

The intended consequences are largely economic, and they are not merely theoretical. When the Canadian province of Quebec began offering childcare for five dollars a day in 1997, employment among mothers of young children rose markedly over the following decade, and some economists have estimated that the resulting tax revenue offset much, perhaps all, of the program's cost. Opponents who dismiss such spending as [[profligate|profligate]] count the bill but not the returns. A subsidy that returns parents, most often mothers, to paid work resembles an investment more than a handout, because the alternative is not zero cost but lost earnings, stalled careers, and a narrower tax base. This benefit also argues for breadth: a middle-income mother whose fees would consume most of her paycheck faces the same incentive to stay home as a poor one, and a program confined to the poorest families would never reach her.

The unintended consequences began with supply. Because care was so cheap, demand quickly outran the number of licensed spaces, and waiting lists became a fixture of family life. That outcome was [[foreseeable|foreseeable]]. Scarce slots tend to go to parents, often comparatively affluent ones, who have the time, information, and flexibility to secure them, so a program designed for everyone can end up subsidizing those who need help least. Much of the rapid expansion, moreover, came through centers of uneven quality. A government that abolishes fees before it has built the capacity to meet the resulting demand is not generous but [[feckless|feckless]]: it has distributed a promise rather than a service, and the families left waiting must still find and pay for care elsewhere.

A second unintended consequence concerns children rather than parents, and it is easier to miss because it surfaces slowly. Economists who studied Quebec's program found that, relative to children elsewhere in Canada, young children in the province showed more anxiety and aggression after it began, and later research suggested that some of these effects persisted into adolescence. Compare the Perry Preschool study, begun in Michigan in the 1960s, in which disadvantaged children who received intensive, well-staffed preschool earned more and were arrested less as adults than children in a control group. The two findings do not conflict. A child whose home offers little stimulation gains from a skilled teacher; a child moved from attentive parental care into a crowded room with rotating staff may lose. The effect of free childcare on children depends less on the subsidy than on what it replaces.

Weighing these consequences, I support free childcare for all families only where a government builds and staffs enough well-run classrooms before it abolishes fees, so that the subsidy buys care rather than a place in line. Until that capacity exists, the [[judicious|judicious]] course is to expand supply first, waive fees for the families whose children gain most, and charge others on a sliding scale. Targeting is not costless: means-tested subsidies often come with eligibility rules whose logic is [[inscrutable|inscrutable]] to applicants, so many eligible families never apply, and programs reserved for the poor tend to lose political support. Those costs argue for making universality the destination, not for declaring it before the classrooms exist. The right question for a legislature is not whether childcare should be free, but whether the care it is about to make free is worth having.

words.meaning_here: loudly and insistently outspoken in pressing their views on universal childcare
recklessly wasteful with public money, as cost-focused opponents charge
predictable in advance from the policy's design: very cheap care would create more demand than supply
words.def: able to be foreseen or predicted.

words.meaning_here: ineffective; it makes a show of generosity but delivers nothing useful
showing sound, careful judgment about what to do first and how far to go
so opaque that applicants cannot work out the reasoning behind the eligibility rules

analysis.verdict: This response earns a 6 because its position is insightful, not merely clear: it exposes the hidden assumption that price is the only barrier and turns a yes-or-no debate into two testable conditions. One extended example, Quebec, is developed through both its intended and unintended consequences and sharpened by a contrast with Perry Preschool, and the prose is precise, varied, and error-free.
analysis.position: By the end of paragraph one the writer takes a conditional but firm stand: "Where both conditions hold, governments should fund free childcare for all families." The final paragraph restates it more sharply, making capacity before fee abolition the deciding test.
analysis.development: Quebec carries most of the argument, and it is developed rather than name-dropped: the essay explains its employment gains, its waiting lists, and its effects on children; it uses the gains to answer the cost objection and argue for breadth, and ties the waiting lists and the child effects to the two conditions. The Perry Preschool contrast then explains why childcare can help one child and hurt another, depending on its quality and on the care it replaces.
analysis.organization: The structure follows the thinking: intended consequence (paragraph 2), the supply condition failing (paragraph 3), the child-outcome condition failing (paragraph 4), then the verdict. Topic sentences such as "The unintended consequences began with supply" signal each step.
analysis.language: Diction is exact rather than ornate ("distributed a promise rather than a service"), and sentence length varies on purpose, from the four-word "That outcome was foreseeable" to long sentences with several clauses. Compact antitheses such as "count the bill but not the returns" show controlled parallelism.
analysis.task: The instruction requires the consequences to shape the position, and the essay labels them openly ("The intended consequences", "A second unintended consequence") before concluding "Weighing these consequences, I support free childcare for all families" with conditions attached.

paragraphs.role: Exposes hidden assumption; sets two conditions
paragraphs.note: Acknowledges other disputes, then shifts the debate from cost to supply and quality and states a conditional position: free childcare is right if both conditions hold, wasteful and harmful if either fails.

paragraphs.role: Intended consequence: mothers' employment and revenue
paragraphs.note: Develops Quebec's labor-market gains, answers the opponents' cost objection from paragraph one, and argues that this benefit justifies a broad program, supporting the favorable half of the position.

paragraphs.role: Unintended consequence: rationing and uneven quality
paragraphs.note: Uses the same Quebec example to show the supply condition failing: waiting lists favor affluent families and quality slips, so a universal promise becomes a broken one.

paragraphs.role: Unintended consequence: effects depend on replaced care
paragraphs.note: Contrasts Quebec's behavioral findings with Perry Preschool's long-run gains to establish the second condition: care helps children only when it improves on what they would otherwise receive.

paragraphs.role: Refined position, concession, policy sequence
paragraphs.note: Lets the traced consequences set the position, prescribes capacity first with targeted fee waivers, concedes the costs of targeting, and closes by reframing the question legislators should ask.

moves.frame: That framing conceals the assumption on which the ... rests, namely that ...
moves.example: That framing conceals the assumption on which the proposal rests, namely that price is the only barrier between families and good care.
moves.use: Early, when the prompt's claim depends on an unstated premise you can name and then test.

moves.frame: The effect of ... on ... depends less on ... than on ...
moves.example: The effect of free childcare on children depends less on the subsidy than on what it replaces.
moves.use: After two examples with opposite results, to name the variable that actually decides the outcome.

moves.frame: Those costs argue for making ... the destination, not for declaring it before ...
moves.example: Those costs argue for making universality the destination, not for declaring it before the classrooms exist.
moves.use: After conceding a counterargument, to absorb it into your position as a matter of timing.

analysis.contrast: A typical 4 or 5 would pick a side on cost or fairness, list benefits (working mothers, child development) and drawbacks (taxes, government overreach), and perhaps cite Sweden or Quebec without describing what actually happened there. It would treat consequences as a pro-and-con list rather than as evidence that sets conditions, and it would miss the supply problem and the point that effects depend on what care replaces.

prompt.statement: Governments should fund research aimed at extending the human lifespan.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Fund Healthspan, Not Mere Duration
essays.essay:
The phrase "extending the human lifespan" hides two different goals. One is to add years to the end of life, stretching out the frailty that already precedes most deaths in wealthy countries. The other is to postpone that frailty itself, so that people remain healthy longer and their decline, when it comes, is brief. I support public funding, but only under three conditions: the research targets the biology of aging rather than the mere prolongation of decline, its benefits remain broadly accessible, and it does not drain resources from cheaper measures that already save lives. These conditions follow from the policy's likely consequences, intended and unintended.

The case for funding rests on a scientific shift. For much of the twentieth century, aging was regarded as passive wear and tear, a process too diffuse to study, let alone alter. Experiments on the roundworm C. elegans helped [[elucidate|elucidate]] the genetics of aging: altering a single gene could roughly double the animal's life, and the long-lived worms stayed active far longer than ordinary ones. The conclusion was [[iconoclastic|iconoclastic]]: aging is a regulated, and therefore potentially adjustable, process. The practical consequence justifies public spending: because heart disease, most cancers, and dementia share advancing age as their greatest risk factor, research that slows aging itself could delay them together rather than one at a time. The added years could then be spent in health rather than in intensive care. Private investors, who need returns they can capture, tend to favor patentable products over openly published basic science, which is why governments should fund it.

The policy fails, however, when longevity is pursued without regard to function, and when success alters behavior in ways no one intended. A case from baseball is instructive. When the surgeon Frank Jobe rebuilt the pitcher Tommy John's torn elbow ligament in the 1970s, he rescued a career that had seemed finished; John pitched for more than a decade afterward. The procedure mattered not because it kept a player on the roster but because it restored a working arm. Its reliability, though, had an unforeseen effect: some players and coaches came to regard it as an upgrade rather than a last resort, an attitude that may help explain the rising number of teenagers who undergo it. Longevity research invites both dangers. Treatments that keep failing bodies alive without restoring vigor would [[immure|immure]] the elderly in nursing homes for additional years. Even in worms, later studies found, some long-lived strains spend longer in a frail state. And the promise of a future cure could tempt citizens and governments to neglect unglamorous prevention, from tobacco control to blood-pressure treatment, that already adds healthy years.

A further condition concerns who benefits. When insulin was isolated in the early 1920s, its discoverers sold the patent to the University of Toronto for a token sum so that no company could monopolize it; a century later, high prices in the United States have driven some diabetics to ration their doses. Longevity research could follow the same arc, with taxpayers financing discoveries that reach mainly those able to pay. A program that serves chiefly to [[gratify|gratify]] the wish of the wealthy to outlive their peers inverts the purpose of public spending. The opportunity cost is equally concrete. Much of the gain in life expectancy between 1900 and 1950 came not from slowing aging but from clean water, sanitation, and better nutrition, which spared children and young adults, and that work remains unfinished: tuberculosis alone still kills more than a million people a year. Pouring money into speculative anti-aging laboratories while such cheap, proven measures languish would be [[profligate|profligate]].

The consequences, then, do not merely decorate my position; they determine it. Governments should fund research into the biology of aging, because the knowledge it yields is a public good that markets will underprovide, and its most plausible payoff is a longer period of health. That support should carry safeguards: open publication of results, pricing commitments for any therapies that emerge, and a budget that never crowds out proven, inexpensive interventions. The proper aim is not to [[banish|banish]] death but to postpone decline. Funding that aim is a sound use of public money; funding mere duration is not.

prompt.statement: Competition among nations has done more to advance science than cooperation has.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Rivalry Accelerates, Cooperation Builds
essays.essay:
Several of the most celebrated scientific episodes of the twentieth century were races, which explains the statement's appeal. Yet the statement treats two kinds of progress as one. Some advances are sprints toward a visible goal that existing knowledge makes reachable; others are the slow accumulation of knowledge too costly, or too widely scattered, for any single country to gather. Competition among nations excels at the first kind and cooperation at the second. Because the second kind is both larger and the precondition of the first, I disagree with the statement, even as I grant the cases in which it holds.

The statement holds when three conditions are met: the target is concrete, the underlying science is largely known, and the obstacle is money and political will rather than ignorance. The space race met all three. When the Soviet Union launched Sputnik in 1957, American newspapers treated the beeping satellite as a national humiliation, and their alarm quickly reached Congress. A legislature that might otherwise have [[dawdled|dawdle]] over appropriations for rockets instead created NASA and poured money into science education. Within twelve years, American astronauts had walked on the moon. The race did yield discoveries, from the radiation belts Explorer 1 detected to lunar samples that reshaped planetary science, but discovery was not what drove it. What rivalry chiefly supplied was urgency: the physics of orbital flight had long been understood, and fear of falling behind turned that knowledge into achievement faster than ordinary budgeting ever would have.

The statement fails when a problem exceeds any one nation's means or when progress depends on results that outsiders can examine. Rivalry [[circumscribes|circumscribe]] the research it pays for: work classified for national advantage cannot be checked by foreign peers, and parallel programs duplicate one another in ignorance. Particle physics shows the alternative. In 1954, twelve European countries, several of them recently at war with one another, founded CERN, pooling funds and talent in a single laboratory. The United States, by contrast, began building a collider in Texas larger than any at CERN, with little foreign support, and Congress canceled it in 1993 as its costs mounted. At CERN's Large Hadron Collider, financed by many nations, physicists detected the Higgs boson in 2012. The arrangement can be [[irksome|irksome]], since every budget must win the approval of member governments year after year, yet that slow consensus proved more durable than one legislature's patience.

The deeper flaw in the statement is that it treats competition and cooperation as alternatives, when the first usually depends on the second. The race for coronavirus vaccines in 2020 was openly national: Washington financed Operation Warp Speed, and Russia named its vaccine Sputnik V, deliberately recalling 1957. Vaccines were authorized before 2020 ended, and national money deserves real credit for that speed, because government funding and advance orders let firms manufacture doses while trials were still under way. Yet those firms began from a genetic sequence that a Shanghai team and a Sydney-based colleague had posted online in January 2020. That was cooperation among scientists, not governments: Chinese authorities reportedly closed the laboratory soon afterward. The statement never says whose cooperation it means, and science often needs this informal kind most: open publication had already carried decades of messenger RNA research across borders. Those same national orders also let wealthy countries claim most early doses, leaving poorer ones a [[miserly|miserly]] share and slowing the vaccines' reach without advancing the science. The press, with its [[inveterate|inveterate]] habit of framing discovery as a contest, called it all a race, obscuring the cooperation that made the race possible.

These cases shape my position as follows. Competition among nations is an accelerant rather than a fuel: when the goal is visible and the knowledge to reach it already exists, a rival's success can jolt a government into spending what it otherwise would not. When the problem is costly, uncertain, or scattered across borders, rivalry breeds secrecy and duplication, and cooperation, whether among governments or among scientists, does the essential work. Since even the sprints that competition wins are run on knowledge that cooperation built, the role of national rivalry in science is real but [[subordinate|subordinate]], however many headlines it has produced.

prompt.statement: In any profession, the ability to explain one's work matters as much as the work itself.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Explanation Matters Where Work Needs Understanding
essays.essay:
The strongest case for this statement comes from professions whose work does not take effect until other people act on it. A public health recommendation that no one follows accomplishes nothing, however sound its science. In such fields explanation is not decoration on a finished product but part of the machinery by which it works, and I readily grant that it matters as much as the analysis it conveys. But that concession rests on a condition the statement never names: the value of the work must pass through someone else's understanding. Where the condition holds, the statement is correct. Where it fails, the statement inflates a useful skill into the equal of the work itself, and a profession that accepts the inflation will reward the wrong people.

Early in the COVID-19 pandemic, American health officials told healthy people they did not need masks, then reversed that advice within weeks. The first advice was [[pithy|pithy]] and confident, as messages meant for millions must be, and its brevity blurred the grounds on which it rested, among them doubts that masks protected ordinary wearers, an underestimate of spread by people without symptoms, and a wish to save scarce masks for hospital workers. The CDC justified its reversal with new evidence of such spread, but the first message had done little to signal that it was provisional, so many people heard a contradiction. Their [[vexation|vexation]] was understandable. Some critics went further and [[upbraided|upbraid]] the agencies for incompetence or even deceit. Because the work could succeed only if millions changed their behavior, an explanation that presented a provisional judgment as settled undermined the work it was meant to deliver.

The condition breaks down, however, in professions whose work acts directly on the world. Anyone who has hired a plumber knows that the measure of the job is whether the pipe stops leaking. A plumber who delivers a [[prolix|prolix]] lecture on water pressure and leaves the joint dripping has failed; one who mutters a few words and leaves a dry floor has done everything the customer needed. The mumbling may be a minor annoyance, but it does not make the floor any wetter. The same logic holds, with far higher stakes, for an anesthesiologist adjusting a dose mid-operation: the unconscious patient depends on correct work, not on anyone's ability to narrate it. Explanation still matters here, in training apprentices and documenting decisions for peer review, but it serves the work rather than standing beside it as an equal.

The statement goes wrong in a second, more troubling way. If explanation counted as much as work, a brilliant explainer of worthless work would be as valuable as a halting explainer of excellent work, and that is roughly the bargain Theranos offered. Its founder, Elizabeth Holmes, described a device that would run many laboratory tests on a few drops of fingertip blood, backing the story with misleading demonstrations and reports doctored to suggest outside validation. Many seasoned investors and distinguished board members accepted her account with [[blithe|blithe]] confidence instead of demanding independent proof that the machines worked. They did not. Patients received unreliable results, the company collapsed, and Holmes was convicted of defrauding investors. The fraud worked because a compelling story was allowed to stand in for evidence. The episode exposes the hidden assumption in the statement: that skill at explaining and quality of work travel together. Often they do not, and a profession that weighs them equally is easiest to fool precisely where its work is hardest for outsiders to check.

Each case moves my position in a specific direction. The mask episode convinces me that the statement holds for a real class of professions, those whose work is finished only in other people's minds. The plumber and the anesthesiologist show that the class has a boundary, beyond which explanation supports the work but does not rival it. Theranos shows what happens when that boundary is ignored: eloquence becomes a substitute for substance rather than a vehicle for it. The ability to explain one's work, then, deserves weight in proportion to how much the work depends on being understood, and it should never outweigh the work itself.

prompt.statement: Hospitals should publish each surgeon's success rates so that patients can choose their doctors.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Disclosure Works Only When Comparison Is Fair
essays.essay:
A surgeon's success rate looks like the purest measure of competence: of the patients she operated on, how many did well? Yet the figure records two things at once—the surgeon's skill and her patients' condition—and the recommendation rests on the [[blithe|blithe]] assumption that the second can be ignored. It also assumes that patients, rather than hospitals, will act on the numbers. I support publishing surgeon-level outcomes, but only under conditions the statement never mentions: the operation must be common and standardized enough for comparison to mean something, the results must be adjusted for patient risk, and someone must watch for surgeons who improve their numbers without improving their care.

The clearest case for comparison comes from Vienna's General Hospital in the 1840s, where two maternity clinics admitted women on alternating days, so their patients were essentially alike. The clinic staffed by physicians and medical students lost far more mothers to childbed fever than the midwives' clinic, and its reputation was so grim that some women preferred to give birth in the street. Ignaz Semmelweis reasoned that doctors were carrying infection from the autopsy room to the delivery ward. The measure he then required, washing hands in a chlorine solution, proved [[efficacious|efficacious]]: deaths in that clinic fell sharply. Because the populations were comparable, the gap reflected what the practitioners did, not whom they treated, which is precisely when outcome comparison is most informative. Patient choice, however, offered only escape; the remedy came from someone who analyzed the difference. Much of the medical establishment rejected Semmelweis's conclusions, which implied that physicians were killing their own patients and thus seemed to [[impugn|impugn]] the competence of the very men asked to accept them. Evidence that indicts a profession is unlikely to be acted on if only that profession sits in judgment of it.

Publication fails, by contrast, when surgeons can improve their numbers more easily by selecting patients than by improving care. In the early 1990s, New York State began publishing risk-adjusted death rates for individual coronary bypass surgeons. Mortality fell substantially, and some low-volume surgeons with poor results abandoned the procedure. But a later survey of the state's cardiac surgeons found that many had turned away high-risk patients, in part to protect their published rates, and critics argued that some of the apparent improvement reflected changes in how risk factors were recorded rather than better surgery. Choice, it turned out, runs in both directions: patients may choose their surgeons, but surgeons also choose their patients. Surgeons' [[vexation|vexation]] at these report cards was not merely wounded pride. Risk adjustment can reduce the penalty for treating sicker patients but cannot capture every feature of a desperate case, so a [[proficient|proficient]] surgeon who accepts the cases her colleagues decline may still rank below them.

Two further circumstances weaken the recommendation. When a surgeon performs an operation only a few dozen times a year, a single death can move the rate by several percentage points, so the published figure measures luck as much as skill. And many patients never choose at all: someone with a ruptured aneurysm is operated on by whoever is on call. "Let patients choose" makes a [[pithy|pithy]] slogan, but even where choice is possible, research on American cardiac report cards suggests that relatively few patients consulted them; much of the benefit seems to have come from hospitals and surgeons responding to scrutiny.

These examples shape a firm but conditional position. Vienna shows that comparison saves lives when patients are alike and only practice differs; New York, that the same comparison can harm the sickest when surgeons choose their patients. Hospitals should therefore publish surgeon-level results for common, standardized operations, with rigorous risk adjustment, minimum case volumes, and measures of statistical uncertainty, while regulators audit how risk is coded and whether high-risk patients are turned away. Where those conditions cannot be met, results should be published for the hospital or surgical team instead. The purpose of disclosure is less to turn surgery into a marketplace than to ensure that a lethal difference in practice, like the one in Vienna, cannot persist merely because the only people sitting in judgment are the ones the numbers indict.

prompt.statement: Cities should protect their remaining green spaces from development, even when more housing is badly needed.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Protect Land for What It Does
essays.essay:
The recommendation treats "green space" as a single, precious category, and that assumption is its weakness. A floodplain meadow, a crowded neighborhood's only park, and a private golf course are all green, but they do different work and serve different people. I agree that some green space deserves protection even when housing is scarce; I do not agree that every remaining patch does. The better test is whether a parcel serves a function no other site could perform, and whether those who gain from keeping it open also bear the cost of the shortage.

The recommendation is plainly sound when green space does physical work that construction would undo. For decades metropolitan Houston spread across prairie and wetland that once absorbed Gulf Coast downpours and [[attenuated|attenuate]] the floods that followed, and some subdivisions rose inside the flood pools of two federal reservoirs. Building there was [[foolhardy|foolhardy]], a wager that the reservoirs would never need that land. When Hurricane Harvey stalled over the region in 2017, they needed it, and many of those homes flooded. The housing was real but not a net gain; it placed families on land whose purpose was to fill with water. The same reasoning covers the lone park in a dense district: for children without yards and older residents who cannot travel far, it has no substitute, and a tower there would shelter some people by taking something essential from many more.

The recommendation fails, however, when preservation is turned against people who need homes. The fight over People's Park in Berkeley shows how. The University of California, short of student beds, planned dormitories there along with apartments for formerly homeless people. Opponents prized the park's protest history and defended the unhoused people camped there, but their lawsuit rested on the California Environmental Quality Act, and an appeals court faulted the university's review for considering neither alternative sites nor the noise student residents might make. Neither ground concerned any work the land itself performed; a law written to protect the environment had been stretched to [[circumscribe|circumscribe]] newcomers' access to a neighborhood. The legislature then amended the statute on both points, and the state supreme court let the project proceed. Those who already have homes can defend open space at little cost, which is why such defenses so easily turn [[sanctimonious|sanctimonious]]; the students and formerly homeless people waiting for those beds, not yet present to object, absorbed every year of delay.

A subtler failure occurs when protection simply pushes development farther out. London's Metropolitan Green Belt, a ring of land around the capital, is defended as a shield for the countryside, and national planning rules still largely bar building on it despite a recent loosening. Yet much of it is private farmland and golf courses rather than parks freely [[accessible|accessible]] to the public. The belt is widely blamed for leaving London short of buildable land and pushing growth past its outer edge into commuter towns whose residents travel back across the protected fields, while owners already settled inside the line keep their views and watch scarcity lift the value of their homes. If that charge is right, the belt's ecological gains are partly offset by longer journeys and by open land consumed beyond it. Protecting land within a line on a map need not protect land in general; it may only move the loss to places where no one is counting.

These cases set the boundaries of my agreement. Houston shows that some land is worth more left open than built on, whatever the shortage; Berkeley and London show that preservation, applied indiscriminately, can protect incumbents rather than nature. A city should therefore refuse to build on land whose value lies in what it does, such as absorbing a flood or giving a crowded district its only open ground, even when housing is badly needed, because a building can be sited elsewhere and a floodplain cannot. Beyond those cases, a blanket rule makes a city [[miserly|miserly]] with its land, hoarding it for people who already live nearby. The question to ask of any green space is not whether it is green, but what it does and for whom.

prompt.statement: Cultural artifacts belong in the countries where they were made, not in the foreign museums that now hold them.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Departure, Not Origin, Decides Belonging
essays.essay:
The statement assumes that where an object was made determines where it belongs, and that assumption hides the question that matters most: how the object left. A Benin plaque and a Chinese export plate both sit in foreign museums, yet they left in morally different ways. I agree with the statement when an artifact was seized by force from a community that still claims it; I reject it when the object departed through fair exchange or when no surviving people or successor state can claim it as its own. Origin is evidence of belonging, not proof of it.

The statement is most persuasive when two conditions coincide: the object was taken by conquest or theft, and the people from whom it was taken survive as a recognizable community. The Benin Bronzes satisfy both. In 1897 a British punitive expedition burned Benin City and carried off thousands of brass plaques and carvings from the royal palace. Many were auctioned to defray the campaign's costs and dispersed among European collections. The plaques served as a visual archive of the royal court, and that court still exists. The claim rests on a living people, not on a modern border: a unified Nigeria did not exist until Britain [[amalgamated|amalgamate]] two protectorates in 1914, centuries after the plaques were cast. Keeping them abroad lets one act of plunder decide where the makers' descendants may study their own past.

The statement falters when either condition is absent. Consider the porcelain China made for eighteenth-century European buyers, some of it enameled to order with a family's coat of arms. Such pieces were made in China, but they were made to leave it; to [[upbraid|upbraid]] a curator in Amsterdam for displaying one is to mistake a sale for a theft. The Buddhist sculpture of ancient Gandhara poses a different difficulty: its artists fused Hellenistic drapery with Indian religious imagery in a region now divided between Pakistan and Afghanistan. A work produced at a crossroads of cultures, under rulers with no modern successor state, fits no single nation cleanly; when its findspot was never recorded, even its country of origin cannot be named. Here the statement does not so much give the wrong answer as give no answer at all.

The most compelling challenge to my position concerns not ownership but survival and education. Its proponents note that encyclopedic museums have protected objects through upheavals that destroyed what stayed behind. In 2001 the Taliban smashed sculptures in Kabul's national museum; in 2003 Baghdad's national museum was looted after the American-led invasion. Encyclopedic museums also teach something no national collection can: a schoolchild in London can walk from Egyptian sculpture to Assyrian reliefs to Greek marble in one afternoon and see that civilizations have always borrowed from one another. This objection cannot be [[discounted|discount]], and one need not [[impugn|impugn]] the sincerity of the curators who advance it.

Even in its strongest form, however, the objection justifies custody, not ownership. Late in the Spanish Civil War, many of the Prado's masterpieces were sent to Geneva under international supervision; afterward, they returned to Madrid, and no one argued that their guardians had acquired them by protecting them. Danger warrants a trust that lasts until conditions change, not a permanent title. The educational argument is weaker still: the universal museum is universal only for those who can obtain a visa. Treating rescue as title would also reward the most [[acquisitive|acquisitive]] museums, which could buy antiquities spirited out of a war zone and call the purchase rescue. Such purchases [[abet|abet]] the very looting the preservation argument deplores.

Where an artifact was made, then, matters less than whether the history of its movement can be justified. When that history is one of seizure from a people who still remember it, return should be presumed, and the holding museum should bear the burden of proof. When it is one of commerce, commission, or genuine rescue, the object may remain abroad, though rescue earns guardianship rather than a deed. Condemning every foreign museum for holding what it did not make is as careless as excusing every acquisition as preservation; the honest task is to ask, object by object, how each arrived where it is.

prompt.statement: Most people value their privacy less than they claim to.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Constrained Conduct Does Not Reveal Value
essays.essay:
Watch almost anyone install a new app and the statement seems self-evident. A woman who tells a pollster that corporate surveillance alarms her will, minutes later, let a free game read her location and contacts. Yet the statement assumes that what people do with their information reveals how much they value their privacy. Conduct reveals value only when people face a real choice whose consequences they can see. I therefore accept the statement only as a description of behavior, and only under three conditions: when the intrusion is abstract, the harm deferred, and the defense tedious. When the intrusion has a face or the choice is posed plainly, it fails even as a description.

Those three conditions describe much of digital life. Privacy policies are so [[prolix|prolix]] that almost no one reads them. Most people click "Accept all" on cookie banners to make them disappear. Shoppers trade their purchase histories for loyalty-card discounts. In each case the cost of protection is immediate and certain, while the cost of disclosure is remote and invisible. No single surrender seems to matter. The damage lies in the accumulation of thousands into a profile no one ever agreed to as a whole. Under these conditions people genuinely behave as if privacy were cheap, and it would be evasive to pretend otherwise.

Change the conditions and the behavior changes with them. Even an [[inveterate|inveterate]] chronicler of her life online, who posts her meals and vacations for hundreds of acquaintances, will tilt her phone away from a stranger on the bus. She curates what she makes public but defends her privacy the moment an intrusion becomes concrete. The same reversal occurs online once the choice is made simple. When Apple began requiring apps to ask users before tracking them across other companies' apps and websites, most users, by widely reported accounts, said no. Their regard for privacy had not suddenly grown; the question had simply become legible.

The most compelling objection comes from the economist's idea of revealed preference. On this view, a user who waves through every tracking request with [[blithe|blithe]] indifference has answered the pollster more truthfully with her clicks than with her words. Professed values cost nothing, the argument runs; what people give up is the only honest measure of what they prize. Explaining such trades away by pointing to tedious banners and clever interfaces treats adults as [[pliant|pliant]] children who cannot be held to their choices. The objection deserves respect: it refuses to let stated ideals excuse contrary conduct. But revealed preference measures value only when the chooser has a genuine alternative and understands the exchange. Both requirements describe how the choice is posed, not how capable the chooser is. The Apple prompt met them; tracking that can be escaped only by abandoning one's phone offers no real alternative.

American courts once embraced the objection's logic and have since begun to limit it. In Smith v. Maryland, the Supreme Court held that a person has no reasonable expectation of privacy in the numbers he dials, because he voluntarily conveys them to the telephone company. That reasoning is the statement translated into law: disclosure proves indifference. In Carpenter v. United States, however, the Court declined to extend it to historical cell-phone location records, holding that the government generally needs a warrant to obtain them. Carrying a phone, the majority reasoned, is practically indispensable to modern life, so the resulting data are not shared in any meaningful sense. In effect, the Court drew the distinction the statement ignores: conduct under constraint does not reveal what people value.

People are not [[disingenuous|disingenuous]], then, when they say privacy matters to them. They act as if they value it less than they claim only in a particular arena: where the threat is faceless, the harm postponed, and the defense an [[irksome|irksome]] daily chore. That arena is large enough to make the statement ring true, yet the statement draws the wrong lesson from it. If privacy erodes chiefly when guarding it is tedious and losing it is invisible, the answer is not to discount what people say they value but to build laws and defaults under which their conduct can finally match it.

prompt.statement: Some argue that schools should group students by ability. Others argue that students of all abilities should learn together.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Group for a Skill, Not a Future
essays.essay:
In most of England and Wales after the Second World War, a handful of tests in arithmetic, English, and reasoning, taken at eleven, largely decided what kind of secondary school a child would attend. Children who passed the eleven-plus, as the tests were known, went to grammar schools that opened the way to university; most who failed went to secondary modern schools, which rarely prepared students for the examinations universities required. Transfers between the two were possible in principle and rare in practice, so a few hours of testing could [[circumscribe|circumscribe]] a child's prospects for decades. The episode poses the grouping debate in its starkest form. Of the two views, the claim that students of all abilities should learn together comes closer to my own, but only in a refined form: the shared classroom should be the default, and grouping should be a temporary instrument for teaching particular skills, never a sorting of children into separate futures.

The case for grouping deserves a serious hearing, because it rests on a real problem rather than on snobbery. A teacher facing thirty children, some still sounding out simple sentences and others ready for algebra, cannot pitch one lesson to all of them; in practice she teaches to the middle. The quickest students learn to [[dawdle|dawdle]], stretching ten minutes of work across an hour because nothing more awaits them, while the slowest fall further behind each week. In cumulative subjects such as mathematics the cost compounds: a student who never mastered fractions cannot follow a lesson on equations, however patiently it is delivered. Nobody thinks a youth orchestra should seat beginners beside its principal players, and advocates of grouping reasonably ask why a classroom should be different.

Where the grouping view goes wrong is in a hidden assumption: that ability is a stable trait a test can read at the moment of sorting. At eleven, a test score reflects much besides aptitude, including the books in a child's home, her maturity relative to her classmates, and whether her parents could pay for coaching. By certifying those advantages as merit, the eleven-plus did more than mirror class divisions; it entrenched a quiet injustice, handing grammar school places disproportionately to middle-class children. Its more [[pernicious|pernicious]] effect worked through expectations. Children are [[pliant|pliant]], and many told at eleven that they belonged in the lower track came to believe it. Their schools, expecting little, set a pace to match and so [[abetted|abet]] the very failure the label had predicted. A gap that was narrow at eleven could widen into a gulf by sixteen, and the system could then cite that gulf as proof that its verdict had been sound.

None of this means that mixing children is sufficient. Putting students of different abilities in one room does not, by itself, teach any of them, and a mixed class taught at a single pace is exactly what advocates of grouping rightly fear. Finland is instructive because it confronted both dangers. In the 1970s it [[amalgamated|amalgamate]] its parallel grammar and civic schools into a single nine-year comprehensive school, and in the mid-1980s it stopped tracking students by ability within those schools. It did not, however, leave struggling students to sink in a common lesson. Many Finnish pupils receive part-time special education at some point: small-group or individual sessions for a particular difficulty, such as reading or speech, while they stay in their regular class. Whatever else explains Finland's high scores on international assessments in the 2000s, its schools show that grouping and a common education can coexist when the grouping serves a specific need and never becomes a separate track.

The debate is usually framed as a choice between sorting and mixing, but the decisive variables are timing, scope, and permanence. Grouping that happens early, covers every subject, and hardens into an identity turns a snapshot of a child into a forecast and then works to fulfill it. Grouping that is tied to a single skill, reviewed every few weeks, and easy to leave is simply good teaching inside a shared school. Students should learn together by default and be separated only for a stated purpose, for a limited time, and with a clear path back.

prompt.statement: Some believe that public health measures justify limits on individual freedom. Others believe that individual freedom should prevail except in extreme emergencies.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Public Health Must Earn Its Limits
essays.essay:
In November 1904, barricades went up in Rio de Janeiro. The government had just made smallpox vaccination compulsory, and the sanitary brigades of Oswaldo Cruz, Brazil's director of public health, were already a resented presence in poor neighborhoods, entering tenements to fumigate rooms and condemn buildings. Within a week, the mandate was withdrawn. The episode, remembered in Brazil as the Vaccine Revolt, poses the question behind these two views in its starkest form: were the rioters defending their liberty or endangering their neighbors? My position lies closer to the first view: public health measures can justify limits on freedom, and not only in extreme emergencies. But a measure does not acquire that justification merely by aiming at health; it must earn it.

It would be a mistake to [[discount|discount]] the case for letting freedom prevail, and the rioters of Rio show why. They were not simply ignorant of medicine. Many had watched the authorities raze their tenements for more than a decade, most recently to clear new avenues. Their [[inveterate|inveterate]] distrust of officials who now claimed the right to enter their homes and pierce their skin was well earned. Defenders of the second view generalize from such experiences: health restrictions fall hardest on those least able to contest them, and powers granted for one crisis tend to outlive it, [[manacling|manacle]] citizens long after the danger has passed. Reserving coercion for extreme emergencies, they argue, [[attenuates|attenuate]] these risks by keeping it rare and conspicuous.

Yet this position rests on a hidden assumption: that danger announces itself in time. Epidemics rarely do. An outbreak whose case count doubles every few days looks negligible for weeks and then overwhelms hospitals; by the time the emergency is undeniable, the modest steps that would once have sufficed no longer do, and only the bluntest restrictions remain. A rule that limits what health officials may do until that moment does not spare freedom; it postpones and enlarges its sacrifice. Many real threats, moreover, are never acknowledged as emergencies. In Ibsen's An Enemy of the People, a doctor discovers that the medicinal baths on which his town's prosperity depends are contaminated and have sickened visitors. Because the remedy would be costly and would close the baths for years, the town refuses to see a crisis; when the doctor presses for repairs, his fellow citizens [[upbraid|upbraid]] him for threatening their livelihoods and declare him an enemy of the people. Ibsen exposes a second assumption: that the only liberty at stake belongs to the person being restricted. The visitor who bathes in poisoned water, like the neighbor exposed to smallpox, never consented to the risk.

None of this, however, vindicates the first view without qualification. The vaccine was [[efficacious|efficacious]]; Cruz's campaign to impose it was not effective. By delivering a sound measure through agents who entered homes uninvited, in a city where the poor were already being displaced, the government turned a medical question into a contest over dignity, and it lost the mandate. Coercion that outruns public trust can undermine the protection it is meant to secure: once the mandate fell, vaccination remained voluntary and sparse, and when a severe smallpox epidemic struck a few years later, many residents sought out the vaccine they had once fought, but only after the disease had reached their streets. The lesson is not that such limits are illegitimate but that their legitimacy depends on conditions the first view takes for granted: the measure must demonstrably work and be the least restrictive option, its burdens must be shared on [[equitable|equitable]] terms, and those who impose it must explain rather than merely command.

I side, then, with those who would let health constrain liberty, but only once the word "justify" is taken seriously. To justify a limit is to offer reasons the people bearing it could accept. Advocates of freedom are right to insist on such reasons but wrong to defer every limit until catastrophe, when there is no longer time for persuasion, only for force. Public health earns its claim on our liberty not by waiting for an emergency but by preventing one, and it keeps that claim only so long as it treats the governed as partners rather than suspects.

Both examples are developed far enough to show what happened and why it matters, and the prose is precise and varied, with superior control of conventions.

The 1904 Vaccine Revolt in Rio does double duty: it gives the freedom view its strongest case in paragraph 2 and then qualifies the first view in paragraph 4. Ibsen's An Enemy of the People shows a real harm that the town refuses to treat as an emergency, and a reason drawn from how epidemics grow (an outbreak "looks negligible for weeks and then overwhelms hospitals") adds an argument that does not depend on either example.
