prompt.statement:
Claim: Professional sports teams should not receive public money.
Reason: New stadiums enrich team owners far more than the cities that pay for them.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Subsidy, Not Public Money, Is the Problem
essays.essay:
"Public money" can mean two quite different things. A city can subsidize a team, paying for a stadium whose revenue flows to the owner, or it can invest in one, committing funds in exchange for a genuine claim on their return. Both the claim and its reason blur this distinction. I agree that teams should not receive subsidies, though not chiefly because owners gain more than cities do, a reason that both misses the real problem and proves too much. Nor would I extend the claim to public money that buys the public a real stake.

Consider the reason first. As a description of most stadium deals, it is largely accurate: sports economists, a group that rarely agrees on much, have repeatedly found that new stadiums produce little measurable growth in local income or employment, while owners pocket much of the premium revenue the buildings generate. As an argument, however, it rests on a hidden premise: that public spending is unjustified whenever a private party gains more from it than the public does. By that standard, states should stop funding universities. A state university graduate captures most of her degree's payoff through higher lifetime earnings, and the state recovers only a fraction in taxes; yet few conclude that public universities are a mistake. The proper test is not whether the public gains more than anyone else but whether it gains enough to justify the cost, compared with what the same money could do elsewhere. The reason is true, in short, but insufficient.

By that test, the claim is nonetheless right about subsidies, for two reasons the argument never mentions. The first is substitution. Much of what a family spends at the ballpark would otherwise have gone to restaurants or movie theaters elsewhere in town, so a stadium mostly relocates local spending rather than creating it; to borrow heavily on the promise of spillovers that rarely appear is [[foolhardy|foolhardy]]. The second is leverage. Leagues keep fewer franchises than there are cities that want one, so any owner can credibly threaten to leave, and that threat makes city councils [[pliant|pliant]]. Baltimore lost the Colts to Indianapolis and its new domed stadium in the 1980s; little more than a decade later, it lured the Browns away from Cleveland with a publicly financed stadium, and Cleveland then built its own, largely at public expense, to secure a replacement team bearing the old name. Each city acted sensibly on its own terms, yet every payment proved that threatening to leave pays, and so [[abetted|abet]] the next owner who tried it. Owners are no more [[acquisitive|acquisitive]] than other businesspeople, and Amazon ran a similar contest among cities for its second headquarters; but league-made scarcity lets an owner reopen the bidding every time a lease nears its end. A city that refuses to pay is not being [[miserly|miserly]]. It is declining to bid in an auction that cities, taken together, cannot win.

Yet the claim, as stated, is too absolute, because not all public money is a subsidy. The Green Bay Packers are owned by hundreds of thousands of shareholders who receive no dividends, and no single investor may hold enough shares to control the team, so there is no owner to threaten departure. When Brown County voters approved a sales tax to help renovate Lambeau Field, they were not paying ransom, and the gains did not flow into a private fortune. The same logic applies to a city that owns its arena and keeps a fair share of its revenue, or that builds a transit station serving a neighborhood as well as a stadium. Such spending is investment, not tribute, and should be judged as such.

What is wrong with most stadium deals, then, is not that someone else grows rich; public spending often enriches private parties, and sometimes that is precisely its purpose. What is wrong is that cities pay for growth that largely fails to materialize, and pay under a threat the leagues themselves manufacture. Public money should reach a professional team only on the terms a prudent investor would insist upon: a real claim on the returns, and a partner that cannot walk away from what the public has built.

words.meaning_here: recklessly risky; borrowing heavily on unlikely spillovers ignores an obvious danger to public finances.
easily controlled; councils give in to owners' demands under the threat of relocation.
encouraged someone in wrongdoing; each payment emboldened the next owner to threaten relocation.
eager to acquire money; owners are no greedier than other businesspeople.
stingy, unwilling to spend; refusing a subsidy is prudence, not stinginess.

analysis.verdict: This response earns a 6 for insight and cogency, not mere clarity. An opening distinction between subsidy and investment organizes the whole analysis, and the essay judges the reason true but insufficient and the claim right for different reasons yet too absolute. Each example is developed far enough to show why it matters, and the prose is precise, varied, and fully controlled.
analysis.position: The qualified position is set out in paragraph 1: "I agree that teams should not receive subsidies" paired with "Nor would I extend the claim to public money". The final paragraph refines it into a rule about an investor's terms instead of repeating it.
analysis.development: Each example carries one step and is explained, not just named: the state-university case shows the reason proves too much ("By that standard, states should stop funding universities."), Baltimore and Cleveland show threats paying off, and the Packers show public money without leverage. Amazon's contest shows owners are no greedier than ordinary firms; what sets them apart is league-made scarcity that lets them reopen the bidding with every lease.
analysis.organization: The opening distinction sets the order: the reason (paragraph 2), the claim right about subsidies (paragraph 3), the claim too broad for investment (paragraph 4), the refined rule (paragraph 5). Signposts such as "Yet the claim, as stated, is too absolute" mark each turn.
analysis.language: Diction is exact (substitution, leverage, tribute), and sentence length ranges from four words ("The first is substitution.") to long balanced sentences. Compressed contrasts such as "Such spending is investment, not tribute, and should be judged as such." give force without ornament.
analysis.task: The instruction demands separate verdicts on the claim and the reason, and the essay states both visibly: "The reason is true, in short, but insufficient." and "the claim is nonetheless right about subsidies". It then limits the claim's absolute wording in paragraph 4.

paragraphs.role: Distinction and qualified position
paragraphs.note: Splits "public money" into subsidy and investment, then states a qualified position: oppose subsidies, deny that the stated reason is their main basis, exempt genuine investment. This three-part map organizes the body.

paragraphs.role: Reason: true but insufficient
paragraphs.note: Concedes the reason's facts, then exposes its hidden premise with the state-university analogy and replaces "whether the public gains more than anyone else" with the right test: whether it gains enough, compared with alternatives.

paragraphs.role: Claim right, for different reasons
paragraphs.note: Applies that test: substitution means stadiums create little new spending, and league-made scarcity gives owners leverage. Baltimore and Cleveland show threats paying off; the Amazon comparison locates the problem in durable leverage, not greed.

paragraphs.role: Limit: where the claim overreaches
paragraphs.note: Uses the community-owned Packers and Brown County's sales tax to show public money with no leverage and no private capture, then extends the logic to city-owned arenas and transit.

paragraphs.role: Refined position in fresh terms
paragraphs.note: Restates the thesis as a rule: the problem is phantom growth and a manufactured threat, not private enrichment, so public money should come only on an investor's terms.

moves.example: "Public money" can mean two quite different things.

moves.example: As an argument, however, it rests on a hidden premise: that public spending is unjustified whenever a private party gains more from it than the public does.

analysis.contrast: A typical 4 or 5 would agree or disagree wholesale, treating the claim and the reason as one, and would list stadium costs and owner profits in general terms. It might name a famous stadium without explaining what happened. It would rarely see that asking who gains more is the wrong test, or that a community-owned team like the Packers is a real exception.

prompt.statement:
Claim: Cities should limit the number of homes rented to short-term visitors.
Reason: Housing is a necessity for residents before it is a source of income for investors.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Regulate Land Use, Not Landlords' Motives
essays.essay:
Whether a city should limit short-term rentals depends less on the morality of landlords than on the arithmetic of its housing. I agree with the claim where homes are scarce and visitors plentiful, and I reject it elsewhere. The reason deserves a separate verdict. It is [[pithy|pithy]], and as a ranking of moral priorities it is true. But it is too broad to single out short-term rentals and too abstract to tell a city when a limit will house anyone. Where the claim is right, it is right for a different reason: renting a home nightly to strangers changes how a building is used, and regulating use is an old power of cities.

The claim holds most clearly where whole apartments are withdrawn from a market that cannot replace them. Venice is the starkest case. Its historic center has lost most of its residents since the mid-twentieth century, and many apartments once home to families are now listed for tourists. Short-term rentals did not start that decline, but they accelerate it: every apartment rented by the night is one fewer available by the year. Residents' [[vexation|vexation]] at rolling suitcases and late-night check-ins is real, yet it is the lesser harm. The more [[pernicious|pernicious]] effect is quiet subtraction. A neighborhood can empty without a single eviction, because each vacancy goes to visitors rather than tenants, and the grocers who served permanent neighbors give way to souvenir shops. Where the housing supply is fixed and tourist demand nearly bottomless, a cap is not hostility to commerce; it is how a city remains a place where people live.

Notice, though, what would justify a cap in Venice. The problem is not that someone earns money from housing; it is that one use of housing crowds out another. Cities have long [[circumscribed|circumscribe]] what owners may do with property because of what a use does to its neighbors, not why the owner chose it. After the Great Fire of 1666, London required that rebuilt houses be made of brick or stone. The rule did not accuse builders of greed; it recognized that one owner's timber could set a whole street ablaze. Zoning rests on the same logic: a residential zone usually excludes hotels, not because hoteliers are wicked, but because hotels bring different traffic, noise, and turnover. An apartment rented to new tourists every few nights, all year, is a hotel in everything but its license. Grounding the claim in land use tells a city what to regulate—the conversion of whole units into full-time lodging—rather than whom to resent.

Grant the reason fully, and it still does not deliver the claim. Long-term landlords also profit from a necessity, yet they house residents, so the reason objects not to profit as such but to profit that displaces residents; whether tourist rentals do that in a given city is a question of fact the reason cannot settle. Nor are hosts reliably the [[acquisitive|acquisitive]] outsiders the reason imagines. The company that did most to turn short-term rental into a global industry began when two San Francisco roommates rented out air mattresses on their floor to help pay rent. For a retiree renting out a spare room, a [[modest|modest]] income from visitors may be what makes staying put affordable. Applied to such hosts, the reason's moral language turns [[sanctimonious|sanctimonious]], and policies written in that spirit punish the wrong people. The reason also falls silent where demand is slack. In a shrinking city full of vacant houses, a cap would return no homes to the market; it would merely deny owners income that might keep aging buildings occupied.

The defensible position is therefore narrower than the claim and sturdier than the reason. A city should limit short-term rentals when housing is scarce and the limit targets whole units converted into year-round lodging; it should spare residents who occasionally share a room or rent out their own home, and expect little from caps where homes are plentiful. Housing is indeed a necessity before it is an investment, but that principle states what a city values, not what it should do. The case for a limit rests on evidence that, in a particular market, tourists are displacing tenants.

words.meaning_here: Brief but forceful; the reason compresses a moral ranking into a few memorable words.
Residents' annoyance and frustration at the noise and disruption of constant tourist turnover.
Harmful in a gradual, subtle way: housing disappears quietly, unit by unit, without evictions.
words.def: having a harmful effect, especially in a gradual or subtle way.

words.meaning_here: Restricted within limits; cities have long limited owners' property uses because of effects on neighbors.
Excessively eager to acquire money; the profit-hungry investor the reason pictures as the typical host.
Relatively small in amount; the limited extra income a resident earns from renting a room.

words.meaning_here: Smugly self-righteous; the reason's moral framing sounds preachy when aimed at ordinary resident hosts.

Venice shows the mechanism ("one fewer available by the year"); London's brick-or-stone rule shows regulation based on a use's effects on neighbors, not on greed; the San Francisco roommates show that hosts can be residents, which breaks the reason's residents-versus-investors split.

Transitions carry the logic, as in "Notice, though, what would justify a cap in Venice."

It then shows the reason objects only to "profit that displaces residents," and whether tourist rentals do that in a given city is a question of fact the reason cannot settle.

prompt.statement: Governments should require every new building to generate some of its own energy.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Mandate the Result, Not the Rooftop
essays.essay:
The appeal of this policy is easy to see. Buildings consume a large share of a city's energy, and a rule that makes each one partly self-sufficient promises cleaner power without waiting for utilities to change. Yet the policy quietly treats the place where energy is produced as if it were the goal itself. The real aim is to burn less fossil fuel at a cost people can bear, and on-site generation serves that aim brilliantly for some buildings and poorly for others. Tracing the likely consequences of the mandate leads me to support a narrower version of it: require self-generation where a building's roof, climate, and use make it cheap and substantial, and hold every other building to a strict energy-performance standard that it may meet in other ways.

Israel offers the most instructive test of such a rule. After the oil shocks of the 1970s, a country with almost no fuel of its own made solar water heaters mandatory on new homes. The intended consequences largely materialized. A rooftop collector and an insulated tank are simple, inexpensive devices, and under a Mediterranean sun they heat a family's water for most of the year without burning anything. Today the great majority of Israeli households heat their water this way, and the savings appear as electricity the national grid never has to produce. The burdens on owners were real but slight: the tanks clutter the skyline, and their periodic upkeep is [[irksome|irksome]], yet these are small costs set against years of nearly free hot water. By any reasonable measure, the mandate proved [[efficacious|efficacious]].

What deserves closer attention is why it worked, because the reasons cut against the word "every" in the statement. The Israeli law demanded one specific form of generation, matched to one specific need, in a climate that rewarded it. Its reach was also carefully [[circumscribed|circumscribe]]. Buildings above a set height were exempted, since a tall tower's roof has too little space for a collector serving every unit. In other words, the policy succeeded in part because it was not universal. The case exposes a subtler risk as well. A statute that names a technology fits the decade in which it is written; if heat pumps or cheaper photovoltaic panels come to outperform the rooftop tank, the same requirement could lock builders into yesterday's hardware. A wise mandate specifies the result it wants rather than the equipment.

The contrasting case is the dense, vertical city, where the casual assumption behind "every" collapses. Imagine the same rule applied to a new forty-story apartment tower in Hong Kong. Its roof is roughly the size of a single floor, while its demand comes from all forty, and neighboring towers shade much of its facade. Because the rule demands only that the tower generate "some" of its energy, a [[miserly|miserly]] share would satisfy it; the developer would install a token array that lights the lobby and changes almost nothing. The consequences would not stop at futility. Every dollar spent on such panels would be added to the price of apartments in one of the world's most expensive housing markets. That same money, spent on better insulation and efficient cooling, or invested in a large solar or wind farm elsewhere, would displace far more fossil fuel. Here the mandate yields a symbolic gain, a real cost, and a forgone opportunity.

Weighed together, these consequences shape my position without reversing it. Buildings stand for half a century or more, so a government cannot afford to [[dawdle|dawdle]]: every structure approved in the meantime will waste energy for decades. The answer is not to abandon the policy but to rebuild it around what made the Israeli law succeed. Low-rise buildings in sunny regions should have to generate a meaningful share of their energy, because for them the obligation is cheap and the payoff large. Towers, buildings on shaded lots, and buildings in cloudy climates should instead meet a demanding performance standard, through efficiency or by financing generation elsewhere. Producing power on the roof is a means; using less fossil fuel is the end, and a good law stays faithful to the end.

prompt.statement: Selective universities should admit some of their students by lottery from among all qualified applicants.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Lotteries Work Only Above a High Bar
essays.essay:
Admission to the most selective universities already involves a great deal of luck. When a university rejects nine of every ten applicants, most of whom could do the work, the outcome often turns on which reader opens a file or which essay strikes a chord. A lottery among qualified applicants would therefore not introduce chance into admissions so much as acknowledge it. I support the policy, but its consequences hinge on two variables that advocates rarely specify: how demanding the definition of "qualified" is, and how much it costs to enter the draw. Set those variables well, and a partial lottery would make admissions saner and more honest; set them badly, and it would make the process even more arbitrary.

The case for a lottery is strongest where competition at the top has outrun anyone's ability to measure differences between candidates. Imperial China offers an extreme illustration. For centuries the civil service examinations were the most prestigious path to office, and because success was rare, preparation consumed whole lives: candidates memorized the Confucian classics and drilled the rigid "eight-legged essay," and many took the examinations again and again into middle age. The system did produce literate officials, but at the margin it rewarded stamina and formal dexterity rather than judgment. South Korea's college entrance examination sustains a similar dynamic today: cram schools run late into the night, and takeoffs and landings are suspended during the test's listening section. Whenever a scarce good is allocated by ever finer distinctions, families pour resources into manufacturing those distinctions, and the richest tend to win. A lottery among applicants who clear a high bar would [[attenuate|attenuate]] the incentive to keep competing, and this consequence is my main reason for favoring it. Beyond that bar, extra test preparation helps only in the contest for seats still filled by judgment, not in the draw.

The second consequence concerns what admission means. Selective universities now defend their decisions in [[prolix|prolix]] statements about "holistic review" that explain everything except why one qualified applicant was chosen over another. Because many of these institutions also favor the children of alumni and donors, their rhetoric of merit can sound [[sanctimonious|sanctimonious]]. No one, by contrast, could [[impugn|impugn]] the legitimacy of a place won in a draw. Graduates who know that chance helped seat them may be slower to treat their success as a verdict on everyone turned away. Both benefits presuppose a high bar; a place drawn from a weak pool would invite doubts about whether its holder belongs.

Yet the same policy fails when the bar is low and a ticket is free. Beijing discovered this with a different scarce good. To curb congestion and air pollution, the city began distributing new license plates by lottery, and because any eligible resident with a driver's license and no car in his or her name could enter at no cost, many with no pressing need entered simply to keep the option open. The pool swelled, the odds became minuscule, and families who needed a vehicle waited for years until the city tilted the draw toward households without a car. In admissions, a loose definition of "qualified" would invite the same dynamic: applications would multiply, odds would collapse, and the university could no longer assemble a class with particular strengths. Nor would a pure draw correct inequality; if the qualified pool already overrepresents affluent students, chance will faithfully reproduce that skew. It would therefore be [[foolhardy|foolhardy]] to fill an entire class by lot or to set the threshold so low that admission becomes a sweepstakes.

My position, then, is conditional but firm. A selective university should fill a meaningful share of its seats by lottery when its standard for "qualified" is demanding enough that every applicant in the pool would thrive there, when entering the pool requires a complete and serious application, and when the remaining seats stay available for deliberate choices that no draw can make, such as admitting the rare prodigy or the student from a community the university has long neglected. Under those conditions, chance performs honestly a task that judgment now performs badly. Without them, a lottery merely exchanges one arbitrary process for another and calls the exchange fairness.

prompt.statement: People who hold power are remembered more for their failures than for their achievements.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Failure Is Memory's Default, Not Its Law
essays.essay:
In 756, as rebel armies closed in on Chang'an, the Tang emperor Xuanzong fled west. At Mawei, his own guards refused to go farther until his beloved consort, Yang Guifei, was put to death, and he gave way. That scene, retold in Bai Juyi's poetry and centuries of drama, is what most people know of Xuanzong. Historians still call his early reign the Kaiyuan golden age; in legend it is mainly the height from which he fell. Such cases make the statement seem self-evident, and I agree that failure is memory's default. It is not, however, memory's law. Failure prevails when a ruler's achievements have vanished and no one in power has a stake in remembering them; when an achievement remains in plain sight, or his heirs depend on it, the balance tips the other way.

Xuanzong's story shows why failure is the default. A collapse supplies a narrative, complete with villains, victims, and a moral; prosperity supplies only a condition. His fall had a full cast. There was An Lushan, the frontier general who had [[inveigled|inveigle]] his way into the emperor's confidence and then rebelled. There was the Yang clan, raised to high rank and showered with imperial [[largesse|largesse]]. And there was the emperor himself, who had taken his son's wife, a detail that let moralizing historians recast him as an aging [[libertine|libertine]]. His achievements offered no comparable drama: full granaries and safe roads rarely generate anecdotes. When the poet Du Fu celebrated them, he wrote after the rebellion, mourning a prosperity already lost. Even Xuanzong's son, enthroned while his father fled, had little reason to burnish the old man's reputation. With his prosperity long gone from view, a vivid catastrophe to his name, and no heir invested in his glory, Xuanzong fits the statement almost perfectly.

The statement fails, however, when those who inherit power need a predecessor's achievements. Mao Zedong presided over the Great Leap Forward famine, which killed tens of millions, and over the Cultural Revolution, during which Deng Xiaoping was twice purged. Yet Deng, even as he eased out Hua Guofeng, the successor Mao had [[anointed|anoint]], refused to repudiate Mao. The Communist Party's 1981 resolution judged Mao's contributions primary and his errors secondary, a verdict often summarized as seventy percent right and thirty percent wrong. Such bookkeeping might sound [[facetious|facetious]] when the debit column includes a famine, but it was meant in earnest: to discredit the founder would have been to discredit the Party that ruled in his name. Many historians outside China, who answer to no party, center his story on the famine and the Cultural Revolution; inside China, his portrait still hangs over Tiananmen Gate. The [[discrepancy|discrepancy]] arises not from the record but from who controls the remembering.

Visible achievements resist oblivion as well. In the 1960s Lee Kuan Yew launched Singapore's "Garden City" campaign, lining its roads with trees; in the late 1970s he gave his government ten years to clean the fetid Singapore River, and the deadline was met. Lee's record includes a genuine failure and a darker stain: his "Stop at Two" campaign helped push birth rates so low that Singapore has spent decades trying to raise them, and he detained opponents without trial. Yet both are recalled mainly by demographers and critics; residents pass through his successes daily. At his death, Singaporeans queued for hours to mourn him. Here both conditions operate: the achievement stands in plain sight, and the party he led, which still governs, has every reason to keep his name attached to the trees and the river.

Taken together, these cases set the limits of my agreement. The statement is right about which way memory drifts: failure makes the better story and, left unchecked, crowds out achievement. But it wrongly assumes that memory is a neutral ledger of deeds; in fact, memory is anchored by what the past leaves standing and edited by those who come after. Xuanzong had neither an anchor nor a friendly editor; Mao's memory rests chiefly on its editors, Lee's on both. How the powerful are remembered depends less on the balance of their deeds than on what survives them and on who inherits the telling.

prompt.statement: Public trust is harder to rebuild than to build in the first place.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Right About Mendacity, Wrong About Misfortune
essays.essay:
The statement assumes that an institution rebuilding public trust starts over, only with more to prove. In fact, its footing depends on what its fall taught the public. Trust is a forecast that an institution will behave well when no one is checking, and a first reputation usually rests on little more than the absence of reasons for doubt. If the fall supplies such a reason by exposing deliberate deception, rebuilding is indeed harder than building. If it reveals only bad luck, and the institution responds at real cost to itself, rebuilding can be easier, because the crisis furnishes evidence of character that a quiet reputation never provides. I agree with the statement, then, but only for the first kind of case.

Volkswagen's diesel scandal shows the statement at its most accurate. For years the company marketed its diesel cars to American buyers as clean and efficient, a campaign that proved [[duplicitous|duplicitous]] in the strictest sense. While professing concern for the environment, Volkswagen had equipped those cars with software that recognized emissions tests and ran the pollution controls at full strength only then; on the road, the cars emitted nitrogen oxides at many times the legal limit. Researchers at West Virginia University, testing the cars on ordinary roads, documented the discrepancy in 2014. For more than a year the company [[prevaricated|prevaricate]], blaming technical problems, and admitted the scheme only in 2015, when regulators threatened to withhold approval of its new models. The chief executive resigned, and the costs ran to tens of billions of dollars.

Yet the bill is not what makes the case instructive. When Volkswagen first won the confidence of buyers and regulators, it needed only to be presumed honest; no one had reason to test its claims on the open road. After the scandal, it could apologize to customers, plead with regulators for leniency, and pledge reform, but each act was a statement, and statements were precisely what the deception had devalued. Worse, the damage does not heal cleanly. The suspicion it leaves proves [[recrudescent|recrudescent]]: years later, even a routine recall can revive it, because the public now holds a ready explanation for every anomaly. Tellingly, Volkswagen's worldwide sales recovered quickly, but the presumption of honesty did not, even for its rivals: regulators stepped up on-road testing of other carmakers' diesels. What returned was not trust but verification, a costlier and more grudging substitute.

Johnson & Johnson's experience in 1982 shows where the statement fails. That autumn, seven people in the Chicago area died after taking Tylenol capsules that someone had laced with cyanide once the bottles were on store shelves. The company was a victim, yet confidence in its flagship painkiller collapsed almost overnight. Unlike Volkswagen, it had no need to [[supplicate|supplicate]] for forgiveness; its task was to act, and it did. Although the deaths were confined to one metropolitan area, it recalled Tylenol capsules nationwide, halted its advertising, and within months reintroduced the product in tamper-resistant packaging that soon became the industry norm. About a year later, the brand had regained most of its lost market share. The damage proved short-lived because the crisis showed consumers something years of marketing never could: how the company behaved when doing the right thing was expensive. The rebuilt trust rested on firmer ground than the original and took far less time to secure.

These two cases do not merely illustrate my position; they set its limits. Where the breach was deliberate, as at Volkswagen, an institution must rebuild against evidence it supplied itself, a far harder task than building on a clean slate. Where the institution was a victim, as Johnson & Johnson was, a costly response can produce sturdier trust than the presumption that came before. Even an institution at fault may recover quickly if its error was honest: a newspaper that promptly corrects a mistake is usually forgiven, while one shown to have printed a story its editors knew to be false rarely is, however quickly the retraction comes. The statement, in short, is right about [[mendacity|mendacity]] and wrong about misfortune; what makes trust hard to rebuild is not how badly it was broken but what its breaking revealed.

prompt.statement: Universities should award degrees for demonstrated skills rather than for time spent in courses.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Time as Proxy, Time as Route
essays.essay:
The proposal to award degrees for demonstrated skills rather than for time spent in courses has become [[modish|modish]] among education reformers, and it rests on a sound intuition: a diploma should certify what a graduate can do, not how long she sat in class. Yet it assumes that time and skill are rival measures of one quality, when time in fact does two different jobs. Sometimes it is a crude proxy for knowledge that an examination could verify directly, and then the recommendation is right. Sometimes it is the only practical route to a competence that no single demonstration can reveal, and then abandoning it would be a mistake.

The recommendation is most plainly advantageous for adults who arrive with skills in hand. A network technician with a decade of experience who enrolls in a conventional program may have to sit through courses on tasks she has performed for years, because the credit hour, descended from the Carnegie unit, was designed to count instructional time rather than learning, as the Carnegie Foundation itself has acknowledged. Western Governors University has built its model around the alternative: students advance by passing assessments whenever they are ready and pay a flat rate for each term, so the mastery they bring shortens the degree and lowers its cost. Critics of seat time pose a question that can sound [[facetious|facetious]] but deserves a serious answer: why should a student who could pass the final examination in the first week sit through the rest of the semester? For such students, the time requirement protects no standard; it simply [[confounds|confound]] attendance with learning and charges them for the confusion.

Where competence means reliability across many situations rather than success in one, the recommendation becomes a liability. Medicine, where an unearned credential endangers patients, is instructive. Since the 2010s, American residency programs have rated trainees against competency milestones, a deliberate move toward demonstrated skill, yet specialty boards still require a minimum period of accredited training before certification. The retention of time is not mere inertia. A simulation can confirm that a resident recognizes sepsis when it is [[florid|florid]], with fever, plunging blood pressure, and an obvious infection; a good one can even include an elderly patient whose only sign is new confusion. In practice, atypical presentations come in endless variety and arrive unpredictably, often at three in the morning, and a trainee meets enough of them only through time on the wards. Here time is not a lazy proxy for skill but the means of acquiring it, and the same holds for any degree that qualifies its holder to act in conditions no examiner can stage.

A subtler danger is that demonstrated skill quietly shrinks to whatever is easy to demonstrate. American schools offer a precedent: after the No Child Left Behind Act tied sanctions to reading and mathematics scores, many districts reported cutting time from science, social studies, and the arts, which did not count toward the law's yearly targets. Degrees awarded solely for assessed competencies would feel the same pull. Skills easy to specify in advance would crowd out those that resist a rubric, such as the knack for framing a question worth asking or the feel for a discipline that a student absorbs from a professor's [[digressions|digression]] rather than from the syllabus. Nor does speed benefit every student. A [[gawky|gawky]] eighteen-year-old who mumbles through his first class presentation may need four years of seminars and rewritten drafts more than an early diploma, yet a model that rewards testing out would push him toward the exit.

These examples lead me to narrow the recommendation, not reject it. The useful question is not whether to measure skill or time, but which job a program's hours are doing. When they merely stand in for knowledge a test can verify, as with the technician, they should go; when they provide exposure to unpredictable cases or room for growth that unfolds slowly, as on the hospital ward or in the first years of college, they should remain as a floor beneath demonstrated skill rather than yield to it. Universities should combine the two as each field requires and be candid about what each diploma certifies.

prompt.statement: Consumers should be willing to pay more for products made in environmentally responsible ways.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Pay for Proof, Not Promises
essays.essay:
American drivers once paid extra for Volkswagen's diesel cars, persuaded by advertising that "clean diesel" offered strong mileage with a clear conscience. In 2015, regulators revealed that the cars' software engaged full pollution controls only during emissions tests; on the road, they emitted nitrogen oxides far above legal limits. Even their strong mileage came partly from the cheat, since the engines ran with their controls turned down. What buyers could verify had been bought with a harm they could not see, and the environmental part of their premium purchased nothing but a story. The episode exposes the recommendation's hidden premise: that a higher price reliably buys a cleaner product. I agree that consumers should be willing to pay more, but only when the environmental benefit can be verified and the premium changes how goods are made, not merely how buyers feel. Even then, private willingness to pay should supplement public rules, not replace them.

The Volkswagen case is extreme, but its logic is general. When buyers cannot verify a claim, a willingness to pay more is less a reward for virtue than an invitation to counterfeit it. Few firms are as elaborately [[duplicitous|duplicitous]] as Volkswagen, whose cheating surfaced only when independent researchers tested the cars on real roads, a check no ordinary buyer could perform. Most green marketing misleads more quietly. Packaging is crowded with [[florid|florid]] language about harmony with nature, and labels such as "eco-friendly" often have no legal definition. Such words flatter the buyer's conscience, and a manufacturer that spends on them rather than on a cleaner factory can [[inveigle|inveigle]] well-meaning shoppers into paying for its advertising. Worse, an honest firm that bears the real cost of cleaner production can be undersold by a rival that merely claims it, so indiscriminate premiums reward the wrong companies.

Under other circumstances, paying more is shrewd. Early American buyers of Toyota's Prius hybrid paid a noticeable premium over comparable conventional compacts. Unlike Volkswagen's customers, who could track their mileage but never their nitrogen oxides, Prius owners could check the central claim themselves: burning gasoline releases carbon dioxide in proportion to the fuel consumed, so a longer-lasting tank meant a visible reduction. Some buyers chose the car mainly because it had become [[modish|modish]] among Hollywood celebrities, but their motives hardly mattered, since the benefit never depended on anyone's sincerity. Their premiums also changed how cars are built, helping turn the hybrid from a curiosity into a standard option across much of the industry. Yet the Prius was an easy case, since every gallon saved was money the owner kept; conscience and self-interest pointed the same way.

When the two diverge, even honest premiums hit a ceiling: environmental harms are shared, but the cost falls only on those who choose to pay. The ozone layer began to recover not because shoppers paid extra for virtuous hair spray but because the 1987 Montreal Protocol and its amendments phased out chlorofluorocarbons nearly worldwide. Volunteers alone could not have done this: a family that bought a costlier ozone-safe refrigerator would have gained no more protection than its neighbors. Enforcement was imperfect, as smuggling showed, but because the rule bound every producer, no company could lawfully profit from polluting. A voluntary premium works the opposite way: it taxes the conscientious and the affluent, exempts everyone else, and lets a firm sell a clean line to wealthy buyers and a dirty one to the rest.

Taken together, these cases turn my agreement from a principle into a set of conditions. Volkswagen shows that a premium for an unverifiable claim rewards [[mendacity|mendacity]]; the Prius, that one paid for a measurable change can reshape an industry, especially when it also repays the buyer; the ozone treaty, that a benefit belonging to everyone is best secured when no one may opt out. These lessons yield a rule: consumers should be willing to pay more when they can confirm what the extra money buys and when early demand can make a cleaner technology commercially [[viable|viable]] and cheap enough to become the norm. Otherwise, they should press for standards that make the clean choice and the cheap choice the same.

prompt.statement: Most people who achieve great success owe more to luck than to talent.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Talent Qualifies, Luck Selects
essays.essay:
Successful people tend to tell their stories as tales of talent rewarded, mentioning a [[providential|providential]] break only in passing; skeptics tell the same stories in reverse. Both assume that luck and talent are independent ingredients, so that crediting one means discrediting the other. They are not. If luck means whatever shapes an outcome without being chosen or earned by its beneficiary, then luck does more than supplement talent: it often produces the talent later admired, and it nearly always sets the size of the reward. I therefore largely agree with the statement. Talent is necessary for great success, but at the highest levels it is common, while the opportunities that turn it into greatness are scarce, and what is scarce decides who wins.

The least visible luck disguises itself as ability. Youth hockey and soccer leagues group children by a fixed cutoff date, so a child born just after it may be nearly a year older than a teammate born just before the next one. At nine, that year is enormous. Coaches picking select teams see one child who is strong and well coordinated and another who is slighter and still [[gawky|gawky]], and understandably [[confound|confound]] maturity with promise. The chosen children receive better coaching, more practice, and stiffer competition, so by adolescence their advantage has become genuine skill. Study after study finds players born just after the cutoff overrepresented on elite youth teams and in professional leagues. Wherever early selection steers resources toward the apparently gifted, an accident of timing can harden into real ability, and the adult who succeeds will sincerely credit talent alone.

Luck also sets how far talent can carry its owner, as South Korea's industrialization shows. After Park Chung-hee took power in 1961, his government nationalized the banks and directed cheap credit toward the heavy and export industries it wanted built; officials, not markets, decided who received it. In effect, the state [[anointed|anoint]] a handful of family-owned firms as national champions. Hyundai, a construction company that had never built a ship, became a giant of shipbuilding with state support. Its founder, Chung Ju-yung, was unquestionably able, but so were many entrepreneurs who never enjoyed such backing. Talent was not idle, since firms that missed export targets risked losing the government's favor. Still, what separated a prosperous local company from a global conglomerate was largely the state's choice, which turned on politics, timing, and connections no founder fully controlled.

The most compelling challenge to the statement is that luck does not repeat, whereas talent does. One lucky bet proves little; decades of success do not look like chance. Warren Buffett sharpened this argument in a celebrated talk at Columbia University. He granted that if hundreds of millions of people flipped coins, roughly two hundred would win twenty times in a row; but if a striking share of those winners came from one school of thought, chance would be a poor explanation. The investors he profiled shared one intellectual ancestor, Benjamin Graham. The argument is sound: talent is real and, given enough evidence, detectable. Yet notice what it concedes. In a large field, spectacular streaks are all but guaranteed, so great success alone is weak evidence of skill. Buffett himself, in a phrase that sounds [[facetious|facetious]] but is not, says he won the "ovarian lottery" by being born in the United States, where his gift for allocating capital happened to command enormous rewards. His talent explains why he outperformed other investors; it does not explain why outperformance made him one of the richest people alive.

Great success, then, requires talent, but it comes to only a few of the many who have it. Talent earns a place in the crowd of plausible contenders; luck, whether a birth date, a government's favor, or the economy one is born into, decides who is lifted out of it. Because contenders have talent in abundance and luck in short supply, most great success does owe more to luck than to talent, though never to luck alone. That conclusion should [[discomfit|discomfit]] the successful, but it calls for humility, not cynicism about effort, and for attention to the talented whom luck passed over.

prompt.statement: Fame is more often a burden than a reward.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Recognition Rewards; Exposure Burdens
essays.essay:
The word "fame" covers two experiences that the statement treats as one. The first is recognition: being esteemed for one's work by people competent to judge it. The second is exposure: being watched, as a person, by strangers who neither know nor care what the work was. Recognition is almost always a reward; exposure, almost always a burden. I therefore agree with the statement, but not for the reason it implies. Fame is not inherently heavy; technology has made exposure cheap and left recognition as costly as ever, so most fame today is the burdensome kind.

Marie Curie lived through both in a single year. In 1911 she won her second Nobel Prize, awarded by scientists who understood what her work on radium had accomplished. That same year, newspapers exposed her relationship with the married physicist Paul Langevin, printed her private letters, and recast a widowed scientist as a foreign [[libertine|libertine]] who had wrecked a French household. A crowd gathered outside her home, and a Nobel committee member urged her to stay away from the ceremony. She went to Stockholm anyway, replying that the prize honored her discoveries, not her private life. Her reply states the distinction exactly. The prize was recognition, a verdict on her work; the scandal was exposure, a public hunger for her person that her achievements had made worth feeding.

The pre-YouTube internet showed what exposure looks like when no recognition precedes it. Classmates of a [[gawky|gawky]] Canadian teenager found a video he had recorded of himself swinging a golf-ball retriever like a lightsaber and posted it online without his consent. Millions watched. Strangers produced remixes and mocking commentary, forgetting that the subject was a real child. Each commenter may have meant only to be [[facetious|facetious]], but the jokes added up to harassment so severe that he left school. He became one of the most recognizable faces online, yet no one recognized him for anything. What happened to him by accident now happens by design: platforms [[anoint|anoint]] new celebrities by algorithm, favoring whatever provokes a reaction, and embarrassment provokes reliably. Recognition still requires years of work and a qualified judge; exposure can arrive in an afternoon with neither. That asymmetry is why the statement holds more often than not.

The strongest objection is that this account notices fame's costs because they are vivid and overlooks its rewards because they are diffuse. Fame, an opponent would argue, is a currency: achievement earns it, and it buys money, access, and influence. Curie herself spent it. In 1921, American women, rallied by a magazine editor, bought her a gram of radium, which President Harding formally presented at the White House; her celebrity, not her scientific standing alone, paid for further research. The opponent would add that the famous rarely renounce fame, and people who keep what they could discard presumably value it. This objection should [[discomfit|discomfit]] anyone who treats fame as a simple curse.

Neither half survives the distinction. The radium went to a woman whom scientists had twice judged worthy of a Nobel Prize, first for research on radiation and then for discovering radium itself; the public was ratifying their verdict, which makes the gift recognition, and therefore a reward. The donors were honoring her laboratory, not her letters. The second half fails because exposure, unlike wealth, cannot be handed back. A millionaire can give away a fortune, but no one can choose to become unknown. Greta Garbo left films in her [[prime|prime]] and spent nearly fifty years refusing interviews, yet photographers trailed her through Manhattan until her death. She could [[jettison|jettison]] her career; she could not jettison her face. That the famous keep their fame proves only that it is irrevocable, not that it is welcome.

Fame, then, is a reward when it is the residue of work that competent people have judged, and a burden when it is attention cut loose from any such judgment. The statement is right about frequency, but the reason lies in our tools rather than in fame itself: we now manufacture the second kind far faster than the first. The question worth asking about anyone's fame is not how far it reaches but what, exactly, it recognizes.

prompt.statement: Some argue that the most important scientific work is now done by large teams. Others argue that the decisive ideas still come from individuals working alone.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Teams Make Solitary Insights Decisive
essays.essay:
The two views in this debate seem opposed only because they answer different questions. The claim for individuals concerns where ideas begin; the claim for large teams concerns where ideas become knowledge. Once they are separated, I find the team view closer to my own position, though only in amended form. Most of the important work in science is now done by large teams, and even the decisive ideas that still arise in single minds rarely arise in minds that work entirely alone. The teams that matter most, however, are those built to give such minds room.

The case for the lone thinker deserves a serious hearing, because conceptual leaps rarely come from committees. In 1964 Peter Higgs [[distilled|distill]] into a paper of barely two pages a mechanism by which certain elementary particles could acquire mass, and the other theorists who reached similar conclusions that year worked in groups of two or three. No consortium voted that idea into existence. Yet the paper was only a beginning. Others soon built the mechanism into what became the Standard Model, and later experiments supported it indirectly, but the particle it required eluded detection for nearly half a century. Only in 2012 did two collaborations at CERN, each with thousands of members, find it, using a machine that no individual could have designed, funded, or operated. The individual view is right about where the idea came from but wrong about what made it decisive. An idea becomes decisive through confirmation, and confirmation in modern science is a collective enterprise.

A case that seems at first to support the opposite view actually strengthens the team view. During the Vietnam War, China launched a secret program, Project 523, to combat the drug-resistant malaria that was sickening soldiers in Southeast Asia. Hundreds of researchers at dozens of institutions screened synthetic compounds and traditional remedies. Tu Youyou, who led one group, found that extracts of sweet wormwood produced promising but inconsistent results. Returning to a fourth-century medical handbook by Ge Hong, she noticed a recipe that called for steeping the herb in water instead of boiling it, and reasoned that heat was destroying the active ingredient. A low-temperature extraction proved strikingly effective in animal tests. Her encounter with that ancient text can look [[providential|providential]], but it resolved a puzzle that only large-scale, systematic screening could have produced. Tu and her colleagues went on to test the extract on themselves and on patients and to isolate the pure compound; other groups determined its structure. The Nobel Prize she shared in 2015 reopened a debate in China over whether one name should stand for a collective achievement. Her insight was genuinely hers, but it was not achieved alone.

Still, the individual view carries a warning that the team view must heed: an organization can smother the very minds it depends on. Bell Labs had a [[munificent|munificent]] patron in AT&T, whose telephone monopoly funded long-term research, and there John Bardeen and Walter Brattain built the first transistor in 1947 in a group led by William Shockley. Shockley, stung at being left out of the breakthrough, worked largely alone and within weeks conceived the junction transistor, a more practical design that displaced the original. The laboratory absorbed even this jealous, solitary effort: colleagues there helped turn his design into working devices. The company Shockley later founded in California fared differently. He recruited brilliant young scientists but wanted [[acolytes|acolyte]] rather than colleagues, and in 1957 eight of them left to found Fairchild Semiconductor, the company from which Intel and much of Silicon Valley's chip industry descended. The variable that matters is not head count but tolerance for dissent. A team that waves off every odd hunch as a [[digression|digression]] will execute its plans and discover little.

I therefore side with those who credit large teams, though not for the usual reason of sheer scale. Teams matter because they supply what the solitary thinker cannot: a puzzle worth solving, instruments to test a solution, and colleagues who can turn a private hunch into public knowledge. The most important science today comes from teams wise enough to leave one of their members alone at the right moment.

so luckily timed that it seems to have been arranged by fate
lavishly generous with money, describing AT&T as the funder of Bell Labs' research
devoted, unquestioning followers who would never challenge their leader

Every example is explained far enough to show why it matters, the position is qualified and earned, and the prose is precise, varied, and controlled.

Each case ends with its lesson stated outright, for example "it was not achieved alone."

Transitions carry the logic, such as "A case that seems at first to support the opposite view" and "Still, the individual view carries a warning."

Diction is exact rather than ornate ("smother the very minds it depends on"), and the five target words sit in standard collocations such as "a munificent patron."

It would treat the views as simple opposites instead of separating conception from confirmation, and it would likely end with "both matter." A 6 names the condition, here tolerance for dissent, that decides when teams succeed.

prompt.statement: Some believe that a good education makes students comfortable with uncertainty. Others believe that a good education gives students firm answers they can rely on.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Firm Methods, Provisional Conclusions
essays.essay:
Before the 2016 presidential election, most prominent forecasting models made Hillary Clinton an overwhelming favorite, and FiveThirtyEight, which gave Donald Trump roughly a three-in-ten chance, was criticized by some commentators for inflating his prospects. When Trump won, many concluded that the forecasters had failed. But an outcome assigned a thirty percent probability is no fluke; it occurs about as often as a .300 hitter gets a hit. The failure lay less in the most careful model than in an audience taught to hear every forecast as a promise. That episode draws me toward the view that a good education should make students comfortable with uncertainty, although I would revise it in two ways: the proper goal is not comfort but competence, and that competence depends on the firm answers the opposing view rightly prizes.

The case for firm answers deserves more respect than it usually receives. Much of what students learn is settled, and treating it as open is not sophistication but negligence: no one wants a pharmacist who is comfortable with uncertainty about a lethal dose, or an accountant who regards compound interest as a matter of opinion. Firm answers also free the mind for harder work. Alfred North Whitehead observed that civilization advances by extending the number of important operations we can perform without thinking about them, and a good teacher's achievement is to [[distill|distill]] centuries of argument into rules students can apply without relitigating them. By contrast, the [[modish|modish]] classroom slogan that there are no wrong answers looks less like humility than abdication. A student who treats every claim as equally open has not made peace with uncertainty; that student has simply stopped distinguishing the probable from the absurd.

Yet the firm-answer view rests on an assumption it rarely states: that answers stay firm, and that the world will pose its problems in the form the textbook anticipated. The 1998 collapse of Long-Term Capital Management shows what happens when it fails. The hedge fund counted two Nobel laureates in economics among its partners, and its strategy relied on models that treated historical relationships among bond prices as stable enough to justify enormous borrowing. In the [[ebullient|ebullient]] markets of the mid-1990s, the fund earned spectacular returns that seemed to vindicate those models. Then Russia defaulted on its debt, investors fled to the safest assets, and relationships the models had deemed reliable broke down at once. By late September the fund had lost most of its capital, and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York brokered a rescue by a consortium of banks. The partners lacked not knowledge but the disposition to be [[discomfited|discomfit]] by their own precision: to ask whether the world still resembled the past on which their models were built.

What reconciles the two views is a distinction between firmness of method and firmness of conclusion. Well-educated people should hold certain tools, such as the arithmetic of probability and the rules of evidence, with complete confidence, precisely so that they can hold their conclusions provisionally. Journalism shows the cost of reversing these priorities. News stories often relegate a poll's margin of error or a study's limitations to the final paragraphs, as though uncertainty were a [[digression|digression]] from the story rather than part of it. Readers raised on that convention learn to take the headline as the answer, which is how a thirty percent chance came to be heard as no chance at all. Indeed, the forecaster criticized for inflating Trump's chances had applied a firm method more rigorously than most rivals, allowing that polling errors in similar states might move together, as they did.

The view that education should make students comfortable with uncertainty thus comes closer to my own, but only once its central word is replaced. Comfort is the wrong aim; a person entirely at ease with not knowing has little reason to find out. A good education should instead produce graduates who hold methods firmly and conclusions loosely, who can say how confident they are and why, and who will [[jettison|jettison]] even a cherished answer when the evidence turns against it. Such graduates need firm answers, but as instruments of inquiry, not substitutes for it.

made uneasy; the partners were never unsettled by how precise their models seemed

to discard an answer once the evidence no longer supports it

analysis.verdict: This response earns a 6 because its position goes beyond clear to insightful. It accepts the uncertainty view but replaces "comfort" with "competence" and shows that competence depends on firm answers. Every example, from the 2016 forecasts to Long-Term Capital Management, is told far enough that its relevance is explicit, and the prose is precise, varied, and economical.

analysis.language: Diction is precise and compressed ("looks less like humility than abdication"), and sentence length ranges from the eight-word "Journalism shows the cost of reversing these priorities" to long, balanced sentences. Target words sit in standard collocations such as "ebullient markets" and "discomfited by."
analysis.task: The instruction asks for both views and a choice between them. Paragraph 2 gives firm answers their strongest case ("deserves more respect than it usually receives"), paragraph 3 argues for uncertainty, paragraph 4 reconciles the two views, and paragraph 5 says which view "comes closer to my own."

prompt.statement:
Claim: People should distrust any expert who never expresses uncertainty.
Reason: Genuine expertise includes knowing the limits of one's knowledge.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Trust Calibrated Confidence, Not Performed Doubt
essays.essay:
The reason offered here is nearly beyond dispute: an expert who cannot tell where her knowledge ends is hardly an expert at all. The claim, however, does not follow from it as neatly as it appears, because the reason concerns what experts know while the claim concerns what they say, and the two can come apart. A specialist may know full well where her field's limits lie and see no reason to mention them on a settled question; hired advocates may advertise uncertainty precisely because the evidence is against their employers. I therefore accept the claim only conditionally: when an expert addresses a genuinely open question and still speaks without qualification, distrust is warranted, though not always for the reason the statement gives.

Forecasting is the clearest case. Over roughly two decades, the psychologist Philip Tetlock collected predictions from political and economic experts and found that self-critical thinkers who qualified their judgments outperformed confident ones who forced every event into a single theory; the experts most in demand by the media, moreover, tended to be among the most overconfident. The pattern makes sense. Uncertainty is [[intrinsic|intrinsic]] to elections, markets, and wars, and an expert who never acknowledges it has misunderstood the problem. Media incentives then amplify the error: television bookers prefer the [[ebullient|ebullient]] guest who promises a landslide to the subdued one who calls the race a coin flip, and confident forecasters soon acquire [[acolytes|acolyte]] who repeat their predictions without checking their records. Here the reason does genuine work: these pundits lacked exactly the sense of their own limits that expertise requires.

Sometimes, though, the claim is right for a different reason. Before the 2008 financial crisis, the major credit rating agencies gave their highest grade to a vast number of securities built from subprime mortgages, and a AAA rating carries no error bars. Investors who distrusted those ratings were vindicated when the securities were downgraded en masse. Yet the analysts were not simply blind to the limits of their models; internal messages later made public showed that some of them privately doubted the ratings they were issuing. The agencies were paid by the very banks whose products they graded, and that arrangement, more than ignorance, produced the [[discrepancy|discrepancy]] between private doubt and public confidence. Distrust was justified, but the statement's reason, which locates the problem in what experts fail to know, misdiagnoses it.

The claim fails outright when the question is settled. A climate scientist who will not hedge on whether human activity is warming the planet may [[discomfit|discomfit]] a reporter trained to present both sides, but her refusal reflects the evidence, not arrogance. For years after the scientific consensus had formed, the journalistic norm of balance led American newspapers to treat the matter as an open dispute, so it was the reporter's instinct, not the scientist's confidence, that deserved suspicion. Properly understood, the reason cuts against the claim here, since knowing the limits of one's knowledge includes knowing where those limits do not reach.

A subtler problem comes from the opposite direction. The statement assumes that expressed doubt reflects honest self-knowledge, but doubt can be a tactic. For decades, scientists funded by the tobacco industry [[prevaricated|prevaricate]] about the evidence that smoking causes lung cancer, insisting that the link was unproven, that other causes had not been excluded, and that more research was needed; one company's internal memo described doubt itself as its product. In that campaign, uncertainty was not the mark of honesty but the instrument of [[mendacity|mendacity]].

What the statement is reaching for is a test of calibration, and expressed uncertainty is only a crude proxy for it. The expert worth trusting is not the one who hedges most but the one whose confidence tracks the evidence: firm about what is established, tentative about what is open, and able to say which is which. Unvarying certainty about unsettled questions should make us suspicious; so should unvarying doubt about settled ones. A listener who wants a practical test could do worse than to ask an expert what evidence would change her mind, and to notice whether she has an answer.

words.meaning_here: inherent; uncertainty is a built-in feature of elections, markets, and wars.
words.def: belonging naturally; essential.

devoted, uncritical followers who repeat a pundit's predictions without checking them.
a mismatch between analysts' private doubts and the confident ratings they published.
words.def: an illogical or surprising lack of compatibility or similarity between two or more facts.

words.meaning_here: make a reporter uneasy or flustered by refusing to supply a second side.
spoke evasively to dodge the truth that smoking causes lung cancer.
deliberate, persistent lying; here, the tobacco industry's long campaign of deception.

analysis.verdict: This response earns a 6 because its position is insightful, not merely clear. It separates what experts know from what they say, then arrives at a calibration standard that the prompt never mentions. Every example is developed until its relevance is explicit, and the prose is precise, varied and error-free.
analysis.position: The writer accepts the reason but limits the claim to one condition: an expert who meets an open question and "still speaks without qualification." The closing paragraph sharpens this into calibration: "firm about what is established, tentative about what is open."

Two paragraphs show where the claim holds (for the stated reason, then for a different one), one shows where it fails outright (settled questions), one shows that expressed doubt can mislead in the opposite direction (strategic doubt), and a synthesis closes. Turning sentences such as "Sometimes, though, the claim is right for a different reason." signal each shift.

analysis.task: The instruction asks for separate verdicts on the claim and the reason, and the essay delivers them visibly. In paragraph 2 "the reason does genuine work," in paragraph 3 it "misdiagnoses it," and in paragraph 4 "the reason cuts against the claim here."

paragraphs.note: Shows that refusing to hedge on climate science reflects the evidence, identifies journalistic false balance as the real problem, and turns the reason itself against the claim.

paragraphs.role: Exposes hidden assumption: doubt equals honesty
paragraphs.note: The tobacco industry's manufactured doubt shows that expressed uncertainty can be a tactic of deception. This does not refute the claim; it reveals that doubt, too, is an unreliable signal of honesty.

paragraphs.role: Refines position into a calibration test
paragraphs.note: Replaces the prompt's crude signal with calibration: confidence should match the evidence. Compresses the earlier conditions into one balanced sentence and ends with a practical question readers can apply.

moves.frame: The ... concerns what ..., while the ... concerns what ..., and the two can come apart.
moves.example: because the reason concerns what experts know while the claim concerns what they say, and the two can come apart
moves.use: When a prompt's reason and claim address different things; name the gap early and organize around it.

moves.frame: ... was justified, but the statement's reason, which locates the problem in ..., misdiagnoses it.
moves.example: Distrust was justified, but the statement's reason, which locates the problem in what experts fail to know, misdiagnoses it.
moves.use: When an example supports the claim but for a cause other than the stated reason.

moves.frame: Properly understood, the reason cuts against the claim here, since ... includes ...
moves.example: Properly understood, the reason cuts against the claim here, since knowing the limits of one's knowledge includes knowing where those limits do not reach.
moves.use: When the reason, read carefully, implies the opposite of the claim in some cases.

analysis.contrast: A typical 4 would judge the claim and the reason together, treat any admission of uncertainty as proof of honesty, and name examples such as a famous scientist or a collapsed company with little explanation. A typical 5 would address both and explain its examples soundly, but would miss the gap between knowing and saying, the incentive explanation, and the possibility that expressed doubt is itself a deceptive tactic.

prompt.statement:
Claim: A society's most important rules are the ones it never needs to enforce.
Reason: The strongest rules are those people follow out of conviction rather than fear.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Conviction Carries Rules, Enforcement Guards Them
essays.essay:
An [[acolyte|acolyte]] of Confucius would accept the claim and its reason as a single truth. Confucius taught that people ruled by punishments merely evade them, while people guided by virtue and ritual learn shame and correct themselves. The reason restates this teaching, which I largely accept: rules held by conviction outlast rules held by fear. The claim, however, does not follow. The reason concerns a rule's strength, how reliably it is obeyed; the claim concerns its importance, how much depends on its being obeyed. The claim also treats conviction and enforcement as rivals; China's early empires suggest that they are partners and that the most important rules are those a society rarely enforces but must always be ready to enforce.

The Qin supplies the reason's best evidence. Under Shang Yang's Legalist reforms, Qin rulers governed through rewards, harsh punishments, and collective liability that made neighbors answerable for one another's crimes. This machinery of [[coercion|coercion]] mobilized soldiers and grain efficiently, and in 221 BCE the Qin unified China. Fifteen years later, the dynasty was gone. According to the historian Sima Qian, the first great revolt began when rain-delayed conscripts, convinced that lateness meant execution, judged rebellion no more dangerous than obedience. Excavated Qin statutes merely fine latecomers to labor service; if that rule bound garrison conscripts, which historians dispute, the penalty was overstated. Either way, fear governs through belief, not statute. Rule by fear holds only while obeying seems safer than defying; once the conscripts concluded otherwise, the fear that had secured compliance drove them to revolt. Nor had fear won any allegiance: within months, rebels proclaimed kings of Chu, Zhao, and other conquered states, drawing on [[recrudescent|recrudescent]] loyalties that force had silenced, not dissolved.

At first glance, the Han seems to vindicate the claim. Yet it did not [[jettison|jettison]] Qin law; its statesmen denounced Qin cruelty but kept much of the code. What the dynasty added, slowly, was a creed: by the Eastern Han, Confucian learning had become the basis of official training. Han rule, later described as Confucian on the surface and Legalist underneath, lasted about four centuries, with one brief interruption. Han emperors claimed the Mandate of Heaven, but their order's endurance was not [[providential|providential]]; it was built from law and creed. Conviction carried the daily burden of order, while law stood behind it for those conviction never reached. Even filial piety, which Confucians treated as the root of virtue, remained enforceable: under Han law, an unfilial son could be punished, not merely shamed. The Han thus supports the reason, because its cultivated loyalties outlasted Qin fear, but it undermines the claim: what the Han rarely had to compel, it could always compel.

If the Qin shows what fear without conviction produces, a modern case shows what conviction without vigilant enforcement permits. In 2008, Chinese parents learned that infant formula from trusted brands, notably Sanlu, contained melamine. Dealers had watered down raw milk and added this nitrogen-rich chemical to fool protein tests that measured only nitrogen. Hundreds of thousands of infants fell ill, and several died. Few rules command more conviction than the rule against poisoning children, and most dairy farmers presumably never considered breaking it. That is precisely the problem. Conviction is a majority phenomenon, but catastrophe can be the work of a [[duplicitous|duplicitous]] few. The graver the harm a violation causes, the less a society can rest on conviction alone.

[[Distilled|distill]] to one principle, the lesson is that conviction and enforcement do different work. Conviction makes a rule cheap to maintain and slow to erode, as the Han discovered and the Qin did not; enforcement guards the margin, where a few people untouched by conviction, like the melamine dealers, can inflict disproportionate harm. The reason is therefore right about which rules endure, but the claim mistakes endurance for importance. If self-sustaining rules deserve special honor, it is for a different reason: they free a society's limited capacity for coercion to concentrate on the few who will not comply. The most important rules are those whose violation a society can least afford; a wise society cultivates enough conviction that it seldom has to enforce them, but never mistakes that rarity for an absence of need.
