analysis.verdict: This response earns a 6 because its position is insightful rather than merely clear: it accepts the reason, rejects the claim, and shows why by separating a rule's strength from its importance. One historical example is developed in depth across two paragraphs and then tested against a contrasting case, and each example's relevance is explained, not just named. The language is precise and varied, with superior control of conventions.
analysis.position: The writer splits the prompt early: "rules held by conviction outlast rules held by fear" is accepted, but "The claim, however, does not follow." The final paragraph restates the position in new terms: a wise society "never mistakes that rarity for an absence of need."
analysis.development: Each example comes with its mechanism: the Qin conscripts show that "Rule by fear holds only while obeying seems safer than defying," and the writer turns a disputed source into a further point, "fear governs through belief, not statute." The revived kingdoms show fear left "loyalties that force had silenced, not dissolved," and the melamine case explains how dealers beat "protein tests that measured only nitrogen" and why "a duplicitous few" can defeat widespread conviction.
analysis.organization: The intro sets up two distinctions. The extended example runs across two paragraphs (Qin, then Han): the Qin paragraph opens with its verdict on the reason, and the Han paragraph closes with a verdict on both the reason and the claim. The contrasting case opens with a bridge that names its opposite angle, and the conclusion pulls all three cases into one principle, "as the Han discovered and the Qin did not."
analysis.language: Sentence variety is deliberate: a five-word punch ("That is precisely the problem."), paired semicolon clauses, and a balanced antithesis that ends both halves on the same verb, "what the Han rarely had to compel, it could always compel." Target words carry argumentative weight without glosses: "recrudescent" describes loyalties that broke out again once fear faltered, and "duplicitous" fits dealers who sold doctored milk as genuine.
analysis.task: The claim and the reason are judged separately and visibly: "The Han thus supports the reason" while "it undermines the claim." The conclusion even saves part of the claim "for a different reason," exactly what the instruction asks for.

prompt.statement: Governments should cap the prices of essential medicines.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Cap the Monopoly, Not the Discovery
essays.essay:
Every price paid for a medicine can buy two things: the pill in the patient's hand and the discovery that made it possible. The statement conflates them. Most medicines on the World Health Organization's essential medicines list are decades old and off patent, so when one becomes unaffordable, its price rewards not invention but a lapse in competition. For a patented medicine, by contrast, the price finances discovery. Because the consequences of capping each kind of price differ, so does my position: governments should cap the prices of old essential medicines, though never so low that manufacturers stop making them, but should cap patented ones only in markets that pay little toward research.

Capping old medicines is easiest to defend because its intended consequence comes almost free. In 2015, a company acquired Daraprim, a 1950s-era treatment for a parasitic infection that can kill people with AIDS, and raised its price more than fiftyfold overnight. Nothing [[intrinsic|intrinsic]] to the medicine had changed. The firm kept generic rivals out by restricting distribution so that they could not obtain samples for testing. A federal court later banned the scheme's architect from the industry, but only years after patients had paid. Such firms tout assistance programs, yet a patient who must beg for a drug that costs little to make has not been granted access. She has received [[largesse|largesse]], which the giver may withdraw at will. A cap would have prevented the harm at once while destroying nothing but the profits of an unearned monopoly.

Set carelessly, however, a cap produces an unintended consequence that makes my support conditional: pushed toward the cost of production, it removes not only exploitation but the reason to manufacture at all. Recurring shortages of cheap generic injectables in American hospitals, including basic chemotherapy drugs, show the pattern: when margins are thin, few firms make a drug, spare capacity vanishes, and one factory's failure can empty shelves nationwide. In The Doctor's Dilemma, George Bernard Shaw [[distills|distill]] the moral cost of scarcity into a single choice: a physician whose tuberculosis treatment can reach only a few patients must decide between an honest, impoverished colleague and a gifted but unscrupulous artist. Scarcity does not abolish the question of who gets treated; it merely moves the answer from the price tag to a doctor's judgment, a waiting list, or luck. A cap must therefore be a ceiling against exploitation, never a price so low that it hands every oncologist Shaw's dilemma.

For patented medicines, the chief consequence of a cap is deferred and invisible: drugs never developed because investors no longer expect a success to repay the failures behind it. No one marches for a cure that was never invented, which makes such caps politically tempting. The industry dresses this warning in [[florid|florid]] language, but the warning itself is sound. Its broader claim, that every high price finances discovery, is [[dubious|dubious]]. In 2001, amid global outrage, dozens of drug companies abandoned a lawsuit against a South African law permitting cheaper imports of patented medicines. Generic competition later slashed the cost of antiretroviral therapy, helping bring treatment to millions of Africans. Yet new HIV drugs kept arriving, financed overwhelmingly by revenue from wealthy markets. What endangers innovation is not a cap as such but a cap imposed where research is paid for. There, governments should bargain as large buyers instead, paying little for a trivial reformulation but rewarding a genuine breakthrough with a sum [[munificent|munificent]] enough to cover the failures behind it. No fixed ceiling can draw that distinction.

Champions and critics of the policy should both be [[discomfited|discomfit]]: it is right for some prices and wrong for others, and its consequences reveal which. A cap is the proper remedy where a price is mere rent: on old medicines whose makers face no competition, and in poor markets that were never going to fund research. It defeats itself where it squeezes margins until manufacturers leave or falls on the revenue that pays for the next cure. A government that keeps both risks in view can make essential medicines affordable without discovering, too late, that a medicine no one will make is unaffordable at any price.

prompt.statement: Public officials should be required to publish their personal financial holdings every year.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Disclosure Diagnoses but Does Not Cure
essays.essay:
Requiring public officials to publish their financial holdings every year rests on an attractive premise: that conflicts of interest wither once they are exposed. I support the requirement, but in a form both narrower and stronger than the statement suggests. The statement treats "public officials" as one category and assumes that an annual list of holdings is what keeps them honest. Yet the consequences of disclosure depend on two variables the statement ignores: how quickly the information appears and how much power the filer holds. A rule blind to both will be too weak for senators and too intrusive for career administrators.

Consider the United States Senate in early 2020. After lawmakers were briefed on the novel coronavirus, several senators, or their spouses, sold substantial amounts of stock shortly before the market collapsed. Richard Burr, then chairman of the Intelligence Committee, had publicly expressed confidence in the nation's preparedness, yet in a single day in February he sold dozens of stock holdings. Kelly Loeffler, newly appointed to the Senate, reported sales that began on the day of a closed briefing on the virus. Both denied acting on nonpublic information. No subpoena exposed these trades; reporters simply read the transaction reports that the STOCK Act of 2012 requires members of Congress to file within weeks of a trade.

What followed shows the reach and the limits of disclosure. The Justice Department closed its inquiries without bringing charges, but the filings had already [[discomfited|discomfit]] both senators. A published form cannot reveal an official's motive; it records only what the filer says was sold, and when. Whatever Burr's reasons, public reassurance paired with private selling looked [[duplicitous|duplicitous]], and voters could weigh it without waiting for a prosecutor. Burr stepped aside as committee chairman after federal agents seized his phone, Loeffler and her husband pledged to exit individual stocks, and the episode revived proposals to ban congressional stock trading. Disclosure worked as a diagnostic test, not a treatment: it identified the problem, and the remedies came from elsewhere. These trades surfaced only through the senators' own reports, so publication is a poor defense against outright [[mendacity|mendacity]]; a filer willing to lie can simply omit an account. Its strength is exposing conduct that may be lawful and still troubling. Timing mattered as well: reports filed within weeks reached voters while the sales were still news, whereas an annual inventory would have surfaced them months later.

The case for publication weakens, however, as the filer's power shrinks. The STOCK Act also required that the financial reports of tens of thousands of senior executive-branch employees, mostly career civil servants, be posted online in searchable databases. After an association of senior executives sued and a study by the National Academy of Public Administration warned that the databases could endanger national security and personal safety, Congress repealed that requirement for most of them about a year later. Technology explains why that reversal was sound. A form kept in an ethics office is available to anyone who requests it; a searchable database can be mined in bulk by people who would never have asked. A career administrator's debts reveal far less about the misuse of public power than a senator's trades, because the administrator's discretion is much narrower. Yet a sortable list of financially stretched employees is valuable to anyone hoping to [[inveigle|inveigle]] one of them into betraying secrets. Here the intended benefit nearly vanishes while the unintended cost remains.

These consequences point to a more precise position. Publication should be required, but its scope and frequency should track power. The more discretion officials hold over regulation, markets, or the distribution of federal [[largesse|largesse]], such as the billions that flowed to vaccine developers during the pandemic, the more promptly they should report each trade, and the more readily disclosure should be paired with divestment or a trading ban. For officials with narrower discretion, filing with an ethics office, open to anyone who asks but never posted in bulk, secures most of the benefit at a fraction of the risk. Disclosure diagnoses conflicts of interest; it does not cure them, and a policy that mistakes the diagnosis for the cure will disappoint the public it was meant to reassure.

prompt.statement: Expertise in one field tends to make people overconfident when they speak about other fields.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Instinct Overreaches, Method Travels
essays.essay:
The statement treats expertise as a single possession, but it is really two. One is trained instinct: the ability, built through long practice, to see the right answer at a glance. The other is method: knowledge of how a field earns, tests, and revises its answers. Instinct cannot tell that it has crossed a border; it feels as sure in a strange field as in a familiar one, so experts who trust it [[extrapolate|extrapolate]] from a lifetime of sound hunches to questions far afield. Method consists of questions rather than answers, and questions travel well. I therefore agree with the statement only in part: expertise breeds overconfidence when people carry their instincts into other fields, and unusual care when they carry their methods.

Ezra Pound illustrates the first case. Few poets have had a surer ear: his cuts turned T. S. Eliot's sprawling draft of The Waste Land into the taut poem readers know. Between the wars, however, Pound embraced Social Credit, a [[heterodox|heterodox]] monetary theory, and fused it with an obsession with usury. During World War II he [[averred|aver]], in broadcast after broadcast on Italian state radio, that usurers, whom he increasingly identified with Jews, had caused the war. Nothing had trained him to judge monetary policy, yet he pronounced on it as confidently as on a line of verse. His economics was not a separate vice; it was his poetic gift operating where it had no jurisdiction. The broadcasts lent a great poet's prestige to antisemitic propaganda and led to his indictment for treason.

Pound's overreach could only persuade; in law, the same error can compel. A novelist who garbles economics on a talk show commits a [[gaffe|gaffe]] that listeners are free to ignore, but a justice who misjudges a scientific question sets precedent that lower courts must follow. In Buck v. Bell (1927), Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr., among the most admired American jurists, wrote the opinion upholding a Virginia law permitting forced sterilization of people deemed hereditarily "feeble-minded." Holmes did not defy the science of his day; many leading biologists then endorsed eugenics. But deference is not verification. He treated the movement's claims as [[incontrovertible|incontrovertible]], took the record's diagnoses on faith, and capped his argument with an epigram: "Three generations of imbeciles are enough." The line has the compression that made his prose famous, and that is the problem: a gift for settling legal questions in a phrase was turned on a biological question no phrase could settle. Historians have found little evidence that the woman at the center of the case was intellectually disabled.

The statement fails, however, when experts travel with their methods. Anton Chekhov, a physician and celebrated writer, could have written about the penal colony on Sakhalin Island on reputation alone. Instead, in 1890, he crossed Siberia and went hut to hut, conducting his own census of the island's convicts and settlers. The resulting book reads like a field survey; its authority comes from the counting, not the name on the cover. Law has institutionalized the same move. In Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals (1993), the Supreme Court told federal judges to examine the methods behind scientific testimony rather than the conclusions an expert witness offers, asking, for instance, whether a theory has been tested and what its error rate is. Those questions were borrowed from science and its philosophers, and courts apply them unevenly, but the habit of screening evidence before a jury hears it was law's own.

These cases shape my position in two ways. First, they locate the danger: it is greatest for the most accomplished, because the more reliable an instinct has proved at home, the more trustworthy it feels abroad. Pound and Holmes overreached not despite their brilliance but partly because of it. Second, they show the remedy is not less expertise but a different use of it: held as questions rather than verdicts, the same expertise made Chekhov and the Daubert Court more careful, not less. Expertise, then, does not by itself produce overconfidence. It supplies a feeling of mastery and a habit of verification; whether experts outside their fields sound like Pound or like Chekhov depends on which of the two they bring along.

departing from mainstream economic thinking; outside accepted doctrine
declared firmly and confidently as true a claim he had no training to judge

Every example is developed far enough to show what happened and why it matters, complications such as Holmes's deference to the science of his day are conceded rather than hidden, and the prose is precise, varied, and economical.

prompt.statement: Great teachers are those who make themselves unnecessary.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Unnecessary for Answers, Needed for Eyes
essays.essay:
The statement is right about the direction of good teaching but wrong about its endpoint. Instruction that leaves students permanently dependent has failed at its most basic task, and in that sense every good teacher works toward her own obsolescence. Yet the statement rests on an [[implicit|implicit]] assumption that learning has a finish line: a fixed body of knowledge a teacher can hand over before stepping aside. Where that assumption holds, the statement is an excellent test. Where it fails, as it does in skills that no one ever finishes mastering, the greatest teachers make themselves unnecessary as suppliers of answers while remaining valuable as observers who see what the learner cannot.

The statement holds most clearly when knowledge can be codified and the learner's goal is self-reliance. When Meiji Japan set out to industrialize in the late nineteenth century, its government hired foreign engineers, physicians, and teachers at considerable expense. It did not, however, count on these experts to train their replacements out of goodwill; it made their departure part of the plan. At institutions such as the Imperial College of Engineering, foreign professors trained Japanese successors, and as those graduates gained experience, the government gradually replaced most of its foreign staff, though some experts remained for many years. In effect, the program succeeded to the degree that the country learned to [[dispense|dispense]] with its teachers. For skills like surveying a rail line or running a telegraph office, continued dependence is simply a cost.

The statement also exposes how teachers make themselves necessary without meaning to. A lecturer who [[enthralls|enthrall]] a packed hall may make difficult material feel effortless, yet students who understand only while she is speaking have borrowed her understanding rather than built their own. A teacher who greets every mistake with [[histrionic|histrionic]] sighs teaches students to perform for her approval rather than to judge their own work. Taiichi Ohno, usually credited as the architect of Toyota's production system, made a practice of withholding answers. In a widely retold story, he would draw a chalk circle on the factory floor, leave a manager standing in it for hours, then ask what the manager had seen, sending him back if the answer was thin. Rather than point out the idle workers and excess inventory himself, Ohno [[goaded|goad]] his managers into seeing them, because a manager who relied on Ohno's eye would be helpless the day Ohno left the floor.

The statement fails, however, where a skill has no ceiling and the learner's own perception is the limiting factor. The surgeon Atul Gawande has described how, years into a successful practice, he sensed he had stopped improving and invited a retired surgeon who had once trained him to watch him operate. The older man came away with notes on the position of Gawande's elbow, the aim of the overhead light, and the arrangement of the drapes. Gawande drew a comparison with professional tennis players, who keep coaches throughout their careers even though few coaches could beat them on the court. Such a teacher supplies not knowledge the student lacks but a vantage point the student can never occupy: the view from outside one's own hands.

Taken together, these cases do not lead me to split the difference; they lead me to relocate the line the statement draws. The Meiji professors and Ohno made themselves unnecessary as sources of answers, and their greatness lay in that withdrawal. Gawande's teacher had once done the same, yet he remained necessary as a source of perception, and nothing about that need diminished him. Read literally, the statement would have us fault teachers whose students still call on them, as though continuing need proved the first lessons had failed. In fact, the call [[exonerates|exonerate]] such teachers, because it shows those lessons worked: only a surgeon who had mastered the basics could profit from a note about the position of an elbow.

Greatness in teaching, then, is less a matter of becoming unnecessary than of knowing what to give away. A great teacher is [[magnanimous|magnanimous]] enough to hasten the day a student no longer needs her answers and honest enough to stay while that student still needs her eyes.

prompt.statement: Parents should limit the time their children spend on screens to one hour a day.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Limit the Feed, Not the Clock
essays.essay:
The strongest case for a one-hour limit has less to do with children than with the companies that court them. Advertising-supported platforms earn more the longer a user stays, so autoplay and the endless feed are built to [[enthrall|enthrall]], and a seven-year-old's self-control is no match for engineers paid to keep her watching. For a young child alone with a tablet full of short videos, a firm daily limit is plainly advantageous: it is simple to enforce, ends the nightly bargaining over "five more minutes," and protects sleep and outdoor play. I grant this argument in full. Its force, however, rests on an assumption [[implicit|implicit]] in the recommendation: that every minute in front of a screen resembles a minute in that feed.

That assumption is false, and once it falls, the recommendation shrinks from a universal rule to a sound default for one kind of use. The error lies in treating a screen as an activity rather than a medium: no one would limit a child to an hour of paper a day, since paper carries both junk mail and Tolstoy. When Sesame Street premiered in 1969, many American households could not receive it clearly. Economists comparing areas of strong and weak reception found that preschoolers in the former were later more likely to be in the grade appropriate for their age, especially in disadvantaged areas. Television helped children stay on track in school when the program was designed to teach. A one-hour cap would have left room for the program, but only by coincidence, since a rule that counts minutes cannot tell Sesame Street from cartoons. It measures time because time is easy to count, not because time is what matters.

The limit becomes actively harmful when a screen is the only channel to something irreplaceable. Imagine an eight-year-old in Manila whose mother, like many Filipino women, works as a domestic helper in Hong Kong. On a video call the mother sees what no text message conveys: whether her daughter is still the [[vivacious|vivacious]] child she left behind or has grown quiet and withdrawn. Under a one-hour rule, a forty-minute call would leave twenty minutes for everything else, including her online homework. Age compounds the problem. The one-hour figure echoes the American Academy of Pediatrics' 2016 guidance for children ages two to five, and to [[extrapolate|extrapolate]] it to a fifteen-year-old is to stretch advice beyond the age group it was written for. That guidance set no number for children six and older, asking instead for consistent limits on media time and content and for keeping media from displacing sleep, physical activity, and other healthy behaviors. A parent who shuts the laptop on a teenager learning to code obeys the rule while interrupting the sustained concentration that the feed tends to erode.

A limit that children find arbitrary also tends to teach evasion rather than restraint. In 2011 South Korea barred children under sixteen from online gaming between midnight and six in the morning. Many teenagers logged in with an adult's identification number, studies suggested the curfew did little to lengthen adolescents' sleep, and the government repealed it about a decade later. Households reproduce that dynamic in miniature. A child who is [[chastised|chastise]] each time she overshoots an hour that seems arbitrary learns to hide her phone under the pillow, not to ask whether the next video deserves her attention.

My agreement, then, is real but narrow. The feed persuades me that parents cannot [[dispense|dispense]] with limits; Sesame Street and the call to Hong Kong, that a limit should attach to the kind of use rather than to the clock; the Korean curfew, that a limit children find arbitrary breeds evasion. For entertainment engineered to hold attention, especially in a young child's hands, one hour is a sensible ceiling that I would enforce without apology. As a universal rule, however, it confuses the container with its contents. Parents should budget screen time as a careful household budgets money, [[stinting|stinting]] on the autoplaying feed and spending freely on the call home, the coding project, and the program that teaches. The question worth asking of any stretch of screen time is not how long it lasts but what it replaces.

prompt.statement: Newspapers should stop reporting public-opinion polls in the weeks before an election.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: A Brief Pause, Not a Long Silence
essays.essay:
The recommendation rests on two questionable assumptions: that the harm of election polling lies in the numbers themselves, and that keeping polls out of newspapers keeps them away from voters. The first is only half true, since the damage usually comes from when and how polls are reported; the second is false. I therefore accept the proposal only in a sharply narrowed form. A pause in the final day or two can protect voters from claims they have no time to test, but a weeks-long blackout would leave readers knowing less than the campaigns, which never stop polling.

Some circumstances do favor silence. Consider a hypothetical: two days before a close election, a little-known firm releases a poll showing one candidate's support collapsing. The survey may be sloppy or commissioned by a rival, yet no one has time to check it, and the campaign's protests would sound [[histrionic|histrionic]] and self-serving. A sensational headline proclaiming the campaign in free fall could persuade its supporters to stay home. Nor does the harm depend on panic: even the most [[phlegmatic|phlegmatic]] voter could not learn before casting a ballot that the survey was an outlier. In that narrow window, a poll ceases to be information and becomes an unanswerable assertion. Over weeks, horse-race coverage does subtler damage. Daily tracking numbers [[goad|goad]] trailing candidates into reckless attacks timed for the next news cycle. Reporters treat each [[gaffe|gaffe]] less as evidence of judgment than as the cause of the next dip. The first harm justifies a brief pause. The second would survive even a long one, since reporters would simply keep score with cruder gauges, from crowd sizes to party insiders' hunches.

The strongest case against a long blackout comes from an election in which the pollsters imposed one on themselves. In 1948, every major poll showed Thomas Dewey comfortably ahead of Harry Truman. One prominent pollster declared the race over in September and stopped surveying; the others stopped a week or two before Election Day. Truman, meanwhile, crisscrossed the country in a [[resolute|resolute]] whistle-stop campaign whose late effect went unmeasured. The consensus seemed so settled that when a printers' strike forced the Chicago Daily Tribune to go to press before most returns were in, its editors trusted their Washington correspondent's confident call and printed "Dewey Defeats Truman," a front page the victorious Truman soon held aloft. The surveys had methodological flaws, but their early silence turned an error into a certainty. A newspaper blackout would make that condition the rule: it would not erase published polls but freeze them, leaving voters to reason from old numbers as if the race had stopped moving. Since that error grows with each day of silence, the length of a blackout is not a detail; it is the whole question.

Technology makes the second assumption untenable. A newspaper blackout silences only newspapers; it does not stop campaigns from commissioning private polls, investors from buying them, or partisans from posting numbers, real or invented. For decades France barred publishing polls in the week before a vote, yet once foreign news sites began posting French surveys online, the ban mainly separated voters who knew where to look from those who did not. After the country's highest appeals court held the ban incompatible with freedom of expression, lawmakers cut the blackout to the eve and day of the vote. A long ban therefore yields not an electorate free of polls but one that receives them from the least accountable sources, stripped of sample sizes, margins of error, and editorial scrutiny.

These cases locate the danger not in polls but in their timing and their telling. The principle that should remain [[inviolate|inviolate]] is the voter's opportunity to weigh evidence before acting on it. A survey released too late to be scrutinized denies that opportunity; so does a weeks-long silence that leaves voters with stale figures and anonymous leaks. A pause of a day or two, roughly where France itself settled, honors the principle. Beyond that window, the better remedy is not silence but discipline: averages rather than single surveys, margins of error stated plainly, and more attention to what candidates propose than to where they stand.

prompt.statement: Most environmental problems can be solved by technology rather than by changes in behavior.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Technology Fixes Harms, Not Appetites
essays.essay:
Few environmental problems have been solved by persuading millions of people to live differently, and the statement draws its force from that record. Appeals to conscience ask individuals, most of them unconcerned about dangers they cannot see, to accept daily inconvenience for a distant benefit; a sewer or a safer chemical, once in place, works whether anyone cares or not. I therefore agree with the statement wherever the harm comes from a substance or process that can be replaced. It fails, however, where the harm is consumption itself, and even its successes depend on a kind of behavior it overlooks.

Victorian London shows why engineering so often succeeds where exhortation cannot. The city's sewage flowed into the Thames, which also supplied much of its drinking water, and cholera struck repeatedly. No campaign for personal cleanliness could have broken that cycle, because households did not control the water that reached them. What broke it was public engineering: an 1852 law moved water intakes above the tidal Thames and required filtration, and Joseph Bazalgette's intercepting sewers later carried waste downstream. Many of the sewers' champions believed that cholera spread through foul air, not water; the system worked anyway, because machinery does not require even its builders to understand it. Yet the main drainage was approved only after the "Great Stink" of 1858, when the river's stench rattled even the most [[phlegmatic|phlegmatic]] members of Parliament. The engineering was decisive, but it arrived through public decisions to mandate and fund it.

The recovery of the ozone layer follows the same pattern, with an instructive addition. In the 1970s chemists Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland warned that chlorofluorocarbons, then common in refrigerators and spray cans, could destroy stratospheric ozone; the discovery of a seasonal hole over Antarctica in the 1980s gave their warning urgency. The remedy asked no one to give up refrigeration. Manufacturers developed substitute compounds, and the Montreal Protocol committed governments to cut production of the old ones. Because the alternatives were affordable, signatories had little temptation to [[renege|renege]]; as the evidence accumulated, they tightened the schedule instead. By making the right choice inexpensive, technology made political agreement possible.

The most compelling challenge to my position comes not from moralists who prize personal virtue but from economists. In 1865 William Stanley Jevons argued that more efficient steam engines had increased Britain's coal consumption, because efficiency made coal-powered work cheaper and therefore more common. Cities offer a modern version of his paradox: widening a congested highway attracts new driving until congestion returns, a pattern called induced demand. From such cases a critic could [[extrapolate|extrapolate]] a general law: because technology lowers the cost of using nature, it invites us to use more of it, so only restraint can solve the problem.

That efficiency can backfire in this way is [[incontrovertible|incontrovertible]]; that all technology must do so does not follow. The paradox applies when technology makes a harmful activity cheaper, not when it separates the activity from the harm. A more efficient engine invites more coal burning, but refrigerators multiplied while the ozone layer began to recover, because the harm lay in the coolant, not in cooling. When the replacements proved to be potent greenhouse gases, the 2016 Kigali Amendment answered with another substitution, not less refrigeration. The objection therefore [[tempers|temper]] the statement rather than refuting it. In fisheries, where the damage is the quantity consumed, sonar and larger trawlers only hasten depletion, and here the critic is right: behavior must change. Even then, the change rarely comes from conscience alone: Stockholm cut congestion by charging drivers to enter its center, altering behavior through prices rather than sermons.

The statement, then, is right about the instrument and wrong about the alternative it dismisses. Technology is the most dependable remedy for harms that can be engineered out of daily life, because it does not wait for people to become virtuous. But it does not end the need to choose. Each success here began with a public decision to build the sewer, ban the chemical, or price the road, and where the harm is sheer appetite, no invention can [[exonerate|exonerate]] the consumer, whose choice to consume less cannot be handed off to a machine.

prompt.statement: Scientific knowledge should never be kept secret from the public.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Withhold the Recipe, Never the Risk
essays.essay:
The claim that scientific knowledge should never be kept secret is right as a presumption and wrong as an absolute, and its error hides in the word "knowledge." That word covers three different things: conclusions about how the world works, data drawn from identifiable people, and technical methods useful chiefly for causing mass harm. Conclusions, above all those concerning risks the public bears, should never be concealed. The other two may sometimes be restricted, but only under narrow conditions, and only when the restriction is itself made public.

The statement holds most firmly when a finding bears on dangers ordinary people face, because those who want such a secret kept are almost always those who gain from keeping it. Henrik Ibsen dramatized this logic in An Enemy of the People, in which a doctor discovers that his town's lucrative spa baths are contaminated. The mayor and the leading citizens, dreading the cost of repairs, insist that publication would ruin the community, and they [[foment|foment]] such hostility toward the doctor that a public meeting declares him the people's enemy. The Tuskegee syphilis study shows that the same logic can survive publication. For four decades the United States Public Health Service tracked untreated syphilis in hundreds of Black men in Alabama and reported its results in medical journals, yet the researchers, who needed their subjects untreated, hid from the men what mattered most to them: that they had syphilis, not merely "bad blood," and, once penicillin became the standard cure, that they could be treated. Openness among experts is not openness with the people a finding concerns. The study ended only when a whistleblower, ignored for years inside the agency, took it to the press. That exposure was [[fortuitous|fortuitous]]; nothing in the system required it.

The statement fails, however, when the "knowledge" in question is really information about particular people. In 2013 European researchers published the genome of HeLa cells, a line grown from tissue taken without consent from Henrietta Lacks, a Black patient treated at Johns Hopkins in 1951. Because a genome carries information shared by relatives, publication exposed her living descendants to scrutiny they had never consented to. The sequence was withdrawn, and the family, [[magnanimous|magnanimous]] toward institutions that had repeatedly taken from them without asking, agreed with the National Institutes of Health on controlled access, with relatives helping to review requests. Yet the restriction concealed nothing about how cells work; every conclusion drawn from the data remains publishable.

The strongest challenge to my position is not that the public cannot handle the truth, an argument with an embarrassing pedigree, but that some knowledge confers capability rather than understanding. A finding that a town's water is contaminated arms citizens to protect themselves; a detailed method for causing mass casualties arms only the rare person who wishes to use it, and one such person may be enough. On this view, the benefit of disclosure is diffuse while the harm is concentrated and irreversible, so even a small chance of misuse outweighs it. I have no [[qualms|qualm]] about conceding its force; it is why the design details of nuclear weapons remain classified in every country that possesses them. But the argument justifies less than it seems to. It licenses withholding a recipe, never concealing that a risk exists or what a society should do about it: citizens know that nuclear weapons exist and can debate whether to build them without knowing how. And because danger is the excuse every advocate of secrecy reaches for first, as Ibsen's mayor shows, the decision to withhold cannot rest with those who would gain from silence. A committee empowered to suppress dangerous findings will, sooner or later, find [[heterodox|heterodox]] ones dangerous too.

Scientific knowledge, then, should never be secret in the sense that matters most: no finding about the risks people face, and no conclusion about how nature works, should be hidden from those it concerns. What may be withheld is narrower than defenders of secrecy suggest: a person's data, guarded on that person's behalf, or a method of mass harm, guarded under rules the public can inspect. A secret whose justification cannot be stated openly has already revealed whose interests it serves.

prompt.statement: Some people believe that history should be taught mainly as a story of national achievement. Others believe that it should give equal attention to national failures.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Failures Belong in the Same Story
essays.essay:
The argument for teaching history mainly as a story of national achievement deserves more respect than its critics, myself among them, usually grant it. A nation is not a natural object but a standing agreement, renewed whenever citizens pay taxes or accept defeat at the polls, and such agreements rest partly on affection. A [[fledgling|fledgling]] state assembled from rival regions may share little beyond a story of what its people accomplished together, and a curriculum that greets children with nothing but crimes risks persuading them that the common enterprise is not worth joining. No sensible teacher wants to [[chastise|chastise]] nine-year-olds for wrongs committed before their grandparents were born.

Yet the argument holds only while the achievements are real and the story is complete enough to survive scrutiny. Pride that depends on omission is brittle. A history that must [[embellish|embellish]] its victories and pass over its defeats does not abolish the defeats; it surrenders them to whoever will tell them, and the student who first hears of them from a [[heterodox|heterodox]] online commentator rather than a teacher draws a corrosive conclusion: the official story was a sales pitch. The deeper flaw is an assumption both views share, that achievements and failures are separate ledgers between which a syllabus must divide its hours. Many of a nation's finest achievements are corrections of its own failures, and a history that omits the failure cannot explain the achievement. The second view therefore comes closer to my own, with one revision: failures deserve not equal time but a place in the same story.

The American government's treatment of Japanese Americans during the Second World War shows why. Federal authorities removed more than 100,000 people of Japanese ancestry from the West Coast, most of them citizens, and held them in camps for much of the war; the Supreme Court upheld the exclusion in Korematsu v. United States. Four decades later, a congressional commission concluded that the policy had grown out of racial prejudice and wartime hysteria rather than military necessity, and in 1988 Congress formally apologized and granted reparations to surviving internees. That apology ranks among the finest acts of American self-government because no court ordered it. But a course built around achievement could not teach it without first teaching the camps. Omitting them would ask students to admire a remedy for an injury they were never shown, and would, in effect, [[exonerate|exonerate]] a government that had already confessed the wrong in law.

Candor also costs less than critics fear. German schools teach the Nazi era in unsparing detail, yet Germany is a confident democracy allied with most of the countries it once invaded, not a nation paralyzed by shame. Japan, a stable democracy on good terms with much of Asia, is a subtler case. Its government formally apologized for colonial rule and wartime aggression in the 1990s, but textbook screening and later politicians' equivocations have drawn repeated protests from China and South Korea, reviving old [[animosities|animosity]]. Its diplomatic [[liability|liability]] is not silence but a gap: when classrooms seem to soften what leaders conceded, neighbors doubt the apology itself.

Still, the second view, read literally, overreaches. "Equal attention" implies a quota, as if a history course were an audit that tallied disgraces against triumphs until the columns balanced. A syllabus that dwelt on failures for their own sake would produce exactly the cynicism the first view fears. Ordinary life suggests a better standard. We distrust the friend who claims never to have broken a promise, and we tire of the one who apologizes endlessly and changes nothing; we rely on the friend who, having [[reneged|renege]] on a commitment, can say plainly what went wrong and how she set it right.

Nations earn considered loyalty the same way. Their failures belong neither in a ceremonial footnote nor in an arithmetic half of the syllabus, but in the same story as the reforms they provoked, a story honest enough to include failures, like the treaties broken with Native nations, that no reform has fully repaired. Taught that way, history offers students something sturdier than pride: evidence that their country has been wrong before, has sometimes known it, and has occasionally found the will to make amends.

prompt.statement: Some people believe that the best way to honor the past is to preserve its monuments unchanged. Others believe that each generation should be free to reinterpret or remove them.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Honor Is Revisable, Evidence Is Not
essays.essay:
Arguments about monuments often proceed as if a statue were the past itself. It is not. A public statue is commissioned by a particular generation to tell a particular story, so the demand that it remain unchanged quietly grants one earlier interpretation permanent authority over all later ones. Still, that observation does not settle the dispute, because "monument" covers two different things: the record, which preserves evidence of what happened, and the tribute, which declares who deserves admiration. The evidence a record carries should remain [[inviolate|inviolate]]; the honor a tribute confers is a judgment each generation may revisit. My position is closer to the second view, though it imposes a stronger duty of preservation than that view's advocates usually concede.

The preservationist view deserves its strongest hearing where a monument functions as a record. The barracks and ruined gas chambers of Auschwitz have been preserved as a museum since shortly after World War II, not because anyone admires them but because their physical presence rebuts those who would deny what happened there. Altering such a site to suit present sensibilities would weaken its testimony for people not yet born. Germany followed similar reasoning when it rebuilt the Reichstag in the 1990s, keeping much of the Cyrillic graffiti that Soviet soldiers had scrawled across its walls in 1945, although those inscriptions record the nation's defeat in its own capital. A generation ought to have [[qualms|qualm]] about editing evidence of this kind, because its successors may need precisely what it finds uncomfortable. Where a monument is evidence, honoring the past does mean leaving that evidence alone.

The same view fails, however, when a monument is a tribute rather than a record. Many Confederate statues in the American South were erected not in the years after the Civil War but decades later, during the Jim Crow era. They gave bronze form to the Lost Cause, a narrative that [[embellished|embellish]] the story of the war with chivalrous generals and contented slaves while recasting a rebellion fought to preserve slavery as a principled defense of states' rights. To keep such a statue unchanged is not to honor the past; it is to honor a later generation's flattering revision of it, broadcast from a community's most prominent public spaces. When Virginia removed Robert E. Lee's statue from Monument Avenue in Richmond, the former Confederate capital, it did not erase the Civil War. The war remains in archives, on battlefields and in museums. What the state withdrew was an endorsement, and a living community is entitled to decide whom it endorses. Here the second view is not merely permissible but correct.

Yet the freedom to remove has its own failure conditions, which is why my agreement is qualified. A rule that lets each generation discard whatever offends it leaves every monument at the mercy of the most easily offended, as the Taliban showed in 2001 when they condemned the Bamiyan Buddhas as idols and blew them up. Process matters as well. Public argument over statues easily turns [[histrionic|histrionic]], with one camp insisting that relocating a single figure erases history and the other treating every delay as complicity. When statues come down overnight in that atmosphere, opportunists seize on the spectacle to [[foment|foment]] resentment among people who were never persuaded. The wiser course lies between these extremes. After the fall of communism, Budapest neither smashed its statues of Lenin, Marx and Hungarian communist leaders nor left them presiding over public squares; it moved many of them to Memento Park, an open-air museum on the city's outskirts, where they stand as artifacts of a dictatorship rather than objects of veneration. Removed from honor, they remain available as evidence.

Neither view, then, survives intact. Freezing every monument in place mistakes deference to the generation that carved the past in stone for reverence toward the past itself, while unlimited freedom to remove treats an inheritance as disposable property. The position I find most defensible is that each generation may decide whom it celebrates in public but holds the physical record in trust for its successors. It may take a general off his pedestal; it should be far slower to take him out of the record.

prompt.statement:
Claim: Nations should work to preserve endangered languages.
Reason: Each language contains knowledge that exists nowhere else.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Document for Knowledge, Revive for Speakers
essays.essay:
Campaigns to save endangered languages usually lead with scholarship: every language, the argument runs, encodes knowledge found nowhere else. I agree that nations should work to preserve endangered languages, but not chiefly for this reason. The premise about unique knowledge is true as far as it goes, yet it justifies recording a language rather than keeping it alive. The stronger case rests on the people who speak it, and that case also shapes what preservation should mean.

Consider the reason first. Advocates often argue that a dying language takes irreplaceable knowledge with it, and some cases bear them out. Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr, an Aboriginal language of northern Queensland, describe space by compass direction rather than left and right; they say a cup sits north of a plate and track their orientation with an accuracy that has fascinated cognitive scientists. That a language can hold such knowledge is not in doubt. What does not follow is that the language must stay alive for the knowledge to survive. Researchers needed living speakers to uncover the compass system, but their findings now sit in grammars, recordings, and published studies that would outlive the language. A recording, admittedly, cannot sustain the habit of always knowing where north is, but the reason as stated concerns what a language contains, not who lives by it. Taken alone, then, it would excuse a government for [[stinting|stinting]] on support, paying a few linguists to record the last fluent speakers and calling the obligation met.

The claim rests on firmer ground: what speakers lose when a language slips away. Anyone who has watched an immigrant family knows the three-generation pattern: grandparents who speak only the old language, parents who regard it as a [[liability|liability]] at school and work, and grandchildren who cannot follow their grandmother's stories. Nothing unique is lost to humanity, since the language still thrives in the old country, yet the family has plainly lost something. When the same thing happens to a whole people, the shift is rarely [[fortuitous|fortuitous]]; economic pressure drives much of it, and governments have often hastened it by design. In New Zealand, the evidence of such design is [[incontrovertible|incontrovertible]]: generations of Māori children were punished for speaking their language at school, and by the 1970s few learned it at home. The revival that followed did not rest on knowledge. Elders, working with the Department of Māori Affairs, opened preschool "language nests," or kōhanga reo, where children heard only Māori. Māori claimants then [[averred|aver]] before the Waitangi Tribunal that the Crown had pledged by treaty to protect the language; the Tribunal agreed, and Parliament made Māori an official language. Public support, seen this way, is not a [[magnanimous|magnanimous]] gesture by a majority toward a minority. It is closer to restitution for a harm the state helped cause.

Grounding the duty in speakers rather than in knowledge also [[tempers|temper]] the claim by changing what "preserve" should mean. The word suggests a museum piece kept untouched behind glass, and a language maintained by decree alone risks becoming one: studied, examined, and seldom spoken. Ireland has required Irish in its schools since independence, yet far more citizens have studied it than speak it daily outside the classroom; compulsion bred familiarity, and in some quarters resentment, but not a community of speakers. The Irish-medium schools, or Gaelscoileanna, that parents have chosen in growing numbers since the 1970s have done far better. The Māori nests followed the same pattern: families chose them, elders staffed them, and the state funded the nests rather than running them. Nations should therefore fund immersion schools and broadcasting, and grant official recognition, wherever speakers want them, while accepting that a community choosing freely may let its language go.

The stated reason, then, is true but points to the wrong remedy. Unique knowledge explains why scholars should document endangered languages; it cannot explain why a nation should spend public money so that children go on speaking them. That obligation arises from the speakers, many of whom lost their language to pressure their own governments applied, and it is best met by giving them the means, though never the command, to speak it again.

analysis.verdict: The essay takes an insightful, qualified position: it accepts the claim but shows that the stated reason supports documenting a language, not keeping it alive. Each example (Guugu Yimithirr, an immigrant family, the Māori revival, compulsory versus chosen Irish schooling) is developed far enough to show why it matters. The prose is precise, varied, and well controlled, which matches the ETS description of a 6.
analysis.position: The opening agrees with the claim "but not chiefly for this reason," then names the alternative ground: "The stronger case rests on the people who speak it." The conclusion refines that position rather than repeating it.
analysis.development: Each example is explained, not just named. Guugu Yimithirr first shows that a language can hold unique knowledge, then shows that findings gathered from living speakers now sit in "grammars, recordings, and published studies." Ireland supplies both sides of the choice: compulsory classes produced study without speech, while schools "that parents have chosen in growing numbers" did far better.
analysis.organization: The paragraphs follow the instruction's logic: the reason is tested (P2), the claim is rebuilt on a better reason (P3), the claim is limited (P4), and the refined position closes the essay (P5). Transitions carry the argument; for example, "Grounding the duty in speakers rather than in knowledge" links P3 to P4.
analysis.language: Word choice is exact and economical ("pledged by treaty," "stinting on support," "restitution"), and strong words are saved for strong claims: "the evidence of such design is incontrovertible." The series "studied, examined, and seldom spoken" compresses what the Irish case then illustrates.

The reason is "true but points to the wrong remedy," while the claim stands on a different ground. The essay illustrates both situations this instruction is designed to test: a true reason that is insufficient, and a sound claim that needs a better reason.

paragraphs.note: Restates the argument fairly, agrees with the claim, rejects knowledge as its main support, and previews both the better ground (speakers) and the limit on what preservation should mean.

paragraphs.note: Concedes the reason with the Guugu Yimithirr compass system, then shows that findings gathered from speakers survive in published work, so the reason alone justifies archiving, not living preservation.

prompt.statement:
Claim: Advertising aimed at young children should be banned.
Reason: Young children cannot tell the difference between persuasion and information.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Protect Children From Motive, Not Persuasion
essays.essay:
The reason offered here rests on firm empirical ground, yet it supports less than its proponents assume. Young children do struggle to recognize persuasion, but they struggle equally with persuasion that nearly everyone approves of, so the reason alone cannot justify a ban. The claim is nonetheless correct under specific conditions: when the advertising is commercial, when it sells products whose costs a child cannot weigh, and when a ban can be drawn tightly enough to stop the message rather than merely relocate it. Under those conditions I support a ban, but on grounds the stated reason leaves out.

The reason deserves its due. Developmental research generally finds that most children under about seven or eight do not grasp that a commercial is trying to sell them something; the youngest often cannot tell where a program ends and an advertisement begins. A five-year-old [[enthralled|enthrall]] by the cartoon tiger on her cereal box sees a friend offering advice, not a salesman closing a deal. This matters because the usual alternative to regulation is education: teach children to recognize advertising, and they will discount it. If the gap closes only with age, however, no curriculum can close it sooner, and the remedy fails precisely among the children the reason describes. For the youngest viewers, the reason does not merely favor restriction; it eliminates the gentler alternative.

What the reason cannot do is explain what is wrong with advertising, because the same incapacity applies to persuasion we rightly welcome. For decades Singapore has run public campaigns urging citizens to keep streets clean and treat one another with courtesy, and it has [[embellished|embellish]] their plain slogans with catchy songs and, for the courtesy drive, a smiling cartoon lion. A six-year-old who absorbs these messages is no better at recognizing them as persuasion than at recognizing a toy commercial; she simply learns that littering is shameful. Few would object to shaping a child's habits this way. If an inability to detect persuasion were the decisive harm, a consistent ban would sweep away the anti-littering poster along with the candy advertisement.

The claim survives on a different ground: whose interest the persuasion serves. Singapore's campaigns ask the child to do something good for herself and her city; the cereal tiger asks her to want something that profits its maker, often at the expense of her health. Advertisers [[aver|aver]] that parents, who hold the wallet, remain the final judges, yet this defense describes the strategy rather than justifying it. The parent is the real target, and the child is the instrument used to [[goad|goad]] that parent into purchases he or she would otherwise refuse. Where the product harms the child in ways she cannot foresee, that strategy deserves prohibition. Chile adopted roughly this approach, restricting how foods high in sugar, salt, saturated fat, or calories may be marketed to children, and the cartoon tiger vanished from Chilean cereal boxes. Because the rule targeted defined products, regulators knew what to look for.

The claim fails, however, wherever a ban cannot follow the money. Marketing to children has increasingly moved from the commercial break into the content itself: online videos in which a [[vivacious|vivacious]] child unwraps new toys for an audience of other children, sometimes with a manufacturer's money behind the camera. A ban written for television spots does nothing about such videos and may make matters worse, since banished persuasion returns as entertainment and [[renders|render]] the line between selling and showing harder to see, aggravating the very confusion the reason identifies. A ban that cannot reach sponsored content is a gesture, not a remedy.

The defensible position, then, is narrower than the claim and grounded differently from the reason. Commercial advertising that sells young children products they cannot evaluate, and that recruits them as lobbyists within their own households, should be banned, provided the ban is defined by who pays and what is sold rather than by the format of the message. Children's inability to recognize persuasion explains why they need protection; it does not tell us what to protect them from. That answer lies not in the child's mind but in the advertiser's motive.

decorated the campaigns' plain slogans with attractive additions: catchy songs and a cartoon mascot.
state firmly and confidently, as a defense, that parents are the final judges.
prod or provoke the parent into buying something against his or her better judgment.
lively and animated in a charming way, which makes the child an appealing on-screen presence.
causes to become; makes the line between selling and entertainment harder to see.

Each example is developed until its relevance is explicit, and the prose is precise and varied, with no wasted words.

The claim then holds only under three named conditions, and the last paragraph restates it as a precise rule, a ban "defined by who pays and what is sold" rather than by format.

The recurring tiger ties paragraphs 2 and 4 together, and the Singapore campaigns carry the contrast from paragraph 3 into paragraph 4.

paragraphs.note: Replaces the stated reason with conflict of interest, contrasts Singapore's campaigns with the cereal tiger, shows the parents-decide defense restates the tactic, and cites Chile's targeted, enforceable food-marketing restriction.

moves.example: If an inability to detect persuasion were the decisive harm, a consistent ban would sweep away the anti-littering poster along with the candy advertisement.
moves.use: Test whether a reason is sufficient by applying it consistently to a case everyone accepts.

moves.frame: ... aver that ..., yet this defense describes the ... rather than justifying it.

moves.use: Turn the opponent's standard counterargument into evidence for your own position.

moves.frame: ... explains why ...; it does not tell us ...
moves.example: Children's inability to recognize persuasion explains why they need protection; it does not tell us what to protect them from.
moves.use: Show that a true premise supports only part of a conclusion, especially in claim-and-reason prompts.

analysis.contrast: A typical 4 or 5 would treat claim and reason as one, agreeing that children are vulnerable and therefore ads should be banned, perhaps adding a token counterargument about parental responsibility. Its examples would be generic (sugary cereal ads, obesity) rather than chosen to test the reason. It would miss that the reason proves too much and that a format-based ban can relocate persuasion rather than stop it.

prompt.statement: Social media companies should be required to let users turn off personalized content recommendations.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: An Off Switch Is Only a Floor
essays.essay:
Few regulatory proposals sound as modest as an off switch. Requiring social media companies to let users disable personalized recommendations seems to demand only one more item in a settings menu while promising people more control over what they see. I support the requirement, but tracing its likely consequences persuades me that a bare switch would accomplish far less than its advocates expect. The policy rests on an [[implicit|implicit]] assumption that offering people a choice is the same as giving them control. Whether that assumption holds depends on how the switch is designed and on what lawmakers allow its existence to excuse.

The intended consequence is real but narrower than it appears. A ranked feed is built to maximize engagement, and few things engage people as reliably as outrage and fear. Myanmar offers the starkest illustration. Before the military's 2017 campaign of violence against the Rohingya, Facebook was effectively the internet for millions of people there, and its engagement-driven feed helped spread posts that [[fomented|foment]] hatred against the largely Muslim minority. United Nations investigators named the platform a major channel for that hatred, and the company conceded it had been too slow to act. Escaping that feed, however, does not mean finding a neutral one. Which posts reach the top of a chronological feed may seem a matter of [[fortuitous|fortuitous]] timing, but the feed rewards whoever posts most often, and organized propaganda campaigns post constantly. In a large experiment during the 2020 American election, Facebook and Instagram users who were switched to chronological feeds spent less time on the platforms but saw more political content and more posts from untrustworthy sources, and their polarization did not measurably change. Ranking systems, it seems, filter as well as amplify. What the switch reliably changes is not the quality of the feed but who decides its order.

Two unintended consequences shape my position even more. The first is mundane: most users will never touch the switch. Defaults are powerful, as a well-known comparison of organ donation policies shows. Austria, which presumed consent unless citizens objected, counted nearly its entire population as potential donors, while neighboring Germany, which required citizens to opt in, counted only a small fraction as consenting donors. The two countries are culturally similar; the default, not generosity, explained most of the gap. A recommendation switch buried three menus deep would work like Germany's opt-in form, and the problem is worse than inertia. The users most [[enthralled|enthrall]] by an endless, personalized feed are precisely those least likely to seek a way out. Nor can the matter be left to goodwill: a company that offers the option voluntarily can [[renege|renege]] on that commitment as soon as engagement sags. Since a hidden switch, or one that quietly resets, would [[render|render]] the policy meaningless, I would support only a requirement that makes the option prominent and keeps it in force until the user reverses it.

The second consequence is subtler and more troubling: the switch could help [[exonerate|exonerate]] the very companies whose default feeds most people will keep using. Once opting out is possible, a platform accused of amplifying extremism can reply that anyone who disliked its recommendations was free to turn them off. History suggests the defense works. After Congress required health warnings on cigarette packs in the 1960s, tobacco companies pointed to those labels in court as evidence that smokers had knowingly accepted the risk, a defense that helped them win case after case. An off switch invites the same maneuver, shifting responsibility from those who design a system to those it was designed to keep scrolling. The requirement should therefore serve as a floor rather than a settlement: platforms must remain answerable for what their default feeds promote, whether or not a switch exists.

My position, then, is a conditional yes. A meaningful off switch deserves to be mandated, not because a chronological feed is healthier, a claim the evidence does not support, but because it returns to users a decision platforms now make for them. That case holds only if the switch is designed to be used and only if lawmakers refuse to mistake it for the whole remedy. Choice is where accountability begins, not where it ends.

Each example is developed until its relevance is explicit, the consequences visibly reshape the position into specific conditions, and the prose is precise and varied.

paragraphs.role: Second unintended consequence: shifted blame
paragraphs.note: Argues the switch could become a corporate alibi, supports the claim with cigarette warning labels used as a legal defense, and concludes that the mandate must be a floor, not a settlement.

prompt.statement: Patients should have the right to read every note their doctors write about them.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Open the Chart, Protect the Record
essays.essay:
The statement assumes that a doctor's note is a fixed document and that the only question is who may see it. In practice, opening notes to patients changes how well they understand their care, what doctors write, and when hard news arrives. Weighing those consequences, I believe patients should have a broad, easily exercised right to read their medical notes. The statement as written, however, goes further than the consequences support: a narrow class of notes can do real harm when read, and even ordinary notes can wound when they arrive at the wrong moment.

The most important consequence is the one the policy intends: patients who read their notes understand their care better and act on it more reliably. When the OpenNotes study invited patients at three American health systems to read their primary care notes, many participating physicians had [[qualms|qualm]] about letting patients see what they wrote; they expected floods of anxious questions and offense at frank remarks about weight or drinking. Both fears proved largely unfounded. Most patients said they understood their health better and felt more in control, many reported taking their medications more faithfully, and when the study ended, none of the doctors chose to stop sharing. This result matters to my position because it undercuts the paternalistic premise behind restricted access: that patients are too fragile to handle what their physicians think of them.

A second consequence is less obvious: once patients can read their notes, doctors begin writing for them. Much of this change is welcome. Shorthand that is harmless among colleagues becomes a [[gaffe|gaffe]] when the patient reads it; a man who finds "SOB" in his chart may not know that it means shortness of breath, and phrases such as "claims to have quit smoking" read as accusations. Writing for a second audience pushes clinicians toward language that is accurate without being cryptic or accusatory, but the same pressure can push them toward vagueness. A physician who suspects that a patient's back pain is partly driven by depression may leave that suspicion out of the note rather than upset its reader, and the record other clinicians rely on grows thinner. This consequence shapes my position as much as the first: a right to read is worth having only if the notes stay honest, so the policy must insist that they remain complete and candid.

The third consequence concerns timing and the reader's state of mind, and here an unqualified right breaks down. When rules under the 21st Century Cures Act took effect in 2021, many American health systems began posting notes and test reports to patient portals immediately, and some patients learned that they had cancer by opening a pathology report online, alone, before any doctor had called. A [[phlegmatic|phlegmatic]] reader may take "concerning for malignancy" in stride; an anxious one may spend a sleepless weekend imagining the worst. A few notes carry graver risks. For a patient in the grip of a persecutory [[delusion|delusion]], a psychiatric note calling the belief false may seem proof that the doctor is part of the plot, and a note recording a spouse's report of the patient's violence could endanger the spouse. Even those rules permit withholding information when its release would endanger someone. To make the right [[inviolate|inviolate]], as the word "every" does, would sacrifice real people to the tidiness of a principle.

None of these hazards justifies returning to the days when the chart belonged to the doctor. A policy that releases lab values and discharge summaries while [[stinting|stinting]] on the clinical narrative would forfeit the very benefits that made openness worth pursuing. The better rule is full access by default, [[tempered|temper]] by a few narrow exceptions that are decided case by case and disclosed to the patient. Control over timing, meanwhile, should rest with the patient: anyone who would rather hear grave results from a clinician than from a screen should be able to delay the release of those results. What patients are ultimately owed is not access to every word but an honest record they can read, and the right should be shaped to serve that end.

prompt.statement: People are more likely to change their beliefs through personal experience than through argument.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Experience Strikes Harder, Argument Reaches Farther
essays.essay:
I agree with the statement only in part. It captures something true about how minds change, but it mistakes the force of experience for its reach. When a belief concerns something people can test in their own lives, a single experience often accomplishes what years of argument could not. Many of the beliefs that matter most, however, concern effects too slow, too diffuse, or too rare for any one life to reveal, and for those beliefs argument is not the weaker instrument but the only one. Even where experience seems to triumph, it frequently succeeds by activating an argument heard long before.

Consider the longtime smoker. For years his family may [[berate|berate]] him for the habit, and his physician may [[reiterate|reiterate]] the risks at every visit, yet he keeps smoking, and each new argument seems only to harden his resistance. Then he suffers a heart attack. [[Convalescent|convalescent]] and badly shaken, he may give up cigarettes within weeks, with little further prompting. Physicians see this reversal so often that they treat a hospital stay for a heart attack as an unusually promising moment to help patients quit. Two features of experience explain its power. First, it converts a statistic about other people into a fact about oneself: the danger he had filed under strangers' misfortunes now lives in his own chest. Second, experience has no author. An argument comes from someone, and accepting it means conceding to that person; a heart attack wins no debate, so yielding to it costs nothing in pride. In cases like this, the statement is plainly right.

The same belief, however, reached the wider public by an entirely different route. Most Americans who came to accept that smoking kills did not learn it from a heart attack or a diagnosis; they learned it from an argument, developed in the epidemiological studies of the 1950s, codified in the Surgeon General's 1964 report, and repeated for decades in warning labels and public campaigns, even as the tobacco industry [[assailed|assail]] the science. Experience could never have taught this lesson to a whole population. Smoking's deadliest harms, from lung cancer to heart disease, typically appear many years after the habit begins, so for many smokers the experience arrives too late to act on, if it arrives at all. Worse, because the danger is a matter of probability, experience often teaches the wrong lesson: many people know a heavy smoker who lived into old age. On questions like this, experience is silent or misleading, and only argument, built on the painstaking comparison of many thousands of smokers with nonsmokers, can reveal what no individual can see. That argument prevailed, changing the beliefs of millions. Here the statement fails, and it fails precisely where experience has nothing reliable to offer.

Taken together, these cases sharpen my position in two ways. Because both involve the same belief, the decisive variable cannot be its content; it is whether the relevant evidence can reach a person through ordinary life in time to matter. Where it can, experience is the stronger teacher; where it cannot, argument must do the work alone. The cases also expose a false rivalry in the statement. The smoker who quits after his heart attack does not read the event unaided; he grasps its meaning because his doctor's argument, made years before, supplied the explanation. That argument never failed. It merely lay [[quiescent|quiescent]], waiting for an event to give it urgency. Experience provided the motive; argument had long since provided the meaning.

The statement, then, is right about which force strikes harder and wrong about which reaches farther. Experience can [[exorcise|exorcise]] a dangerous illusion in a single night, as no lecture can, but it touches only the beliefs one life can test, it often comes too late, and even when it succeeds it tends to complete an argument rather than replace it. For everything slower, larger, or less visible, argument is our only [[recourse|recourse]], and the most valuable arguments may be those that seem to fail at first but are remembered when experience finally arrives.
