prompt.statement: Historical events are better understood through the lives of ordinary people than through the decisions of leaders.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Whose Choices Actually Made the Event
essays.essay:
The statement hides an ambiguity in the word "understood." To understand a historical event can mean knowing what it was like to live through it, or knowing why it happened. For the first, the lives of ordinary people are nearly always the better guide. For the second, they are the better guide only when the event was built from countless small choices rather than imposed by a few people on everyone else. I therefore concede the statement more ground than conventional histories do, but not all of it. Vietnam's economic reforms of the 1980s show the statement at its strongest, and Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge shows where it breaks down.

The standard account of Doi Moi, the "renovation" that turned one of Asia's poorest countries into one of its fastest-growing economies, is a story about leaders. In December 1986, confronting food shortages and triple-digit inflation, the Communist Party's Sixth Congress began moving the country from central planning toward a market economy. This account is not false; the Congress did decide, and its decision bound the nation. In leader-centered histories, however, ordinary people appear only as a [[plaintive|plaintive]] chorus, enduring the shortages that wiser policy relieves. What such histories cannot explain is why the leadership changed course rather than enforcing collective farming more harshly, or why the reforms took the form they took.

The answer to both questions lies in the rice paddies. For years before 1986, farmers had quietly withdrawn effort from collective land and poured it into the family plots they were allowed to keep, which proved far more productive. Peasants who appeared politically [[quiescent|quiescent]], staging no uprisings and issuing no manifestos, were in effect voting with their labor. A few bold provincial officials, risking their careers, [[contravened|contravene]] Party policy by secretly letting cooperatives contract fields to individual households. Hanoi first condemned these arrangements, then partly sanctioned them in 1981, and finally embraced them: a 1988 resolution made the household, rather than the collective, the basic unit of farming. By the end of the decade, a country that had depended on imported rice was exporting it. The 1986 timing, admittedly, came partly from the top: a botched currency reform had sent prices soaring, and the death of Party chief Le Duan opened the way for reformers. But the direction reform took was shaped in the villages, where farmers had already hollowed out the collectives and, with local officials, invented their replacement. Here ordinary lives were not [[tangential|tangential]] to the event but at its core, and a historian who read only Party resolutions would mistake the signature for the authorship.

The statement fares worse when power is concentrated enough to override the many. On April 17, 1975, the Khmer Rouge captured Phnom Penh and began driving its entire population into the countryside. Hospital patients were forced into the streets. Within four years, starvation, overwork, and execution had killed well over a million Cambodians. Survivors' memoirs are indispensable for grasping the atrocities the regime [[perpetrated|perpetrate]]; no study of its leaders can convey what it meant to leave one's home at gunpoint. Yet these accounts cannot explain why a capital was emptied, because the cause did not lie with the people who walked out. It lay in the agrarian fanaticism of a small, secretive, [[despotic|despotic]] leadership determined to abolish money, markets, and urban life itself. In Phnom Penh, ordinary people were not the authors of history but those on whom it was inflicted.

These cases shape my position from both sides. Vietnam persuades me that the statement is truer than leader-centered histories admit; Cambodia keeps me from accepting it whole. The difference is not simply between freedom and dictatorship, since both countries were ruled by communist parties that tolerated no opposition. It lies in what each event required. A harvest depends on the daily cooperation of millions who can quietly withhold it; an evacuation at gunpoint requires only orders and obedience. Even obedience is a choice, but the regime's soldiers, zealous or coerced, could carry out the order, not reverse it. The historian's first task, then, is not to choose between the palace and the village but to discover, case by case, whose choices actually made the event.

prompt.statement: Museums should abolish admission fees, even if that means fewer special exhibitions.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Free the Collection, Not the Exhibitions
essays.essay:
The recommendation treats a museum as one institution with one price of entry, but most large museums are two institutions sharing a building. The first, the permanent collection, works much like a public library: it is held in trust for the public, and its value grows with frequent, casual use. The second, the program of special exhibitions, works more like a theater season: each show is assembled at great cost, runs for a few months, and disappears. Separate these functions, and the recommendation turns out to bundle a sound proposal with a poor bargain. I agree that permanent collections should be free wherever public funding can sustain them, but I would not sacrifice exhibitions to that end, nor would I urge free entry on museums that lack public support.

The case for free admission is strongest for the library function. In 2001 Britain ended admission charges at the national museums that still imposed them, and visits rose sharply. Yet the larger gain is the kind of visit free entry permits. Anyone who has lived near a free museum knows the pattern: a visitor can stop in for ten minutes at lunch or spend a [[languid|languid]] afternoon in a single gallery, certain she can return next week. A ticket encourages the opposite habit, a dutiful march through every room to get one's money's worth, followed by years of absence. Here the recommendation's goal is plainly right.

The "even if" clause, however, openly accepts the loss of exhibitions but underestimates how large that loss would be. Exhibitions are not ornaments; they are where much of a museum's intellectual work happens. They are expensive to mount, since lenders are exacting about light and humidity and fragile loans must be crated, insured, and often escorted by couriers. The expense buys what a permanent installation rarely offers: an argument. A seventeenth-century Dutch still life can be densely [[allusive|allusive]], its skull, hourglass, and extinguished candle speaking of mortality, yet a casual visitor may see only a handsome arrangement of objects. An exhibition that gathers dozens of such paintings and explains their conventions teaches that visitor to read the whole genre, and the lesson carries back into the free galleries. A museum that traded exhibitions for free entry would open its doors to a collection that seldom changed, and the [[repercussions|repercussion]] would outlast any single season: fewer catalogs, less research, fewer reasons to return. On this count the recommendation would do real harm.

The library analogy also exposes a second weakness: libraries are free because taxes pay for them. A small historical society may rely on ticket sales for much of its budget; abolishing fees there would cause a [[precipitous|precipitous]] drop in revenue. Gifts, memberships, and savings from canceled exhibitions might narrow that gap, but a small museum usually has few wealthy patrons and few exhibitions to cancel, so it has little [[recourse|recourse]] once ticket revenue vanishes and often must cut hours, staff, or conservation. Even the Metropolitan Museum of Art, which had let visitors pay what they wished for decades, began charging out-of-state visitors a fixed fee in 2018, after the share paying the full suggested amount fell steeply; New York State residents and students from New York, New Jersey, and Connecticut could still pay what they chose. The Met's rule may look [[finicky|finicky]], yet it reveals a distinction the recommendation ignores: who bears the fee. For a tourist who has crossed an ocean, admission is a trivial part of the trip; for a family across town, it may decide whether they visit once a year or once a month.

These examples lead me to accept the recommendation's aim while rejecting its terms. The useful question is not whether museums should charge but for what, and to whom. Where public money sustains a collection the public already owns, its galleries should be free, and public budgets, not the exhibitions that make those galleries intelligible, should bear the cost. A museum without such support should not adopt free entry as a gesture it cannot afford. Free permanent collections, ticketed exhibitions, and fees placed where they deter the fewest visitors would deliver nearly everything the recommendation promises without the sacrifice it demands.

prompt.statement: Public libraries should become community centers rather than mainly places to borrow books.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Access, Not Activities, Defines the Library
essays.essay:
The strongest case for turning libraries into community centers comes from public health. Studying Chicago's 1995 heat wave, the sociologist Eric Klinenberg compared two adjacent, similarly poor neighborhoods with strikingly different death rates and argued that far fewer elderly residents died where busy streets and shops drew people outdoors and into one another's sight. Libraries do the same work; many cities open them as cooling centers and train staff to reverse opioid overdoses with naloxone. Where the library is a neighborhood's only free indoor space, following the recommendation is plainly advantageous, and [[plaintive|plaintive]] appeals to the library's literary mission sound less like principle than like nostalgia. Yet the heat-wave refuge works for a reason the recommendation overlooks: the library asks nothing of the people it shelters. Libraries should adopt community functions that widen free access, but they should not become community centers "rather than" libraries, which would erase what no other institution offers.

The recommendation assumes that a library's purpose is lending. But lending was only one expression of a deeper function: offering knowledge and a public room to anyone, unconditionally. Fewer loans, then, do not leave the building idle. A community center gathers people around activities; a library gathers them around access. The difference matters most to people who come to be left alone: the retiree reading the papers at a [[languid|languid]] pace, the teenager whose family's crowded apartment offers neither a desk nor silence. The library is where the teenager [[surmounts|surmount]] that disadvantage; she needs a table, a shelf of books, and no one asking her to join anything. A library defined by programming measures success by attendance, and the solitary reader, who appears on no sign-up sheet, becomes invisible to whoever sets its budget.

Victorian England shows that the two functions can coexist when access comes first. The Public Libraries Act of 1850 let larger English and Welsh boroughs, with ratepayers' consent, levy a modest rate for free libraries, and its supporters hoped reading rooms would draw working men from the alehouse. The rooms did become social places, crowded with laborers reading newspapers few of them could afford, but the crowd assembled around print, not a calendar of events; community was the by-product of access. Recent British experience supplies the first circumstance where conversion does harm. After austerity began in 2010, many councils closed branches or folded them into "community hubs," and critics argued that the label concealed shrinking book budgets and volunteers replacing trained librarians. When a library is [[subsumed|subsume]] into a hub, the building may survive while the institution inside it quietly disappears.

The second harmful circumstance is subtler, and medicine offers the clearest analogy. A 1986 federal law requires hospitals that accept Medicare to screen anyone arriving at their emergency departments and to stabilize, or appropriately transfer, those with an emergency condition, regardless of ability to pay. For some uninsured patients, that open door has become a substitute for primary care. Such openness is humane, but an emergency room is a poor place to manage diabetes, which demands continuity rather than crisis care, and a backstop that cannot say no makes it easy to postpone building the clinics those patients need. Many urban libraries are already overwhelmed by people other institutions have failed: people without homes, people in psychiatric crisis, people who are simply lonely. Declaring the library a community center would turn that burden into policy, letting a city cut outreach workers and cite the library as proof the need is met. However [[mettlesome|mettlesome]], a librarian with a naloxone kit is not an addiction clinic.

The heat wave argues for expansion; the hubs and the emergency room argue for limits. Together they turn my answer from a verdict into a test. A community function belongs in the library when it extends free, unconditional access to knowledge or shelter and no better institution can provide it. It does not belong there when it crowds out the collection and the quiet, or lets a city retire services it ought to fund elsewhere. The library has always been a community institution; its distinctive gift is a public room where no one is required to participate, a gift worth protecting even if borrowing declines.

prompt.statement: Complete honesty is not always the best policy in public life.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Secrecy Built to End, Not to Last
essays.essay:
Whether the statement is wise depends on what "complete honesty" means. If it means never lying, the statement is a dangerous license, since an official permitted to lie when convenient will find it convenient often. If it means disclosing everything one knows the moment one knows it, the statement is plainly true. I agree with it only in this second sense, and even then the exceptions are narrow. Withholding is justified only when three conditions hold: disclosure would chiefly help someone intent on harm, the silence has a definite end, and the delay could be defended once revealed. Where those conditions fail, and above all where citizens must act on what they are told, nothing short of full candor will do.

The statement holds most clearly in computer security. When researchers find a serious flaw in widely used software or hardware, the norm is coordinated disclosure: the company responsible is told privately and given time to fix it before the details go public. The processor flaws known as Meltdown and Spectre stayed under such an embargo for months while patches were prepared. Immediate, complete honesty would have handed criminals a blueprint for attacks no one could yet block. What justifies this silence is its structure. The information would have helped attackers far more than users, the secrecy carried an expiration date, and when it ended, the researchers published everything, so the decision to wait could itself be judged.

Remove those conditions and the case for reticence collapses, nowhere more visibly than in public health. As concern grew in Britain that "mad cow disease" might spread to people, the government chose reassurance; the agriculture minister even tried to [[mollify|mollify]] anxious consumers by offering his young daughter a hamburger before television cameras. Officials did not, strictly speaking, lie. They projected a confidence the evidence did not support, itself a form of dishonesty. When the government later announced a probable link to a new, fatal variant of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, beef sales went into a [[precipitous|precipitous]] decline. The deeper [[repercussions|repercussion]] fell on trust: public confidence in food-safety assurances crumbled, and an official inquiry judged the campaign of reassurance a mistake. Here there was no adversary to arm. A prion cannot read a press release; only the public could use the information, by deciding what to eat. Nor would veiled warnings have helped, since hints alert the well-informed and leave everyone else [[oblivious|oblivious]].

The most compelling challenge to my position comes not from those who want more secrecy but from those who want none. Any exception, they argue, will be administered by the very people it benefits. Officials are blamed for panic but rarely for silence, so even sincere ones overrate the dangers of disclosure; the claim that the public cannot handle the truth has long been the favorite excuse of [[despotic|despotic]] governments. The objection is right that an official's own conviction is no safeguard. In the Tuskegee study, the U.S. Public Health Service [[perpetrated|perpetrate]] a deception lasting four decades, concealing from hundreds of Black men in Alabama that they had syphilis and withholding penicillin even after it became the standard cure. But my conditions rest on structure, not sincerity. In coordinated disclosure, a researcher can announce a fixed deadline and publish when it passes, whether or not the company is ready; Tuskegee, by contrast, depended on its subjects never learning the truth and ended only after a whistleblower went to the press. Secrecy that an outsider can end differs in kind from secrecy built to last; forbidding both sacrifices real protection to prevent an abuse the distinction already excludes.

Saying everything at once, then, is not always the best policy, but the exceptions are few and sharply bounded. An official may stay silent for a time when speaking would chiefly arm an adversary, when someone other than the official can end the silence, and when the full record will be published afterward so the delay can be judged. When the people being protected are also the ones who must act, as patients, consumers, or voters, the only defensible policy is to tell them what is known, what is not, and how sure anyone can honestly be.

prompt.statement: Charitable giving does more good when it is anonymous.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Silent to Recipients, Visible to Everyone Else
essays.essay:
The statement treats anonymity as a single virtue, but a donor can be hidden from two distinct audiences: the person who receives the gift and the public at large. These two silences do different work. Concealing the giver from the recipient usually does more good, because it spares the recipient a debt of gratitude and denies the giver any claim to deference. Concealing the giver from the public usually does less good, because it removes both the example that draws others into giving and the scrutiny that keeps giving honest. I therefore accept the statement in its first sense and largely reject it in its second.

The case for hiding the giver from the recipient goes back at least to Maimonides, who in the twelfth century ranked the gift in which neither party knows the other second only to helping a person become self-sufficient, and judged it better for the poor not to know their benefactor than the reverse. The logic is simple: a gift with a face attached creates a relationship, and relationships between benefactor and beneficiary are rarely equal. Anyone who has watched a struggling relative accept help from a prosperous one has seen how quickly assistance hardens into a ledger: the recipient must attend the right gatherings, defer to the right opinions, and write a [[plaintive|plaintive]] note of thanks that doubles as a plea for further help. Miss one family dinner, and the recipient may spend weeks trying to [[mollify|mollify]] a slighted benefactor. A recipient who does not know the giver owes no one that performance.

Hiding the giver from the public is another matter. Generosity spreads by example, and example requires visibility. The Giving Pledge, launched in 2010, asks billionaires to commit publicly to giving away most of their wealth, on the premise that a public promise moves peers as a private check cannot. The same logic works when an office passes around a sign-up sheet for a colleague's funeral costs: each name on the sheet makes the next easier to write. Visibility also permits scrutiny. In 2019 it emerged that the MIT Media Lab had accepted money from Jeffrey Epstein, years after his conviction for a sex crime involving a minor, and had recorded his gifts as anonymous to keep them from public view. Anonymity there protected no one's modesty; it let an institution take money it could not openly accept without appearing to [[condone|condone]] his crimes.

The strongest objection to my view is that publicity does not merely multiply gifts; it bends them. Donors who expect credit gravitate toward what can carry a name, such as a stadium or a university wing, and away from operating budgets, rural clinics, and other needs no one will engrave. A smaller sum given quietly, the objector concludes, may do more good than a larger one given for applause. This objection is right about naming but wrong about knowing. What distorts giving is glorification, not disclosure: the plaque, the gala, the name carved over the door. A plain public record of who gave how much to whom would preserve example and scrutiny while offering vanity little to feed on, and it would let anyone judge whether accepting a gift [[contravenes|contravene]] an institution's principles. Anonymity does not cure misallocation; it merely hides it from anyone who might object.

Public anonymity does more good under one condition: when exposure invites reprisal. In NAACP v. Alabama in 1958, the Supreme Court refused to let the state force the organization to surrender its membership lists, which named the ordinary people whose dues sustained it. At a time when segregationists [[perpetrated|perpetrate]] violence against civil rights supporters, anonymity was not modesty but protection. The exception is narrow. Anonymity also spares a donor from being [[inundated|inundate]] with requests, but that convenience belongs to the giver; it does not make the gift do more good.

Generosity, then, does the most good when it is anonymous to the people it helps and visible to everyone else: discreet enough to spare the recipient a debt, public enough to invite imitation and scrutiny. Only where visibility would endanger the giver should the second silence be added to the first.

prompt.statement: Some people believe that scientific findings should reach the public only after experts agree on them. Others believe that the public should see science as it develops, disagreements included.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Disclose the Evidence, Withhold the Certainty
essays.essay:
Both views frame the question as a choice between speaking and staying silent, but silence is never neutral. While experts wait to agree, the public does not suspend judgment; it acts on what it already believes and listens to whoever is willing to talk. The first view rightly fears that half-formed science will mislead; the second rightly insists that people who live with the consequences of a question are entitled to watch it being answered. My own position is closer to the second view, with one refinement: the public should see evidence as it develops, disputes included, but firm advice should wait for agreement. Where the balance falls depends on two questions: who bears the cost of waiting, and whether the public is being informed or instructed.

The first view is most persuasive when a preliminary finding reaches the public not as information but as a prescription. Early in the COVID-19 pandemic, plasma from [[convalescent|convalescent]] patients was promoted in the United States on the strength of uncontrolled data and given to large numbers of hospitalized patients. That hasty embrace carried a cost beyond false hope: because the treatment was easy to obtain, American researchers struggled to enroll patients in the randomized trials that could have tested it. Britain's large RECOVERY trial later showed that plasma did not improve survival. Yet the harm came not from the public glimpsing early data but from officials presenting an untested hypothesis as routine treatment. The case vindicates caution about prescriptions, not secrecy about evidence.

The first view fails, and fails badly, when the cost of delay falls on the public and those who can delay agreement profit from it. In the 1950s, residents of Minamata in southern Japan developed an illness that caused numbness, tremors, and worse; some children were born with it. Within a few years, researchers at Kumamoto University had traced it to organic mercury in wastewater from the Chisso Corporation's chemical plant. Chisso and its industry allies [[assailed|assail]] the finding and floated other culprits, including wartime munitions supposedly dumped in the bay. Meanwhile, Chisso's own hospital director had induced the disease in cats fed the plant's wastewater, and the company suppressed the results. With experts portrayed as divided, the government did not officially blame Chisso's wastewater until 1968, and the plant kept discharging mercury for most of that time. The first view assumes a [[disinterested|disinterested]] arbiter who will announce agreement once the evidence warrants it. At Minamata, the power to withhold consensus became a license to keep polluting.

Openness has a failure condition too. In 2020, the public was [[inundated|inundate]] with claims drawn from unreviewed preprints, and one early manuscript, withdrawn within days, nonetheless fed rumors that the virus had been engineered. Disclosure without context is not transparency; it is noise. Yet much of the public's confusion came from too little candor rather than too much. Americans told that healthy people did not need masks, and weeks later that they should cover their faces in public, were understandably [[nonplussed|nonplussed]]. The reversal reflected new evidence that people could spread the virus before feeling sick, but the first advice had blended uncertain science with a practical aim, saving scarce masks for health workers, and presented the mixture as settled fact. Had officials called the evidence thin, kept the shortage separate from the science, and labeled their advice provisional, the change would have read as learning, not incoherence.

The real question, then, is not whether the public should see unsettled science but in what form. The first view fuses two acts, disclosing evidence and recommending action; by withholding evidence to avoid premature advice, it lets whoever can stall agreement decide when the public learns anything. I would separate them. Evidence and the disputes around it belong to the public once they are credible, honestly labeled to show how settled they are; firm recommendations belong only to what has survived scrutiny, and advice that cannot wait should announce itself as provisional. Trust that took years to build can suffer a [[precipitous|precipitous]] fall when confident advice is reversed. Science owes the public its doubts as well as its conclusions. What it should hold back is not information but a certainty it has not yet earned.

prompt.statement: Some believe that people are shaped mainly by their upbringing. Others believe that people are shaped mainly by the choices they make as adults.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Choice Decides What Childhood Is For
essays.essay:
Children do not choose their parents, their first language, or the habits of discipline or neglect around them, and by the time they can reflect on these influences, they have already absorbed them. Proponents of the first view rightly insist on this, since much of what we call character is laid down before we are old enough to consent to it. Yet advocates of adult choice point to what the first view struggles to explain: people with similar childhoods often become different adults, and some turn sharply from the paths their childhoods seemed to set. I find the second view closer to the truth, but only in a qualified form. Upbringing supplies the material a person works with and, in extreme cases, can damage the capacity to work at all; within those limits, adult choices determine what the material becomes.

The tennis player Andre Agassi offers the strongest case I know for the first view. His father, a former Olympic boxer from Iran, was determined that his son would become the best player in the world. He modified a ball machine the boy came to call "the dragon," required him to hit thousands of balls a day, [[berated|berate]] him when he faltered, and sent him away at thirteen to a Florida tennis academy. Nearly everything Agassi could do on a court he had learned under [[duress|duress]]. The method worked as designed: he turned professional at sixteen and won Wimbledon in his early twenties. Yet in his memoir, Open, he wrote that he had always hated tennis, which makes his success look less like his own achievement than like the handiwork of a [[despotic|despotic]] father. If the story ended there, the first view would win outright.

It did not end there. By late 1997, despite three major titles, Agassi had fallen outside the top hundred and, by his own later admission, had used crystal methamphetamine. The first view predicts what should have followed: a man trained toward a goal he never chose abandons it once the trainer's grip loosens. Instead, Agassi chose to start over. He played the sport's minor-league circuit, rebuilt his conditioning, and in 1999 won the French Open, completing a career Grand Slam. He never [[exorcised|exorcise]] his resentment of the game; what changed, by his own account, was that he now played for reasons he had chosen rather than inherited, which later included funding a school he founded for disadvantaged children in Las Vegas. The comeback did not erase his upbringing. It [[subsumed|subsume]] his father's project within a larger purpose of his own. That pattern, I suspect, is typical: adult choice rarely escapes childhood, but it decides what childhood will be used for.

A darker case marks the limit of the second view. Under Nicolae Ceausescu, Romania's orphanages held many thousands of children with almost no individual care. After his regime collapsed in 1989, British families adopted some of these children, and researchers followed them into adulthood. Those who had spent under six months in the institutions fared about as well as British-born adoptees. Many who had stayed longer still showed attention and social difficulties in their twenties, along with emotional problems that emerged in adolescence, despite loving adoptive homes. These were not failures of will; the deprivation had impaired the very faculties that deliberate choice requires. The case does not [[refute|refute]] the second view, but it exposes an assumption its advocates rarely state: that a capable chooser exists before the choosing begins. Upbringing does much to build that chooser, and when it fails badly enough, it leaves deficits that no amount of later resolve can fully [[surmount|surmount]].

The second view, then, comes closer to my own, provided it is properly bounded. Childhood shapes much of what a person carries into adulthood, and in its rare catastrophic failures it can limit how much choosing that person can do. For most people, however, whose childhoods leave them imperfect but capable of deliberation, the deciding force lies in the uses to which they put what they were given. Agassi could not choose his childhood. He could choose what it would serve, and that decision, more than the regimen that preceded it, made him who he became.

prompt.statement:
Claim: Writers and artists should not be expected to explain their work.
Reason: A work that needs explanation has already failed.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Unclear Work Fails; Unfamiliar Work Waits
essays.essay:
To say that a work "needs explanation" can mean two different things. A work may be unclear: its maker meant something and failed to convey it. Or it may be unfamiliar: it says what it means, but to an audience that lacks the knowledge or habits it presupposes. The stated reason [[subsumes|subsume]] the second kind under the first; that is its central error. I largely accept the claim that writers and artists should not be expected to explain their work, but not because explanation signals failure. The better reason is that an artist's explanation tends to shrink the work it explains. Even so, the claim yields when a work occupies shared public space.

For unclear work, the reason is nearly right, and commercial design shows why. The design theorist Don Norman argued that a door needing a "Push" sign is a badly designed door: its shape should tell the hand what to do, and the sign admits it does not. Advertising works under the same discipline. A billboard gets only the seconds a driver spends passing it, so copy that requires a second reading has already lost its audience, and good copywriters purge every trace of accidental ambiguity. Literature is not exempt. A novel whose plot cannot be followed because its prose is careless is not redeemed by an author's note; the note is a patch, and the patch confirms the failure.

Unfamiliar work is another matter. Nguyen Du's Tale of Kieu, widely regarded as Vietnam's greatest poem, is densely [[allusive|allusive]], drawing on Chinese poetry, history, and legend. Its first scholar-readers, steeped in the Chinese classics, recognized most of those references unaided. A Vietnamese student today, educated in the Romanized script, is often [[nonplussed|nonplussed]] by the same lines and needs an annotated edition. Nothing in the poem changed; its audience did. If needing explanation were proof of failure, a masterpiece would have failed sometime in the last century. Kieu also shows that a work can need explanation at one level while succeeding at another: for generations, villagers who could not have named a single source memorized and recited its verses, because its story and music required no gloss. Whether a work needs explanation is a fact about the distance between a work and its audience, not a verdict on the work.

Notice, though, that Kieu's footnotes were written by scholars, not by Nguyen Du. The context an unfamiliar work needs can come from anyone, and usually comes better from someone other than the author, whose explanation carries an authority that hardens into an answer key. T. S. Eliot added notes to The Waste Land for its first book edition; he later admitted adding them partly to fill out a slim volume and regretted sending readers chasing sources instead of reading the poem. That is the real case for the claim.

The claim does have a limit. A work in shared public space confronts people who never chose to see it, and its maker can fairly be asked to account for its purpose, though not to decode its meaning. When Maya Lin, then a Yale undergraduate, won the competition to design the Vietnam Veterans Memorial, critics [[assailed|assail]] her abstract black wall, sunk into the earth, as a monument to shame. She defended the design publicly, arguing that the names themselves were the memorial. The wall was built as she designed it, but only after opponents were [[mollified|mollify]] by the promise of a statue and a flagpole nearby, a concession she opposed. The memorial's later history [[refutes|refute]] the stated reason as neatly as Kieu does: visitors now need no explanation, finding a name and seeing their own faces reflected beside it in the polished granite.

The claim, then, is sound in most cases but rests on the wrong foundation. Needing explanation is not a symptom of failure; it is often the cost of distance, whether across centuries, as with Kieu, or across habits of seeing, as with Lin's first critics. Only an unclear work is condemned by its need for a gloss. An unfamiliar one deserves patience, and its maker owes the public, at most, an account of what the work is for, never the key to what it means.

prompt.statement:
Claim: After a natural disaster, communities should rebuild where they stood rather than relocate to safer ground.
Reason: A community's ties to its place are worth more than the protection that moving would provide.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Ties That Travel, Hazards That Return
essays.essay:
The claim and its reason deserve different verdicts. Taken as a general rule, the reason is false: no attachment to a place is worth more than the lives a predictable hazard will take there. Yet the claim itself is right more often than that verdict implies, and for a reason its authors never offer. Relocation frequently fails to deliver the protection it promises, because the ties it severs are not sentimental luxuries but the means by which people earn a living and look after one another. Whether a community should rebuild where it stood therefore depends on two questions the statement ignores: whether the hazard will return with lethal force, and whether the community can move without coming apart.

When the hazard is certain to return and likely to kill, the reason collapses. In 1985 Colombia's Nevado del Ruiz volcano erupted, melting part of its ice cap and sending mudflows that buried the town of Armero and killed most of its residents. Armero stood on deposits left by earlier mudflows from the same mountain, the most recent in 1845. The volcano had lain largely [[quiescent|quiescent]] since then, but it stirred for about a year before erupting, and a hazard map published weeks beforehand showed the town at high risk. The danger was neither hidden nor unprecedented; it was simply discounted. Colombia did not rebuild the town. Survivors were resettled elsewhere; many have marked the sites of their lost homes with tombstones, turning the ruins into a memorial. Their attachment is genuine, but it cannot justify rebuilding in the path of the next mudflow. Armero shows that honoring a place and living on it are different obligations.

Where the hazard recurs but can be survived, however, the claim regains ground, though not because attachment outweighs safety. After severe floods along the Zambezi in the 2000s, Mozambique's government urged tens of thousands of floodplain residents to resettle permanently on higher ground. Many kept returning to the lowlands to plant, judging that the land above the floodplain could not feed large families. In ordinary years the river that occasionally devastates the valley is [[languid|languid]] and dependable, keeping its fields better watered and more fertile than the uplands. The families' ties were a matter not of nostalgia but of economics, and a [[precipitous|precipitous]] relocation that ignored them did not remove people from danger; it left them commuting into it. In such places, rebuilding near the fields, with better warnings and sturdier houses, may protect more people than a move they will not sustain. Relocation is fragile: it works only when land, water, and work move with the people, and it fails quietly when any one stays behind.

Even deep ties do not by themselves support the claim, for the reason rests on a hidden assumption: that a community's ties reside in the soil rather than in its people. Ties to neighbors and institutions, unlike ties to fields, can travel. When a levee failed during the Mississippi River flood of 1993, the village of Valmeyer, Illinois, went under. Most residents backed moving the village to bluffs several hundred feet higher, where it was rebuilt with federal help. Many residents settled elsewhere, and the population took years to recover, but because a core of neighbors chose to move together rather than being ordered to, Valmeyer survived as a village instead of dissolving into scattered households. Resettlement imposed by decree, in contrast, [[contravenes|contravene]] a principle that disaster planners increasingly accept: those who bear a risk should help decide how it is managed. The ties the reason invokes are real, but most of them [[buttress|buttress]] the case for moving communities whole, not for leaving them in harm's way.

A doctor may send a [[convalescent|convalescent]] patient home early because familiar surroundings aid recovery, but no doctor discharges a patient to a burning house. Communities deserve the same judgment. They should rebuild where they stood when the hazard is rare or manageable and their livelihoods are bound to the site; they should relocate when the danger is sure to return and likely to kill, moving together and on terms they help set. The reason names something real, but it treats a condition for recovery as if it outranked survival.

prompt.statement: Schools should stop assigning letter grades and give students written evaluations instead.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Narratives for Teaching, Grades for Sorting
essays.essay:
The proposal to replace letter grades with written evaluations rests on an unstated assumption: that the two do the same job and are therefore interchangeable. They do not. A grade is a signal sent outward, to parents, colleges, and employers who must compare students quickly; a written evaluation is a message sent inward, to a student who needs to know what to do next. A single letter [[subsumes|subsume]] mastery, effort, improvement, and even punctuality, and no reader can tell which produced it. It therefore serves the outsider tolerably and the learner poorly. Tracing the likely consequences of abolishing grades leads me to a qualified position: schools should make written evaluations their primary form of feedback, especially in the early years, but should keep a coarse grade wherever outsiders must compare students, because outright abolition would quietly penalize the very students it aims to help.

The policy's intended consequence, better feedback, is real, and it is largest where the stakes of comparison are lowest. When a ten-year-old brings home a C-plus in science, the letter invites a frustrated parent to [[berate|berate]] her and tells neither what went wrong; a paragraph noting that her lab reports are careful but her conclusions outrun her data gives both something to work on. Youth sports offer a parallel. Norway's sports confederation forbids the formal ranking of young children: they play and compete, but without official standings or national championships, and coaches are urged to stress skill and enjoyment over results. Comparison is postponed until it can mean something. Norway has nonetheless led the medal table at recent Winter Olympics. That record does not prove the approach caused the success, but it does [[refute|refute]] the notion that withholding early scores must breed complacency.

The unintended consequences emerge where comparison cannot be postponed. Abolishing a grade does not abolish the competition it summarized; it forces whoever does the sorting to find another signal, and the substitute can be cruder than the original. Medical education recently ran this experiment. When Step 1 of the United States Medical Licensing Examination switched from a three-digit score to pass/fail, the aim was to end a consuming fixation on that number. Residency programs, [[inundated|inundate]] with far more applications than they could read closely, did not stop ranking; they shifted weight to the next available number, the Step 2 Clinical Knowledge score. Many observers also warned that programs would lean harder on the prestige of an applicant's medical school, which reflects where a student was admitted rather than what she did there. The anxiety did not disappear; it moved. A high school that drops grades in the name of equity may likewise push colleges toward a school's name or a family's connections, signals that favor the already advantaged. That risk alone persuades me that grades must survive somewhere.

A second unintended consequence concerns the evaluations themselves: good ones are expensive to write and hard for strangers to read. The University of California, Santa Cruz, opened with narrative evaluations in place of grades, yet over later decades made letter grades the norm. As enrollment grew, writing an assessment for every student in crowded lecture courses became a heavy burden. Students worried that graduate and professional schools would be [[nonplussed|nonplussed]] by transcripts with paragraphs instead of a grade point average, and with reason: calibrating wording so that "excellent" means the same thing from one instructor to the next is [[finicky|finicky]] work, and no outsider can tell whether it was done. A hasty evaluation decays into boilerplate praise for being a pleasure to have in class, which tells a student as little as a B does while costing the teacher far more.

Weighed together, these consequences call for a division of labor rather than a replacement. Written evaluations should carry the teaching, from the first report card onward, because they tell a learner what no letter can. A coarse grade should survive only at the few junctures where strangers must compare students, and even there it should travel with the narrative rather than in place of it. A school that abolishes grades outright will not end ranking; it will merely surrender ranking to proxies it can neither see nor correct.

prompt.statement: Developers should be required to include affordable homes in every new residential building.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Mandate the Outcome, Not the Method
essays.essay:
The proposal to require affordable homes in every new residential building joins a worthy goal to a blunt instrument. The goal, neighborhoods in which teachers, nurses, and bus drivers can afford to live where they work, deserves the force of law, because it collides with local interests that a voluntary program can leave undisturbed. The instrument, however, hinges on the word "every," which ignores how differently a forty-story tower and a twelve-unit walk-up respond to the same obligation. Tracing the policy's likely consequences, intended and unintended, leads me to support a binding requirement on developers, but one that prescribes an outcome rather than a single method.

The case for compulsion rests on what happens without it, and New Jersey supplies the evidence. In its Mount Laurel decisions of the 1970s and 1980s, the state supreme court held that zoning that shut out lower-income families [[contravened|contravene]] the state constitution and that each growing town owed its region a fair share of affordable housing. The first ruling announced that duty but left compliance largely to the towns, and for years most simply stalled. Only after the second ruling let builders sue exclusionary towns and win court-ordered approval for projects that set aside lower-income units did the state begin to [[surmount|surmount]] that resistance. The episode shows that a legal duty moves reluctant towns only when someone with a profit motive can enforce it. Its sequel is just as instructive. Eager to [[mollify|mollify]] furious suburbs, the legislature then let towns pay poorer cities to absorb part of their obligation, an arrangement that critics denounced as a purchased exemption and lawmakers eventually abolished. A requirement is necessary, then, but a requirement riddled with exits is merely a price list.

Subtler [[repercussions|repercussion]] follow from the word "every." In costly markets, where affordable units are priced below their cost to build, the requirement acts as a charge on each new project, and that charge does not fall evenly. A luxury tower in a [[buoyant|buoyant]] market can recover the loss through its penthouses; a modest building in an outer neighborhood often cannot. Consider a hypothetical developer weighing twelve apartments on a narrow lot where rents are moderate: if two must be priced well below cost, the project may no longer pay for itself, and the lot stays vacant. Repeated across a city, such decisions could cause a [[precipitous|precipitous]] drop in exactly the mid-sized construction that adds homes more cheaply than towers do. Fewer new homes mean higher rents for everyone, including the families the policy was written to protect. A rule imposed on every building can thus yield fewer affordable homes than a rule imposed on some.

Even where affordable units are built on site, satisfying the letter of a rule can betray its purpose. In the 2010s a luxury tower on Manhattan's Upper West Side won extra floor area from the city and a state-authorized property-tax exemption by including affordable apartments, then placed those units in a separate section with its own entrance, nicknamed the "poor door." The arrangement was legal, and it did create affordable homes; it also announced, through the building's design, that the two groups of tenants were not meant to be neighbors. The outcry led New York to bar separate entrances in buildings receiving those benefits. The lesson is not that mixing incomes within a building is futile but that a count of units is a poor proxy for the goal. Any city that adopts this policy must remain [[vigilant|vigilant]] about how affordable homes are delivered, not merely how many appear.

These consequences point toward a policy that is firmer than the proposal in some respects and more flexible in others. Large projects should be required to include affordable homes, with density bonuses offsetting the cost so that the obligation does not become a tax on new supply. Smaller buildings should contribute proportionally to a fund that builds in the same neighborhood, never in some distant town. And every affordable unit should share the entrances and amenities of its market-rate neighbors. What deserves a mandate is not an affordable unit in every building but an affordable home in every neighborhood, offered on equal terms.

prompt.statement: Most organizations fail not because of bad ideas but because of poor execution of good ones.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Execution Explains Failure Only for Proven Ideas
essays.essay:
The statement rests on an assumption that sounds harmless: that an idea can be judged good or bad apart from how it is carried out. For borrowed ideas that assumption is usually sound; for genuinely new ones the only way to learn whether an idea is good is to execute it, and there separating the two merely shields flawed ideas from blame. Whether the statement holds therefore depends on one condition: whether an organization is borrowing an idea that has already worked or staking itself on one that never has. For the first kind I largely agree; for the second I do not.

Where an idea has been proven elsewhere, failure usually does lie in execution. Consider the 2013 launch of HealthCare.gov, the federal insurance marketplace. The concept was hardly novel; Massachusetts had run a similar exchange for years. Yet the site buckled on its first day and remained barely usable for weeks. The causes were managerial: the agency coordinated dozens of contractors itself, no one was clearly accountable for the whole, and the pieces were scarcely tested together. What the launch lacked was not vision but [[rigor|rigor]]. Once the administration made a single contractor accountable for the whole and brought in outside engineers, the same marketplace enrolled millions within months. When better execution of an unchanged idea succeeds, we can say with confidence that execution was the culprit. Most organizations resemble this case. A new restaurant or clinic copies a model that has worked thousands of times; when it fails, the likelier cause is how it was run, though even a proven model can suit one neighborhood poorly.

The calculus changes when an idea has never been proven, because its quality then includes its fit with the people and conditions it will meet, and only practice reveals that fit. After the Arusha Declaration of 1967, Julius Nyerere [[exhorted|exhort]] rural Tanzanians to leave scattered homesteads for ujamaa villages, where they would farm collectively and receive schools and clinics. The vision was humane. Yet it was unproven: no one knew how farmers, or the land, would respond to dense settlement. When persuasion moved too few families, villagization became compulsory, and in the 1970s millions were resettled, often on sites chosen for administrative convenience rather than fertile soil. The [[ramifications|ramification]] spread nationwide: harvests faltered, and although drought compounded the damage, Tanzania was soon importing grain. Defenders blame overzealous officials, yet the plan itself rested on a [[doctrinaire|doctrinaire]] conviction that planned villages would prosper whatever the soil, the rainfall, or the farmers' own judgment. Once families refused to move, coercion was not a lapse in execution; it was a foreseeable consequence of an idea that depended on farmers' consent yet had no answer when they withheld it.

Even where it holds by count, the statement is dangerous as a general rule: it hands the authors of every failed plan a ready excuse. Jonathan Swift [[lampooned|lampoon]] this habit of mind three centuries ago. In Gulliver's Travels, the projectors of the Academy of Lagado promise that one laborer will do the work of ten and that they can ripen crops in whatever season they choose. None of their schemes works yet; the countryside lies waste, and a nobleman who farms the old way prospers yet is scorned. What gives the satire its bite is the projectors' [[pomposity|pomposity]]: they speak of unfinished inventions as if the world's improvement depended on them. Each setback becomes a reason to press harder, never evidence against their plans. An organization that attributes every failure to the poor execution of a good idea speaks in their voice.

My position, then, is conditional but firm. If an idea proven elsewhere fails, the fault most often lies in execution, and counted by sheer number, such failures probably predominate. When failures are weighed by consequence, however, the balance shifts: many of the costliest belong to governments and ventures attempting the unproven, and there an idea unsuited to the people and conditions it meets is not a good idea badly executed; it is a bad idea. The useful question after any failure is not whether the idea was good in the abstract, but whether a better-run attempt at the same idea has ever worked.

prompt.statement: A person's character is revealed more clearly by small daily choices than by moments of crisis.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Daily Baseline, Crisis Stress Test
essays.essay:
In May 1939, before a game in Detroit, Lou Gehrig took himself out of the New York Yankees' lineup. He had played in 2,130 consecutive games, a streak built on showing up every day and playing through broken fingers, but an undiagnosed illness was draining his strength, and he believed he was hurting the team. Which revealed his character more clearly: the streak or the decision to end it? I largely agree that small daily choices are the better evidence of who a person is, because they are numerous and unforced. Yet routine leaves some virtues untested and some motives ambiguous, and often only a crisis can supply the test or resolve the ambiguity.

For most traits, the statement holds. A single dramatic act can be shaped by adrenaline, an audience, or the strangeness of the moment; a pattern sustained across years is far harder to explain away. When Barbara McClintock's claim that genetic elements could jump between sites on chromosomes met with puzzlement in the early 1950s, she staged no protest. She simply refused to [[relent|relent]]: season after season she planted maize at Cold Spring Harbor, pollinated it by hand, and studied its mottled kernels, until similar mobile elements turned up in bacteria and she received an unshared Nobel Prize in 1983. No single day of that work says much about her; the decades say nearly everything. Small choices are also revealing because nothing compels them. A basketball player who is [[insolent|insolent]] toward referees in meaningless preseason games cannot blame playoff pressure; when almost nothing is at stake, almost nothing but the person explains the conduct.

The statement fails, however, in two kinds of cases. The first involves virtues that ordinary life seldom tests: routine can show whether someone is honest or kind, but it rarely asks anyone to stay composed while a life hangs in the balance. In June 2021, when Christian Eriksen collapsed in cardiac arrest during a European Championship match in Copenhagen, Denmark's captain, Simon Kjær, was among the first to reach him, made sure his airway was clear, and gathered teammates into a ring that shielded Eriksen from the cameras while medics revived him. Nothing in a defender's job resembles a teammate's heart stopping on the field, so years of steady play could not have revealed that composure. One evening says little about how reliably he would act that way again, but it is the only evidence there could be. The second case involves motives that daily life allows to coexist. For years, playing every day served both whatever pride Gehrig took in the streak and his duty to the team, so the streak alone could not show which mattered more. Only when his body's growing [[frailty|frailty]] set those motives against each other did the answer appear: he surrendered the streak rather than burden the team.

These cases shape my position by exposing a [[tacit|tacit]] assumption in the statement: that daily choices and crises measure the same thing, so that one must be the sharper instrument. They do not. Daily choices establish a baseline, showing what a person values and how reliably; crises are stress tests, and a stress test means little without a baseline. Gehrig's farewell at Yankee Stadium in July 1939 shows this dependence. Stricken with an incurable disease that had ended his playing career, he might have been forgiven for turning [[morose|morose]]; instead he told the crowd he considered himself the luckiest man on earth. From someone without his record, the line might sound like bravado. We accept his [[equanimity|equanimity]] at face value because of how he had conducted himself on thousands of ordinary afternoons.

I agree with the statement, then, but only within limits: small daily choices reveal character more clearly, while crises reveal it more completely. Ordinary choices are many and free of excuses, so their pattern is hard to mistake. Crises, by contrast, test virtues that routine seldom summons and rank commitments that routine lets sit comfortably side by side. A fair judgment of anyone needs both: the long record of ordinary days to tell us who a person is, and the rare hard moment to tell us what that person will refuse to give up.

prompt.statement: Organizations should evaluate employees by the results they produce rather than by the hours they work.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Reject the Clock, Question the Tally
essays.essay:
The best argument for this recommendation is that results are what an organization wants, while hours measure only what the work costs. Counting hours rewards the plodding employee over the efficient one, and an [[officious|officious]] manager who notes who leaves before six teaches everyone to display diligence rather than practice it. I grant this argument, but it holds only when the measured result closely tracks what the organization truly wants, lies within the employee's reach, and appears before she is evaluated. The recommendation rests on the [[tacit|tacit]] assumption that all three conditions always hold. Where they do, judging employees by results is advantageous; where any one fails, a results standard can distort work as badly as a time clock. I therefore agree with the recommendation's rejection of hours far more than with its faith in results.

Rwanda's health system shows the recommendation at its best. In the mid-2000s, after district pilots, the country extended nationwide a scheme paying health centers for the quantity and quality of specified services, payments that could fund staff bonuses. An impact evaluation found that, compared with centers in comparison districts given equivalent extra funds without performance conditions, the paid centers recorded substantial increases in clinic births and preventive checkups for young children; the performance condition, not the extra funding, made the difference. The measured result, moreover, lay close to the real goal: a clinic delivery is not itself a healthy mother and newborn, but skilled care at birth is among the best protections for both. Yet the same evaluation exposed a limit: completion of the recommended prenatal visits, which required repeated returns, did not improve. The evaluators found the largest gains in well-paid services needing little provider effort; lower payment may explain part of the prenatal gap, but the pattern suggests results-based pay works best where the result lies within the worker's reach.

Journalism shows what happens when the other conditions fail. When some digital publishers tied writers' pay to page views, the metric favored headlines engineered for clicks over reporting that took weeks to verify; page views became a [[proxy|proxy]] for journalistic value, and writers learned to serve the proxy. Investigative work uncovers a deeper flaw. In 2001 the Boston Globe's Spotlight team began examining how Boston's Catholic archdiocese had concealed sexual abuse by priests. For months it published nothing, even as it won over reluctant sources and persuaded a judge to unseal lawsuit documents. The 2002 stories prompted investigations of dioceses nationwide, and by year's end the cardinal who led the archdiocese had resigned. Had the Globe's editors [[harangued|harangue]] the team each month for its lack of stories, the investigation might never have reached print. Its value arrived late, depended on many hands, and could not be measured until the work was done.

These cases shape my position, but they do not rehabilitate hours: however long the Spotlight reporters worked, their timesheets could not have shown an editor whether they had a story. They reveal, rather, that "results" is not one thing. An organization judging by results must first [[disentangle|disentangle]] what lies within an employee's reach from what lies beyond it; Rwanda's nurses could secure a mother's one-time decision to deliver in a clinic far more readily than her repeated return visits. It must also [[delineate|delineate]], in advance, which outcomes count and over what horizon, since a reporter judged by the quarter and one judged over two years are doing different jobs. Where that definition is possible, results are the fairer standard. Where it is not, the alternative is not the time clock but informed judgment. Someone who understands the work can judge its quality long before its results appear.

My position, then, is narrower than the recommendation without opposing it. Results deserve to be the standard when they closely track the real goal, lie largely within the employee's control, and appear on a schedule the organization can wait for. Beyond those conditions, a [[doctrinaire|doctrinaire]] commitment to results merely replaces one crude count with another. The recommendation is right to abandon the clock; its error is to assume that whatever can be tallied at the end of a quarter is what an organization most values.

prompt.statement: Professionals such as doctors, engineers, and lawyers should have to retake their licensing examinations every ten years.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Retest the Changes, Not the Calendar
essays.essay:
In January 1995, the Great Hanshin earthquake struck Kobe, tipping an elevated stretch of the Hanshin Expressway onto its side. Surveys later found that buildings designed before Japan tightened its seismic code in 1981 had collapsed or been badly damaged far more often than newer ones. Their engineers had largely followed the rules of their day. The disaster poses the question behind this recommendation: what becomes of professionals whose knowledge stops at the year they were licensed? I agree that a license should not certify competence for life, but not that retaking the same examination every ten years is the way to renew it. Retesting helps where knowledge is explicit and periodically overturned; it does little where competence lives in the body or in deep, narrow expertise.

The recommendation would be advantageous where knowledge is codified and revised in discrete steps, and where practitioners work without close supervision. Seismic codes are rewritten after destructive earthquakes, each revision encoding lessons paid for in lives. An engineer licensed before such a change who now works alone, judging whether an old apartment block can be safely renovated, might apply superseded assumptions confidently, with no colleague to catch the error. Medicine offers a parallel. Once researchers showed that the bacterium Helicobacter pylori causes most peptic ulcers, a brief antibiotic regimen [[supplanted|supplant]] the long-term acid suppression, and sometimes the surgery, that physicians had relied on. A doctor who stopped learning in the 1970s would still treat ulcers as a disease of stress and acid. In such circumstances, an examination on current standards is a fair, efficient safeguard: the answers are settled, and a failing score exposes the gap that endangers the public.

Yet the recommendation rests on a hidden assumption: that what deteriorates in a professional is what the licensing examination measured. Advocates take that assumption for granted, but it fails, and retesting loses its advantage, in two common circumstances. The first is when competence is partly [[corporeal|corporeal]]. Much of a surgeon's skill resides in steady hands, sharp eyes, and the stamina for long operations, and the danger that grows with age is [[frailty|frailty]]: a slight tremor, dimming vision, flagging endurance. A written test, whatever its [[rigor|rigor]], detects none of these. Worse, an aging surgeon who passed easily would return to the operating room with a fresh certificate and an unexamined tremor. The second is specialization. A licensing examination tests the broad minimum expected of a novice. A hand surgeon twenty years into practice has sensibly let the details of obstetrics fade, much as a tax attorney has let criminal procedure lapse. Missing such questions would reveal nothing about the safety of their work.

Professionals who resist retesting are easy to caricature, and the [[pomposity|pomposity]] of the senior partner who treats any examination as an insult is real enough. A further objection, however, is not [[captious|captious]]. A recurring high-stakes examination has consequences beyond measuring competence: above all, it changes what people study. Imperial China recruited officials through civil service examinations, and under the Ming and Qing dynasties candidates had to master the rigidly formatted "eight-legged essay." Critics complained that the system rewarded skill at the examination rather than at governing, and the Qing court, struggling to modernize, dropped that format and in 1905 abolished the examinations altogether. A decennial licensing exam would invite the same drift in milder form, pulling professionals away from the problems their patients and clients bring and toward easily scored questions.

These examples shape my position without reversing it. They argue not against accountability across a career but against the calendar and the entry-level examination as its instruments. The Kobe and ulcer cases call for testing that follows the field: when a seismic code or a standard of care changes, practitioners should be examined on the change, whether it arrives after three years or fifteen. The aging surgeon calls for late-career assessment of hands and eyes, not memory. The specialist and China's examination history call for judging professionals by audits of their actual work, not a test designed for beginners. A license should be renewed against the demands of the work its holder does today, not against a syllabus that both the field and the holder have outgrown.

prompt.statement: Societies make more progress by rewarding individual competition than by encouraging cooperation.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Let Groups Compete, Not Colleagues
essays.essay:
The statement takes it as [[axiomatic|axiomatic]] that competition and cooperation are rivals, so that a society must choose between them. That opposition holds at only one level. People can compete against those they work beside, or cooperating groups can compete against other groups; the first arrangement pays a person for outdoing colleagues, the second for helping colleagues outdo everyone else. Only the first, the "individual competition" the statement praises, forces a choice between rivalry and cooperation. I agree that competition drives progress, often more reliably than goodwill does, but not that pitting individuals against their own colleagues is the best way to harness it. Societies advance fastest when cooperating groups compete and individuals are rewarded for what they contribute rather than for whom they defeat.

Team sports show the second arrangement at work: teams compete fiercely, but none wins unless its members play for one another. At the 2004 Olympics, the United States sent a hastily assembled team of professional basketball stars; Argentina sent a squad whose core had played together for years and had beaten American professionals at the 2002 world championship. Argentina beat the Americans in the semifinal and won gold, while the favorites settled for bronze. The Americans had more individual talent, but the Argentines had learned to anticipate one another's movements and to pass up a good shot for a teammate's better one. Tellingly, the American program then asked its stars to sign on for several years rather than a single summer, and reclaimed the gold in 2008. Here competition did produce progress, but what it rewarded was cooperation.

Competition among individuals inside a group works the other way, and education shows the damage most clearly. Under a strict grading curve, only a fixed share of a class can earn top marks, however much the whole class learns. A student who explains a hard concept to a struggling classmate risks her standing, and the rational response is to hoard notes and study alone. The [[ramifications|ramification]] reach beyond the transcript. Explaining an idea is among the surest ways to master it, so the curve penalizes the very activity that produces understanding, and habits [[ingrained|ingrained]] in school follow students into laboratories and hospitals, where work is done in teams. Partly for this reason, many American medical schools now grade their early courses pass/fail: a physician trained to see every classmate as a threat is poorly prepared for a profession in which patients' safety depends on what colleagues tell one another.

The most compelling challenge to this view comes from economic history. Much of Vietnamese agriculture, above all in the North, was long organized into collectives that pooled the harvest and divided it by work points, which tracked attendance far better than effort. Officials could [[exhort|exhort]] members to labor for the common good, but output stagnated. The state [[relented|relent]]: reforms begun tentatively in 1981 and broadened in 1988 let households farm allocated plots under multiyear contracts and sell their surplus, and Vietnam soon turned from importing rice to ranking among the world's leading exporters. Defenders of the statement call this decisive: cooperation failed, and individual reward succeeded. I accept the evidence but not the inference. The collectives were not cooperation that farmers chose; they were a [[doctrinaire|doctrinaire]] scheme imposed from above. They failed because they severed reward from contribution. Nor did the reforms set farmers against one another. They made the household, a small group whose members genuinely cooperate, the unit of reward, and one family's bumper crop took nothing from its neighbors. The case shows that cooperation cannot be commanded or left unrewarded, not that progress requires setting individuals against one another.

The real question, then, is not whether to prefer competition or cooperation but where to stage the contest and what to reward. Rivalry between teams, firms, and laboratories punishes complacency, and its prizes go to those who cooperate best. Rivalry among members of the same team, each ranked against the others, teaches people to withhold exactly what the group needs. A society that lets cooperating groups compete, and rewards people for what they add, will outpace both one that preaches solidarity without reward and one that turns every colleague into an opponent.
