prompt.statement: The internet has made people better informed but worse at judging what is true.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: The Internet Shifted Verification onto Individuals
essays.essay:
In early 2020, a message passed from phone to phone assuring readers that if they could hold their breath for ten seconds without coughing, they were free of the new coronavirus. The same phones could reach the World Health Organization in a few taps, and the agency soon listed the claim among the myths it was correcting. Recipients held both the falsehood and its refutation in their hands; what many lacked was a dependable way to choose between them. I agree that many people now misjudge what they read, but the statement errs in treating being informed and judging truth as separable. The internet has made people better supplied with claims, not better informed, and the culprit is less decaying judgment than a transfer of labor: verification has moved from institutions to individuals ill-equipped to perform it.

The statement treats being informed as a matter of quantity, but to be informed is to hold true beliefs; seeing more claims one cannot evaluate leaves a person no better informed. A generation ago, editors did much of the sorting before a claim reached the public; a newspaper reader inherited that fact-checking without noticing it. Search engines have rebuilt some of that sorting for health questions, but a scroll through social media still [[yields|yield]] clinical guidance, testimonials, and miracle cures in one undifferentiated stream. Faced with that stream, people err in opposite directions: some believe too readily; others mistake [[captious|captious]] objections for critical thinking and dismiss a health agency's correction outright. Both errors trace to the same missing step: no one sorted the claims first.

The law has long understood this. A trial is a deliberately information-poor setting. Rules of evidence generally exclude hearsay, and cross-examination lets each side test opposing witnesses; these procedures help [[disentangle|disentangle]] what a witness observed from what the witness heard or assumed. American judges likewise instruct jurors not to research the case online and have declared mistrials when jurors disobeyed. These safeguards serve fairness to the parties as well as accuracy, but both rest on one premise: a claim should be tested before it shapes a verdict. A juror who looks up the defendant is better informed than fellow jurors only in the crudest sense; in the sense that matters, that juror is worse positioned to judge, because the new claims never faced the [[rigor|rigor]] of the adversarial process and neither party could answer them.

The strongest challenge to my view comes from those who find today's [[lugubrious|lugubrious]] eulogies for trustworthy news historically naive, since the age they mourn never existed. Gatekeepers, they note, were often wrong, and their errors persisted because readers could not verify them. The internet supplied the means: readers can now compare a news report with the full speech it describes, and when the journal Nature compared a sample of Wikipedia's science articles with Britannica's, the encyclopedia anyone may edit fared surprisingly well. On this view, people judge no worse than before; their mistakes are simply more visible. I concede most of this, but the objection's best example confirms my argument. Wikipedia succeeds because it rebuilt the gatekeeping it seemed to abolish: it demands cited sources and lets editors contest changes in public. Where such procedures exist, the internet has sharpened judgment; where they are absent, as in a forwarded chain message, judgment falters however much information lies a few taps away.

The internet, then, has not so much corrupted human judgment as revealed how much of it we once delegated to others. People become informed, rather than merely supplied, only when some procedure stands between a claim and their belief in it. The remedy is not to [[harangue|harangue]] users about their gullibility, since a lecture hands them one more claim to judge, not a better way of judging. It is to rebuild verification wherever people encounter information: in platforms that flag frequently forwarded messages, in schools that teach students to cross-check sources, and in readers who meet an alarming claim with enough [[equanimity|equanimity]] to wait a day and ask who stands behind it. Judgment has always been a collective achievement; the internet has simply enlarged each individual's share of the work.

prompt.statement: Some argue that a free press must be protected even when it publishes harmful falsehoods. Others argue that the press must be held accountable for the harm it causes.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Accountable to the Injured, Not to Power
essays.essay:
Much of the conflict between these views stems from an ambiguity in the phrase "held accountable." The press can be accountable to power, when officials decide which reports are false and punish their publishers. Or it can be accountable to the injured, when a person damaged by a specific falsehood must prove to an independent court that the publisher acted knowingly or recklessly. The first view is, at bottom, a warning against accountability to power; the second is persuasive chiefly as a defense of accountability to the injured. My position lies closer to the first view, because no government can be trusted to decide which falsehoods are harmful. Yet the press deserves protection from the censor, not from every consequence of a lie.

The case for accountability deserves a serious hearing, because falsehood does real harm. During Rwanda's 1994 genocide, the radio station RTLM branded Tutsi as cockroaches and broadcast the names of people to be hunted down; no principle of press freedom worth defending would have sheltered it. Defenders of the press often treat it as [[axiomatic|axiomatic]] that the remedy for false speech is more speech, assuming that truth, given time, will overtake error. Yet a widely cited study of Twitter found that false stories spread farther and faster than true ones. When a fabrication reaches millions before any correction appears, the contest is not fair, and those harmed in the interval have a legitimate [[grievance|grievance]].

Stated without qualification, however, the second view assumes something history rarely provides: an impartial judge. Without one, "harmful falsehood" tends to mean whatever embarrasses the powerful. In an 1898 open letter, Émile Zola accused French army leaders of shielding the real spy in the case of Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish captain wrongly convicted of treason. To the high command the letter was [[insolent|insolent]], and the army, itself the supposed victim, had Zola prosecuted for libel. The presiding judge repeatedly barred questions about the Dreyfus case, though the truth of Zola's charge turned on it. Convicted, then convicted again in his absence after the first verdict was annulled because the wrong party had filed the complaint, Zola fled to England. His central charge proved true, but the state did not fully [[relent|relent]] until 1906, when France's highest court cleared Dreyfus. Satire is equally exposed, since it is false by design: a cartoon that [[lampoons|lampoon]] a prime minister as a foreign ruler's puppet depicts something literally untrue, and that exaggeration is its point.

Accountability to the injured is what the second view rightly demands, yet even a private lawsuit can serve the censor. In New York Times v. Sullivan, an Alabama jury had awarded a Montgomery official a large libel judgment over a civil rights advertisement that misstated minor details and never named him. Had the verdict stood, any [[captious|captious]] official could have combed critical coverage for small mistakes and turned each into a ruinous lawsuit. The Supreme Court instead required public officials to prove that a publisher knew a statement was false or recklessly disregarded the truth. That standard forgives honest error without immunizing deliberate lies. In 2023 Fox News paid more than three-quarters of a billion dollars to settle a voting-machine company's suit over false claims that the company had rigged the 2020 election. The trial judge had already ruled the statements false, leaving a jury to decide whether Fox had acted knowingly or recklessly; the network settled just after the jury was seated.

The real choice, then, is less between protection and accountability than between two answers to one question: who decides what is false? A society that lets officials decide will punish dissent and call it correcting error. A society that requires injured parties to prove deliberate or reckless falsehood before independent judges can keep its press free without making it lawless. With that refinement, I side with the first view: freedom to publish must be the rule, and liability a narrow exception reserved for knowing or reckless falsehoods that injure identifiable people. Some harmful falsehoods will escape any remedy. That cost is real, but it is smaller than the cost of a press that must convince officials of its accuracy before it dares to publish.

prompt.statement: Some people believe that cities should grow upward, with tall buildings. Others believe that cities should spread outward, giving each resident more space.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Build Up, Then Give the Ground Back
essays.essay:
Debates about urban growth usually take it as [[axiomatic|axiomatic]] that space is something a resident owns, an assumption that tilts the question toward the outward view before the argument begins. Measured by floor area and yard size, the detached house wins easily. If we count instead the space a resident actually uses, including streets, parks, and markets, the upward view comes much closer to my own position. I would refine it, however. Height is worth pursuing only when a city returns the land that height saves to the people living in the towers.

The outward view deserves a fair hearing, because it answers physical needs that no planner should wave away: daylight in every room, sleep undisturbed by footsteps overhead, a yard where children can run. Postwar American suburbs gave millions of working families their first houses, and many still regard such a home as the core of a decent life. Yet the [[ramifications|ramification]] of that choice extend well beyond the property line. Where development is [[sparse|sparse]], buses cannot run often enough to be useful, so nearly every errand requires a car. Each new subdivision consumes farmland or forest and adds pipe and pavement that later generations must maintain. The private gain is real, but much of its cost is paid by the public.

Singapore shows what deliberate upward growth looks like. Much of its population once lived in crowded shophouses and squatter villages, and in 1961 a fire at the Bukit Ho Swee settlement left thousands homeless in one day. A small island with little land to spare could not answer that crisis by spreading out. The Housing and Development Board, formed the year before, accelerated its building program and within a few years had completed tens of thousands of flats, in blocks that grew taller over time. Today most Singaporeans live in public housing, the great majority as owners on long leases.

What makes the example persuasive is not the towers' height but what that height bought. Because homes were stacked, land remained for everything else. Singapore's master plans [[delineate|delineate]] the land reserved for housing, industry, and green space years before construction begins. Each new town has its own schools, parks, and town center, and later towns are organized around rail stations. Even the open ground floors of many blocks, known as void decks, host weddings, funerals, and old men playing chess. A family on the twentieth floor may have a modest flat, but it is hardly [[bereft|bereft]] of space; its space has simply moved from private to shared.

The strongest objection comes from St. Louis, where the Pruitt-Igoe towers, praised in the 1950s as model public housing, were being demolished within two decades of opening. Footage of the implosions, replayed for decades in documentaries and lectures, made the complex a byword for failure. For many critics of high-rise housing, the demolition remains [[conclusive|conclusive]] proof that ordinary families cannot live well in the sky. But height alone did not doom the towers. Once height is [[disentangled|disentangle]] from the conditions around it, other causes come into view: income ceilings restricted the complex to low-income families, its upkeep depended on rents that fell as residents left, and St. Louis was losing jobs and population while remaining sharply segregated. When elevators broke and windows shattered, the housing authority could not afford repairs. Pruitt-Igoe lacked precisely what makes Singapore's towers work: residents of mixed incomes who own their homes, shared ground that people actually use, and steady spending on maintenance. The comparison also shows when the outward view wins: a city unable to sustain that investment may do less harm by letting families spread out.

The real choice, then, is not between tall and wide. A city that stacks its poorest residents in towers and walks away will repeat Pruitt-Igoe, while a sprawling city grants residents ample private room but quietly bills them in driving time, fuel, and vanished countryside. Cities should build upward wherever they are willing to return the saved ground as transit, parks, and common rooms, and maintain the towers as long as people live in them. Built that way, a city gives each resident more space than any single lot could provide.

prompt.statement:
Claim: Personal ambition does more good than harm to society.
Reason: Ambitious people create the businesses, discoveries, and works of art that benefit everyone.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Ambition Helps Where Rank Requires Achievement
essays.essay:
The claim treats ambition as a single trait, but the word names two appetites. One is the desire to accomplish something: to explain how a disease spreads, to build a bridge that stands. The other is the desire for rank: to be admired, deferred to, and placed above others. The second appetite breeds [[pomposity|pomposity]], but its real danger is not that it is ridiculous. The first is satisfied only by producing something real; the second, by anything that confers rank, including flattery, intimidation, and borrowed credit. I agree that ambition does more good than harm, but only where a society makes rank depend on accomplishment. The reason offered, though true as far as it goes, cannot show this: it counts what ambition builds and ignores both what it destroys and what makes it build at all.

Ambitious people do found companies, make discoveries, and produce art. But the reason keeps a ledger with one column; good and harm cannot be weighed by listing only the good. It also assumes that these creations benefit "everyone," though benefits and costs often fall on different people. Robert Moses, who reshaped New York for four decades, built Jones Beach, the Triborough Bridge, and hundreds of playgrounds. He wanted power at least as much as any project, and bridge tolls made him largely independent of elected officials. That same appetite drove the Cross Bronx Expressway through settled working-class neighborhoods, displacing thousands of residents and leaving a trench of traffic and exhaust the borough still lives beside. Motorists from across the region gained; families who had no say in the route paid. Where residents organized effectively, as Jane Jacobs and her allies did against his planned Lower Manhattan Expressway, his ambition met its limit.

If the reason fails, the claim may still hold for a different reason. In the early 1950s, James Watson and Francis Crick were racing Linus Pauling to determine the structure of DNA, and their ambition was not always admirable. They relied partly on X-ray evidence from Rosalind Franklin that reached them without her knowledge, and Watson's memoir later portrayed her as a [[morose|morose]], combative colleague, a caricature her biographers have since dismantled. Yet the prize they wanted could not be won by flattery or seniority. A proposed structure had to fit the X-ray data and the molecule's chemistry, and any competent rival could check whether it did. Pauling's three-stranded model failed that test and was quickly discarded; the double helix passed it and became a cornerstone of molecular biology. Science converts even unlovely ambition into public goods because the only durable way to rise in it is to be verifiably right. The race cost one scientist her due credit; its benefits were public.

Remove that discipline and the same appetite turns destructive. Trofim Lysenko rose to dominate Soviet biology by promising rapid gains in crop yields and denouncing Mendelian genetics as bourgeois pseudoscience. His claims rested on poorly controlled trials, but under Stalin careers depended on political favor, not on results others could check. With the state behind him, his critics lost their posts; Nikolai Vavilov, the country's leading plant geneticist, died in prison; and Soviet genetics was crippled for a generation. The catastrophe owed less to one man's moral [[frailty|frailty]] than to a system that rewarded it. Where rank is won by telling the powerful what they want to hear, ambitious people will tell them, and the costs spread from a rival's reputation to an entire discipline and the farms it was meant to serve.

Ambition, then, is easy to [[lampoon|lampoon]] and impossible to abolish, and its effects depend less on the people who have it than on the paths open to them. The claim holds where rank is earned through work others can test: markets with real competition, sciences that demand replication, cities whose residents can stop a highway. It fails where rank flows from favor. By counting only the bridges and the breakthroughs, the reason credits ambition alone with what ambition and its constraints achieved together. The wiser course is not to [[exhort|exhort]] the young to want less but to ensure that the surest way to rise is to do something worth doing.

sullen, gloomy, and bad-tempered, as Watson unfairly depicted Franklin
a weakness of character; one man's susceptibility to the temptations of status and favor
to ridicule publicly through satire or caricature
to urge earnestly, as in lecturing young people to be less ambitious

prompt.statement:
Claim: Children should learn to cook in school.
Reason: Few skills affect lifelong health as much as knowing how to prepare one's own food.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Teach Cooking as Choice, Not Cure
essays.essay:
Children should learn to cook in school, but the reason offered for that claim promises more than any classroom can deliver. Three things are easily confused here: knowing about cooking, being able to cook, and actually cooking, day after day. Only the third has much bearing on lifelong health, yet the reason credits the benefit to "knowing how," as if knowledge turned into habit by itself. It does not. Once the three are told apart, however, the claim can stand on firmer ground: a school can reliably make children able to cook, and that ability is worth having even if it never becomes a daily routine.

The history of cooking on American television shows how loosely these things are connected. Julia Child's The French Chef, launched in 1963, was built to send viewers into their own kitchens; when she fumbled the flip of a potato pancake, she pushed the pieces back into the pan and assured her audience that mistakes were survivable. The Food Network later put cooking on screen around the clock, but the genre changed character. In prime time, contests in which chefs race a timer [[supplanted|supplant]] programs that set out to teach. Michael Pollan, in The New York Times Magazine, described the resulting paradox: Americans were watching more cooking than ever while time spent cooking at home had been shrinking for decades.

This decline exposes the reason's hidden premise. People who cook frequently do eat better, but the reason attributes the difference to knowledge. If information were the active ingredient, a nation saturated with cooking demonstrations should have been cooking more, not less. More plausibly, the binding constraints were time and habit, and, as Pollan argues, the food industry has long told people they are too busy to cook. A defender of the reason will reply that viewers learned about cooking, not how to cook, and that is true; but the reply puts all the weight on practice, which the next case tests. Still, the same history shows what school can offer. The knowledge cooking requires is largely [[corporeal|corporeal]]: it lives in the hand that knows when dough is ready and the nose that catches garlic beginning to burn, and no amount of watching puts it there. A class in which children chop, measure, and taste every week supplies exactly what those viewers lacked; a class that merely [[harangues|harangue]] them about sugar offers nothing a screen could not.

A contrasting case from business tests whether such practice is enough. Blue Apron, the meal-kit company that went public in 2017, sold adults this kind of hands-on practice: pre-measured ingredients and illustrated recipe cards delivered weekly. The service required no shopping or planning and little prior skill, yet the company struggled to keep subscribers, and its share price fell steeply after its debut. Price explains some of that churn, and canceling a subscription is not the same as abandoning the stove. Even so, the churn is a warning: if adults who paid to skip shopping and planning so often canceled, a school cannot assume that practice will harden into habit. Taken seriously, the warning defines the conditions under which the claim holds. A single semester of recipes is little more than a meal kit with a grade attached. Instruction is likely to stick only if it runs for years and begins while routines are still forming, before adult life fills every evening with demands that seldom [[relent|relent]].

Even when the habit lapses, the ability retains a value the reason overlooks: the reason judges cooking by its typical effect, not by what it makes possible. An adult who cannot cook depends entirely on what restaurants and manufacturers choose to sell; when a diagnosis of diabetes demands a different diet, or a layoff cuts off the income that paid for takeout, the most direct remedy is out of reach. A child raised where no one cooks is [[bereft|bereft]] of the example most people learn from; school may be that child's only teacher. The strongest case for cooking classes, then, is not that they secure lifelong health, which no single skill can guarantee, but that they spare children a future in which someone else always decides what is for dinner.

prompt.statement: Governments should provide a basic income to every adult citizen, whether or not that person is employed.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: A Floor, Not a Replacement
essays.essay:
Charles Darwin never drew a salary. He lived on family wealth and spent some twenty years assembling the evidence for natural selection, often working only a few hours a day because of chronic illness. Few employers would have tolerated that pace, and few patrons would have funded so uncertain a project. Darwin is the [[archetype|archetype]] of the gentleman scientist, and his case suggests that the most valuable thing an unconditional income buys is not comfort but time. A universal basic income promises everyone a far smaller share of that freedom. Whether the policy is wise, however, depends on two questions the statement leaves open: how large the payment would be, and what it would replace. Weighing its likely consequences, I support a modest income that sits beneath existing aid and oppose any version designed to dismantle that aid.

The consequence critics fear most is that people will stop working. Many treat it as [[axiomatic|axiomatic]] that unconditional cash breeds idleness, yet the evidence does not bear this out. Since the early 1980s, Alaska has paid nearly every resident an annual oil dividend, and economists who studied it found no decline in overall employment, only a modest rise in part-time work. Finland's two-year trial, which paid randomly selected unemployed adults a monthly sum with no obligation to seek work, found that their employment changed little, though they reported less stress. Where versions of the policy have been tried, the collapse of the work ethic that critics predict, often in [[lugubrious|lugubrious]] tones, has not materialized. Still, neither case is [[conclusive|conclusive]]: Alaska's dividend is too small to replace a wage, and Finland paid only a sample of unemployed adults, who knew their payments would end. The evidence shows that small or temporary payments leave work largely intact; it cannot tell us what a payment large enough to live on would do.

A second consequence, less often discussed, may matter more. Conditional programs demand proof of job searches, periodic recertification, and reports of every extra shift, and an [[officious|officious]] caseworker can cut a family's benefits over a single missed appointment. This machinery is costly to run and deters many eligible people from applying. Worse, it sets a trap. When benefits shrink as earnings rise, a recipient who accepts a better job can end up barely ahead, or even behind. A universal payment cannot be lost by earning more, because everyone receives it regardless of income. A modest floor would also free some families from conditional aid altogether. Paradoxically, the policy that critics accuse of discouraging work may weaken a disincentive to work that conditional aid itself creates.

The decisive consequence, however, is cost. A payment generous enough to live on, sent to every adult, would require steep tax increases or the absorption of existing programs. The second path appeals to critics of the welfare state: the political scientist Charles Murray has proposed replacing nearly all transfer programs, Medicare and Medicaid included, with a single annual grant, only part of which must buy health insurance. Here the policy turns dangerous, because a flat payment treats unequal needs as equal. A healthy young adult and a wheelchair user who needs a paid aide every day would receive the same grant, though their daily costs differ enormously. If basic income were allowed to [[supplant|supplant]] disability benefits and public health coverage, the people whose needs are greatest would be left [[bereft|bereft]] of the support they can least afford to lose.

These consequences do not point one way; they diverge according to design. As a floor beneath existing aid, a basic income appears to leave work intact, gives every adult one income that no caseworker can revoke, and softens the penalty for earning more. As a substitute for that aid, it trades the welfare of the most vulnerable for administrative tidiness. Darwin's fortune paid for his years of unhurried thought and the many physicians he consulted; a modest basic income can buy a little of the first and almost none of the second. Governments should guarantee every adult a modest income, but they should treat it as the foundation of a safety net, never as an excuse to tear the rest of the net down.

prompt.statement: Workers should have a legal right to ignore work messages outside working hours.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Protect Silence, Price Availability
essays.essay:
The strongest objection to this policy is not that employers deserve round-the-clock access; it is that much modern work no longer has clean "working hours" to protect. A parent who leaves at three for school pickup may prefer to clear her inbox at nine, and a law forcing her employer to fix her hours would be an [[officious|officious]] intrusion, substituting a legislator's clock for an arrangement both parties chose. Some messages, moreover, genuinely cannot wait, as when a server fails. The flexibility argument, however, holds only for workers who can decline without paying for it. It assumes that answering at nine is a choice; where silence is quietly penalized, flexibility becomes another name for permanent availability, the very condition the proposed right targets. I therefore support the right, but its likely consequences persuade me that its form matters more than its existence.

The first consequence exposes a hidden assumption in the statement: that what workers lack is permission to ignore a message. College sports suggest otherwise. For decades the NCAA capped required athletic activities for Division I athletes at twenty hours a week in season, yet athletes in its own surveys reported spending far more, because workouts labeled voluntary did not count against the cap and few players hoping to start regarded them as optional. The rule held on paper and eroded in practice, less because coaches defied it than because each athlete assumed the teammate who showed up would earn the playing time. A bare right to ignore messages would invite the same arithmetic: anyone could leave the late email unread, the most eager would answer anyway, and their response time would become everyone's standard. This consequence pushes my position beyond the statement: a right to ignore means little unless the law also forbids reprisal for using it.

The second consequence pulls the other way: a rule drawn too rigidly can relocate work instead of reducing it. When the body that accredits American residency programs capped trainees' hours, first at an average of eighty a week and later by shortening first-year residents' shifts, the intended consequence was better-rested doctors; an unintended one was more frequent handoffs, each a chance for knowledge about a patient to slip between departing and arriving physicians. Longer intern shifts were later restored, partly out of concern that shorter ones had fragmented care without shrinking the work. An after-hours right drafted bluntly could repeat that error: messages ignored at night would pile into a frantic morning, or the late shift would migrate to contractors the law does not cover. The right must therefore bend for roles in which availability is the job itself.

A well-designed law can reconcile these two pressures. Australia's 2024 statute lets employees refuse to monitor, read, or respond to after-hours contact unless refusal would be unreasonable, judged by factors such as the reason for the contact, the employee's role, and whether the worker is paid to stay available. That last factor is the hinge. Australian law also bars employers from punishing a reasonable refusal, closing the trap of the "voluntary" workout. I would add one requirement: employers must [[delineate|delineate]] in advance which roles demand after-hours availability and pay for it, giving urgent work a legitimate home rather than a hidden one. The most valuable consequence of such a law is not that messages [[cease|cease]] but that availability acquires a price. Once evening access costs something, managers will [[disentangle|disentangle]] real emergencies from mere convenience: the failed server from a passing thought about next quarter's slides.

At stake is not a few minutes of typing but the difference between being off duty and merely being away from one's desk. Workers who are never fully released do not become more dedicated; they grow distracted at dinner and [[morose|morose]] by Sunday evening. Rest is what lets a nurse, a coach, or an engineer meet the next morning's genuine emergencies with [[equanimity|equanimity]]. The right to ignore work messages deserves to become law, then, but as protection against penalty rather than mere permission, paired with a duty on employers to name, and pay for, the hours they truly need. Framed that way, the law does not forbid urgency; it makes urgency honest.

prompt.statement: Nations are shaped more by their geography than by their leaders.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Geography Sets the Price, Leaders Choose
essays.essay:
The claim that geography shapes nations more than leaders do is attractive because geography is permanent and leaders are not: mountains outlast dynasties. Yet the statement treats the two as rival forces, when in practice geography acts largely through what people know and what their leaders decide. Terrain, climate and disease set the price of every option a nation faces; leaders choose which option to buy. I therefore accept the statement only in a qualified form. Geography is decisive when its constraints are binding and no one yet knows how to loosen them. Where those constraints are slack, or where knowledge has loosened them, leaders matter more, whether they rise to that freedom or abuse it.

Where geography operates through disease, the statement holds. Late in 1801, Napoleon, then the most [[redoubtable|redoubtable]] soldier in Europe, sent an army under Charles Leclerc to Saint-Domingue to reassert French control. The army was beaten less by its opponents' muskets than by yellow fever, carried by a mosquito that thrived in the island's heat and rains. Many locals had survived the disease in childhood and were immune; the newcomers were not, and the fever [[ravaged|ravage]] their ranks, killing Leclerc himself. Toussaint Louverture, the colony's governor, grasped this asymmetry and urged his general Jean-Jacques Dessalines to burn what could not be held and let the rainy season do the rest. Dessalines, who had defected to the French before they seized Toussaint, later led the rebels to victory. Napoleon, his New World ambitions undone, sold Louisiana to the United States in 1803, and Haiti declared independence in 1804. Veterans who had remained [[imperturbable|imperturbable]] under fire in Europe lost to an ecology, and the side that prevailed was the one that read it correctly.

The statement fails, however, when geography is generous and leaders [[squander|squander]] what it provides. Ukraine's black-earth soils are among the most fertile on earth, and the region had long exported grain. Yet in 1932 and 1933 millions of Ukrainians starved. Poor weather and crop disease may have shrunk the harvest, but a bad harvest in a granary does not by itself produce mass starvation; policy does. Stalin's government, having forced peasants onto collective farms, imposed grain quotas they could not meet, seized food from villages that fell short, and barred the starving from leaving, while still exporting grain. The famine exposed not the poverty of Ukraine's fields but the [[turpitude|turpitude]] of leaders who would sooner let villages starve than admit their policy had failed. Blaming the deaths on soil or climate is [[sophistry|sophistry]] that would hand every tyrant a ready alibi.

These cases shape my position by exposing the conditions that the statement leaves unstated. Geography dominates when its constraints are binding and slow to change, as they were for nonimmune troops before anyone knew how yellow fever spread. Leaders dominate when those constraints are slack, as on the Ukrainian steppe, and above all when a poor harvest makes a population's needs [[exigent|exigent]], because then how quickly and how fairly a government responds decides who survives. Binding constraints, moreover, need not stay binding. France's attempt to cut a canal across Panama collapsed in the 1880s, in part because yellow fever and malaria killed thousands of its workers. After Walter Reed's commission in Cuba confirmed that mosquitoes transmit yellow fever, the physician William Gorgas, backed by Theodore Roosevelt when administrators balked at the cost, had standing water drained, buildings screened and houses fumigated until the disease vanished from the Canal Zone. The canal opened in 1914. The isthmus's heat and rains had not changed; its standing water had, and that change was the work of new knowledge and of leaders willing to pay for it.

Read this way, the statement describes starting conditions, not destinies. Geography decides which paths lie open and how steep each is; leaders decide which path is taken, and the more a society understands its environment, the more of its fate passes from the terrain to those who govern it. That transfer guarantees nothing. Armed with new knowledge, Gorgas made a deadly isthmus safe enough to build a canal; armed with unchecked power, Stalin's regime starved the farmers who worked some of the richest soil in Europe.

prompt.statement: The value of a university education lies chiefly in the habits of mind it builds, not in the knowledge it transmits.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Habits of Mind Are Built from Knowledge
essays.essay:
In a 1910 report, the educator Abraham Flexner surveyed every medical school in the United States and Canada. He found many to be profit-making ventures where students memorized lectures and graduated with little laboratory work and scant contact with patients. His remedy, which helped remake American medicine, resists the terms of the statement: Flexner wanted physicians who reasoned like experimental scientists, yet insisted that they first spend years mastering the laboratory sciences. Was he reforming what students knew or how they thought? The question exposes the statement's hidden assumption: that knowledge and habits of mind can be pulled apart, and knowledge [[relegated|relegate]] to second place. I agree that habits are a university's more durable gift, but only insofar as they are built out of knowledge, not in place of it. The statement holds where knowledge is perishable or easily obtained elsewhere; it fails where knowledge is the very material of judgment.

The statement holds, first, when knowledge loses its relevance. For centuries, imperial China chose officials through examinations that rewarded memorizing the Confucian classics and mastering the rigid eight-legged essay. Successful candidates commanded an immense body of learning, but it was learning built to be reproduced, not tested against the world. When the Qing confronted industrialized powers in the nineteenth century, reformers blamed the system for producing officials who could recite commentaries but not meet the crisis, and the court abolished the examinations in 1905. The statement holds, too, when knowledge loses its scarcity. Courses from elite universities are now free online, yet, despite reminders and deadlines, most enrollees never finish. The scarce resource is no longer knowledge but the habits needed to absorb it: the discipline to persist, the instinct to ask what counts as evidence, the willingness to revise a belief. A university is best placed to supply those habits, since a teacher, unlike a recorded lecture, can [[cajole|cajole]] a student into rewriting a muddled draft.

Yet the statement fails where knowledge is the substance of judgment rather than its ornament. In a classic study, the psychologists William Chase and Herbert Simon briefly showed chess players of different strengths a position from a real game; the master recalled far more of it than the novice. When the pieces were arranged at random, his advantage largely disappeared. What looked like a superior habit of mind was, in large part, a vast memory of meaningful patterns. Medicine works the same way. A medical student trained always to build a differential diagnosis has an admirable habit, but that habit remains [[inchoate|inchoate]] until she knows which diseases belong on the list and which findings rule them out. None of this is the grumbling of a [[curmudgeon|curmudgeon]] who misses recitation drills; it is what research on expertise keeps finding.

These cases do not cancel each other out; each shapes a different part of my position. The examination halls and the unfinished online courses persuade me to accept the statement's ranking, because when facts grow stale or cheap, habits keep their value. The chessboard and the hospital ward persuade me to reject the opposition it draws, because habits are made from facts. It is fashionable to [[deprecate|deprecate]] memorization and to demand that universities teach students how to think, not what to think. A curriculum built on that slogan turns out graduates who can dismantle any argument but build none. Cut loose from knowledge and rewarded for winning, argument soon degenerates into [[sophistry|sophistry]]. The Qing examiners erred in the opposite direction, prizing knowledge that never became a habit of inquiry. Both failures rest on the same assumption: that one can be cultivated without the other.

The value of a university education, then, lies neither in knowledge nor in habits alone but in the conversion of one into the other. The laboratories Flexner championed mattered not because they replaced the textbook but because they forced students to use it: to predict, to test, and to watch a confident hypothesis fail at the bench. A university earns its keep when the facts it teaches are worked so thoroughly that they harden into reflexes of judgment. The statement describes that endpoint well; it errs in imagining a route to it that bypasses knowledge.

prompt.statement: Writers should publish anonymously so that readers judge their work rather than their reputations.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Anonymity for Judgment, Not for Testimony
essays.essay:
The recommendation rests on a tidy assumption: that an author's reputation is only noise, a residue of fame and prejudice that keeps readers from seeing the page. Sometimes it is. Reputation in this first sense, which I will call public image, includes celebrity, an author's sex or politics, and gossip about her [[peccadilloes|peccadillo]], none of which reveals whether a paragraph is any good. A celebrated author's name can carry a weak book as easily as a scandal sinks an [[estimable|estimable]] one. But reputation has a second sense as well: accountability, the standing of a known person who can be questioned, contradicted, and held responsible for what she has written. Anonymity removes both at once. As a first approximation, then, I endorse the recommendation for imaginative work, which can be judged from the page alone, and reject it for factual work, which asks readers to accept claims on the author's word.

Fiction offers the clearest case. Mary Ann Evans published her first novel, Adam Bede, as George Eliot, and she had good reason to hide. She was a woman in a literary market that condescended to women novelists, and she lived openly with George Henry Lewes, a married man. Under her own name, Adam Bede might well have been dismissed as the work of a fallen woman. Under a pseudonym, it was read as a novel, and its success [[burnished|burnish]] the reputation of an author the public could not identify. Within months, gossip and a false claimant to her books forced the secret out. The disclosure drew some snide commentary and worried her publisher, but it came after the verdict: a critic who now wished to [[excoriate|excoriate]] the novel would have had to explain away his own praise. The pseudonym had hidden only her public image, which had no bearing on her prose.

Reputation in the second sense, however, is not a prejudice to be filtered out but evidence to be weighed. The Sixth Amendment guarantees a criminal defendant the right to confront the witnesses against him, because testimony cannot be assessed apart from the person giving it: whether she bears a grudge, stands to gain, or has lied before. Several states also let lawyers impeach a witness with a prior conviction for a crime involving moral [[turpitude|turpitude]]. An anonymous accuser cannot be impeached by her record, and lying costs her nothing. The same logic governs factual writing, which asks readers to believe what they cannot verify: an unsigned exposé of boardroom wrongdoing leaves them unable to tell evidence from revenge. Here the author's name is not a distraction from the work but part of it, a pledge that someone will answer if the account proves false.

Yet the dividing line is not simply between fiction and fact, as the Federalist Papers show. Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay defended the proposed Constitution under the single pseudonym Publius. Pen names were routine in that newspaper debate—opponents of ratification wrote as Brutus and Cato—and Hamilton's role was widely suspected. Whatever the motive, the essays did not need their authors' names: their claims about faction, representation, and the separation of powers were arguments any reader could test for himself. This example forces me to sharpen my original distinction. The real question is not whether a work is imaginative or factual but whether it can be judged from the page. A novel and a closely reasoned argument can be; testimony cannot.

These examples leave me in qualified agreement. Where a work asks only to be read, a writer may reasonably withhold her name. Where a work asks to be believed, the name is part of the claim, and withholding it shifts the burden of trust onto readers with no means of bearing it. Even in the first case, permanent anonymity is a blunter tool than the recommendation's purpose requires. Fair judgment demands only that evaluators not know the author while they evaluate, as in double-blind peer review and many literary contests. Once the verdict is rendered, the name can come out: Evans never chose her moment, yet Adam Bede kept its standing. Anonymity, then, is most valuable as a temporary condition of judgment, not a permanent condition of authorship.

analysis.verdict: The essay earns a 6 for insight and cogency, not just clarity. It splits "reputation" into public image and accountability, draws a provisional line between imaginative and factual work, and then lets the Federalist Papers genuinely revise that line rather than merely illustrate it. Each example (Eliot, the Confrontation Clause, the Federalist Papers) is developed far enough to show what happened and why it matters, complications included, in precise, controlled prose.

The final paragraph restates the refined position in fresh words, calling anonymity "a temporary condition of judgment."
analysis.development: Each example is explained, not just named: the essay says why Evans hid, admits her exposure had costs, and shows why it mattered that it "came after the verdict." The Sixth Amendment is used for its rationale, that testimony depends on "whether she bears a grudge, stands to gain, or has lied before," which the essay backs with impeachment rules and carries over to an unsigned exposé.

Transitions carry the logic: "Reputation in the second sense, however," and "Yet the dividing line."
analysis.language: The diction is exact without being showy, as in "explain away his own praise" and "a pledge that someone will answer." Sentence length ranges from "Sometimes it is." to long cumulative sentences such as the one explaining the Sixth Amendment. Parallel openings ("Where a work asks only to be read" and "Where a work asks to be believed") give the conclusion its balance.
analysis.task: The instruction asks for circumstances in which the recommendation helps and circumstances in which it does not, plus how those examples shape the position. Paragraph 2 supplies the advantageous case and paragraph 3 the disadvantageous one. Because paragraph 1 offers its fiction-versus-fact line only "As a first approximation," paragraph 4 can truthfully say: "This example forces me to sharpen my original distinction."

prompt.statement: Universities should judge applicants by what they have accomplished rather than by their test scores.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: When Test Scores Protect the Disadvantaged
essays.essay:
In 2022, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology reinstated the testing requirement it had held in [[abeyance|abeyance]] during the pandemic. Its admissions office explained that scores helped it spot well-prepared applicants whose high schools offered no advanced coursework. A test long criticized as a tool of privilege was restored in the name of the disadvantaged. The episode exposes the assumption behind judging applicants by accomplishment rather than test scores: that accomplishment is the fairer measure. The recommendation springs from an [[estimable|estimable]] impulse: to reward what students have done, not one morning's performance. I agree that accomplishment should outweigh a score, but only when applicants have had comparable chances to accomplish something and the accomplishment closely resembles the work the program demands. Where either condition fails, discarding scores throws away useful evidence; where opportunity is unequal, it hurts precisely the students the reform means to help.

Following the recommendation is plainly advantageous when the work itself can be observed before admission. A conservatory does not admit a cellist on the strength of a written theory exam; it asks her to play, because an audition samples the very work she would do there. Many biomedical doctoral programs reached a similar conclusion, dropping the GRE after analyses at several of them suggested that, among admitted students, scores did little to predict who would publish or finish the degree. A year of experiments is not a proxy for research ability; it is research ability on display. Laboratory positions do cluster at wealthy universities, but where summer programs recruiting from colleges with few labs have widened access, a test score adds little to a substantial research record.

Following the recommendation becomes harmful, however, where accomplishment depends on chances only some applicants receive. A student cannot win a science fair her school never enters. Medicine offers a cautionary case. When the first licensing exam American medical students take went pass/fail in 2022, one aim was to ease their fixation on a single number. Competition for residencies did not vanish; by most accounts, it migrated to the next scored exam and, more troublingly, to research output and school prestige. A licensing exam asks every student the same kinds of questions, about a [[distended|distend]] abdomen or a failing kidney; a research record asks, in effect, whether someone opened a laboratory door. Students at little-known schools and graduates of foreign ones kept the later exam but lost the score residency programs had weighted most heavily, their earliest chance to outscore peers from famous institutions. Those peers, surrounded by faculty who publish, appear more readily on author lists. Tutoring can nudge a score upward, but a record of activities is far easier to [[burnish|burnish]].

These cases shape my position in two ways: they supply the conditions on which my agreement depends, and they blur the line the recommendation draws between accomplishment and testing. Many celebrated accomplishments are tests in disguise. International Mathematical Olympiad medals are won on a timed written exam, and even the audition praised above is a test performed before judges. Conversely, a rigorous exam can [[substantiate|substantiate]] what a thin transcript only hints at, as when a student from a school without calculus earns a top mathematics score that reveals a talent no activity list would have flagged. The useful question is not whether evidence comes as a score or a record, but whether it is hard to buy and close to the work ahead.

Universities should therefore rely chiefly on accomplishment when the work can be sampled directly and the chance to do it has been widely shared, and keep scores in view wherever that chance has depended on wealth or connections. Testing's most [[redoubtable|redoubtable]] critics will object that scores, too, rise with family income. They do, but dropping scores only hides that advantage in activity lists, where it is harder to detect. Where opportunity is unequal, a test is not the enemy of fairness but often its last defense: the one measure a gifted student with no one to vouch for her can still claim on equal terms. An admissions office that grasps this will neither worship scores nor [[disdain|disdain]] them; it will ask what each applicant's circumstances allowed her to prove.

prompt.statement: Professional codes of ethics do more to protect professionals than to protect the public.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Enforcement, Not Text, Decides Who Benefits
essays.essay:
The statement treats a professional code of ethics as a single instrument, but most codes are two documents bound together: one sets out what practitioners owe the people they serve, the other what they owe one another. The Hippocratic Oath shows the seam, pledging to keep the sick from harm while binding the physician to treat his teacher as a parent and teach the teacher's sons without fee. Whether codes favor professionals depends on which half is enforced and, above all, by whom. Because professions have usually policed themselves, I largely agree with the statement, but for a reason it does not name: the fault lies less in what codes say than in who enforces them.

The guild half has long served its authors. The American Medical Association's first code, adopted in 1847, barred members from consulting with "irregular" practitioners such as homeopaths. The clause was billed as a safeguard against quackery, though regular physicians' bleeding and purging arguably harmed patients more than homeopathy did; its clearest effect was to shut out competitors. Medical and legal codes also banned advertising, shielding practitioners from price competition. Outsiders dismantled those bans in the late 1970s: the Supreme Court on commercial-speech grounds for lawyers, the Federal Trade Commission on antitrust grounds for physicians. Discipline shows the same tilt. A board of practitioners finds it easy to censure a [[peccadillo|peccadillo]] that embarrasses the profession, such as a garish advertisement, and hard to pursue a respected colleague whose negligence harms patients: the first threatens the guild's image, the second only people outside the room.

Protections for the public, by contrast, have often failed when most needed. Germany's 1931 guidelines on human experimentation, among the strictest of their era, required consent. Under the Nazi regime they fell into [[abeyance|abeyance]], and physicians at Dachau and Auschwitz subjected prisoners to freezing, high-altitude and sterilization experiments. Such atrocities owed nothing to a gap in the rules: the state that had issued the guidelines now sponsored their violation. The Nuremberg Code was issued not by a medical society but by judges at a war-crimes tribunal, enforcers at last independent of the offenders. Democracies are not exempt. At Tuskegee, the U.S. Public Health Service tracked untreated syphilis in hundreds of Black men for four decades, long after penicillin became standard therapy. Its results appeared in medical journals; the profession was not deceived, merely undisturbed. What ended the study in 1972 was a news report, not a disciplinary hearing.

The strongest challenge is that I have judged codes by their spectacular failures and ignored their daily work. Confidentiality is the best case. Because physicians are bound to secrecy, patients disclose drug use and sexual histories and seek testing for stigmatized infections such as HIV, to the public's benefit far more than any doctor's. Even the guild's self-interest serves outsiders: a profession that wants to be trusted has every reason to expel members guilty of moral [[turpitude|turpitude]]. And physicians themselves, in the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki, supplied many principles of modern research ethics.

This objection is right about what codes say and wrong about where their force comes from. Codes do shape everyday conduct and often articulate a protection before any law does. But confidentiality reassures patients less because physicians swear to it than because law stands behind it; the HIV cases doctors must report stay private under public-health statutes, not the oath. The incentive to expel [[miscreants|miscreant]], moreover, competes with an incentive to hide them, since every public expulsion advertises that the profession harbored one. Helsinki did not stop Tuskegee, which ran eight more years, nor did the Public Health Service's own 1969 review panel, which recommended that it continue; only after the scandal did Congress write review boards into law. The profession supplied many principles; the public supplied the teeth.

A code of ethics, then, is best read as a first draft of the public's protections, effective to the degree that enforcers with no stake in its violation stand behind it. Left to the guild that wrote it, a code does more to [[burnish|burnish]] the profession's image than to restrain its members; entrusted to courts, legislators and independent reviewers, the same words become a shield for the people they claim to serve.

words.meaning_here: a minor lapse, such as a garish ad, that embarrasses the profession without endangering anyone
suspension in practice: the 1931 consent rules were never repealed but went unenforced under the Nazis
base, shameful conduct serious enough to justify expelling a member from the profession
wrongdoing practitioners whose public expulsion would reveal that the profession had harbored them
to polish or enhance the profession's public image, as opposed to actually restraining members

analysis.verdict: This response earns a 6 because its position is insightful, not merely clear: it splits most codes into a guild half and a public half and locates the real problem in enforcement rather than in the text. Every example is developed far enough to show why it matters, and the strongest objection is stated fairly, partly conceded, and then answered.
analysis.position: The essay takes a qualified stance in paragraph 1, agreeing "but for a reason it does not name": the fault is who enforces codes. The ending sharpens this into a proportional claim: a code works to the degree that "enforcers with no stake in its violation stand behind it."
analysis.development: Examples are explained, not just named: the 1847 consultation clause is shown to have guarded a market because regular physicians' "bleeding and purging" were arguably worse than homeopathy. Nazi Germany shows demanding rules failing because "the state that had issued the guidelines now sponsored their violation," and Tuskegee shows the profession "was not deceived, merely undisturbed."
analysis.organization: The opening distinction drives the structure: paragraph 2 covers the guild half, paragraph 3 the public's protections, and paragraphs 4 and 5 test the enforcement claim against the best objection. Signposts such as "Protections for the public, by contrast" keep the logic visible.
analysis.language: Diction is exact and compressed, as in the elliptical "the second only people outside the room." Short sentences such as "Democracies are not exempt." break up longer ones, and target words sit in standard collocations such as "fell into abeyance" and "guilty of moral turpitude."

Paragraph 5 concedes "Codes do shape everyday conduct" before answering on enforcement, noting that "Helsinki did not stop Tuskegee."

prompt.statement: A community is held together more by shared rituals than by shared beliefs.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Rituals Bind Because They Permit Disagreement
essays.essay:
In the days before Tet, the highways out of Ho Chi Minh City fill with motorbikes carrying migrant workers home to the provinces, gifts strapped behind the seats. The reunions that follow are seldom occasions of [[unalloyed|unalloyed]] joy: old arguments about politics and money resurface, and the young field pointed questions about marriage. Yet on New Year's Eve, with those quarrels held in [[abeyance|abeyance]], the whole family stands before the ancestral altar and lights incense. Ask its members what, if anything, the ancestors perceive, and their answers will diverge; ask them when to bow, and they will agree at once. That contrast is why I largely agree with the statement: shared practice binds more durably than shared conviction because it can hold together people who disagree. Still, rituals rest on one thin belief: that the people beside you are worth the trouble. When that belief fails, no ceremony can replace it.

Rituals bind so well because they ask so little of the mind. The same bow can be made by a devout Buddhist, a Catholic or a skeptic who sees it as courtesy toward the dead. Most participants hold only [[inchoate|inchoate]] ideas about what the ceremony accomplishes, and nothing forces them to settle those ideas. Even the family [[curmudgeon|curmudgeon]], who scoffs at talk of spirits, lights his incense with everyone else. A late arrival or a perfunctory bow is a [[peccadillo|peccadillo]] forgotten by morning. A creed offers no such slack: a community founded on propositions must demand assent to them and then police that assent.

The Chinese Rites controversy shows what happens when belief polices practice. Following Matteo Ricci, Jesuit missionaries let converts keep honoring Confucius and their ancestors, judging the rites civil rather than religious. Rival orders objected, and Rome ruled the rites a superstition incompatible with the faith, a verdict not reversed until 1939. The Kangxi Emperor, who had tolerated the missionaries, took the ruling as an [[affront|affront]], a foreign claim to authority over Chinese custom, and eventually banned missionary preaching. The episode exposes the statement's hidden assumption that rituals and beliefs are rival bonds. Belief divides precisely when it dictates ritual, because ritual is where membership becomes visible: a convert's private convictions troubled few neighbors, but his absence from the family rites told every neighbor he had left the fold.

The most compelling challenge to my position is that ritual is downstream of belief. A gesture means something only because someone believes it does, so a ritual emptied of conviction should decay into theater. The late Soviet Union seems to prove the point. Its Red Square parades continued into its final years, yet once faith in communism faded, the marching did nothing to keep the union from dissolving. On this account, I have mistaken a symptom of cohesion for its cause.

The objection is right about one kind of ritual and wrong about another. Soviet parades existed to display assent to a doctrine, and they faced upward, toward the reviewing stand; when the doctrine lost credibility, so did the parades. Rituals that face sideways, toward those performing them alongside you, can outlast the doctrines attached to them. Japan's shrine festivals are centuries older than State Shinto, the emperor-centered ideology the Meiji state laid over them. When that ideology was dismantled after 1945, the festivals went on facing sideways; Tokyo residents still carry portable shrines through their own streets, though many profess no religion. What such rituals require is not doctrine but the thin belief named at the outset: that one's neighbors are worth gathering for. Where that belief survives, ritual can carry a community through the collapse of an official creed; where it has vanished, no parade can restore it.

The statement, then, is right about the rival it names but misleading if taken to mean that ritual can dispense with belief. Shared rituals hold a community together better than shared doctrines because they let members disagree about what the community means while agreeing that it matters. That agreement is itself a belief, the most modest a community can require, and ritual renews it whenever people return, to a family altar or a festival street, to stand beside one another.

words.meaning_here: pure and complete; the reunion's joy is mixed with quarrels and awkward questions
temporary suspension; the quarrels are set aside during the rite but will resume
half-formed and vague; participants have never worked out what the ceremony does
the grumpy, complaining relative who scoffs at the rite's beliefs yet still lights his incense
a small, forgivable fault; minor lapses of respect during the rite are easily excused
an insult; the emperor resented Rome's claim to judge Chinese custom
words.def: an action or remark that causes outrage or offense; insult; offense; slight; snub; slur

analysis.verdict: The essay earns a 6 for insight and cogency, not just clarity. It takes a qualified position, draws two original distinctions (doctrine versus a 'thin belief' in one another; rituals that face upward versus sideways), and explains why each example matters. It states the strongest objection fairly and answers it, in precise, varied prose with no padding.
analysis.position: The position comes early and is qualified: "That contrast is why I largely agree with the statement", followed at once by the limit, that rituals "rest on one thin belief." The last paragraph restates it in new words: rituals let members disagree about what the community means "while agreeing that it matters."
analysis.development: Each example is explained, not just named: the Tet altar shows rituals tolerating disagreement, and the Chinese Rites controversy shows belief splitting a community once it polices practice. The Soviet parades give the objection its force, and Japan's shrine festivals, far older than the State Shinto laid over them, show ritual outlasting an imposed ideology.
analysis.organization: The essay follows its argument rather than a template: scene, then why rituals bind, then a historical case that exposes the prompt's hidden assumption, then the objection, then a distinction that answers it, then the refined claim. The 'thin belief' set up in paragraph 1 comes back in paragraphs 5 and 6, which ties the essay together.
analysis.language: The diction is exact and concrete ("they faced upward, toward the reviewing stand"). Short sentences alternate with long balanced ones, such as the semicolon pair in paragraph 1 (quoted in full under Moves), which sets "their answers will diverge" against "they will agree at once." Each target word appears in its usual collocation, for example "held in abeyance" and "unalloyed joy."
analysis.task: Paragraph 4 gives the objection its strongest form, that "ritual is downstream of belief," with a real case, and ends by turning it on the writer: "I have mistaken a symptom of cohesion for its cause." Paragraph 5 concedes part of it and answers the rest with a distinction instead of a denial.

prompt.statement: Some people believe that the purpose of art is to represent the world as it is. Others believe that art should imagine the world as it could be.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Imagination Is the Purpose, Accuracy the Obligation
essays.essay:
The strongest case for art that simply represents the world comes from one of the twentieth century's most systematic attempts to make art imagine it instead. In the 1930s, Stalin's government bound Soviet artists to socialist realism, a doctrine that asked them to portray life not as it was but as the revolution would make it. In the same decade that famine killed millions in Ukraine and Kazakhstan, leaving starving children with [[distended|distend]] bellies, official canvases and posters celebrated ruddy collective farmers and abundant harvests. Art that imagined a better world became an alibi for a worse one. Defenders of the first view are right to [[deprecate|deprecate]] such work, and right to suspect that every picture of the world as it could be carries the same temptation.

Yet the lesson stops short of where it seems to point. Socialist realism did not fail because it imagined; it failed because it passed off its imagining as fact, erasing the distance between the world as it is and the world as it could be. Pure representation, moreover, is less a rival purpose than a method, and no artist can practice it without choosing. Every frame excludes far more than it includes, and what remains must be shown in some light: to paint a drunk as a [[miscreant|miscreant]] rather than as a casualty is to pass judgment on him. To judge the world by any standard is already to imagine it otherwise. The first view thus names art's most dependable instrument rather than its purpose. The second view comes closer to my own, with one refinement: art exists to imagine the world as it could be, but it must keep the actual world in plain sight so that the distance between them is measured rather than concealed.

William Hogarth grasped this in 1751, when he published the paired prints Gin Lane and Beer Street in support of a campaign against the cheap gin ravaging London's poor. Gin Lane is not a report. It is a nightmare assembled from real materials, a picture less of where the city stood than of where it was heading: a drunken mother lets her infant slip over a railing, houses collapse, and only the pawnbroker, the distiller, and the undertaker prosper. Beside it, Hogarth placed an imagined alternative, a street of stout, cheerful tradesmen in which the pawnbroker's shop is the one building falling into ruin. Neither print carries the argument alone. By itself, Gin Lane would merely condemn the city for its vice, and Beer Street, frankly idealized, would only [[wheedle|wheedle]] its viewers with a portrait of the citizens they might become. Together they turn a public health crisis into a choice between two possible cities.

Even art devoted to strict accuracy works this way. When Andreas Vesalius published De humani corporis fabrica in 1543, he corrected many errors that had survived for more than a millennium under the authority of Galen, whose anatomy rested largely on the dissection of animals. Vesalius's own former teacher [[lambasted|lambaste]] the book in Galen's defense, but the corrections held. Here, surely, is the realist's triumph: the human body drawn, systematically and in full, from the human body. Yet the plates are anything but neutral. Their flayed figures, often modeled on the corpses of executed criminals, stand upright in open countryside and gesture as though alive. The title page shows Vesalius himself dissecting before a crowd; older anatomy scenes had shown a professor reading from a chair while a barber did the cutting. Vesalius's version pictures medicine as it could be: a profession that learns by looking. Accuracy gave the vision its authority, and the vision gave the accuracy its purpose.

The two views pose a false choice, but not an evenly balanced one. Realists are right that imagination cut loose from the facts turns into propaganda, and that no vision of a better world deserves trust if it hides the present one. Still, a faithful picture of the world matters for what it lets viewers conceive: a different city, a different way of practicing medicine. Art's purpose is to make other worlds thinkable; its obligation is to show this one truthfully enough that the comparison holds.

words.meaning_here: Swollen outward by pressure from within; here, the bellies of children starving in famine.
To express disapproval of; realists rightly object to art that hid famine behind images of plenty.
A wrongdoer or villain; depicting the drunk as someone to blame rather than as a victim.
To coax by flattery; alone, Beer Street would charm viewers rather than make an argument.
Criticized harshly and at length; Vesalius's former teacher attacked the book to defend Galen.

analysis.verdict: This response earns a 6 because its position is insightful, not merely clear: it reframes the prompt as a distinction between art's purpose and its instrument. Each example (socialist realism, Hogarth's paired prints, Vesalius's Fabrica) is developed far enough to show what happened and why it matters to the argument. The prose is precise, varied in rhythm, and essentially free of errors.
analysis.position: The writer sides with the second view but refines it at the end of paragraph 2: art should imagine the world as it could be while keeping the actual world visible. The key reason is that depiction always judges, as in painting a drunk "as a miscreant rather than as a casualty." The last sentence restates the position as a purpose and an obligation: "Art's purpose is to make other worlds thinkable".
analysis.development: Each of the three examples does distinct work. Soviet socialist realism gives the opposing view its strongest case, Hogarth's prints show exaggeration and idealization working as a pair, and Vesalius shows that even strict accuracy serves a vision. Each example is explained rather than name-dropped, as in "Neither print carries the argument alone."
analysis.organization: The essay follows the concession-first shape: paragraph 1 grants the realist case, and paragraph 2 turns with "Yet the lesson stops short of where it seems to point." Paragraphs 3 and 4 then escalate to the case hardest for the writer, signaled by "Even art devoted to strict accuracy works this way."
analysis.language: Diction is precise and economical ("an alibi for a worse one"), and sentences range from six words ("Gin Lane is not a report.") to long, balanced constructions. Target words carry their exact connotations: alone, Beer Street "would only wheedle its viewers," which names flattery as the print's limit.
analysis.task: Both views get a substantive hearing: the realist view receives its strongest example, is credited again in paragraph 4 ("Here, surely, is the realist's triumph"), and is credited once more in the conclusion. In paragraph 2 the writer states explicitly which view "comes closer to my own" and why.

paragraphs.note: Grants the opposing view its best evidence: Soviet socialist realism celebrated abundance during famine. Ends by conceding that any imagined world carries the same temptation, which sets up the limit.

paragraphs.note: Relocates the failure to passing imagination off as fact, argues that depiction always judges (a drunk as miscreant or casualty), so representation is a method, then states the refined position.

paragraphs.role: Second example: nightmare and ideal as a pair
paragraphs.note: Hogarth's prints, made to support an anti-gin campaign, pair an exaggerated Gin Lane with an idealized Beer Street; alone, one would only condemn, the other only wheedle. Together they pose a choice between two cities.

paragraphs.role: Hardest case: even anatomical realism imagines
paragraphs.note: Vesalius's Fabrica, lambasted in Galen's defense, is the realist's best ground, yet its lifelike figures are far from neutral, and its title page pictures a reformed medicine; the closing chiasmus fuses accuracy and vision.

paragraphs.role: Refined position in fresh words
paragraphs.note: Credits the realists once more, then restates the thesis as a split between purpose (make other worlds thinkable) and obligation (show this one truthfully).

moves.example: Socialist realism did not fail because it imagined; it failed because it passed off its imagining as fact
moves.use: After conceding a damaging example, relocate its failure to a narrower cause your position can absorb.

moves.frame: The first view thus names ...'s most dependable ... rather than its ...
moves.example: The first view thus names art's most dependable instrument rather than its purpose.
moves.use: When an opposing view describes a means, reclassify it as a tool serving your goal.

moves.frame: ...'s purpose is to ...; its obligation is to ...
moves.example: Art's purpose is to make other worlds thinkable; its obligation is to show this one truthfully enough that the comparison holds.
