analysis.contrast: A typical 4 or 5 response would pick a side in the first sentence, give one paragraph to each view, and cite examples such as Guernica or Orwell's 1984 without explaining what they show. It would treat the views as equal rivals and end by calling both important. This essay instead grants the opposition its best case, locates its precise limit, and reclassifies representation as art's instrument.

prompt.statement: Some argue that science advances mainly through bold ideas that go beyond the available evidence. Others argue that it advances mainly through careful observation and the patient accumulation of data.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Outrunning the Evidence, Not Evading It
essays.essay:
The debate hangs on a phrase that sounds precise but is not: what does it mean for an idea to go "beyond the available evidence"? An idea can outrun the evidence, claiming more than the data yet show while staking itself on observations that could prove it wrong. Or it can evade the evidence, floating so free of any test that nothing could count against it. Only the first sort of boldness advances science; the second breeds dogma. Seen this way, the two views are partners rather than rivals: an idea that outruns the evidence is idle until careful observation catches up. Still, the idea is the senior partner, which is why the first view comes closer to my own: science advances mainly through bold ideas that outrun the evidence, while careful observation decides which of them survive.

The second view pictures the scientist as an [[imperturbable|imperturbable]] recorder, unmoved by hope or fashion, and its strongest evidence comes from the birth of modern astronomy. For some two decades, the Danish nobleman Tycho Brahe charted the positions of the planets with a precision unmatched by any astronomer before the telescope. Johannes Kepler, who worked from those records after Tycho's death, was no timid empiricist; he had begun his career by proposing that the orbits of the six known planets were spaced by the five regular solids, nested one inside another. Yet when his best circular model of Mars missed Tycho's observations by about eight minutes of arc, he refused to dismiss the gap as error, which would have been boldness of the evasive kind. The struggle to close that gap led him to elliptical orbits. Here data disciplined imagination, and the second view is right to be [[chary|chary]] of any idea that has not faced such a reckoning.

Even this story, however, does not show that accumulation by itself moves science forward. Tycho's tables did not announce ellipses; Tycho himself, who knew them best, died convinced that the Earth stood still. The records yielded the ellipse only when Kepler dared to abandon the perfect circle, an assumption astronomers had held since antiquity. The data delivered the verdict, but a bold idea had to pose the question.

In Victorian London, an evasive idea and an outrunning one competed to explain the same disease. Most physicians blamed cholera on miasma, a poison in foul air; since foul air was everywhere, almost any pattern of deaths could be read as its work. William Farr, the leading medical statistician of his day, tabulated cholera deaths with exemplary care and found that mortality fell as elevation rose, which he read as a sign that tainted air hung heaviest over low ground near the river. Hindsight makes it tempting to [[excoriate|excoriate]] the miasmatists, but their failure was not a lack of diligence; it was the elasticity of the idea their diligence served. John Snow argued instead that cholera spread through contaminated water, long before germ theory won acceptance. His notion of the agent remained [[inchoate|inchoate]], some unseen matter that multiplied in the bowel, yet his hypothesis made specific predictions. During the 1854 outbreak in Soho, he found deaths clustered around a single public pump on Broad Street. He also compared households supplied by two water companies, often on the same streets and sharing the same air, and found that customers of the company drawing from a sewage-fouled stretch of the Thames died at far higher rates, a pattern foul air could not easily explain. Snow's inquiries were laborious, but they were not mere accumulation; they were tests that only a bold idea could have designed.

None of this demotes observation; it assigns observation its proper office. Carefully gathered data are the court in which bold ideas stand trial, and that court eventually convicted both the perfect circle and miasma. But a court does not choose its own cases. A scientist who holds judgment in [[abeyance|abeyance]] until the facts accumulate may wait indefinitely, because facts do not add up to knowledge until someone has risked a claim worth testing. Science moves forward when an investigator ventures beyond the evidence in a direction the evidence can follow, and then submits that venture to observation as exacting as Tycho's.

prompt.statement:
Claim: Governments should not fund the arts.
Reason: Art that cannot attract private support does not serve the public.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: A Price Is Not a Verdict
essays.essay:
The case against public arts funding is strongest when made not by philistines but by people who take both art and taxation seriously. Taxes are compulsory and donations are not, so a theater that survives on private money has at least persuaded real people that its work is worth paying for, while a guaranteed grant can keep a tired institution alive long after anyone cares what it produces. American philanthropy has an [[estimable|estimable]] record, too: many of the country's great museums began as the projects of individual donors. Yet the market test has a precise limit: it registers only value that someone can be charged for, and much of what art contributes to public life cannot be sold to anyone. That limit is why I reject the stated reason almost entirely and accept the claim only in a far narrower form.

Behind the reason lies an unstated assumption: that private support measures public value. It does not. Private support means support from whoever has money to give, and an opera company that must [[wheedle|wheedle]] donations from a few wealthy patrons soon learns to stage what they enjoy. More fundamentally, some goods fail to attract private money not because no one values them but because no one can capture the value they create. Basic science is the classic case. In 1945, Vannevar Bush urged the federal government to fund it, arguing that industry, driven by commercial necessity, would neglect inquiry whose payoff was uncertain and distant. The National Science Foundation grew out of that argument, whose logic is now standard economics: published knowledge benefits everyone, so no firm can capture the full return on producing it. Nobody concludes that physics unable to attract investors fails to serve the public. Applied to art, the reason is no sounder; it is [[sophistry|sophistry]] dressed up as realism, mistaking a price for a verdict.

Much of the art that shapes a city obeys the same logic. In the late 1850s, New York began building Central Park on a vast tract of Manhattan, following a design by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux; it was a work of landscape art on a scale few private patrons would have attempted. The park's benefits are [[tangible|tangible]]: they reach everyone who walks through it, enrich owners of nearby property, and improve the health of a crowded city. Yet none of that can be billed to a single buyer. Large-scale private support came only after the park existed: a nonprofit conservancy founded more than a century later now raises much of the money for its upkeep. Here the reason gets the sequence backward, treating as a precondition what is often a consequence.

The claim deserves a fairer hearing than its reason, because it has a better defense: public money gives politicians leverage over expression. In 1989, members of Congress [[lambasted|lambaste]] the National Endowment for the Arts for indirectly subsidizing work by Andres Serrano and Robert Mapplethorpe that they considered blasphemous or obscene; several years later, Congress cut the agency's budget sharply and ended most of its grants to individual artists. Peer review did not shield the agency, because Congress's leverage was the power of the purse itself. The danger is real, but it calls for dispersal, not abolition: public money spread across many independent funders, so that outrage over a single work cannot starve everything else. Private patronage has censors too; donors simply exercise their veto quietly, by declining to give.

The absence of private support, then, is a question rather than a verdict. Sometimes it means that a work has no audience, and there the reason is true but too weak to carry the claim: it would justify declining to fund that work, not withdrawing from the arts. Elsewhere it means that the work's value is diffuse, delayed, or shared by people who never paid, which is precisely when public money can do what private money cannot. Governments should therefore be [[chary|chary]] of subsidizing art that already sells and of any arrangement that lets officials reward art that flatters them, while funding without apology the art whose beneficiaries can never be sent a bill.

coax money out of patrons by flattery and charm
reasoning that sounds plausible and hardheaded but is actually unsound
real and definite; the park's benefits clearly exist even if no buyer can be billed

prompt.statement:
Claim: Every citizen should learn basic statistics.
Reason: Most public debates now turn on numbers that people cannot evaluate without such knowledge.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Sort the Numbers Before Judging Them
essays.essay:
The claim that every citizen should learn basic statistics is sounder than the reason offered for it. I agree that statistical reasoning belongs in every citizen's education, provided "basic statistics" means habits of thought about chance and evidence rather than a repertoire of formulas. The reason, however, overstates two things: how many of the numbers in public debate an introductory course would equip anyone to evaluate, and how many debates genuinely turn on numbers at all. The claim survives both objections, but it needs a different, more modest justification.

The claim and the reason stand on the firmest ground when a debate hinges on a simple figure framed misleadingly. In 1995, British regulators warned that newer oral contraceptives doubled the risk of dangerous blood clots compared with older formulations. The warning was accurate, but the absolute increase was tiny: roughly one additional case a year for every several thousand women. Many women abandoned the pill in alarm, and the next year brought a measurable rise in unintended pregnancies and abortions. Because pregnancy itself raises clotting risk more than these pills do, the scare exposed many women to a larger risk of the very harm they feared. No course can make an anxious reader [[imperturbable|imperturbable]], but a reader trained to ask "doubled from what?" can read such headlines calmly, not from indifference but from understanding. That one question is precisely what a basic course can teach. Here the reason is simply true.

The reason weakens when the decisive numbers come from methods no introductory course could teach. Early in the COVID-19 pandemic, when little was yet known about the virus, governments closed schools and businesses partly on the strength of epidemic models whose assumptions about transmission and mortality even specialists disputed. In such [[exigent|exigent]] circumstances, a citizen who had mastered means, medians, and margins of error was scarcely better placed to audit those projections than one who had not; both had to decide whom to trust. Nor is statistical training an [[unalloyed|unalloyed]] good. A smattering of the subject often teaches people that numbers can be manipulated without teaching them to distinguish manipulation from honest uncertainty, and so leaves them [[chary|chary]] of relying on any figure. The cynic who dismisses all models because some proved wrong has merely traded credulity for an equally reflexive suspicion. For such numbers, basic statistics offers not the power to evaluate but the habit of calibrated trust: asking how a figure was produced, what it assumes, and whether its authors acknowledge what they do not know.

The reason fails more fundamentally when a debate is not, at bottom, about numbers. In 2016, the news organization ProPublica reported that COMPAS, an algorithm some American courts used to predict reoffending, wrongly labeled Black defendants as high risk far more often than white defendants. Its maker replied, also accurately, that a given score meant roughly the same likelihood of reoffending in both groups. Researchers soon proved that when two groups reoffend at different rates, no imperfect predictor can equalize error rates across groups while keeping each score's meaning constant. The numbers could not settle the dispute; it turned on which kind of unfairness a just society should find more [[repugnant|repugnant]]. Yet this case supports the claim even as it undercuts the reason. A citizen who understands conditional rates can see that both sides' arithmetic was sound and locate where the arithmetic ends and the moral argument begins. That skill is the best defense against the most respectable form of [[sophistry|sophistry]]: dressing up a contested value judgment as a neutral technical finding.

Every citizen, then, should learn basic statistics, though not because doing so will make each of us a competent judge of every number in public life. Only some numbers yield to an introductory course, and many numerical debates are really about values. The stronger justification is that statistical reasoning teaches people to sort the figures they encounter into three kinds: those they can check for themselves, those they must take on trust from accountable experts, and those that conceal choices belonging to citizens rather than technicians. A curriculum built around that sorting, rather than around formulas, would give the claim the support its stated reason cannot.

urgent and pressing; the circumstances demanded action before better evidence arrived

wary and reluctant, here about trusting any number, honest or manipulated
morally distasteful and unacceptable

prompt.statement: Universities should make all of their lectures freely available online.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Open by Default, Not by Mandate
essays.essay:
The strongest argument for this policy is that giving lectures away does not give away what a university sells. When MIT announced in 2001 that it would publish materials from nearly all its courses through OpenCourseWare, some with lecture videos, the obvious worry was that free content would [[undercut|undercut]] demand for an MIT education. It did not. MIT remains among the world's most sought-after universities, because what its students pay for is not the lectures but carefully selected peers, laboratories, and a credential that employers trust. If the only question were whether free lectures drain demand for degrees, the answer, at least for prestigious universities, would be no. But the policy treats openness as an [[unalloyed|unalloyed]] good. It assumes that free lectures democratize education, and it demands that every lecture be published, whatever the cost. That cost is real: after the Justice Department found Berkeley's free lecture recordings inaccessible to people with disabilities, the university pulled thousands of them from public view instead, a retreat that a mandate would forbid. Traced to their likely consequences, those two features turn a sensible default into an unwise mandate. Universities should publish most of their lectures, but not all, and not in the belief that doing so equalizes opportunity.

Consider first the intended consequence. The democratizing claim assumes that what keeps people from an education is a shortage of lectures, and South Korea's experience suggests otherwise. For roughly two decades its public educational broadcaster, EBS, has offered free online lectures for the college entrance examination, and the government later tied a large share of exam questions to EBS materials to curb spending on cram schools. Yet private tutoring spending kept setting records into the mid-2020s, and many cram schools now sell courses built around the EBS materials. That spending has many causes, so this is no controlled test. Still, the free lecture did not neutralize the advantage that money buys; it became one more thing money could help a student master. Early MOOCs pointed the same way: most surveyed enrollees already held degrees, and few finished.

The word "all" produces a second, unintended consequence. Lectures shade into discussion, so a mandate would reach seminars and bedside teaching, and recording changes what happens in the room. Much valuable teaching depends on provisional speech. A good seminar leader spends half the hour [[cajoling|cajole]] reluctant students into stating what they only half believe, so the class can test it; a clinical instructor discusses a real patient whose details could never be published; a historian in a discussion section argues the strongest version of a position she rejects so students learn to answer it. A ninety-second excerpt, stripped of context, can be enough for strangers to [[excoriate|excoriate]] a professor online. A student who knows every question will be preserved grows wary of asking the naive ones, though they are often the most useful. A mandate to publish everything would turn the classroom into a performance, and the teaching most worth hearing would be the first to disappear.

Nothing here is meant to [[deprecate|deprecate]] what open lectures have achieved. For a self-taught engineer in Hanoi or Lagos, Gilbert Strang's recorded linear algebra course is a genuine gift. But the consequences point toward a narrower policy. Because publishing does not erode the value of a prestigious degree, lecture courses should be open by default. Because recording chills candor, instructors should be free to exempt seminars and clinical sessions. And because free video does not erase the advantages of money and schooling, a university that wants to democratize learning rather than merely [[burnish|burnish]] its reputation should spend the money a mandate would consume on what the video lacks: feedback, mentoring, and pathways to credit.

The real question, then, is not whether lectures should be free; most should be. It is whether publishing a lecture amounts to offering an education, and whether a university should be compelled to record the moments of teaching that depend on going unrecorded. A wise policy would make openness the rule in the lecture hall and a choice in the seminar room, and judge its success not by how many people press play but by how many of them, lacking every other advantage, actually learn.

prompt.statement: Every public construction project should set aside one percent of its budget for public art.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Fund Art Built In, Not Added On
essays.essay:
The phrase "public art" names two different things: art added to a public work and art made of the work itself. The first is the sculpture installed on a finished plaza; the second is the bridge, station, or seawall designed so well that its structure rewards attention. The proposed rule quietly favors the first meaning, because a set-aside is easiest to administer when it buys a discrete object. Traced forward, the rule's consequences lead me to a qualified position: governments should guarantee money for public art, but not by attaching a fixed share to every project.

The rule's intended consequence is valuable. Without a mandate, public art survives only through persuasion: advocates must [[cajole|cajole]] each council and agency, project by project, and when budgets tighten, art is cut first because no one at the table is paid to defend it. A fixed percentage ends that cycle. The [[curmudgeon|curmudgeon]] who calls every dollar spent on sculpture a dollar stolen from asphalt exaggerates the cost: one percent is less than the contingency most engineers build into an estimate. Yet the benefit comes from the guarantee itself, not from the per-project formula, and it could serve art made of public works as readily as art added to them.

The trouble begins with the formula, which ties the art budget to a project's cost rather than to its audience. A highway interchange's enormous cost would inflate its art allotment far beyond what the site could use, while a neighborhood library crowded with schoolchildren would receive barely enough for a mural. Worse, that windfall would likely buy a sculpture stranded beside the ramps: art added to the interchange rather than made of it. The word "every" compounds the problem. When a levee fails or a bridge is condemned, the need for repair is [[exigent|exigent]], and commissioning art, with its competitions and review panels, would only slow the work.

A subtler consequence follows from the very feature that makes the rule attractive. Because the money arrives automatically, no one has to win the public's consent for what it buys. Richard Serra's Tilted Arc, commissioned under a federal program that reserved half a percent of building costs for art, shows the risk. Installed in a Lower Manhattan plaza in 1981, it was a long, curving wall of rusted steel that cut the plaza in two: public art in the first sense at its starkest. Office workers forced to detour around it [[lambasted|lambaste]] it as an eyesore, and after years of hearings and litigation it was dismantled in 1989. The persuasion that a mandate eliminates was never merely an obstacle; it was how public art earned its public.

The deepest consequence may fall on the other ninety-nine percent. When a budget labels one line "art," everything else is implicitly excused from being more than functional. The rule [[relegates|relegate]] beauty to a single subcontract and leaves engineers free to design [[barren|barren]] concourses and plazas, so long as they work. Hector Guimard's Paris Métro entrances, built around 1900, suggest the alternative: not ornaments beside the stations but their doorways, with cast-iron railings and lampposts curving like plant stalks. They were controversial too. Critics mocked the style, his design for the Opéra station was rejected in favor of a more classical one, and many of the entrances were demolished in the twentieth century. Yet the dispute concerned taste, not access: riders who disliked the lampposts still descended the stairs between them, and the survivors are now protected monuments. Art made of a public work may offend some tastes, but it does not force anyone to walk around it.

These consequences, more than any abstract claim about the value of art, decide my position. The guarantee of money deserves to survive; the attachment of a fixed share to each project does not. A wiser policy would pool the one percent into a common fund and spend it where people gather, not where construction is expensive. It would hold the requirement in [[abeyance|abeyance]] during emergency repairs, let communities review each commission before construction, and, above all, put artists on design teams from the outset. The goal should be fewer objects set down beside public works and more public works worth looking at.

analysis.verdict: This earns a 6 because the position is insightful as well as clear: the essay reframes the policy by distinguishing art added to public works from art made of them, and that distinction returns in every body paragraph. The consequences visibly decide a qualified stance, examples are developed honestly (even Guimard's controversies are conceded), and the language is precise and varied with superior control.
analysis.position: The qualified stance closes paragraph 1: "governments should guarantee money for public art," but "not by attaching a fixed share to every project." Paragraph 2 says the benefit "comes from the guarantee itself, not from the per-project formula," and paragraph 6 turns that split into a specific alternative policy.
analysis.development: Examples are explained, not just named: Tilted Arc was "a long, curving wall of rusted steel" that office workers had to detour around, and its fate shows what happens when money bypasses consent. Guimard's entrances were the stations' doorways; the essay concedes they "were controversial too," then shows the dispute "concerned taste, not access." The interchange and the library make the cost-versus-audience problem concrete.
analysis.organization: The opening distinction organizes the body: paragraph 2 says the guarantee could serve "art made of public works as readily as art added to them," paragraph 3 warns of "art added to the interchange rather than made of it," paragraph 4 calls Tilted Arc "public art in the first sense at its starkest," and paragraph 5 finds the second sense in Guimard. Within that frame the consequences escalate: "The trouble begins," "A subtler consequence," "The deepest consequence."
analysis.language: Diction is exact and economical: "relegates beauty to a single subcontract," "the dispute concerned taste, not access," "how public art earned its public." Short sentences ("They were controversial too.") alternate with long, controlled ones, and the final sentence ends on a crisp reversal: "more public works worth looking at."
analysis.task: The instruction asks how consequences shape the position, and the essay says so directly: the consequences "decide my position." Each proposed fix answers a consequence traced earlier: pooling answers cost versus audience, community review answers consent, the emergency pause answers "every," and artists on design teams answer the split between art and design.

prompt.statement: Specialization has made modern people more capable as a group but less capable as individuals.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Specialization Helps Only While Experts Stay Testable
essays.essay:
Much of the statement's plausibility [[stems|stem]] from an ambiguity in what it means to be "capable." Capability can mean self-sufficiency, the power to meet one's needs unaided, or reach, the range of what a person can accomplish with available tools and knowledge. If capability means self-sufficiency, then specialization has diminished the modern individual. If it means reach, then specialization has made individuals more capable than ever. I accept the statement in the first sense and reject it in the second. Yet both point to a third sense, the ability to judge the systems on which one depends, and there the statement's two halves prove less separable than it assumes.

In the sense of self-sufficiency, the statement plainly holds, and modern cities show why. When the electrical grid failed across the northeastern and midwestern United States and Ontario in 2003, tens of millions discovered how much of their everyday competence was borrowed. Subways stopped, elevators trapped office workers, and Detroit, having lost pumping power, advised residents to boil their water. Few city dwellers could have replaced those services; a nineteenth-century farm family, drawing water from its own well and storing food in its own cellar, would barely have noticed the outage. I would [[qualify|qualify]] this concession only slightly: even that family relied on a miller and a blacksmith, so self-sufficiency has always been a matter of degree. Specialization did not create dependence; it deepened dependence and hid it inside systems so reliable that few people learn how they work.

Measured by reach, however, the statement fails, as the history of science reveals. Thomas Young, the English physician who demonstrated that light behaves as a wave and made early progress in deciphering hieroglyphs, is often called one of the last true polymaths. Yet a physics undergraduate today understands light better than Young did, because one course teaches her Maxwell's electromagnetic theory, formulated decades after his death. One might [[object|object]] that the student, unlike Young, cannot begin to decipher an Egyptian inscription. But that comparison pits her against a genius, not his contemporaries. Most of them could neither explain light nor make anything of a hieroglyph. Likewise, sequencing the first human genome occupied an international consortium for more than a decade; today a single physician can have a critically ill newborn's genome sequenced within days to diagnose its disease. What specialists discover does not stay inside their fields; it returns to everyone else as instruments, textbooks, and techniques.

Both cases share a feature the statement overlooks: what an individual can do depends on systems that others build and run. Group and individual capability are therefore not separate ledgers, since specialized systems stay trustworthy only while their users can still [[check|check]] the specialists' claims. The water crisis in Flint, Michigan, shows what happens when they cannot. After the city switched its water source in 2014 to save money, the new supply lacked corrosion control, and lead leached from aging pipes. Residents complained of discolored, foul-smelling water but lacked the expertise to prove their suspicions, and state regulators [[maintained|maintain]] for months that the water was safe. The most [[telling|telling]] detail is that a General Motors plant stopped using city water because it corroded engine parts: the company could see the damage for itself and switch sources, while the lead in residents' water remained invisible. The decisive public evidence came when an outside engineer tested samples residents had collected and a local pediatrician compared children's blood-lead levels before and after the switch.

These cases leave me with a position narrower than the statement's. The blackout confirms that individuals have surrendered much of their self-sufficiency in what is mostly a worthwhile trade; the history of science shows that the same specialization has extended each person's reach. Flint locates the genuine danger: not forgotten practical skills but disarmed judgment, the inability of ordinary people to verify, rather than merely suspect, that experts have failed. Where that capacity is [[wanting|wanting]], the group is not more capable, merely more complicated, and its competence belongs to whoever can hire their own specialists. Specialization strengthens individuals and groups alike only so long as it leaves ordinary people able to test the specialists' claims, not merely doubt them.

analysis.verdict: This earns a 6 because it does more than agree or disagree. It splits "capable" into self-sufficiency, reach, and judgment, and that distinction leads to an insight the prompt hides: group and individual capability cannot drift apart indefinitely. Each example is developed until its relevance is explicit, the conclusion follows directly from what Flint shows, and the prose is precise, varied, and error-free.
analysis.position: A qualified position appears in the first paragraph: "I accept the statement in the first sense" and reject it in the second. The conclusion turns this into a conditional claim: specialization helps only while people remain "able to test the specialists' claims."
analysis.development: Every example states what happened and why it matters. The blackout shows "how much of their everyday competence was borrowed"; Young versus a modern student, and a physician ordering a newborn's genome sequence, show individual reach growing; the General Motors detail contrasts a company that "could see the damage for itself" with residents who could only suspect what was wrong.
analysis.organization: The opening distinction organizes the body: "In the sense of self-sufficiency" (holds), "Measured by reach, however" (fails), then a paragraph that links both cases and tests the link on Flint. The two case paragraphs open by naming their sense, and the third body paragraph opens by stating what both cases share, so the reader always knows where the argument stands.
analysis.language: Diction is exact rather than ornate, as in "not separate ledgers." Sentence length varies deliberately: long, balanced sentences with semicolons alternate with short ones such as "The water crisis in Flint, Michigan, shows what happens when they cannot." Target words sit in natural collocations like "maintained for months."
analysis.task: The essay shows the statement holding (the 2003 blackout) and failing (Young, the newborn's genome), then says explicitly how those cases shape its stance: "These cases leave me with a position narrower than the statement's." The final paragraph assigns each case its specific contribution.

paragraphs.note: Splits "capable" into self-sufficiency and reach, takes a side on each, and previews a third sense, judgment, which will complicate the statement's neat group-versus-individual contrast.

paragraphs.note: The 2003 blackout shows lost self-sufficiency against a nineteenth-century farm family; the concession is then qualified: dependence is old, but specialization deepened and hid it.

paragraphs.role: Case where the statement fails
paragraphs.note: Young versus a modern physics student shows reach growing; an objection is answered by correcting the comparison; a physician ordering a newborn's genome sequence shows specialized knowledge returning to individuals.

paragraphs.role: Hidden assumption, tested on Flint
paragraphs.note: Links the two cases (both depend on systems others run), argues that group and individual capability are entangled, and uses Flint to show what happens when individuals can suspect but not verify specialists' claims.

paragraphs.role: Refined position built from the cases
paragraphs.note: States what each case contributes to the position and ends with a fresh conditional claim: specialization strengthens everyone only while ordinary people can still test experts' claims.

moves.example: If capability means self-sufficiency, then specialization has diminished the modern individual. If it means reach, then specialization has made individuals more capable than ever.
moves.use: Open any prompt whose key term has two defensible meanings; take a side on each.

analysis.contrast: A typical 4 or 5 would agree or disagree outright: a farmer once grew his own food, an office worker cannot, but teams now build skyscrapers. It would name the Human Genome Project without explaining why it matters, treat "capable" as one fixed idea, and end by restating its thesis. It would never notice that a group's competence depends on its members' ability to test experts' claims.

prompt.statement: The subjects students find most difficult are usually the ones most worth studying.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. Consider when the statement might or might not hold true, and explain how those cases shape your position.

essays.title: Only Intrinsic Difficulty Signals Worth
essays.essay:
Anyone who has struggled through a hard course wants to believe the struggle was worthwhile, and the statement flatters that wish. It is half right, and the wrong half rests on a hidden assumption: that difficulty belongs to the subject itself. Much of what students find hard belongs instead to the way a subject reaches them, through the language of instruction, the preparation they lack, or the aims of the institution teaching it. I agree with the statement only when the difficulty is intrinsic: when it could not be removed without removing what the subject has to teach.

Gabriel García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude displays intrinsic difficulty at its purest. The novel follows seven generations of the Buendía family in Macondo, an invented Colombian town, and seems designed to disorient. Sons are named after fathers and uncles until one Aureliano or José Arcadio blurs into the next, and decades collapse into a sentence while a single afternoon stretches across pages. Many first-time readers find that their patience [[flags|flag]] somewhere in the middle generations. It is [[telling|telling]] that many editions print a family tree before the first chapter, as if conceding that readers will get lost.

Yet an edition that removed the confusion, by renaming the characters or straightening the chronology, would destroy the book's argument. The recycled names are no stylistic tic; they enact the novel's claim that the Buendías, and the region they stand for, are trapped in cycles they cannot see. García Márquez treats history the same way, drawing on the 1928 killing of striking banana workers in Ciénaga; in his version, the massacre is followed by a forgetting so complete that a returning survivor is assured nothing happened. A reader who has spent hundreds of pages unable to tell one generation from the next understands from the inside how a people might lose track of its own past. At the end, Aureliano Babilonia, the last surviving Buendía, deciphers an old manuscript that foretold his family's history, just as the reader has been deciphering the novel. A plot summary can relay the facts of Macondo; only the novel [[affords|afford]] the experience of losing one's way among them, and that experience is the lesson. Here the statement holds in full.

Difficulty of another kind runs through Decolonising the Mind, in which the Kenyan novelist Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o recalls his colonial schooling. Pupils caught speaking Gikuyu near the school, he writes, could be caned or made to wear a metal plate declaring them stupid, while English became the language of instruction and the measure of a child's intelligence. It follows that arithmetic or geography could be hard not because the subjects were deep but because they arrived in a language the children were still learning. A pupil who [[buckled|buckle]] under that weight was failing not geography but a language test disguised as geography. In Ngũgĩ's account, the system aimed less to educate than to [[cow|cow]] children into abandoning their mother tongue, and no mark in another subject could offset a failed English paper. One might [[counter|counter]] that even this struggle built perseverance. Perhaps, but perseverance can be learned from difficulties that also teach something, and a child told repeatedly that his language marked him as stupid was at least as likely to learn that he was incapable.

Set side by side, the two cases do not simply balance agreement against disagreement; they locate the line the statement blurs. In García Márquez, the difficulty could not be removed without removing the lesson; in Ngũgĩ's classroom, teaching in a language the children already spoke would have removed most of the difficulty and none of the substance. Because the two kinds feel identical from the inside, difficulty by itself is an unreliable sign of worth. A better question for anyone who must [[husband|husband]] limited time and attention is whether the best possible teacher could make a subject easier without making it poorer. If not, the difficulty is the subject, and the struggle is the education. If so, the difficulty is a defect of delivery and deserves no reverence. Hard subjects are often worth studying, but their worth lies in what the hardness teaches, never in the hardness itself.

analysis.verdict: This earns a 6 because its insight goes past clarity. It exposes the statement's hidden assumption, that difficulty belongs to the subject, and turns it into a test readers can apply. One example is developed over two paragraphs, far enough to explain why its difficulty matters, then tested against a contrasting case, in precise, varied prose with no filler.
analysis.position: The position comes in paragraph 1 and is a condition, not a split verdict: "I agree with the statement only when the difficulty is intrinsic." The last paragraph restates it in new words as a test: "make a subject easier without making it poorer."
analysis.development: García Márquez is not merely named. Two paragraphs show how the difficulty works (repeated names, compressed time) and why removing it would "destroy the book's argument." The Ngũgĩ case uses concrete detail, the metal plate, English as "the measure of a child's intelligence," and an exam no other mark "could offset," to show difficulty with no value behind it.
analysis.organization: The structure follows the thinking: claim and hidden assumption, a two-part extended example (what makes it hard, then why that matters), a contrasting case, then synthesis. "Yet an edition that removed the confusion" turns description into argument, and "Set side by side" signals the synthesis.
analysis.language: The diction is exact and economical, and sentence length ranges from short ("Here the statement holds in full.") to long, balanced constructions. Parallelism makes the key ideas memorable: "failing not geography but a language test disguised as geography."
analysis.task: The instruction asks when the statement holds, when it fails, and how those cases shape the position. Paragraph 3 ends "Here the statement holds in full," paragraph 4 gives the failing case, and paragraph 5 says the cases "locate the line the statement blurs."

paragraphs.note: Grants the statement's appeal, exposes its assumption that difficulty lives in the subject itself, and states the position as a condition: agree only when the difficulty is intrinsic.

paragraphs.role: Extended example, part one: the difficulty
paragraphs.note: Shows concretely what makes One Hundred Years of Solitude hard (repeated names, distorted time) and cites the printed family tree as evidence that the difficulty is real and widely recognized.

paragraphs.role: Extended example, part two: why difficulty matters
paragraphs.note: Argues the confusion is the meaning: names enact historical cycles, the banana massacre shows collective forgetting, and the ending mirrors the reader's labor. Concludes that the statement holds here.

paragraphs.role: Contrasting case where the statement fails
paragraphs.note: Uses Ngũgĩ's colonial schooling, where English was both medium and measure, to show difficulty created by an imposed language rather than the subject; then answers the perseverance counterargument instead of ignoring it.

paragraphs.role: Synthesis: a test, then refined position
paragraphs.note: Explains how the two cases shape the position, proposes the removability test (easier without poorer), and closes by separating a subject's worth from its hardness.

moves.example: It is half right, and the wrong half rests on a hidden assumption: that difficulty belongs to the subject itself.
moves.use: Opening an Issue essay: grant part of the claim, then name the unstated premise you will attack.

moves.example: Yet an edition that removed the confusion, by renaming the characters or straightening the chronology, would destroy the book's argument.

moves.frame: ... are often ..., but their ... lies in ..., never in ... itself.
moves.example: Hard subjects are often worth studying, but their worth lies in what the hardness teaches, never in the hardness itself.
moves.use: Final sentence: restate a qualified position by pinpointing where the real value lies.

analysis.contrast: A 4 would agree or partly agree, list brief examples (a hard math class, a famous scientist) without explaining why their difficulty matters, and end by restating the prompt. A 5 might develop one example well and add a counterargument, but it would still treat difficulty as one thing. Neither would separate intrinsic from incidental difficulty or offer a way to tell them apart.

prompt.statement: News organizations should let their audiences' interests, rather than their editors' judgment, decide which stories receive the most coverage.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Audience Interest as Evidence, Not Verdict
essays.essay:
The recommendation hinges on an ambiguous word. An audience's "interests" may be what it finds interesting or what is in its interest: the stories it will read tonight, or the knowledge it will wish it had possessed a year from now. The statement also rests on a hidden assumption, that public interest exists before coverage and can simply be measured. In fact, readers cannot be curious about a danger that no one has described to them. Seen this way, the issue is less a contest between populism and paternalism than a question of who knows what. I would let audience interest steer coverage when the audience knows something its editors do not, and keep editors in charge when the audience's ignorance is itself the problem.

Following the recommendation would have served the public well in Flint, Michigan. After the city switched its water source in 2014 to save money, residents complained for more than a year about discolored, foul-smelling water, while city and state officials insisted it was safe. The residents were right: the new water was corroding aging pipes and leaching lead into household taps. It is [[telling|telling]] that the story became national news only after independent researchers found elevated lead in tap water and in children's blood; the national press had waited for experts to confirm what residents had long been saying. Had more newsrooms treated the alarm of the people drinking that water as signal rather than noise, the contamination might have surfaced sooner. Here what interested the audience and what served it were identical, and audience concern worked as an early-warning system. Editors who dismiss such concern as mere public clamor mistake their own distance for objectivity.

The recommendation fails, by contrast, when a danger is slow, technical, or unfamiliar. In the mid-1990s, foreign capital poured into Thailand, Indonesia, and South Korea, and many commentators [[waxed|wax]] lyrical about an Asian economic miracle. Beneath the new skylines, banks and companies had piled up short-term loans in foreign currencies to finance property speculation and rapid expansion, a fragility visible mainly in dry financial data. Here the two senses of interest split apart: few readers were clamoring for analyses of short-term debt when they could read about soaring towers and new fortunes. In July 1997, Thailand's currency [[buckled|buckle]] under speculative attack; within months the crisis had swept across the region, and millions of families who had never heard of foreign-currency debt lost their jobs or their savings. Editors hardly distinguished themselves, but their failure argues against the recommendation, not for it: they erred by indulging their readers' appetite for the boom, when the remedy was to give prominence to a story the audience found tedious. A danger often becomes [[pressing|pressing]] long before it becomes interesting.

These two cases sharpen my position in a way neither could alone. Audience interest is reliable evidence about problems people can already see and a poor guide to problems they cannot, since curiosity is bounded by knowledge. It also follows its own rhythm: public attention tends to [[flag|flag]] just as a story moves from scandal to remedy, which is exactly when sustained reporting determines whether anything changes. In Flint, the television crews left long before the last lead pipes were replaced. And because every newsroom must [[husband|husband]] scarce reporting resources, a rule of following demand would not merely reorder the day's headlines; it would decide which beats survive. The first to be [[axed|axe]] would be the desks covering dull subjects such as water regulation, municipal budgets, and bank supervision, precisely where both the Flint disaster and the Asian crisis began.

The sounder arrangement is a division of labor rather than a transfer of authority. When people report trouble in their own lives, their concern should raise a story's priority, and editors should be humble enough to follow. But the decisions about what leads before anyone is curious, and what stays prominent after curiosity fades, belong to editors, because those are the moments when what interests an audience and what serves it come apart. Readers' preferences deserve to be weighed as evidence, never obeyed as a verdict.

prompt.statement: Athletes and entertainers should use their fame to speak out on political issues.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the recommendation. Describe specific circumstances in which following it would or would not be advantageous, and explain how these examples shape your position.

essays.title: Fame Is a Loudspeaker, Not a Credential
essays.essay:
The strongest argument against this recommendation is that fame is not expertise. A sprinter's speed or a singer's range confers no insight into tax policy or immunology, yet a famous face can drown out every informed voice in a debate. In the late 2000s, the actress Jenny McCarthy, citing her son's diagnosis, became the most visible [[champion|champion]] of the claim that vaccines cause autism, a claim that drew its apparent credibility from a study The Lancet later retracted. Her television appearances reached millions of parents who would never open a medical journal, and public health officials spent years dispelling the doubts she helped spread. Celebrity did harm here precisely because it worked: it lent one parent's anecdote the authority of a household name. Not every celebrity intervention looks like this one, however, and the difference defines my position: when athletes and entertainers do speak out, they should use their fame to draw attention to causes, never to borrow authority they have not earned.

That reasoning assumes that every political statement by a celebrity must stand or fall on expertise. Many of the most valuable ones are testimony instead. When Muhammad Ali refused induction into the U.S. Army in 1967, citing his religious faith and his opposition to the war in Vietnam, he claimed no special knowledge of foreign policy. He was answering a question his government had put to him personally, and he paid for the answer: he was stripped of his heavyweight title and kept out of the ring for more than three years, and his conviction stood until the Supreme Court overturned it in 1971. Speaking out cost Ali dearly but served the public: his fame [[afforded|afford]] a private act of conscience an audience that ordinary draft resisters never had, and the price he paid made his stand impossible to dismiss as a stunt. Advantage, in other words, should be measured by what speech does for the public, not for the star.

Technology sharpens this distinction rather than erasing it. A single post can now reach tens of millions of people in seconds, with none of the editors and hostile questions that once tempered a celebrity's public statements. When Taylor Swift ended years of political silence in 2018 with an Instagram post that endorsed two candidates and urged her fans to register, Vote.org reported a sharp surge in registrations within a day. Whatever one thinks of the endorsements, the registrations required nothing of her expertise; she simply pointed an enormous audience toward a civic act whose value is not in dispute. The same machinery carries a false medical claim just as quickly. The platform cannot tell attention from authority, so the speaker must.

These examples [[shape|shape]] my position in a second way: they expose a hidden assumption in the word "should," namely that obliging the famous to speak will make them speak honestly. The cost of speech, however, falls unevenly. In 2019, a Houston Rockets executive's tweet supporting protesters in Hong Kong set off a diplomatic [[row|row]] with Beijing, and Chinese state television stopped broadcasting NBA games. Many of the league's biggest stars, several with lucrative commercial ties to China, chose to [[hedge|hedge]] or to say nothing, and one apologized publicly. Players who had spoken forcefully about racial injustice at home now seemed [[cowed|cow]] by the prospect of losing a market abroad. The contrast is [[telling|telling]], though not because their earlier statements were insincere. Pressure to speak cannot manufacture courage; it yields speech where speech is safe and silence where it is costly, the reverse of what made Ali worth hearing.

The recommendation, then, is right about what fame can do and wrong to treat its use as an obligation. Fame is a loudspeaker, not a credential. Athletes and entertainers serve the public when they turn it toward injustices they have witnessed, burdens they personally bear, or civic acts that need no expertise to endorse; they mislead the public when they use it to settle questions that only evidence can answer. The most credible voices [[husband|husband]] their influence, spending it on causes they know firsthand and accepting the price when it comes; that restraint is precisely why they are believed.

prompt.statement: Cultural heritage is better preserved by living communities than by museums.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Kept Alive Is Not Kept Intact
essays.essay:
Every twenty years, carpenters at Japan's Ise Grand Shrine rebuild its main sanctuaries on adjacent plots and dismantle the old ones, a cycle repeated, with interruptions, for over a thousand years. What Ise preserves is not timber but knowledge, the joinery each generation learns by doing. For such heritage—a craft, a game, a language—the statement is plainly right: a museum can display a chisel, but not the skill of using it. Yet the statement assumes that keeping heritage alive and keeping it intact are the same achievement. They are not: communities preserve heritage by using it, and use changes it. Where the goal is to know what a tradition once was, the museum's fixity, usually dismissed as lifelessness, becomes its chief virtue.

Such change is harmless in a craft but corrosive in a community's memory. In 1907, a commission prompted by the sporting-goods magnate Albert Spalding declared that Abner Doubleday had invented baseball in Cooperstown in 1839. The evidence was largely one elderly man's recollection, but the verdict served Spalding's business and national pride alike: baseball became purely American, not an offshoot of English rounders. Tested against documents, the story was found [[wanting|wanting]]: Doubleday was a West Point cadet that year, and an English children's book printed nearly a century earlier mentions "base-ball." Its believers probably [[harbored|harbor]] no intent to deceive; they remembered what they wished to believe, as communities do. Even the Hall of Fame, opened in Cooperstown for the legend's supposed centennial, displayed the myth for decades: a museum built on a community's story shares the community's wishes. Only a record indifferent to those wishes could [[check|check]] the appetite for a flattering origin.

A second weakness is starker: communities end. Attention to a tradition [[waxes|wax]] and wanes with a people's fortunes; once a people is scattered or absorbed, no one remains to remember. Around 1900, sponge divers raised corroded bronze fragments from an ancient wreck off the island of Antikythera. Scholars soon recognized astronomical gearing, but no living tradition could explain how it worked: its makers' craft had vanished, and nothing comparably intricate is known for a millennium afterward. Because Athens's National Archaeological Museum kept the fragments, researchers could reexamine them with each new technique, from early radiographs to CT scans, until they reconstructed a device that modeled the motions of the sun and moon and predicted eclipses. Museums are often called places where heritage goes to die; here the museum was the only place where heritage could wait.

A thoughtful defender of the statement would [[object|object]] that I credit museums with what they keep and ignore what they take. Many collections hold sacred things taken from communities that still used them, preserved only as a pressed flower is: intact in form, dead in function. Sometimes fixity is itself the injury. The Zuni of New Mexico have asked museums to return carved war-god figures, which their religion requires to weather away in open shrines; kept pristine behind glass, a war god cannot fulfill its purpose.

This is the strongest challenge, and I concede its core: where a community survives and claims its heritage, its judgment should govern, even when it chooses to let something perish. But the Zuni case shows that preservation is sometimes the wrong goal, not that communities achieve it better, and it leaves my two cases untouched: vanished communities and contested histories. It is also [[telling|telling]] that the most famous repatriation dispute, over the Parthenon Marbles, concerns not whether a museum should hold them but which one: the British Museum or the Acropolis Museum, built partly to receive them.

I [[maintain|maintain]], then, that the statement is right about who should control living heritage and wrong about what preservation requires. A community keeps a tradition meaningful by practicing it, which means revising it; a museum and its archive keep it verifiable by refusing to. A culture that trusts only the first will believe its own legends; one that trusts only the second will own a catalog of practices no one performs. Heritage fares best with both: carpenters still raising the sanctuaries at Ise, and a record stubborn enough to tell their descendants when they have misremembered.

prompt.statement: People are happier when they have fewer choices.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the statement. In developing your position, address the most compelling reasons or examples that could be used to challenge it.

essays.title: Fewer Options, Not Less Authority
essays.essay:
The word "choices" does double duty in this statement. It can mean options, the products on a shelf or the headlines on a screen, or it can mean authority, the standing to decide for oneself which options deserve attention. The claim draws its plausibility from the first sense and its danger from the second, and it quietly assumes that whoever removes our options has our interests at heart. I agree that people are often happier with fewer options, but only when the narrowing is done by someone who serves them and leaves their authority intact. When the narrowing serves the narrower, or strips away the right to choose otherwise, the same reduction that felt like relief begins to feel like confinement.

Consider how people take in the news. A reader scrolling a social media feed confronts an endless stream of headlines, each demanding a small decision about whether it deserves a click. Surveys across dozens of countries have found growing numbers of people deliberately avoiding the news, and many say they feel worn out by its sheer volume. A well-edited newspaper [[affords|afford]] its readers something the feed cannot: a few dozen stories, ranked by people whose profession is judging what matters. The reader sees less and understands more. Much of the unhappiness blamed on abundance [[stems|stem]] not from the existence of options but from the labor of sifting them, and an editor performs that labor on the reader's behalf. Yet the reader has surrendered nothing essential. She chose the paper, and she can cancel her subscription tomorrow.

Now hold the act constant and change the actor. After Argentina's military junta seized power in 1976, it narrowed what citizens could read far more efficiently than any editor. Censorship and intimidation kept the official account on most front pages, and journalists who defied the regime risked joining the thousands who were "disappeared." Most of the press [[buckled|buckle]] under that pressure; a small English-language daily that reported on the abductions was a conspicuous exception. Argentines who [[harbored|harbor]] suspicions about vanished neighbors and relatives had few trustworthy sources in their own language against which to test them. Like the newspaper reader, they saw less; unlike her, they also understood less. The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo, who began gathering before the presidential palace in 1977 to ask what had become of their children, were seeking precisely the information the regime had suppressed. What separated the junta from the editor was whose interests the narrowing served and whether the reader could walk away.

The strongest challenge to my position comes from cases in which people seem happier precisely because a grave decision was taken from them. One study compared American parents, who themselves decided whether to withdraw life support from a critically ill infant, with French parents, for whom physicians usually made that decision. The American parents reported more negative feelings afterward. A thoughtful skeptic could [[counter|counter]] that in the gravest choice of all, authority itself was the burden, so my distinction collapses exactly where it matters most. I accept the finding but not the inference. What the French parents were spared was not control over their lives but authorship of a decision in which every option meant loss, and such decisions are rare. The same research produced a [[telling|telling]] result: those who made such decisions felt worse, yet they were reluctant to give up the right to make them. That reluctance shows that people distinguish between being relieved of a burden and being stripped of a power, and that they will accept pain rather than surrender the power.

The statement, then, holds only under conditions it never names. Fewer options make people happier when someone who serves them does the narrowing, as a good editor does for a reader. Surrendering authority itself brings relief only when every option is a loss, and even then people hesitate to give it up. When rulers who answer to no one impose a smaller menu, the result is not peace but enforced ignorance, as Argentines learned under the junta. Happiness depends less on how many choices people have than on who removes the rest, and for whose sake.

essays.title: Automation's Gains Reach Workers Only by Design
essays.essay:
Arguments about automation are usually framed as forecasts about machines, but these two views answer different questions. The first concerns an economy measured across generations: will there be more good jobs in total? The second concerns people measured across a single working life: will the worker displaced today ever find meaningful work again? Both, then, can be true at once, and historically they often have been. The first view comes closer to my own, though it settles only the first question. Automation does create more good jobs than it eliminates, but those jobs reach the people it displaces only when displacement is gradual enough, and institutions responsive enough, to carry them there. Where either condition is absent, the second view is not alarmism but an accurate account of what happens to the displaced.

The mechanization of American agriculture shows the optimistic view at its strongest. Tractors and combines displaced millions of farm workers, but growing cities and factories created new jobs; migration let adults reach them, and schooling prepared their children. Between about 1910 and 1940, small towns, many in farm states, taxed themselves to build public high schools, and the share of young Americans earning a diploma rose from under one in ten to roughly half. Parents who [[championed|champion]] these schools saw that their children's jobs would require reading, arithmetic and bookkeeping rather than a strong back. The schools did not [[stem|stem]] the exodus from the farm; they gave it somewhere to go. Where that investment was withheld, the results were bleaker. Southern sharecroppers, many of them Black, left or were forced off the land as cotton farming mechanized at midcentury, and segregated, underfunded schools had [[afforded|afford]] them few routes into other work. Two conditions made the transition work: the displacement unfolded over decades rather than years, and communities invested in the next generation before the old jobs disappeared.

Britain's handloom weavers in the early nineteenth century show what happens when the second condition fails. The [[telling|telling]] detail is that the power loom did not throw them out of work overnight: their displacement was gradual, but with no schooling or retraining to carry them elsewhere, slowness only prolonged their decline. Their piece rates, already falling as newcomers crowded into weaving, sank further as the power loom spread. Many weavers, too old to learn another trade and too poor to move, stayed at their looms for ever-smaller earnings until the trade all but vanished. Their children found work in the mills, so the optimists' arithmetic held in the long run. For the weavers themselves, however, the pessimists' prediction came true. Eventual recovery is no consolation to someone whose career is shorter than the adjustment.

The pessimists' strongest argument concerns today's automation. Earlier machines replaced muscle, craft and eventually the very bookkeeping those farm parents prized, but workers could retreat into tasks demanding judgment. Software that drafts contracts, reads radiographs and writes code now competes for that refuge, and it spreads in years rather than decades. A transcription department can be eliminated within a single budget cycle; a high school movement takes a generation. This argument makes meeting those conditions more urgent without changing what they are. Optimists who [[maintain|maintain]] that markets will absorb the displaced on their own repeat the error of the governments that left the weavers to market forces. The [[pressing|pressing]] question is not whether new work will appear but whether a fifty-year-old medical transcriptionist can reach it, which depends on paid retraining tied to employers who are hiring.

I therefore side with the first view, but as a claim about what societies can accomplish for workers rather than what technology guarantees them. Over the long run, automation has repeatedly enlarged the supply of good work; left to itself, it has delivered that work to the displaced unevenly and often too late. The optimists are right about the destination, the pessimists about the toll of the journey, and that toll is not fixed. A society that expands schooling and adult retraining as fast as machines take over tasks will vindicate the first view within a single working life; one that leaves adjustment to chance will vindicate the second for the generation caught in between.

prompt.statement: Some people believe that originality is the highest value in creative work. Others believe that mastering a tradition matters more than breaking from it.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss which view comes closer to your own position and explain your reasoning. In developing your position, address both views.

essays.title: Originality as the Reward of Mastery
essays.essay:
Debates about creative work often cast originality and tradition as rivals, as if every artist must choose between rebel and custodian. That framing conceals a doubtful assumption: that originality is a quality a work can possess on its own. In fact, originality is a relation between a work and what preceded it, and only someone who knows what preceded it can achieve it or even recognize it. For that reason, the view that mastering a tradition matters more than breaking from it comes closer to my own, with one refinement. Originality is precious, but it is a poor thing to aim at directly; pursued for its own sake, it tends to yield work that is merely [[novel|novel]], striking for a season and soon forgotten. Mastery is the better aim, provided it means the fluency that makes dissent possible rather than the reverence that forbids it.

The case for originality deserves a serious hearing, because traditions do not defend themselves; institutions do, and institutions can be ruthless. In nineteenth-century France, the official Salon's jury controlled access to buyers and reputations, and it [[cowed|cow]] many young painters into imitating the polished mythological scenes it rewarded. In 1863 it rejected so many submissions that Napoleon III allowed the refused works to be shown separately. That year the emperor bought Alexandre Cabanel's Birth of Venus, a flawless exercise in academic finish, while crowds jeered at Manet's Luncheon on the Grass and critics [[panned|pan]] it as crude and indecent. Posterity reversed that verdict; histories of modern art treat Manet's canvas, not Cabanel's, as a turning point. Defenders of originality are right that a tradition, left to its guardians, can harden into a machine for excluding the new.

It is [[telling|telling]], however, that the rebel in this story was steeped in the tradition he offended. Manet trained for years under the academic painter Thomas Couture and copied old masters in the Louvre. The scandalous Luncheon took the poses of its three foreground figures from an engraving after Raphael, and Olympia, exhibited two years later, restaged Titian's Venus of Urbino with a modern Parisian courtesan, cool and businesslike, in place of the goddess. Manet did not ignore the tradition; he turned it against itself, and the provocation lives in the distance between his sources and his answers. A painter with no command of the old masters could have produced something strange. Only a painter fluent in them could have produced an argument with them. Originality here is not the opposite of mastery but its consequence.

Mastery matters for a second reason that has nothing to do with originality: a tradition stores knowledge no individual could work out alone. City building is creative work too, and its failures are measured in neighborhoods rather than reviews. In the 1920s Le Corbusier proposed razing a large stretch of central Paris for identical glass towers set in parkland, a scheme that treated the street itself as obsolete. Paris was spared, but the tower in the park became a template for postwar public housing, and many such projects were later demolished; poverty and neglect contributed, but so did designs that cut residents off from the street. Jane Jacobs, whose bitter feud with Robert Moses helped kill his plan for an expressway across Lower Manhattan, [[championed|champion]] precisely the kind of neighborhood such planners dismissed as blight. Its crowded sidewalks and mixed uses, she argued, were not clutter but accumulated intelligence: shops drew people onto the street, and people on the street watched over one another. Planners who prized invention over that inherited wisdom often relearned it at great cost.

None of this makes tradition sacred. The Salon's jurors knew their tradition thoroughly and used that knowledge to shut out the future; expertise that hardens into gatekeeping forfeits its authority. My position, then, is that mastery deserves priority because originality worth having cannot be pursued head-on. It arrives as the byproduct of knowing a tradition well enough to see what it has not yet attempted. Artists who [[affect|affect]] indifference to the past rarely escape it; more often they repeat its oldest mistakes without recognizing them. Those who change a tradition have usually studied it closely enough to argue with it.

prompt.statement:
Claim: Organizations should hire for curiosity rather than for credentials.
Reason: Credentials show what someone has learned, but curiosity predicts what that person will learn next.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: What Credentials Prove That Curiosity Cannot
essays.essay:
The strongest argument for this claim is that credentials often measure the wrong thing. A diploma certifies that someone passed certain courses, sometimes in a field that has since changed, and requiring one excludes people who learned the same skills on the job or in the military. This reasoning has led Maryland, Pennsylvania, and several other states to drop the four-year degree requirement for many state jobs. On this point the reason is correct: a credential looks backward. Yet what those states put in the diploma's place is [[telling|telling]]. They did not begin hiring for curiosity; they began hiring for demonstrated skills and experience, a more direct record of what a candidate has already learned. That a credential looks backward is a reason to supplement it, not to discard it. I therefore accept the first half of the reason, reject the second, and endorse the claim only in a far narrower form.

Measured against how people learn, the second half of the reason is found [[wanting|wanting]]. Curiosity predicts what a person will be eager to learn, not what that person will master; the gap is bridged only by discipline, time, and a tolerance for tedium. Everyday experience makes the point. Most of us know someone who bought an expensive camera or a language course in a burst of enthusiasm, spent a few exhilarating weeks with it, and then watched that interest [[flag|flag]] once progress required drills rather than discoveries. Such curiosity is genuine, but it reveals what will catch a person's attention, not what will hold it. A credential, by contrast, testifies to something the reason overlooks: that its holder stayed with a difficult subject long after it stopped being new. A hard-won degree thus predicts future learning too, because it demonstrates the habit of finishing.

A second problem is not what curiosity predicts but whether an employer can observe it at all. A degree can be verified with a phone call; curiosity, in the form a hiring process can see, is easy to [[affect|affect]]. Any candidate who has skimmed a career guide knows to ask probing questions and to describe a weekend project with conspicuous enthusiasm, so a firm that screens for curiosity soon rewards whoever performs it best. Durable curiosity, the kind that does predict learning, reveals itself only over years. The biochemist Katalin Karikó kept studying messenger RNA after her university demoted her for failing to win grants, and the technique she later developed with the immunologist Drew Weissman proved essential to the mRNA vaccines against COVID-19. Such persistence would be invisible in an interview; it was legible only in years of experiments pursued against discouragement. That record is a credential by another name, and an honest version of the claim would concede as much.

The claim also ignores who pays for a hiring mistake. In medicine, aviation, and structural engineering, credentials exist less to forecast growth than to guarantee a floor, because an incompetent practitioner harms patients, passengers, and the public, not merely the employer. No hospital should hand a scalpel to a curious amateur, however quickly that amateur might learn; licensure is how society [[hedges|hedge]] against errors it cannot afford to discover on the job. The balance shifts where mistakes are cheap and reversible, and especially where the work is so [[novel|novel]] that no credential yet exists. A company entering a field too young to have degree programs must bet on the people likely to learn fastest. Here the claim is right, but for a reason other than the one offered: not because curiosity reliably predicts learning, but because there is no credential to hire for.

The useful question, then, is not whether to prefer curiosity to credentials but what each kind of evidence proves. A credential shows that someone learned something difficult and saw it through; curiosity, when it can be detected at all, reveals only where a person's attention is drawn. In most fields the strongest candidate offers both: a mastered foundation and a record of extending it. Curiosity deserves the greater weight only where the work has outrun every existing qualification, and even there it is most trustworthy when it has already left a trail.
