prompt.statement:
Claim: Great art requires suffering.
Reason: Only people who have endured hardship understand the human condition deeply enough to portray it.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with the claim and with the reason on which it is based.

essays.title: Suffering Is a Route, Not a Requirement
essays.essay:
The figure of the suffering artist is so familiar that it can pass for a law of nature. The claim and the reason offered for it, however, deserve separate verdicts. The reason is half right: art that portrays human life does depend on a deep understanding of human experience, and hardship is one way to acquire that understanding, though hardly the only one. The claim fares worse. If "suffering" means the hardships of an artist's life, the claim is false: such hardship is not necessary for great art, and it stifles far more talent than it ripens. The claim becomes defensible only in a sense the reason never mentions.

Consider first what the reason gets right. When Charles Dickens was twelve, his father was imprisoned for debt in the Marshalsea, and the boy spent his days pasting labels on pots of boot blacking in a riverside warehouse. Dickens [[harbored|harbor]] the shame of that period for the rest of his life, confiding it to almost no one, yet it resurfaces throughout his fiction: in young David Copperfield's drudgery at a wine warehouse, and in Little Dorrit, whose heroine is born inside the Marshalsea itself. Few novelists have rendered the humiliation of poverty so exactly, and it is hard to imagine Dickens doing so without having felt it. Still, the example proves less than it seems. Countless London children worked in such places; only one of them wrote David Copperfield. Hardship gave Dickens his material, but it did not give him the eye and the craft that transformed it.

The reason fails, however, at the word "only," which assumes that such understanding must be acquired firsthand. The history of science suggests otherwise. When cholera swept through London's Soho district in 1854, the physician John Snow did not need to contract the disease to work out how it was reaching its victims. He recorded where the dead had lived, asked their households where they drew their water, and traced the outbreak to a single public pump on Broad Street. His insight into a collective catastrophe came from patient, systematic attention to other people's suffering, not from his own. Art often works the same way. Jane Austen spent most of her life among the minor gentry of quiet Hampshire villages, yet few novelists have dissected vanity, snobbery, and self-deception more precisely. No serious critic would [[pan|pan]] Pride and Prejudice because its author never went hungry. Sympathy, in other words, is a discipline of attention; it can be cultivated without being purchased through pain.

Judged on its own terms, the claim is weaker still. Even a sound reason could not carry it, because the reason concerns only art that portrays human life, and much great art, from a Bach fugue to the geometric tilework of the Alhambra, represents nothing at all. Worse, the claim mistakes an obstacle for an ingredient: hardship more often prevents great art than produces it. Virginia Woolf argued in A Room of One's Own that a woman who wishes to write fiction needs money and a room of her own, and that earlier centuries produced so few women writers not for want of genius but for want of both. Van Gogh's case is [[telling|telling]]. His reputation [[waxed|wax]] chiefly after his death, and his anguish now seems inseparable from his canvases, yet he painted in the lucid intervals between his attacks, not during them. Those who [[maintain|maintain]] that art requires suffering read such lives backward, crediting the illness with work it interrupted and forgetting the many whom poverty, sickness, or war kept from ever beginning.

If the claim holds at all, it holds for a reason its defenders seldom give. Great art does exact a kind of suffering: the long frustration of abandoned drafts, the slow acquisition of skill, and failures endured in private. That is the suffering of craft rather than of circumstance. A young poet can [[affect|affect]] despair; no one can fake ten years of practice. Hardship may deepen an artist's understanding, as it deepened Dickens's, but it is neither the only source of that understanding nor a reliable one. What great art requires is the patience, and the means, to give understanding form.

prompt.statement: Scientists who receive public funding should be required to explain their work to the public in plain language.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: An Account, Not a Pitch
essays.essay:
Whether this policy is wise depends on an ambiguous verb. To explain a piece of research can mean to give an account of it: what question was asked, what was found, and what remains unknown. It can also mean to justify it, persuading a listener that the work deserves the money. Anyone who has dealt with a mechanic knows the difference. One mechanic tells you what is broken and how certain the diagnosis is; another delivers a pitch for the premium repair. I support requiring publicly funded scientists to give the first kind of explanation. A plain-language mandate tied to funding, however, tends to slide from account to pitch, and the consequences of that slide lead me to endorse the policy only in a form built to resist it.

The consequences of requiring an account are largely good. Taxpayers have a legitimate claim to know what their money bought, and research that outsiders can follow is harder to dismiss as the hobby of an insulated elite. A less obvious benefit falls on scientists: a researcher who cannot say in ordinary words what a study found has often not fully decided what it found, so the duty to write plainly doubles as a duty to think clearly. The European Union offers a working model: sponsors of drug trials conducted under its rules must publish a lay summary of their results. Because the summary follows the work, it can report what happened rather than what was hoped for, and the rule requires one for a failed trial as firmly as for a successful one.

The pitch is another matter. The National Institutes of Health already asks grant applicants for a few sentences, in language a lay reader can follow, on how their project bears on public health. Written before the funded work begins, those sentences can describe only what a project hopes to achieve, and a request to show relevance invites a promise of better diagnosis or treatment whether or not the project can keep it. The deeper danger arrives when plain descriptions become the basis for judging worth. In the 1970s and 1980s, Senator William Proxmire's Golden Fleece Awards singled out federal spending he considered wasteful, and research with odd-sounding titles was a favorite target. The ridicule worked because a one-line plain summary, stripped of context, could make almost any study sound frivolous.

Consider how a publicly funded study of microbes in Yellowstone's hot springs would have sounded to that audience: curiosity at the taxpayer's expense, a line item easily [[axed|axe]]. Yet an enzyme from one of those microbes, stable at temperatures that destroy most proteins, later made the polymerase chain reaction practical, and with it much of modern genetic testing, including the PCR tests for COVID-19. Basic research rarely knows its payoff in advance, so forcing it to justify itself in plain terms favors work whose benefits are easy to narrate. Scientists, sensing this, will either [[hedge|hedge]] until they say nothing or promise cures they cannot deliver, and both responses erode the trust the policy was meant to build.

These consequences, more than any abstract principle of accountability, decide my position. The most [[pressing|pressing]] question is not whether scientists should explain their work but when, and for what purpose. A sound policy would require a plain account at the end of each funded project, publish it, and keep it out of the review that decides who is funded next. It would also ask what the work did not establish, so that scientists who [[qualify|qualify]] their claims are rewarded rather than penalized. Researchers who [[object|object]] that their work is too technical for general readers are right that simplification loses something, but a plain account need not be complete, only honest about where it stops.

The public is owed an account of what its money bought, not a pitch for what more money might buy. Required in that form, plain explanation would make science more transparent and scientists more rigorous. Required as a test of whether research sounds useful to a lay ear, it would teach scientists to promise rather than explain, and the first projects to go would be those whose value no one, including their authors, can yet describe.

analysis.verdict: This response earns a 6 because its position is insightful, not merely clear. It splits "explain" into an account and a pitch and shows that the policy's consequences depend on which one the rule produces. Every example is carried far enough to show why it matters, the distinction organizes the essay, and the prose is precise, varied, and error-free.
analysis.position: Paragraph 1 ends with a qualified stand: support for "the first kind of explanation," but only "in a form built to resist" the slide from account to pitch. Paragraph 5 turns that condition into concrete design rules: write the account after the project, publish it, and keep it out of funding review.
analysis.development: Each example is developed to its point. The EU rule shows the good consequence because the summary "can report what happened rather than what was hoped for." The NIH relevance statements ("Written before the funded work begins") show why a funding-stage explanation can only promise, and the Yellowstone microbes, traced to PCR and COVID-19 testing, show what plain-language justification would put at risk.
analysis.organization: The opening distinction sets the structure: paragraph 2 treats the account, paragraphs 3 and 4 the pitch, and paragraph 5 draws a policy from both. Pivots such as "The pitch is another matter." and "These consequences, more than any abstract principle of accountability, decide my position." mark the main turns in the argument without falling back on stock transitions.
analysis.language: Sentence length ranges from five words ("The pitch is another matter.") to long, balanced sentences, and the conclusion uses deliberate parallelism ("Required in that form" / "Required as a test"). Target words sit in natural collocations, such as "a line item easily axed" and "qualify their claims."
analysis.task: The instruction asks how consequences shape the position. The essay traces intended effects (transparency, clearer thinking) and unintended ones (promises made before results exist, ridicule of basic research, hedging), then states outright that these consequences "decide my position" and derives its conditions from them.

paragraphs.role: Splits "explain" into account versus pitch
paragraphs.note: Defines two senses of the key verb, makes them concrete with the mechanic, and states a conditional position: support accounts, resist pitches. This distinction structures every later paragraph.

paragraphs.role: Intended consequences of requiring an account
paragraphs.note: Names benefits to taxpayers and to scientists' own thinking, then uses the EU lay-summary rule, which covers failed trials too, to show that an account written after the work can report results instead of hopes.

paragraphs.role: Unintended consequences: the pitch can only promise
paragraphs.note: Uses the NIH relevance statements, written before the work, to show that funding-stage explanations can only promise, then the Golden Fleece Awards to show context-free plain summaries becoming weapons against research.

paragraphs.role: Extended example: basic research put at risk
paragraphs.note: Traces the Yellowstone microbes to PCR and COVID-19 testing, generalizes that basic research rarely knows its payoff in advance, and predicts hedging or overpromising in response.

paragraphs.role: Consequences turned into policy conditions
paragraphs.note: Explicitly ties the traced consequences to the position, proposes timing, publication, and separation from funding review, and answers the objection that research is too technical.

paragraphs.role: Refined position restated in fresh terms
paragraphs.note: Recasts the distinction as what money bought versus what more money might buy, and ends on the cost of the wrong version: basic research nobody can yet justify.

Its examples would be named rather than developed, such as a passing mention of vaccines. It would treat the policy as one thing, so consequences would sit beside the position instead of deciding which version of the policy deserves support, and it would close by repeating the thesis.

prompt.statement: Scientific journals should publish studies with negative results as readily as studies with positive ones.
prompt.instruction: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning. Consider the possible consequences of implementing it and explain how they shape your position.

essays.title: Judge Studies by Design, Not Outcome
essays.essay:
The principle behind this policy is hard to fault; the harder question is what it would do in practice. Tracing its consequences exposes two hidden assumptions. The statement treats journals as the gatekeepers of negative findings, when many such findings never reach an editor, and it treats “negative” as one category, when a precise estimate of no effect and an inconclusive result from a small study are different things. Corrected for both, the policy is one I would [[champion|champion]]: journals should judge a manuscript by the importance of its question and the rigor of its design, ideally before the result is known, and every study should show how much its result can rule out.

The history of reboxetine shows what the absence of such a policy costs. The antidepressant was licensed across much of Europe from the late 1990s, and for years physicians prescribed it on the strength of published trials suggesting it worked. When Germany’s health technology assessment agency reviewed the drug more than a decade later, the manufacturer at first resisted surrendering its complete trial data. Once obtained, the data reversed the picture: most patients studied had been enrolled in unpublished trials, and with those trials counted, reboxetine was no better than placebo and inferior to rival antidepressants. The most [[telling|telling]] feature of the episode is that no published paper needed to be fraudulent. The distortion lay in the gaps between papers.

The reboxetine story reveals the policy’s intended consequence and its limits. The intended consequence is a record whose sum can be trusted: guideline writers and meta-analysts pool published trials, and pooling a filtered sample produces a confident answer to the wrong question. Yet the gap originated with the sponsor, which kept the missing trials in its own files. A promise of fair treatment means nothing to a company that has chosen not to publish, so the policy gains force only when journals use the leverage they hold. When leading medical journals announced in the mid-2000s that they would consider only trials registered before enrollment began, they forced no one to publish, but they made silence conspicuous. Registered reports, a format pioneered at the journal Cortex, go further: editors accept a study on its question and methods before the data exist, so the result cannot [[color|color]] the decision. In a citation economy that rewards [[novel|novel]] and positive findings, that advance commitment keeps “as readily” from becoming a slogan.

A contrasting case tests whether my position must be [[qualified|qualify]] further. Through the 1960s and 1970s, small trials tested streptokinase, a clot-dissolving drug, in heart attack patients. Here the negative results were published, and the consequence was delay: most trials were too small to detect a modest reduction in deaths, many reported no significant benefit, and clinicians remained unconvinced. Large trials led from Italy and Britain in the 1980s finally showed the drug saved lives, yet researchers who later pooled the earlier trials found the benefit detectable more than a decade earlier. A skeptic might [[counter|counter]] that null results should therefore be published less readily. The case argues the reverse. Had the small trials been buried, no pooled analysis could have exposed the missed benefit. What misled readers was interpretation, not publication: the habit of reading “no significant difference” in a small study as proof that no difference exists.

Critics [[pan|pan]] the policy as an invitation to clutter, imagining journals swollen with careless studies whose only distinction is that nothing happened. Editors must indeed ration the attention of reviewers and readers, but judging manuscripts by design rather than outcome does not lower the bar for null results; it raises the bar for positive ones, which could no longer ride a striking finding past a weak method. The streptokinase case justifies the second condition I set at the outset: every study should report the range of effects its data are compatible with, so that readers can tell an informative null from an inconclusive one. Understood this way, the policy deserves support: a null result should face the same test as a striking one, applied where possible before anyone knows which it will be, and be reported so that it claims no more than its evidence can bear.

analysis.verdict: This response earns a 6 because its position is insightful as well as clear: it exposes two hidden assumptions in the statement, and the consequences it traces justify each condition of a qualified endorsement. The one extended example is developed until its relevance is explicit, then tested against a contrasting case that grounds one of those conditions instead of overturning the position. The diction is precise, the sentences vary, and control of conventions is superior.
analysis.position: Paragraph 1 commits early but conditionally: “the policy is one I would champion,” followed at once by the form it must take. The final sentence restates that position in fresh terms: “a null result should face the same test as a striking one.”
analysis.development: The reboxetine case is explained, not just named: the essay says what happened (“most patients studied had been enrolled in unpublished trials”) and why it matters (“The distortion lay in the gaps between papers”). The streptokinase case gets the same treatment, including what later pooling of the trials revealed.
analysis.organization: The essay follows the assigned shape: position (P1), one example over two paragraphs (P2 what happened, P3 what it implies), a contrasting test (P4), and the refined position (P5). Topic sentences carry the logic, for example “A contrasting case tests whether my position must be qualified further.”
analysis.language: Diction is exact and compressed, as in “pooling a filtered sample produces a confident answer to the wrong question.” Sentence length ranges from the five-word “The case argues the reverse.” to long sentences balanced with semicolons and colons.
analysis.task: The instruction asks for consequences that shape the position, and the essay names them and shows their effect. The intended consequence is “a record whose sum can be trusted”; a limit (a promise cannot reach a sponsor who chooses silence) and an unintended consequence (published nulls misread as proof of no effect) each justify one of the conditions attached to the endorsement in P1, and the feared consequence of clutter is answered by the design-based standard set there.

paragraphs.role: Exposes hidden assumptions; states qualified position
paragraphs.note: Names two assumptions in the statement (journals as gatekeepers; “negative” as one category), then endorses the policy only in a defined form. Every later paragraph tests or justifies part of this position.

paragraphs.role: Extended example, part one: what happened
paragraphs.note: Narrates the reboxetine case concretely: licensing, years of prescribing, the agency review, the withheld data, the reversal. Ends with the insight that the harm lay in missing studies, not false ones.

paragraphs.role: Extended example, part two: consequences and limits
paragraphs.note: Draws the intended consequence from reboxetine (a record guideline writers and meta-analysts can trust), then a limit: the sponsor withheld the trials. Journal leverage and review before results exist answer that limit.

paragraphs.role: Contrasting case tests the position
paragraphs.note: Streptokinase shows published null results causing delay, which seems to cut against the policy. The essay reverses the objection: burial would have prevented pooling, so the real fault was misinterpretation.

paragraphs.role: Answers clutter objection; restates refined position
paragraphs.note: Rebuts the clutter objection by showing design-based review raises the bar for positive results, grounds the reporting requirement stated in P1 in the streptokinase case, and closes with the refined position in new words.

moves.example: A promise of fair treatment means nothing to a company that has chosen not to publish, so the policy gains force only when journals use the leverage they hold.

moves.frame: A skeptic might counter that .... The case argues the reverse.

analysis.contrast: A typical 4 or 5 would agree that negative results matter, list generic benefits (less waste, honest science), and cite publication bias or a famous scandal without explaining what happened. It would treat “negative” as one thing, ignore that sponsors rather than editors often withhold studies, and treat the counterargument as a box to tick. It would not let consequences determine the position, so the conclusion would restate the prompt.
